  audit of PR #8157 (rf2-0xd6, a GRANDCHILD via rf2-xc11) -> REOPENED
Descendants trigger it; unrelated merges do not. It follows the DISCOVERED edge transitively, at least to grandchildren.

READ IT AS DESIGN, NOT AS A BUG. When a child of an audit finding lands, re-examining whether the parent is still discharged is a reasonable thing for an audit to do. It only LOOKS like churn because the answer keeps being yes. So do not "fix" it and do not fight it.

THE OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE. A bead with open discovered-from descendants will reopen once per descendant merge, however well you close it. Do not spend a cycle diagnosing each one. Instead: check whether the trigger PR belongs to a descendant, and if so re-close citing the existing discharge. When the LAST descendant has landed there is no further trigger, and that is the point at which a further reopen becomes real information.

HOW TO IDENTIFY THE TRIGGER CHEAPLY. Walk the recent tracker-export commits and print the bead status at each: for c in $(git log --format=%h -8 origin/main -- .beads/issues.jsonl); do git show $c:.beads/issues.jsonl | filter for the id, print status and comment count; done. The commit subject names the audited PR, and the DISCOVERED section of the bead names the descendants. Two facts, one command.

SUPERSEDES the mechanism half of close-reason-does-not-survive-a-reopen-put-the-discharge-in-a-comment. That memory RULE still stands on its own merits — a close reason genuinely does not survive a reopen, so putting the discharge in a comment is still right, and it is what makes the re-close cheap. But it is not why this bead kept reopening.

THE MERGED-PR AUDIT RECORDS ITS FINDING AS A COMMENT, NOT IN THE NOTES FIELD. Grepping notes for AUDIT-REOPEN and concluding from its silence is a FALSE NEGATIVE, and it cost a wrong re-close on 2026-08-21.

MEASURED. rf2-csca8 was closed, then reopened by the post-merge hook. The notes carried no marker, so it was re-closed as a lost write. The marker was a COMMENT created 2026-08-21T00:41:23Z headed 'MERGED-PR AUDIT #8619 — REOPENED THIS EXACT OWNER; NO DUPLICATE BEAD', carrying a substantive statistical defect (an independent Fisher test pinned where the data are paired). The re-close buried it for six minutes.

THE CHECK THAT WORKS, in order:
1. bd comments <id> --json, sorted by created_at descending. This is where the audit writes.
2. comment_count across the reopening commit. It went 15 to 16, which is by itself proof a finding was attached.
3. Only then the notes field.

AND TO IDENTIFY THE WRITER, trace the bead's status through the .beads commits: git log --format=%H --since=... -- .beads/issues.jsonl, then read the bead out of each commit. The flip is attributable to an exact commit — here chore(beads): audit PR #8619 — which distinguishes a deliberate audit reopen from a lost write in one pass. Do this BEFORE re-closing, not after.

A SINGLE BEAD REVERTING WHILE THE REST OF THE BATCH HOLDS is a signal it was reopened deliberately, not that the export time-travelled. 7 of 8 closures held here.

THE AUDIT-REOPEN SCAN MUST READ THE DATABASE, NOT THE EXPORT (2026-08-11; second correction to audit-reopen-scan-over-jsonl and audit-reopen-scan-must-be-time-keyed).

My jq scan reads .beads/issues.jsonl. That file is an EXPORT, refreshed only when a checkpoint runs - so it lags the Dolt database by however long since the last `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh`. Any reopen the audit hook writes AFTER the last checkpoint is invisible to the scan, because the export still carries the pre-reopen row.

CAUGHT LIVE: rf2-hic-076 read OPEN via `bd show` while `jq 'select(.id=="rf2-hic-076")'` on the export reported `status=closed`, complete with a closed_at timestamp. Same bead, two instruments, opposite answers. The audit note (MERGED-PR AUDIT #7852) existed in the database and not in the file.

WHICH INSTRUMENT WINS: `bd show` reads the database and is AUTHORITATIVE. The export is a snapshot. This is the same property CLAUDE.md warns about for a different reason (committing a stale export time-travels the tracker) - the file is downstream of the truth, in both directions.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THE LOOP: the CLOSURE AUDIT is the reliable detector, because it loops `bd show <id>` per id and reads the status FIELD from the database. The jq scan over the export is a convenience for spotting reopens on beads I never touched, and it is only as fresh as the last checkpoint. So: run the closure audit first and trust it; if the jq scan is used, CHECKPOINT IMMEDIATELY BEFORE IT so the export is current, and treat a disagreement between the two as the export being stale rather than the database being wrong.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, third time this session: an instrument that answers from a cached artefact rather than from the source will be confidently wrong exactly when the source has just changed - which is exactly when you are asking. The other two instances were `git branch -r` (a cache, not remote state) and `gh run list --json status` returning lowercase while `gh pr checks --json state` returns uppercase.

A MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN REOPEN A BEAD BY WRITING TO ITS *NOTES* FIELD, WHERE 'bd comments' RETURNS NOTHING (measured 2026-08-17).

THE INSTANCE. rf2-k9rzr was verified CLOSED immediately after PR #8429 merged. On the next full backlog reread it read OPEN with 'bd comments rf2-k9rzr --json' returning an EMPTY LIST. The reopening audit was real and substantial — 'MERGED-PR AUDIT PR #8429 - completeness and implementation-quality correction', arguing that the PR's own replacement prose supplies the decisive counter-evidence to closing its item 5, and that 'the orphan is a two-host cluster, not one diagnostic string'. It was in the NOTES field.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. A mayor sweeping the backlog with 'bd comments <id> --json' sorted by created_at — the obvious and otherwise correct method — sees NO COMMENTS on that bead and reads it as an unremarkable open item with only its original description. The finding is invisible. The bead was reopened for a reason and the reason cannot be seen by the sweep.

THIS IS THE EXACT CASE THE REPAIRED RULE NAMES. PR #8432 removed the false slogan 'a bead's description is a historical document and its comments are the current state' and replaced it with: establish which text is newest by tracker timestamp, never by position, AND NEVER BY WHICH FIELD IT SITS IN. rf2-hic-047 was the counterexample cited when that landed (newest comment 2026-08-12, newer notes mutation 2026-08-15). rf2-k9rzr is the second measured instance inside twelve hours, and the sharper one, because there were zero comments at all rather than merely older ones.

THE PRACTICAL FIX FOR A BACKLOG SWEEP. A comments-only sweep is incomplete by construction. Either walk 'bd history <id> --json' newest-first to the first change in ANY text-bearing field (description, notes, acceptance, design), or — cheaper for a bulk pass — read the rendered 'bd show' and look for a NOTES block, then order what you find by the history's timestamps. Treat 'NO COMMENTS' in a sweep as 'no comments', never as 'nothing new'.

Autonomous-decision mode (Mike, 2026-05-29 overnight): when Mike EXPLICITLY delegates decisions + says keep-moving (e.g. going to bed, 'done by morning'), the mayor DECIDES in-scope design/technical forks itself — per its own recommendations + the job's goals + the pre-alpha-masterpiece stance (ELEGANCE+CORRECTNESS primary) — and proceeds WITHOUT stopping to ask. This supersedes the usual surface-and-await-go / 'don't action floated ideas' posture FOR THE DELEGATED JOB ONLY. Non-negotiable guardrails stay intact: record EVERY decision in the bead notes + merging PR body (so Mike can review/reverse each in the morning); merge only on green CI (--admin = review-bypass only, never past a failing touched-surface gate); worktree-boundary blocks + stance in every dispatch; recover worker deaths (discard degraded partial work, re-dispatch); commit+push bead structure on each signal; keep ai/dashboard.md as the morning hand-off with a running decisions-log. Quality bar does NOT drop to 'keep moving' — the masterpiece stance governs.

Background workers can end with a garbled final message (e.g. 'I will wait for the background task completion notifications') after doing substantial work but BEFORE committing/pushing/opening the PR. Distrust the completion report; verify ground truth: gh pr list --head, git rev-list origin/main..branch (commits), git status --porcelain (uncommitted). piwhsw (2026-06-09) did the full EP-0002 resolver across 8 files but left them all UNCOMMITTED. Salvage: commit the WIP in the worktree (NO beads, NO AI attribution), push, open the PR yourself, bd close --force (epic-blocked), and let CI be the authoritative completeness gate since the garbled ending means the work may be mid-edit.

A BACKGROUNDED GATE CAN RUN IN ANOTHER WORKER'S WORKTREE AND GRADE THEIR DIFF (rf2-g2mxd, 2026-08-03).

THE MECHANISM, and it is the most dangerous false-green found this week. A worker backgrounded its spine as:

    cd <its own worktree> && sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh

THE `cd` DID NOT SURVIVE BACKGROUNDING. scripts/test-fast-pr.sh derives spine_root/diff_root from BASH_SOURCE[0], so a RELATIVE invocation adopts whatever cwd the shell actually has. The run executed entirely inside a DIFFERENT live worker's worktree (slimresid-e7zxb), classified THAT worker's diff, and produced the two-concurrent-spines signature — 13 phantom test_quiet_shadow_node_cljs_test failures — inside someone else's checkout.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE OTHER FALSE GREENS: the result is a REAL colour attached to SOMEONE ELSE'S DIFF. Not a truncated log, not a stale exit code — a complete, internally consistent run that graded the wrong work. The only visible symptom was a foreign path in an mkdocs INFO line NINETY LINES DOWN.

THE RULES:
• INVOKE BACKGROUNDED GATES BY ABSOLUTE PATH: sh /abs/path/to/worktree/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh — never 'cd X && sh scripts/...' for anything backgrounded.
• BEFORE BELIEVING A GATE, CHECK THE ROOT IT RESOLVED, not just its exit code. If the log names a path that is not your worktree, the run is not yours.
• Cross-check its SURFACE CLASSIFICATION against your own diff — a run reporting jvm=false node=false when your diff is full of .cljs is grading something else. (That is how a sibling caught a different collision the same hour.)

PROPOSED REPO FIX, on rf2-g2mxd: have the spine echo its RESOLVED ROOT as line 1 of its output, so the mismatch is visible immediately instead of ninety lines down.

FAMILY: this joins the pipe's exit status, the SIGTERM'd wrapper's exit 0, the shared-scratchpad clobber, the two-valued probe, and the ungated bench lane. The general form is THE INSTRUMENT REPORTED ON SOMETHING OTHER THAN YOUR SUBJECT — and the defence is always the same: verify the instrument was pointed at you before believing its verdict.

BACKGROUNDED IS NOT KILLED — a harness that moves a long gate to the background at the 600s cap does NOT invalidate its exit code (2026-08-05).

MY STANDING RULE, in every brief: "a killed or timed-out run's exit code is MEANINGLESS - read the runner's own terminal marker." That is correct and stays. But a worker today hit the adjacent case and flagged that my rule reads as covering it: the harness moved scripts/test-fast-pr.sh to the background at the 600s foreground cap, THE RUN CONTINUED TO COMPLETION, and it reported exit 0 with PASS fast PR spine. Nothing was killed. The exit code is meaningful.

THE DISTINCTION TO WRITE: a run that is TERMINATED mid-flight has a meaningless code. A run that is DETACHED and later completes has a real one. The discriminator is whether the runner printed its own terminal marker - which is what the rule already tells workers to read, so the fix is to stop implying that backgrounding alone is the hazard.

WHY IT MATTERS: two workers today reported exit codes with an apology attached because they had been backgrounded, and one nearly re-ran a completed 30-minute spine to get a "clean" foreground result. That is wasted wall-clock produced by my own wording.

ALSO WORTH SEPARATING, from the same report: "Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js" in a FRESH worktree with no node_modules is NOT the reap signature. The reap signature is a gate reporting files that PLAINLY EXIST as missing. A worker that has not run npm ci and hits a genuinely absent module has an ordinary environment gap, and the documented junction is the answer. Confusing the two sends a worker looking for a mayor error that did not happen.

BACKLOG COUNTING — `bd list --status=open` EXCLUDES EPIC CHILDREN; `bd ready` includes them. On 2026-07-19 I reported "backlog 49" for many hours while `bd ready --limit 0` held 70. The 23-bead gap was entirely dotted epic-child ids (rf2-vxgfnd.141, .143, .164, .166, .167, .176, .188, .195, .196, .249, .271, .292, .295, .296, .97, .97.1, rf2-6ajm6z.1) plus five (TRIGGER-GATED) P4s. About 16 were genuinely dispatchable and sat undispatched while I ran 2-4 workers and reported the pool as nearly drained.

THIS IS THE SECOND OCCURRENCE of the same failure — the existing memory recount-ready-backlog-each-tick records under-saturating at 1-3 workers while 108 beads were ready. Same cause both times: a count that silently omits a whole class.

THE COUNT TO USE: `bd ready --limit 0 | awk $1=="○"{print $2} | sort -u | wc -l` — field-based, on the ready list, which is the pool that matters for dispatch. Do NOT count `bd list --status=open`, and do NOT grep -c on a bare glyph.

TWO GREP TRAPS HIT WHILE DIAGNOSING THIS, both of which produced silently wrong numbers rather than errors: (1) an unanchored `grep -oE rf2-[a-z0-9]+` over list output counts ids appearing inside DESCRIPTIONS too — that gave 94 against a true 61 earlier in the session; (2) a `^\s*[○◐●]?\s*rf2-` regex matched NOTHING and returned 0 ids, which reads as "empty pool" rather than as a broken pattern. Always sanity-check that ready ⊆ open ⊆ total; if ready > open, the counter is wrong, not the tracker.

SILENT DAMAGE: backticks inside a DOUBLE-quoted shell string are command substitution, so `bd update --append-notes "...`x`..."` silently deletes the backticked terms before bd ever sees them. bd prints its normal success line. Measured 2026-09-01 (rf2-6c12m.33 worker): six terms vanished from a load-bearing sentence and the remaining text STILL SCANNED as English — it read "in plain backticks (, , )" — so nothing on screen looked wrong. Caught only by re-reading the note afterwards.

THIS IS A SIBLING OF THE --notes-REPLACES TRAP, with the same silence and a different mechanism: there the tool destroys content, here the SHELL does, before the tool is reached. Both are invisible until somebody re-reads the bead, which on a held bead may be never.

THE FIX IS THE QUOTING, not the content: use a SINGLE-quoted string (backticks are literal inside single quotes), or a heredoc, or drop the backticks. Single quotes are the cheap default and cost nothing.

WHY IT BITES EXACTLY WHERE IT HURTS: the notes most likely to carry backticks are the TECHNICAL ones — file paths, symbols, commands, keyword spellings — which are also the notes whose precision is the whole point. A prose note about a decision survives; a note recording an exact symbol spelling gets gutted.

ALWAYS PROBE AFTER WRITING a note that mattered: re-read it and check for known content from the start, middle and end. That probe already guards the --notes trap and the >27000-character truncation; it catches this one too, and it is the only thing that does.

THE CHECK-COUNT BAND IS 98 AFTER PR #8264, AND THE MECHANISM IS A *SKIPPED* CHECK (measured 2026-08-15 00:35, re-verified 00:52 AUSEST).

WHAT CHANGED: #8264 (rf2-qpk2l) adds a 'Provenance pins (full corpus)' job to lint.yml, conditioned github.event_name != 'pull_request' so it NEVER RUNS on a PR. It nevertheless appears in every PR's check list as SKIPPED, and gh pr checks --json state | length COUNTS A SKIPPED CHECK. Measured before merging: #8264 read 98 while #8265 read 97 on the same tree.

WHY THIS ONE IS WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY: the previous two band moves came from jobs that actually run. This one moves the band WITHOUT adding a second of CI time, breaking the intuition that the band tracks work done. THE BAND COUNTS CHECK ROWS, NOT EXECUTED JOBS.

A FALSE REFUTATION I ALMOST RECORDED, AND HOW IT RESOLVED — this is the durable half. At 00:52, #8266 had been update-branched onto post-#8264 main, CARRIED the skipped 'full corpus' row, and still read 97. That looked like a refutation: the job present, the count unmoved. It was not. Diffing the check NAMES against #8264 showed exactly one absent row: 'All required checks passed'. THE AGGREGATOR IS NOT CREATED UNTIL ITS needs: RESOLVE, so any PR still in flight reads band-minus-one no matter what its matrix is. #8266 had one check non-green at the time.

SO THERE ARE NOW THREE DISTINCT CAUSES OF A BAND-MINUS-ONE READING, and their remedies differ:
  1. STALE BASE — computed against a superseded matrix. Remedy: gh pr update-branch, then re-read.
  2. GENUINELY ONE CHECK SHORT — a real gap. Remedy: investigate the missing job.
  3. STILL IN FLIGHT — the aggregator has not been created yet. Remedy: WAIT. update-branch is the wrong move and re-triggers everything.
Cause 3 was documented by rf2-nfgib's worker in PR #8254 and is what made this resolvable in one command instead of a misdiagnosis. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS ALWAYS THE SAME: diff the check NAMES, never reason from the count.

DO NOT WRITE 98 INTO .claude/commands/mayor-merge.md YET. Clause 1's own standard, which rf2-nfgib followed for 97, is to confirm on PRs MERGED AFTER the matrix change. As of 00:52 none has merged since #8264, so the evidence is #8264 itself plus one in-flight PR — strong, but not the standard. Confirm on two merged PRs, then file. Writing it early would repeat exactly the over-confidence this record was corrected for.

ALSO NOTE THE DESIGN CHOICES THAT PRODUCED THIS, both deliberate: the job is NOT in the 'Lint required' aggregator, because check_fast_pr_gap.py derives the required set from aggregator needs: and listing it would report a ~50s corpus audit as a missing local spine lane for a job that never fires on a PR; and it is push-conditioned rather than schedule-only because post-merge-workflow-sanity.yml excludes lint.yml on the ground that it 'already runs on push', which a schedule-only job would have falsified for itself while leaving the excuse standing.

THE CHECK-COUNT BAND WILL MOVE TO ~97 WHEN PR #8242 MERGES, AND CLAUSE 5 BITES ON EVERY PR BEHIND IT (2026-08-14 22:30 AUSEST).

WHAT #8242 DOES: it adds an unconditional job, jvm-repo-source-walks, wired into all-required-passed's needs:. That is a MATRIX CHANGE -- a new REQUIRED check -- not a cache tweak or a display-name rename.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, and they are the two clauses that most recently went wrong here.

CLAUSE 1: the band moves. It was measured at 96 on 2026-08-14 (six PRs merged after 9d2c42c234, unanimous, corroborated independently by check_fast_pr_gap.py --list deriving 96 statically). After #8242 lands, expect 97. DO NOT WRITE 97 DOWN AND TRUST IT -- .claude/commands/mayor-merge.md clause 1 says the measurement IS the clause and the constant is only its most recent result, and that file has now been wrong twice (93 while the tree carried 96). Re-measure on PRs merged AFTER #8242.

CLAUSE 5: every PR branched before #8242 was computed against the SUPERSEDED matrix. Their rollups will read 96 and say 'all required checks passed', which is a true statement about the old matrix and says nothing about the one on main. The new required job will not appear in their rollup at all. THIS IS THE EXACT SHAPE THAT ALREADY BIT ONCE: two PRs merged four minutes apart, the first adding a required browser job, the second checked against the base from before it -- the tree happened to be green and only a hand-run audit established it.

SO: after #8242 merges, run gh pr update-branch on every open PR and re-check, rather than reading band-minus-one as 'one job short' or reading a 96 as green. A PR legitimately reading 96 against the old matrix is indistinguishable by COUNT from one genuinely a job short; only updating the branch settles it.

'Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again.' USUALLY MEANS THE PR BRANCH IS OUT OF DATE WITH BASE — THE REMEDY IS 'gh pr update-branch <n>', NOT RETRYING (established 2026-08-07 after seven failed retries).

CORRECTING AN EARLIER MEMORY OF MINE. I first blamed a beads audit hook that pushes 'chore(beads): audit merged PR NNNN' to main after each merge. That hook IS real — I watched main move abb49f1ad4 -> aeadb93841 in eight seconds with no merge of mine — and during a burst it can genuinely race a merge. But it was NOT the cause here: I later confirmed main sat stable at one sha across 21 seconds and three fetches while the merge still refused, seven attempts in, with and without --admin.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE: the PR branch was 83 commits behind main. For a rebase-merge GitHub replays the branch onto base, and a sufficiently stale branch is refused with this message even when the PR reads mergeable=MERGEABLE and mergeState=CLEAN. The message names the base, so it reads like a transient race; it is a staleness condition.

THE REMEDY: 'gh pr update-branch <n>'. It moves the head (here f060635c30) and the PR goes MERGEABLE/BLOCKED pending fresh CI on the new head — which is the honest outcome anyway, since the branch is now tested against the main it will land on.

THE DISCRIMINATOR between the two causes, cheap: fetch origin/main, wait ~10s, fetch again. Moving with no merge of yours = hook queue draining, wait it out. Stable but still refusing = the BRANCH is stale, run update-branch. Check how far behind with 'git rev-list --count origin/<branch>..origin/main' — tens of commits is the tell.

DO NOT confuse either with a 502 from a mutating endpoint, where the mutation may HAVE happened and blind retry is wrong. 'Base branch was modified' is an explicit refusal: nothing happened, and retrying is safe but useless until you fix the staleness.

WHEN A NEW TEST CAUSES WIDESPREAD FAILURES IN UNRELATED SUITES, BASELINE MAIN BEFORE DIAGNOSING. Learned 2026-07-24 by the bench-evidence worker, which caught it on itself.

THE INCIDENT: its first B1 draft used Promise.all over two act() mounts and LEAKED A LIVE ROOT on rejection. That cascaded into 98 FAILURES ACROSS UNRELATED SUITES plus a suite-wide timeout — failures in pilot_field and pilot_overlay, which its change had nothing to do with. It ran the suite with its own new file REMOVED, proved main was green (642 tests, 0 failures), and only then knew the fault was entirely its own.

⚠️ WITHOUT THAT BASELINE IT WOULD HAVE CHASED PHANTOM REGRESSIONS in other people work — and in a repo with several workers in flight, the natural (wrong) conclusion is "someone else broke main".

THE RULE: a broad, cross-suite failure after a LOCAL change is almost always YOUR change leaking shared state, not a real regression elsewhere. Before diagnosing anything: remove your new file (or stash-free equivalent: check out the pre-change tree) and re-run. If main is green, the fault is yours and the blast radius is a CONTAMINATION signal, not a map of what is broken.

THE SPECIFIC HAZARD, worth knowing on its own: in a shared-process test bundle, a LEAKED REACT ROOT contaminates every later suite. Promise.all over concurrent mounts is the classic way to leak one — on rejection the other mount is never released. Fix shape: await each mount IN TURN, disambiguate them, and release in a `finally`. This is the same family as the process-global tables that must be reset between suites; anything holding a live handle across a test boundary poisons alphabetical successors.

RELATED FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER: THE BROWSER LANE DISCARDS CONSOLE OUTPUT ON SUCCESS. Published evidence records are only captured under RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS=1. So a test that intends to inspect emitted evidence sees nothing on a passing run unless that flag is set — another way an assertion can be measuring an empty stream.

`bd update --claim` AUTO-STAGES .beads/issues.jsonl, AND `git commit` TAKES THE WHOLE INDEX — so a worker that claims its bead and then commits carries the tracker onto its branch WITHOUT EVER TYPING `git add .beads`. Found by the rf2-ejb9h worker, 2026-08-08, which caught it in its own commit and stripped it before pushing.

WHY THIS IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE. CLAUDE.md's beads-durability rule is "worker branches carry code, spec, docs and tests — never .beads/issues.jsonl", and every worker brief repeats it. But the rule reads as an instruction about what to `git add`, and the leak does not come through `git add` at all. It comes through the tracker tool staging on the worker's behalf during a step the brief REQUIRES (claim the bead), followed by an ordinary `git commit -m`. A worker can follow every written instruction and still push a tracker snapshot.

WHAT THAT SNAPSHOT DOES IF IT LANDS: .beads/issues.jsonl is a full-database export, so committing a worker's stale copy TIME-TRAVELS THE TRACKER — beads closed since the worktree was cut reopen, beads filed since vanish. PR #6677 landed exactly that: 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral.

THE FIX, worker-side, and it is index-only so the working file is untouched:
  git restore --staged .beads/issues.jsonl
then commit. Do it BEFORE the commit, not after — an amend rewrites a pushed sha.

THE FIX, brief-side: say "your claim auto-stages the tracker; run `git restore --staged .beads/issues.jsonl` before your first commit" rather than only "do not add .beads". The existing wording tells a worker not to do something it was never going to do deliberately.

THE BACKSTOP HELD AND SHOULD KEEP BEING RUN: `sh scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh origin/main` (pass the base ref — bare invocation exits 1 by design) reports "No beads-database paths in this PR diff" and is the gate that catches this if the worker does not. The pre-commit hook in linked worktrees is the other arm, once installed via `sh scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: a worker reporting "I left the staged .beads for your heartbeat" is doing the right thing, not being lazy — the tracker database is the mayor's to commit. Absorb it with the ordinary `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` cycle, which re-exports from Dolt rather than trusting whatever file is sitting there.

TWO bd close hazards, both hit for real on 2026-08-07/08. Pass close reasons and notes via --reason-file / a quoted heredoc, never an inline double-quoted shell string.

HAZARD 1 — RE-CLOSING DOES NOT REPLACE THE STORED REASON. `bd close` on an ALREADY-CLOSED issue prints success and leaves the previous reason in place. The rf2-0fixc worker discovered this the hard way: its first close reason was damaged, it re-closed with --reason-file, bd reported success, and the OLD damaged text was still stored. It had to append a correction note instead. So a botched close is not fixable by closing again — verify with `bd show` and append a correction if the text is wrong.

HAZARD 2 — INLINE DOUBLE-QUOTED STRINGS GET SHELL-MANGLED. Backticks inside a double-quoted argument are COMMAND SUBSTITUTION. The mayor hit this on a `bd remember` call whose body quoted `gate root: <path>` in backticks: bash executed the contents, printed a `gh pr create` usage dump into the middle of the memory, and stored the mangled result — exit 0, no warning. The rf2-0fixc worker hit the same class on a close reason ("shell backtick substitution ate one fragment"). Markdown-ish prose about a codebase is FULL of backticks, so this is not an edge case, it is the normal case.

THE SAFE FORMS:
  bd close <id> --reason-file <file>
  bd update <id> --append-notes "$(cat <<'EOF'
  ...text with `backticks` and $vars, safe because the heredoc marker is QUOTED...
  EOF
  )"
The quoted heredoc marker ('EOF', not EOF) is what disables substitution. An unquoted marker re-opens the hole.

AND SEPARATELY, THE ONE THAT COST REAL DATA: `bd update --notes` REPLACES notes; use --append-notes. See [bd-update-notes-replaces-existing-notes-it-does] — the same session destroyed 57,413 characters of the EP-0038 epic's note history that way.

BD CONFIG UNSET LIES ABOUT CUSTOM STATUSES (found 2026-07-25, rf2-gtynf). 'bd config unset status.custom' reports SUCCESS and a following 'bd config get status.custom' then reads '(not set)' — but the status is NOT retired: 'bd statuses' still lists it, and a bead can still be moved into it (exit 0). The only thing that actually retires a custom status is 'bd config set status.custom ""' (explicit empty string). DETECTION: 'bd statuses' disagreeing with 'bd config get' is the tell — trust 'bd statuses' and an actual move attempt, never the config read. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS BEAD: status.custom lives ONLY in the Dolt DB, never in tracked config, which is the same shape as the issue-prefix trap (rf2-cchlf). A fresh clone has no custom statuses, so 'bd bootstrap' REJECTS any exported row carrying one — proved end-to-end: a DB with the custom status accepted a bead into it, exported, and a fresh 'bd bootstrap --yes' of that export failed exit 1. So a custom status is a fresh-clone bootstrap landmine, not a cosmetic preference. GENERAL RULE: after any bd config mutation, verify with the command that READS THE BEHAVIOUR (bd statuses, an actual state transition) rather than the command that reads the setting — this tool has at least two settings where the config read and the effective behaviour disagree.

bd DB is effectively SHARED across worktrees, not per-worktree. Observed 2026-05-23: the panel-audit worker (running in its own worktree, NO PR) ran 'bd create rf2-ad7zx.5-.11' + 'bd close .4', and those changes appeared in the MAYOR checkout's bd — while the audit worktree's own .beads/issues.jsonl did NOT contain them. GOOD PRACTICE for no-PR workers (audits especially): after the worker finishes, VERIFY the mayor's bd reflects its bead changes (bd show), then commit+push the mayor's .beads/issues.jsonl mirror so origin matches — the beads will NOT arrive via a PR. Also: still push NEW beads to origin BEFORE dispatching workers that must claim them (a fresh worktree seeds from the committed mirror).

bd EXPORT FROM THE WRONG WORKING DIRECTORY SILENTLY RETURNS A DIFFERENT DATABASE (2026-08-14, hit by the rf2-3lrb worker; more dangerous than the encoding trap beside it).

WHAT HAPPENED: a bd export run with cwd in the session scratchpad auto-discovered a DIFFERENT beads database and returned a plausible-looking snapshot — 789 issues where the real tracker has 1130, and 79 "open" carriers of a text block where the true count was 18. Nothing errored. The output had the right shape, the right field names and internally consistent counts. A scripted pass keyed on those numbers would have rewritten the wrong population, or reported a false census, with no signal at all.

THE RULE: run bd export from the REPO ROOT, and CROSS-CHECK the total against bd stats before believing any number derived from it. Two commands, and the second is what makes the first trustworthy. Also note plain bd export drops infra and memory rows — use --all when the count matters.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE ENCODING TRAP: mangled em dashes at least corrupt something visible. A wrong-database export is a complete, coherent, wrong answer — the same failure class as a gate that runs in a sibling worktree and reports its verdict as yours. Both are "internally consistent run about the wrong subject", which is far harder to catch than a broken one.

THE COMPANION ENCODING RULE, now stated correctly and wider than I first wrote it: the damage is the WINDOWS CONSOLE ENCODING, not bd. python -c ... > file mangles U+2014 the same way. The working rule is NO TEXT CROSSES A CONSOLE PIPE OR STDOUT REDIRECT: read with bd show --json redirected to a file and parsed as UTF-8, write with bd update --body-file from a UTF-8 file, and do intermediate reporting from inside Python with an explicit encoding. Verified across two consecutive scripted passes over 19 bead descriptions each: zero U+FFFD.

RUNNING ANY bd COMMAND FROM A WORKER WORKTREE AUTO-STAGES .beads/issues.jsonl AND DIRTIES A BRANCH THAT MUST NEVER CARRY IT (2026-08-10).

FOUND BY the rf2-xlsh worker, which deliberately SKIPPED writing a bd note for exactly this reason and said so in its report. CLAUDE.md already records that bd auto-stages and never commits, but the consequence for a WORKER has not been written down: a worker told to "claim the bead" or "add a note" stages a full-database export onto its own branch, and the PR-boundary rule says worker branches must never carry .beads/issues.jsonl or .beads/metadata.json.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. Every dispatch brief tells the worker to run `bd update <id> --claim` and most tell it to close on PR-open. Each of those stages the export. A worker that then runs `git add -A`, or that commits without checking `git status`, carries the tracker snapshot into its PR. That is the time-travel hazard: the snapshot is whatever the worktree held when it was created, so merging it reopens beads closed since and deletes beads filed since. PR #6677 landed exactly that, 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral.

THE WORKER'S OWN MITIGATION, which is the right one: it did not run bd at all, and cited the bead in the PR title and body instead so the merged-PR audit hook still has its trail. The hook keys on the bead id in the PR text, not on a bd write.

WHAT TO PUT IN BRIEFS: tell the worker to stage explicit paths, never `git add -A`, and to check `git status --short .beads` is empty before every commit. If a brief asks for a bd claim or close, add that those commands stage the export and the worker must unstage it (`git restore --staged .beads`) before committing. A worker that would rather skip the bd write entirely and rely on the PR text is making a defensible choice, not a lazy one.

THE MAYOR OWNS .beads COMMITS. Only the mayor checkout checkpoints the tracker, via sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, which re-exports from Dolt rather than trusting whatever file is on disk.

bd history <id>'s NEWEST ENTRY IS A DATABASE-COMMIT TIME, NOT A BEAD-MUTATION TIME — ON A BUSY TRACKER EVERY BEAD SHARES THE SAME NEWEST TIMESTAMP (measured 2026-08-23 10:03 AUSEST, tip c951fe8ef3).

WHAT I DID AND WHAT IT RETURNED. Asking 'when did each held bead last really change?', I took the max timestamp out of 'bd history <id>' for all 21 open+deferred beads. Every one came back 2026-08-23 09:50:19 — identical to the second, across beads I had not touched in days. That is the reassuring, useless answer: it says everything changed a minute ago.

THE MECHANISM. bd history lists Dolt commits, and every bd write commits the database, so a commit appears in a bead's history whether or not that bead moved. rf2-3t2nq shows 9728 entries; its four newest snapshots (09:50:19, 09:50:18, 09:34:21, 09:06:03) diff to NO FIELDS DIFFERING against their predecessors. Entry counts differ per bead only because a bead's history starts when the bead does (rf2-hic-090 has 7137, being younger).

THE HELP TEXT IS WRONG. 'bd history --help' says it shows 'all commits where the issue was modified'. Measured, it shows all commits, full stop.

THE METHOD THAT WORKS is the one the backlog-reread loop already prescribes, and this is WHY it prescribes it: take 'bd history <id> --json --limit N', walk ADJACENT PAIRS newest-first, diff the embedded Issue snapshot, and stop at the first pair where a text-bearing field (notes, description, status, priority, close reason) actually differs. Two-sided control run at the same tip: rf2-hic-090, which I had appended a note to minutes earlier, reports its first real change at 09:50:19 on 'notes'; rf2-3t2nq, untouched, walks past three identical pairs to a real change at 09:06:03. Across the 21 beads the true newest mutations spread over two days, from 2026-08-22 11:05 to 2026-08-23 09:50 — the actual signal, which the max-timestamp read had flattened to a single instant.

TWO MECHANICAL TRAPS IN RUNNING IT. Pass --limit (default is all, and a full history is thousands of full issue snapshots). And decode the output as UTF-8 explicitly: on this setup the default codec dies with UnicodeDecodeError on any note containing an em-dash or a curly quote, which is most of them.

bd's --json OUTPUT CARRIES CRLF ON THIS SETUP, SO EVERY ID YOU LOOP OVER ENDS IN A CARRIAGE RETURN — AND THE LOOPS BUILT ON IT RETURN A CLEAN, REASSURING, WRONG ANSWER (2026-09-03).

MEASURED. 'bd list --status open --limit 0 --json | jq -r .[].id > ids.txt' writes lines ending ^M$ (confirmed with cat -A). Any subsequent 'git log --grep=$id' or 'grep -F $id' therefore searches for 'rf2-xxxxx\r' and finds nothing.

WHAT IT COST HERE. The backlog-reread loop's done-in-tree sweep — the one check loops.md section 3 says NOTHING ELSE PERFORMS — reported ONE open id with a merged-history hit. Run correctly it reports THIRTEEN. And the single hit is what made the broken run look like a clean run: a wholly empty result would have sent me looking, while one plausible hit read as a survey that found almost nothing. That is the same shape loops.md records for the empty per-agent scratch sink, reached through a line ending.

WHY THE CONTROLS DID NOT CATCH IT. I ran both controls the method asks for — an invented id returned 0, a known-merged id returned a hit — and BOTH PASSED, because I typed those two ids as literals on the command line rather than drawing them from the pipeline. A control that does not travel the same path as the data is not a control for that path. THE CONTROL THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: take an id FROM the pipeline that you know is in the history, and assert a non-zero count.

THE FIX IS ONE FILTER: pipe through 'tr -d \r' immediately after jq, every time. Do it at the source of the list, not at each use.

AND PREFER ONE GIT CALL PLUS LOCAL MATCHING over N git invocations in a loop: 'git log origin/main --oneline -n 4000 > hist.txt' once, then grep -F each id against that file. Faster, and the history file is inspectable when a count surprises you — which is how this was diagnosed at all.

I MADE THREE COUNTING/PARSING ERRORS IN ONE BOARD REREAD, ALL FROM GREPPING bd OUTPUT INSTEAD OF READING ITS STRUCTURE (2026-08-06).

1. FALSE ZERO ON EPIC CHILDREN. I counted open children with grep -cE "^[○◐●] rf2-2rtt6\." and got 0 while 21 were open. `bd list` renders a TREE: children are prefixed with box-drawing characters (├── ○ rf2-2rtt6.1 ...), so a column-0 glyph anchor never sees them. My follow-up "format-independent" attempt with ^.{0,4} ALSO failed, because those box characters are multi-byte.

2. A CYCLE THAT DOES NOT EXIST. I reported rf2-2rtt6.106 and .112 as mutually blocking, from grep -A4 after "BLOCKED BY|DEPENDS". That window swept the FOLLOWING "BLOCKS" section into the reading. The truth is a clean chain: .106 DEPENDS ON .103 and BLOCKS .112. bd show prints DEPENDS ON and BLOCKS as SEPARATE SECTIONS and a fixed -A window crosses the boundary.

3. A WRONG EXPLANATION OF THE open/ready GAP. I told the operator that `bd ready` includes dotted epic children which `bd list --status=open` omits. On this board that is FALSE — ready is a strict SUBSET of open, and the gap is exactly the DEPENDENCY-GATED beads. (An older memory records the opposite for a different board state; do not carry either as a standing fact — derive it.)

THE RULE: bd output is STRUCTURED (tree prefixes, named sections, cross-reference blocks), so line-oriented greps read it wrong in at least three distinct ways. For a COUNT, extract ids unanchored (grep -oE "rf2-[0-9a-z]+(\.[0-9]+)*" | sort -u) and know that this also catches ids in DISCOVERED FROM / BLOCKS / PARENT cross-references, so it OVER-counts unless you scope it. For a RELATIONSHIP, read the named section with a range address (sed -n "/^DEPENDS ON/,/^$/p"), never a fixed -A window.

AND THE STANDING TELL: `bd blocked` reported 0 while six beads were dependency-gated and unreachable. `blocked` is a STATUS FIELD, not a computed dependency state — a bead can be ungettable without ever being marked blocked. Reading blocked=0 as "nothing is gated" is a false clean.

WHY THIS KEEPS HAPPENING TO ME SPECIFICALLY: every one of these was a cheap proxy for a real question — a glyph for a row, a fixed window for a section, a remembered rule for a derivation. It is the same error the codebase keeps yielding (a gate reading raw YAML as executable, a checker counting matching files instead of bytes), committed in my own instrument. BEFORE QUOTING A NUMBER OR A RELATIONSHIP FROM bd, ASK WHAT WOULD HAVE TO BE TRUE FOR IT TO BE MEASURING SOMETHING ELSE.

bd search matches TITLES ONLY and excludes closed issues by default, so 'No issues found' is routinely VACUOUS. Measured 2026-08-22 in three directions: a phrase in a bead's NOTES ('loud-box-safe') returns 0; a phrase in a DESCRIPTION ('verified reverse-domain group') returns 0; phrases in TITLES ('fused reader array', 'quiet-box window') return 1 each; a nonsense token returns 0. The tool's own help confirms it: 'Text queries search titles' and 'excludes closed issues by default'. --desc-contains is a FILTER requiring a positional title query, not a standalone description search, so it cannot answer 'find any bead mentioning X' either. THE COST IS REAL: searching for the second-clock-driver work returned 'No issues found' twice, which reads identically to 'nobody filed it' and would have justified filing a duplicate. Grepping .beads/issues.jsonl instead found FOUR carriers in one command, two of them closed, including rf2-xc0bw which held the work. THE RULE: to ask whether the tracker knows about X, grep the JSONL export (it carries description, notes, comments and close reasons); use bd search only for titles, and pass --status all when you do.

bd show --json CARRIES ONLY FORWARD EDGES: enumerating CHILDREN through it returns a VACUOUS ZERO (2026-08-23).

MEASURED. A bead's JSON record carries exactly two list fields: labels and dependencies. There is NO children, discovered, discovered_from or blocks key. So a probe like [x for x in d.get('children',[])] finds nothing because it looked at nothing -- and a blank from a wrong field name is indistinguishable on screen from a blank meaning "no such edges exist".

THE BACKLOG LOOP ASKS FOR EXACTLY THIS ENUMERATION and warns that a prefix scan misses generated ids -- a child of rf2-hic-090 can be rf2-8mlfj, sharing nothing. So the JSON route looks like the rigorous answer to that warning and is worse than the prefix scan: the prefix scan at least finds the same-family ones.

THE WORKING INSTRUMENT is the TEXT output, whose reverse edges live in sections the JSON does not project:
  bd show <id> | awk '/^(BLOCKS|DISCOVERED)/{f=1} /^(COMMENTS|LABELS)/{f=0} f' | grep -oE 'rf2-[a-z0-9-]+' | sort -u
Run over fourteen open beads this returned nine with reverse edges and four ids never examined before (rf2-xomo, rf2-sxhu, rf2-8mlfj, rf2-v04s) -- all closed days earlier, so the pass was null, but only the text route could establish that.

THE CONTROL THAT CAUGHT IT: when a structural probe returns zero across EVERY item, dump the record's actual keys before believing it. One command -- print every list-valued field with its length -- showed labels and dependencies and nothing else, which is what turned a clean null into a known gap.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the day's recurring one: a query against a field that does not exist fails silently and reassuringly. Confirm the field exists before trusting its emptiness.

bd show --json PIPED THROUGH THE SHELL ON THIS BOX MANGLES NON-ASCII — REDIRECT TO A FILE INSTEAD (2026-08-14, caught by rf2-prbe worker on its first read).

SYMPTOM: U+2014 (em dash) comes back as replacement characters, inflating a 2644-char description to 2660. Redirecting to a file and reading it as UTF-8 round-trips exactly.

WHY IT MATTERS: any scripted rewrite of bead text reads the current description, edits one part, and writes it back. If the read was piped, every em dash in the WHOLE description is silently corrupted on write-back — not just the part being edited. The rf2-prbe pass would have corrupted em dashes across 19 bead descriptions, and the hic worker-protocol block is full of them. The worker caught it before the pass ran.

THE RULE: for any bd read whose output will be written back, redirect to a file. Never pipe. This is the same family as the never-pipe-a-gate rule but a different mechanism — that one loses an exit status, this one loses bytes.

ALSO WORTH KEEPING from that pass: the hic worker-context block is BYTE-IDENTICAL across all 88 carriers (1543 chars, exactly one occurrence per bead, one distinct variant), so an exact-string anchor works and a fuzzy match is unnecessary. Verify a scripted tracker rewrite by exporting the whole tracker before and after and diffing: the rf2-prbe pass confirmed exactly 19 of 1123 descriptions changed, every delta exactly +267 chars, with zero movement in title, status, priority, type, owner, labels or dependencies.

bd show PRINTS COMMENTS LAST, SO piping bd show <id> to tail LANDS IN COMMENTS AND NOT ON THE NEWEST NOTE (2026-08-23, hit twice in one session).

THE SECTION ORDER bd show emits: DESCRIPTION, then NOTES, then DEPENDS ON / BLOCKS / DISCOVERED, then COMMENTS. Comments are ordered by their OWN dates and can be far older than the newest note. So a tail of the whole output reads old text that LOOKS newest because it is last on screen.

MEASURED ON TWO BEADS THE SAME AFTERNOON:
- rf2-85og2: 1299 lines total, NOTES span 42-567, COMMENTS span 572-1299. A tail landed at ~line 1290 on a comment saying the bead still owes a quiet-box window and that a second driver plus donor arm "wants its own bead". The genuine newest note (2026-08-22 17:06:29) says the OPPOSITE: the quiet-box half is satisfied and authorised, U1/U2's window was taken in PR #8676, and what remains wants an operator ruling or a subject that does not yet exist.
- rf2-9wmqd: same shape. Its own banner names the cause in its own words -- "bd show prints COMMENTS last, so the bottom of its output is two superseded worker reports saying item (c) is still owed. It is not." Item (c) landed in PR #8680.

BOTH ERRORS RAN IN THE SAME DIRECTION: they reported work as OWED that had already been done, which reads as diligence and manufactures a backlog that does not exist.

THE METHOD ALREADY SAYS a tail "is not a read-the-newest method". What it does not say is the mechanism on THIS tool, which is what makes the failure reproducible rather than occasional.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD:
1. Find the section boundaries first -- grep -nE on line-anchored DESCRIPTION|NOTES|COMMENTS|DEPENDS ON|BLOCKS|DISCOVERED over the captured output -- then read the TAIL OF THE NOTES BLOCK only.
2. Confirm with bd history <id> --json by walking adjacent snapshot pairs newest-first to the first change in a text-bearing field; that gives the real mutation time of the newest note.
3. On any bead whose notes run to tens of thousands of characters, ADD A SCANNABLE BANNER as the newest note. rf2-9wmqd's banner is the model and states its own justification: the notes were ~50,000 characters with no scannable marker, so each tick re-derived the answer at that cost.

*** 'bd show <id> | tail -N' DOES NOT GIVE YOU THE NEWEST NOTE. IT ROUTINELY GIVES YOU AN OLDER ONE. *** Measured 2026-08-16 02:03 on rf2-hic-047.

THE MEASUREMENT. 'bd show rf2-hic-047' renders 127 lines. The NEWEST note — MERGED-PR AUDIT #8317, dated 2026-08-15 — sits at LINE 79. An OLDER note, dated 2026-08-12, sits at LINE 111, thirty-two lines FURTHER DOWN. So 'tail -10' returns the 2026-08-12 text and hides the 2026-08-15 audit entirely.

WHY, structurally: audit notes are appended INTO THE DESCRIPTION BLOCK, while dated operator comments render afterwards in a separate COMMENTS section. The two are not interleaved chronologically. 'tail' lands in COMMENTS, which is frequently the older material, and the description's own tail — where the merged-PR audits live — is invisible to it.

WHAT IT COST. I briefed rf2-hic-047 from the 2026-08-12 comment, calling it 'the newest note', and told the worker its job was a versioned virtualizer re-audit. The actual newest note asked for something else and smaller: virtualizer-recipe.md lines 25 and 34 still teach h/fn, which does not exist. The worker read the bead properly, followed it over the brief, and reported the difference — which is the only reason the right repair landed. It also found the comparison correction had ALREADY landed in #8317 on 2026-08-13, so my brief's premise was doubly stale.

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED SLIP. The whole session's dispatch discipline is 'READ THE BEAD BOTTOM-UP, the newest note governs' — and I have been executing that with 'bd show | tail -N' roughly twenty times. Every one of those reads may have shown me the wrong end of the bead. It plausibly explains the rf2-vz6dg brief too, where I led with the description's headline and the worker had to tell me the live charge was elsewhere.

*** THE CORRECT READ, and it is barely more expensive: ***
  - Read the FULL 'bd show <id>' when the bead is short enough. Do not sample either end.
  - When it is long, find the newest material by DATE, not by position: 'bd show <id> | grep -n "MERGED-PR AUDIT\|202[0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]"' gives you every dated marker WITH ITS LINE NUMBER, and you then read around the LATEST DATE rather than the LAST LINE.
  - Never write 'the bead's newest note says' on the strength of a tail. Quote the date you read it from.

AND THE BRIEFING RULE THAT SAVED IT STAYS LOAD-BEARING: every dispatch says 'READ THE BEAD BEFORE THIS BRIEF, AND READ IT BOTTOM-UP — where the bead and this brief disagree, THE BEAD GOVERNS, and say in your report what differed.' Workers caught FIVE stale or wrong premises in my briefs tonight because of that clause. It is the backstop for exactly this class of mayor error, and it is worth more than any single brief being right.

bd update --append-notes <text> APPENDS to a bead's notes with a newline separator. bd update --notes <text> REPLACES them outright and says nothing about what it destroyed.

MEASURED 2026-08-21. Earlier the same session --notes silently overwrote a standing warning on rf2-y1jkm ("DO NOT REDISPATCH THIS BEAD... It is on Mike's queue"); recovering it needed a walk of git log --format=%H -- .beads/issues.jsonl parsing each revision's JSONL. --append-notes removes the need for the read-modify-write entirely.

THERE IS NO --notes-file. bd update accepts --body-file (description) and --design-file (design) but notes take their text as an ARGUMENT only, so a long multi-line note goes through --append-notes with the text passed directly (subprocess arg, or a shell quoted string). Do not reach for a --notes-file flag; it errors 'unknown flag'.

ALSO: printing bd's own stdout back through Windows-native Python dies on cp1252 for its success glyph. Use encoding='utf-8', errors='replace' on subprocess, and do not echo bd's output verbatim.

bd update --claim is a NO-OP on a bead already assigned (e.g. assignee=Mike Thompson) — it silently won't flip status to in_progress, so the bead keeps showing as open/dispatchable and a cron tick can dispatch a duplicate worker. Use 'bd update <id> --status in_progress' to force it. Hit during the post-ELK dispatch (lamdfl showed dispatchable while a worker was already building it).

bd update --notes REPLACES existing notes; it does NOT append. Use --append-notes (documented: "Append to existing notes (with newline separator)").

THIS IS NOT A THEORETICAL HAZARD — IT CAUSED REAL DATA LOSS ON 2026-08-07. An acting mayor used `bd update <id> --notes "..."` on six beads across one session and destroyed the accumulated note history on four of them. Worst case: rf2-2rtt6, the EP-0038 programme epic, went from 57,413 characters of notes to 1,698 — every operator direction, every delegated ruling, the whole kill-criteria walk-in state, replaced by a single new paragraph. rf2-emvod 4,128 -> 565; rf2-jo60g and rf2-w3yxd similarly overwritten.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS, and this is the important part: `bd update --notes` prints a cheerful "✓ Updated issue: <id> — <title>" and exits 0. Nothing warns, nothing diffs, and the loss is invisible unless you re-read the bead and remember roughly how long it used to be. The mayor above ran six such calls over ninety minutes and only noticed when a memory search surfaced this very key by coincidence.

RECOVERY, PROVEN, because .beads/issues.jsonl is a full-database export committed on every checkpoint:
  1. Pick a checkpoint commit predating the first bad --notes call: `git log --oneline -- .beads/issues.jsonl`
  2. `git show <sha>:.beads/issues.jsonl > /tmp/old.jsonl`
  3. Parse both old and current JSONL, and for each damaged id build notes = old_notes + a dated separator + current_notes. Start the record from the CURRENT one so status, close reason and every other field keep today's values — only the notes field is merged.
  4. Write those records to a repair JSONL and `bd import --allow-stale <file>`. Plain `bd import` REFUSES with "Kept local state for N issue(s) with the same updated_at but different content" — that guard is correct and --allow-stale is the right answer here precisely because the repair record carries current state.
  5. Re-run `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` before verifying: `bd show` reads the DATABASE, but any check against .beads/issues.jsonl reads the EXPORT, which is stale until re-exported. Verifying against the stale export will tell you the repair failed when it succeeded.

THE RULE: use --append-notes for every additive note. Reserve --notes for the case where you have deliberately constructed the complete replacement text — which in practice is only ever a repair like the one above.

bd update --notes REPLACES THE NOTES FIELD — READ THE EXISTING NOTE BEFORE WRITING ONE, AND APPEND (measured 2026-08-21, and it nearly cost a wrong dispatch).

WHAT HAPPENED. I read the measurement-lane ORDER off rf2-0puue's notes, saw rf2-y1jkm
named in it, and wrote a note on rf2-y1jkm saying it was the next lane item and should
be dispatched the moment the box freed. I never read the note already on rf2-y1jkm.
`bd update --notes` replaced it.

WHAT I DESTROYED WAS THE WARNING THAT WOULD HAVE STOPPED ME. The overwritten note ended
"DO NOT REDISPATCH THIS BEAD. A new worker would re-derive the same impossibility and
refuse again, at full cost. It is on Mike's queue." It also recorded WHY: criterion 2
cannot be met as written, no commit carries both halves, and the choice between striking
the criterion and authorising a spliced-tree measurement is the operator's. The bead also
carried defer_until roughly a month out, which no free bench slot discharges.

SO THE FAILURE IS CIRCULAR AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES IT DANGEROUS: the note that would have
prevented the write was deleted BY the write, and nothing on screen said so. The success
line reads identically either way.

TWO RULES, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT ACTUALLY SAVES YOU.

1. Never write a note without reading the current one first. Recover-then-append:
   read the existing notes, concatenate your addition below a dated header, and write
   the whole thing back. A note is a shared, accreting record, not a scratch field.
2. WHEN BRIEFING FROM A BEAD, READ THAT BEAD — not a sibling that merely NAMES it. A
   lane order, a remainder table or a parent's child list tells you a bead EXISTS in a
   programme; it does not tell you that bead is dispatchable, and the disqualifying
   fact lives on the bead itself. This is `mayor-dispatch.md`'s "the mayor's own earlier
   note is the most dangerous stale source" arriving one step earlier: here the stale
   source was another bead's roster, and I then MANUFACTURED the confirming note myself.

RECOVERY, WHICH IS CHEAP AND WORTH KNOWING. `.beads/issues.jsonl` is a full-database
export committed on every checkpoint, so an overwritten field is recoverable: walk
`git log --format=%H -- .beads/issues.jsonl`, parse each revision's JSONL for the bead
id, and take the newest revision whose field predates your write. That is how the note
above was restored verbatim.

RELATED: [[bd-write-from-wrong-cwd-silently-discarded]] — the other quiet bd failure
found the same day. Both share one defence: verify the tracker's STATE after a write,
never the tool's report of it.

bd update --notes REPLACES the notes field; it does NOT append, despite its help text reading 'Additional notes'. Use --append-notes (help: 'Append to existing notes (with newline separator)'). MEASURED 2026-08-22: five beads lost ~72,800 chars of accumulated notes in one session -- rf2-uelji 23641->3094, rf2-9wmqd 46569->3294, rf2-hic-063 8319->2027, rf2-hic-090 3729->1766, rf2-0puue 3218->2504. Nothing errors and bd prints a success line, so the loss is invisible until someone re-reads the bead. It has now happened at least twice: rf2-y1jkm carries an earlier mayor's account of destroying the very warning that would have stopped them. RECOVERY WORKS and is cheap: .beads/issues.jsonl in git history is a full export, so the pre-damage notes are in any checkpoint commit before the update -- extract with git show <rev>:.beads/issues.jsonl, rebuild as old + '\n' + current, and write back. THE ARGUMENT-LENGTH CEILING sits between 26736 and 49864 chars on this shell: a longer --notes value fails SILENTLY (non-zero exit, no message). Split at line boundaries into <=18000-char chunks, first via --notes then --append-notes, and verify by content probes from the start, middle and end rather than by exact length (chunking shifts it by a byte or two). And note the export is STALE until bd export runs -- checkpoint before measuring, or you will read the pre-update file and think the write failed.

A bd WRITE FROM OUTSIDE THE REPO PRINTS SUCCESS AND PERSISTS NOTHING — VERIFY EVERY bd WRITE BY READING IT BACK (measured 2026-08-21).

WHAT HAPPENED. Two tracker writes in one mayor tick were lost silently. Both were
issued from the session scratchpad directory, because the natural shell idiom is to
write the payload to a file and pass it in one compound command:

  cd "$SCRATCHPAD" && cat > note.txt <<'EOF' ... EOF
  bd update rf2-y1jkm --notes "$(cat note.txt)"

bd printed the full success line naming the correct bead and title. The write did
not reach the store. The identical command re-issued with the working directory at
the repo root landed immediately, same payload, same byte count.

IT FAILS OPEN AND IT ANNOUNCES NOTHING. There is no error, no warning, no non-zero
exit. The success line is indistinguishable from a real one, and it names the right
bead, which is what makes it convincing.

READS ARE NOT AFFECTED, WHICH IS WHY IT IS HARD TO SEE. Measured directly: from the
scratchpad, bd show returned the bead's CURRENT notes and bd memories returned real
matches from the shared store. So a read-back performed from the same wrong directory
would have looked fine. Only writes vanish.

THE DISCRIMINATING TEST, run both directions: bd remember issued from the scratchpad,
then bd memories for that key issued from the repo root, returns "No memories
matching". The write is not merely invisible from elsewhere; it is not there.

TWO THINGS IT IS NOT. It is not the checkpoint reverting the write — tested directly
by landing a note, running scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, and re-reading it: the note
survived and the export grew by the expected row. And it is not payload length,
character content or heredoc quoting — the same 1,630-byte file landed unchanged from
the right directory.

THE RULE. Never let a bd write inherit a cd. Build the payload file with an absolute
path and invoke bd with the working directory at the repo, and READ THE WRITE BACK
from the repo before believing it — for bd update, bd remember, and any close whose
reasoning you would not want to re-derive. This is the same class as the empty-export
and reverted-close hazards CLAUDE.md already carries under Beads durability: the
tracker's failures are quiet, and the only defence that has ever worked is verifying
the state rather than reading the tool's own report of it.

FOUR BEAD CLOSURES SILENTLY REVERTED IN ONE SESSION, ALL AFTER THEIR PR MERGED (2026-08-04).

THE PATTERN. rf2-2rtt6.84, .85, .86 and .96 were each closed by their worker when its PR opened. Each PR then merged. Each bead later read OPEN again, with no close reason on it. Nothing in the loop surfaces this: the ready count simply goes up, and a mayor reporting "45 ready" is reporting reopened finished work as outstanding. Two of the four were only found because the operator asked why there were no background workers; the other two were caught by a per-tick closure re-check added after that.

WHAT IS COMMON TO ALL FOUR. Every one is a bead whose worker closed it at PR-open time rather than after merge, and every one is in a burst where multiple beads were being written by concurrent workers and the mayor was checkpointing .beads/issues.jsonl on its heartbeat. The plausible mechanism is the export/re-import cycle: bd auto-stages an export, the checkpoint commits it, and a later re-import from a snapshot taken before the close reinstates the older row. It matches the earlier rf2-51uz1 finding (a bd close evaporating when a checkout of .beads reverted the export) but here no checkout happened -- so the trigger is not identical and I have NOT established the cause.

THE OPERATIONAL RULE, which works regardless of cause: RE-CHECK EVERY BEAD CLOSED THIS SESSION, EVERY TICK, AND RE-CLOSE WHAT REVERTED WITH EVIDENCE FROM THE TREE. Not from memory, and not from the worker's report -- name the file or commit that proves the work landed. The method's bootstrap.md carries this instruction; I wrote it this morning and then stopped executing it for several hours, which is how two of the four went unnoticed.

DETECTION IS CHEAP AND MUST BE MECHANICAL: keep the list of ids closed this session, and each tick run bd show on each, parsing the STATUS FIELD rather than grepping the record (grepping matches 'open' inside titles -- that mistake cost a false clean report earlier). A one-line loop is enough.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: a reverted close makes finished work look outstanding, which invites a SECOND dispatch of the same bead. That already happened once today for a different reason (rf2-2rtt6.83, two workers, seventy seconds apart, both doing the full job). Reverted closes are a standing supply of duplicate-dispatch candidates.

A BEAD'S DESCRIPTION READS FIRST AND CAN BE OLDER THAN ITS COMMENTS — I DISPATCHED THE SAME ALREADY-DONE WORK TWICE (rf2-2rtt6.31, 2026-08-04).

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched rf2-2rtt6.31 ("re-take HD-008's donor rows") and, having learned that paraphrase loses distinctions, quoted its DESCRIPTION verbatim into the brief — WHAT TO DO, WHY, the BLOCKED-BY note, the FENCES, and the pre-registered ~1.13-1.22x prediction. All accurate. All superseded. A 2026-08-02 COMMENT on the same bead records that the work was ALREADY DONE and PUBLISHED: commit 1ac48c4a0b, PR #7378, every commissioned deliverable present in hd8-composed-donor-arm.md — the re-take section, the provenance table with SHA and both reproduce commands, all three adapter runs, rows published beside the originals, the bulk row fenced against rf2-d2tzk by name, and the stop rule stated plainly. The worker read the whole record, found the conflict, refused to take a second draw, and told me. Its closing line: "this is the SECOND dispatch to re-take rows that were already taken. The bead's description and its newer comment describe different work, and the description is what reads first."

THE MECHANISM, and it is not the same as the NOTES-vs-COMMENTS blindness. That earlier failure was a tool that could not SEE a field. This one is ordering: bd show prints DESCRIPTION before COMMENTS/NOTES, a description is written once at filing and rarely amended, and comments accrete. So the OLDEST text is the most prominent and reads as current. Quoting the description verbatim — the very discipline I adopted to stop paraphrase errors — made this WORSE, because it lent stale text the authority of a direct quote.

THE RULE: BEFORE DISPATCHING, READ THE BEAD BOTTOM-UP. The newest comment or note is the operative one; the description is the oldest thing on the record. If they describe different work, the later text governs and the description is history. Say so explicitly in the brief rather than quoting the description as though it were live.

COROLLARY FOR VERIFICATION: "is this already done?" is answered by the tree and the bead's own tail, not by the bead's status. rf2-2rtt6.31 was OPEN with its acceptance ALREADY PUBLISHED — open meant "residual items remain", not "the work has not been done". Check what is on main before commissioning a measurement; a published row is cheaper to read than to re-take, and re-taking one after reading its result creates a selection opportunity that invalidates both draws.

WHAT THE WORKER DID RIGHT, and it is the general lesson: it declined the second draw because "having read the published results, taking a competing draw without a pre-registered rule for which one counts is exactly the selection opportunity the brief forbids." Reading a result changes what a later measurement means. That is true whoever takes it.

Bead-structure git hygiene (Mike 2026-05-29): commit + push .beads/issues.jsonl on each meaningful bead signal (create / close / decision recorded / dispatch-claim batch) so bead state is never stranded locally. Mayor commit-guard allow-lists .beads/issues.jsonl + root MEMORY.md, so the mayor may commit it directly. Cadence 'as you see fit' = after each dispatch pass / merge-close / decision batch, not every micro in_progress flip. Sequence: git add .beads/issues.jsonl; git commit -m 'chore(beads): ...'; git pull --rebase; git push. No AI attribution in the message.

A BEADS AUDIT HOOK PUSHES TO main AFTER EVERY MERGE, WHICH MAKES 'Base branch was modified' FIRE ON THE NEXT MERGE (observed 2026-08-07).

WHAT HAPPENS. After each PR merges, a hook commits 'chore(beads): audit merged PR NNNN' and pushes it to main — asynchronously, seconds later. During a merge burst those commits arrive between your calls, so main is moving the whole time. GitHub then refuses the next merge with 'GraphQL: Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again. (mergePullRequest)'.

WHY IT LOOKS LIKE SOMETHING ELSE. The PR reads mergeable=MERGEABLE and mergeState=CLEAN when you check, because it IS clean — the refusal is about the base moving between the mergeability computation and the merge call, not about the PR. I retried five times, including once alone with nothing else running, and diagnosed conflicts, recompute lag and the branch being 83 commits behind before checking whether main itself was moving. It was: abb49f1ad4 -> aeadb93841 in eight seconds with no merge of mine.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, one command: 'git fetch && git rev-parse origin/main', wait a few seconds, run it again. If the sha changes with no merge of yours, the hook queue is still draining. That is faster than any amount of PR-side diagnosis.

WHAT TO DO. Do not retry in a tight loop and do not force anything. Let the audit-commit queue drain — merge the rest of the batch, let the hooks land, then merge the straggler in a later tick when main is quiet. A merge burst of N PRs generates N audit commits, so the last PR in a burst is the most likely to be refused.

RELATED, and do not confuse them: a 502 from a mutating endpoint may mean the mutation DID happen and must not be blind-retried. 'Base branch was modified' is different — it is an explicit refusal, nothing happened, and retrying is safe. Read the error TEXT.

BEADS CHECKPOINT GUARD — the shell precedence trap that truncated the export (2026-07-25). The mayor's checkpoint guard was written as: if [ $L -gt 500 ] && ! git diff --quiet X || ! git diff --cached --quiet X. Shell parses this as (A && B) || C, so the C clause ALONE was sufficient — the size guard was bypassed entirely and a 0-line issues.jsonl was committed and pushed (2541 deletions, commit 9c79500371). ALWAYS write the guard as a standalone gate first: L=$(wc -l < .beads/issues.jsonl); if [ $L -lt 2000 ]; then echo ABORT; exit; fi — then do the commit unconditionally inside. Never combine the size check with a dirtiness check using && / || on one line. RECOVERY (fast, no data loss — the Dolt DB is unaffected by a JSONL truncation): bd export --all -o <scratchpad>/regen.jsonl, compare 'wc -l' against the last good version (git show <good-sha>:.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l), cp over .beads/issues.jsonl, commit + push. Restored in commit 3389497f55. ALSO: on this Windows setup 'git cat-file -p ref:path' and 'git show ref:path' piped to Bash wc -l return 0 due to path-separator mangling — verify with PowerShell ((git cat-file -p 'ref:path' | Measure-Object -Line).Lines) or you will misread a healthy file as empty.

Before dispatching a bead, run: git log --oneline --grep='<bead-id>' origin/main. Workers fix a bead and name it in the commit message, but the bead never gets closed — FOUR beads in one session (rf2-xx4ty, rf2-wd9im, rf2-d89rs, rf2-6tags partially, rf2-vuylw) were already fully landed on main and burned a worker slot each to rediscover. The fixing commit almost always carries the bead id, so this one-line grep reclaims the slot for free. It is strictly cheaper than the 'grep for the alleged broken symbol' check the bootstrap already mandates, and catches a different case: not 'someone else fixed it incidentally' but 'this exact bead was fixed and left open'. Related: [[an-audit-that-reopens-an-issue-may-already-be-stale]].

Before dispatching any review-wave/senior-review bead, gh-screen it first: gh pr list --state merged --search '<bareid> in:title'. Prior sessions routinely leave merged beads OPEN/IN_PROGRESS (bd close didn't persist across dolt rebase races) — this session 6 workers no-op'd on already-merged beads (6nx8y/hzttr/h2yvs/uvfph/065xo/utvst via PRs #3304/#3310/#3321/#3303 + commits) before the screen was added. The screen is authoritative; a git-log bare-id grep misses already-CLAIMED beads (they're excluded from status=open scans). Mandatory pre-dispatch gate.

THE BENCH RUNNER EXIT CODE IS NOT THE VERDICT, AND I BRIEFED A WORKER THAT IT WAS (2026-08-19).

I wrote into rf2-77gz8 dispatch: "the bench runner own captured exit code is the verdict for the window". That is WRONG, and the worker caught it at source.

THE FACTS. p0_run.cjs --only alloc documents a NON-ZERO expected exit. All 20 runs of that window exited 1. Nineteen were admissible. One (run12) failed its positive CONTROL, read low, and was excluded from the verdict — while exiting 1 exactly like the nineteen good ones.

SO THE EXIT CODE DISCRIMINATES NOTHING HERE. Admissibility is decided by three other things: the positive CONTROLS, READ-BACK VERIFICATION (zero unverified read-backs), and the PER-WINDOW CERTIFICATE. A worker that took my instruction literally would have counted run12 as admissible, folding a control-failing run into a 20-run series and shifting the level it reports.

WHY THIS IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE. The general rule elsewhere in the method — capture the runner own exit code, never the harness reported one — is correct and load-bearing, and it makes "exit code is the verdict" sound like the same rule. It is not. That rule says WHOSE number to read. It does not say the number MEANS pass. For an instrument whose whole job is to refuse, a non-zero exit is the NORMAL case and the verdict lives in the artefact the run produced.

THE RULE: for any measurement runner, brief the ADMISSIBILITY CRITERIA the record actually states — controls, read-back, certificate — and say what the expected exit code IS so the worker can tell a normal refusal from a crash. Never write "the exit code is the verdict" for an instrument that refuses by design.

TWO MORE OF MY PREMISES IN THE SAME BRIEF WERE STALE, both because I quoted a bead instead of re-deriving: the mode rate ("one-in-three to one-in-eight") came from an older corpus and had diluted to 1 in 7 once a sibling six runs merged; and the bead run labels are CHRONOLOGICAL, not filenames, so "run 2" is bisect-1. Read against the filenames its published figures do not reproduce; read correctly, every one does.

A SCANNERS SAFETY ARGUMENT SHOULD BE ABOUT ITS FAILURE DIRECTION, NOT ITS COMPLETENESS (2026-08-06, rf2-t4j7c, PR #7609).

THE SITUATION: a gate needed to stop scanning comment text as if it were code. The obvious objection is that a comment-blanker which is not a real JS lexer will mis-scan — and this one deliberately does NOT model regex literals, while the riders it scans CONTAIN regex literals.

THE ARGUMENT THAT MAKES IT SAFE ANYWAY, and it is the reusable part: A MIS-SCAN BLANKS CODE, AND BLANKED CODE MAKES AN ASSERTION FIRE, NEVER FALL SILENT. So the failure direction is toward a false RED, which is loud and gets fixed, rather than a false GREEN, which is the class this whole project keeps finding. The worker stated that direction IN THE FILE rather than leaving the next reader to rediscover it.

GENERALISE: when a cheap approximation stands in for a correct parser, do not argue that the approximation is good enough. ARGUE WHICH WAY IT FAILS. An approximation that fails toward refusal is fine in a gate; the same approximation in a REDACTOR or an elision check would be catastrophic, because there the same imprecision leaks. Same code, opposite verdict, decided entirely by which direction the error runs.

THE DEFECT IT FIXED, for the pattern: lane_cache_wiring.test.cjs claimed the clear and release use the same build id and NEVER COMPARED THEM. Reproduced on unmodified main — a rider with resetLaneBuildCache(IMPL, CLEAR_BUILD) against spawn [..., release, RELEASE_BUILD, ...], two constants naming DIFFERENT builds, passed discovery, require, clear-before-spawn and the no-literal check at exit 0. A second rider whose only resetLaneBuildCache( was COMMENT TEXT, clearing nothing, also passed.

THE CONTROL THAT PROVES THE FIX GENERALISES: a legitimate EIGHTH rider using a const named LANE_BUILD rather than BUILD passes. That is what shows the gate compares IDENTIFIERS rather than having memorised the seven it ships with — a fixture set drawn only from the existing corpus cannot distinguish those two.

AND AN HONEST IMPOSSIBILITY, worth copying rather than papering over: the mutation that would have proved the check live on a REAL driver could not be run, because the harness classifier blocked editing and even COPYING reads_ladder_run.cjs. Rather than claim a proof it could not take, the worker argued vacuity closed structurally — sameBuildId has exactly one silent path (no clear call at all) and clearsFirst fails in precisely that case, and all seven riders pass clearsFirst, so two real identifiers were compared on each. A stated structural argument beats a missing measurement claimed as done.

ALSO: it ran a full CRLF-converted pass UNPROMPTED, because CRLF anchoring has silently no-opped mutations in this lane before — same class as the heredoc backslash-stripping trap. Clean, 36/36.

A BLIND "git checkout HEAD -- .beads" AFTER A CHECKPOINT REVERTS CLOSES MADE BY CONCURRENT WORKERS (2026-08-09).

WHAT HAPPENED. On one 21:08 reread, TWO beads that had been closed earlier read OPEN again: rf2-hic-000 (closed on PR #7711, merged ae77d063e) and rf2-hic-002 (closed on PR #7712, merged b8805eb8a). Both were verified still landed on main; nothing was owed. They were tracker artefacts, not regressions, and both were re-closed with evidence.

THE LIKELY MECHANISM, and it matches the hazard CLAUDE.md already documents for a single close (rf2-51uz1) — scaled up by concurrency. The mayor loop runs: beads-checkpoint (re-export from Dolt, commit) -> git checkout HEAD -- .beads -> pull -> push. With SIX workers closing their own beads at unpredictable moments, a close that lands AFTER the checkpoint's export but BEFORE the checkout is written back out of existence: the checkout restores the pre-close file, and bd re-imports it over the database. The documented single-agent version is the same bug with a smaller window.

THE FIX, and it costs nothing. The checkout exists only because an uncommitted .beads/issues.jsonl makes git pull abort. So TEST FIRST instead of clearing unconditionally:
    git status --short .beads     # blank => clean => DO NOT checkout, just pull
Only clear it when it is actually dirty. After the checkpoint has just committed, it is normally already clean, so the checkout is pure downside. Verified on this tick: status was blank, the pull succeeded with no checkout, and both re-closes survived the push.

AND ALWAYS RE-VERIFY AFTER. Read the status FIELD on the stable bead id for everything closed this session, every tick. No notification announces a revert; the session's closed-count silently overstates until someone looks. Two reverts appeared in a single tick here, and only the field read caught them.

THE SUBSTITUTE FOR "MONITOR ARMED, WAITING" IS A FOREGROUND UNTIL-LOOP THAT BLOCKS IN-TURN (rf2-e3i6y worker, 2026-08-03).

SEVEN workers stranded in one day by ending a turn to wait on something outside it — a completion notification, a backgrounded gate, an armed Monitor. Prohibitions did not stop it; each worker found a new mechanism to wait on. What finally worked is a CONCRETE SUBSTITUTE ACTION, stated by the worker that used it: "I blocked IN-TURN with a foreground until-loop, which works and does not end the turn — that is the pattern that should replace 'Monitor armed, waiting'." Several workers also blocked in-turn past the 600s tool cap in repeated increments, successfully.

SO BRIEF THE SUBSTITUTE, NOT THE BAN: "if a gate outruns a single call, block in-turn with a foreground loop that re-checks the log; never end a turn expecting to be woken."

AND THE UNTIL-LOOP ITSELF CAN BE FAIL-OPEN — this is the sharp part. That worker's loop matched on '|FAIL' as its terminal alternative, and INCIDENTAL FIXTURE OUTPUT ('-> FAILED' from a POM self-test) tripped it: the loop reported MARKER SEEN while 'PASS fast PR spine' was still absent, and the spine was in fact alive at pid 550478 and later finished green. So the waiting instrument reported on the wrong string.

THE RULE THAT CATCHES IT: match ONLY the runner's own terminal marker, anchored, and never a generic failure word that fixture output can contain. Absence of the marker beats presence of anything else. This is the same family as the pipe's exit status, the SIGTERM'd wrapper's exit 0, the clobbered scratchpad, and the backgrounded gate that graded another worktree — THE INSTRUMENT REPORTED ON SOMETHING OTHER THAN THE SUBJECT — and it is worth noticing that the family now includes the tools workers write to watch their own work.

A BRANCH SURVEY TAKEN EARLIER IN THE SAME TICK IS NOT EVIDENCE AT DELETION TIME (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: during a hygiene reap I surveyed all local branches and recorded worker/xrayfinish-v1fg3 as ahead=0 - no commits beyond origin/main. Minutes later, in the same tick, I deleted it as a no-work leftover. Git printed 'was 7c1cd84b54', which did not match the tip my survey had seen. The worker had committed in the interval. The branch carried TWO commits and 18 files replaying salvaged work onto a current base, none of it in origin/main.
