FAN-OUTS DEFEAT PRE-LOOP GUARDS — a check taken BEFORE a loop does not fence the loops later iterations. Found by rf2-sdeae (P1, #6361, 2026-07-18). rf2-qfrh4 had fenced every epoch-restore SEAM on the exact-ownership token, but three of those seams are fan-outs: the guard ran once, then the loop kept invoking callbacks that could seat a successor mid-flight. Three interleavings were constructed on the same thread, inside the callback, between the read and the write. Sharpest: the quiesce chain first hook (:machines/on-frame-restored!) destroys frame A and seats B; A second hook (:http/abort-in-flight-for-frame!) then aborts B in-flight requests — a dead frames tail mutating a live successor. RULE: when auditing an ownership or liveness guard, ask whether the guarded region contains ITERATION or CALLBACK RE-ENTRY. If it does, the guard must travel INTO the region (widen the token through the loop) rather than gate its entry. FIX SHAPE that worked: an ORDER fix, not a new gate — detach-slots! removes slots in one swap-vals!, THEN aborts the detached values, so no host side effect runs inside the retriable swap. The sibling timers/release-frame! already did this; the work-ledger table was the odd one out, so the fix converged on established local discipline instead of inventing a mechanism. BONUS SIGNAL WORTH COPYING: the adversarial re-entrancy case exposed unbounded amplification — a callback re-entering release-frame! re-read the not-yet-dropped slot and re-aborted it 1101 times in the red run. If a re-entrancy test produces a COUNT rather than a boolean, the count is the evidence. Related: rf2-uhouu (#6339) collapsed two reads into one atomic decision; this is the same discipline in the opposite direction — the decision existed and had to travel.

A FENCE NEEDS BOTH SIGNALS, AND I DROPPED THE OLD ONE BECAUSE THE NEW ONE HAD JUST BITTEN (2026-08-15 14:15 AUSEST). WHAT I GOT WRONG. I briefed worker/stale-uvazt that 'skills/reagent-migration/** is FREE — verified at dispatch against every open PR and every live worktree.' IT WAS NOT. origin/worker/mount-7mtcf held SEVEN of the twelve files, including evals/evals.json. The worker found it, tested liveness properly (merge-base --is-ancestor says NOT merged, so not a rebase leftover; tip 1d576c2a8b at 13:29; bead still open; no PR yet) and correctly REFUSED half the cluster as blocked. HOW I MISSED IT, AND THIS IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. I ran inside each live worktree and read mount-7mtcf as CLEAN. It WAS clean — because it had COMMITTED its work. The committed three-dot diff (git diff --name-only origin/main...worker/) is the signal that would have shown those seven files, and I did not run it for that path. SO I INVERTED THE VERY TRAP I HAD JUST LEARNED. Earlier today rf2-42bj2 established that a worker at ZERO COMMITS looks empty by three-dot diff while holding real working-tree edits — so I started checking porcelain. Then I quietly stopped checking the diff, because porcelain was the signal that had recently caught something. The two signals answer DIFFERENT questions and neither subsumes the other: git diff --name-only origin/main...worker/
-> what the worker has COMMITTED git status --porcelain (inside the worktree) -> what it has NOT yet committed A worker mid-task flips between them: uncommitted early, committed at milestones, and CLEAN-BUT-COMMITTED for the whole stretch between a commit and its PR. That last state is invisible to porcelain and is exactly where mount-7mtcf sat. THE RULE IS THEREFORE: RUN BOTH, ALWAYS, AND UNION THE RESULTS. Adding a third check (PR state) separates a live holder from a rebase-merged ghost, but it does not replace either of the first two. WHY IT COSTS: an omitted holder is a stale-NARROW fence, which mayor-dispatch.md itself names as the expensive direction — two workers on one file merge-conflict and can silently revert each other. Here it cost half a cluster instead, only because the worker re-derived rather than trusting me. GENERAL FORM, since this is the second time today I have done this shape: WHEN A NEW CHECK IS ADDED BECAUSE THE OLD ONE FAILED, THE OLD ONE IS STILL REQUIRED. The new check exists because the old one was insufficient, not because it was wrong. Same error as clause 5's job-key count, where zero turned out to be necessary and not sufficient.

MY FENCES ARE ENUMERATIONS, NOT RULES — AND A WORKER CROSSED ONE SILENTLY (2026-08-11).

WHAT MY BRIEFS SAY: "Your surface is X. You are fenced out of spec/*, .github/workflows/*, package.json, shadow-cljs.edn. Worker A holds Y, worker B holds Z." That is a NAMED SURFACE plus a LIST OF FORBIDDEN PATHS. A file that is in neither is UNDEFINED, and the worker has to guess.

WHAT HAPPENED: rf2-hic-030's worker was fenced to native.cljc|.cljs plus new test files, and out of the four hot-zone paths. It edited implementation/hicasso/resources/clj-kondo.exports/.../config.edn — neither named nor forbidden. I found it by reading its PR diff, not from a report.

I ALMOST GOT THIS WRONG IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION. The directory belongs to another live worker (areduce-ka4d), so at a glance it read as a collision and I nearly told it to back the change out. Reading the actual FILE list showed no overlap — areduce holds hooks/*.clj, the README and the fixtures; config.edn is untouched by it. And the change was RIGHT: :lint-as clojure.core/defn because defcomponent is defn-shaped, with n/$ and n/props deliberately getting nothing so the grammar is not restated in a second place that can drift. Enforcing the fence mechanically would have destroyed a good decision.

THE TWO FAILURES THE ENUMERATION ALLOWS: a worker crosses silently into a contended file (a real collision nobody sees until the merge), or a worker DOESN'T make a correct small change because it was not obviously permitted.

THE FIX, one clause added to the fence paragraph in every brief:

  "Your surface is <X>. Anything outside it: if the change is trivially additive and the file is held by nobody, make it and SAY SO IN YOUR REPORT. If it is contended, hot-zone, or more than trivially additive, STOP and report instead."

That converts a list into a RULE, makes the crossing visible either way, and keeps the judgement with the worker — which is the stance. I already write the stop-and-report form for ANTICIPATED crossings (a new build id, an npm script, a new :rf.error/* id); this generalises it to the unanticipated ones, which are the only ones that surprise me.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a diff shows a file outside the brief's surface, READ THE FILE LIST OF EVERY OTHER LIVE WORKER BEFORE REACTING. Directory-level overlap is not collision. I check this now; I nearly did not.

A POLLING PROCESS IS INVISIBLE TO THE STRANDED SWEEP'S WRITE CLOCK — IT MOVES EXACTLY ONE FILE, $GIT_DIR/FETCH_HEAD (measured 2026-08-23 10:28 AUSEST).

WHAT SIX SWEEPS GOT WRONG. The worktree pr-audit-8445 was read on seven consecutive stranded sweeps and reported each time as silent for hours: file-tree newest write 03:13:10, git index 03:38:20, both static. Each sweep correctly declined to reap it, but on the reasoning 'cannot tell from spacing alone'. It was in fact alive the whole time. Reading .git/worktrees/pr-audit-8445/FETCH_HEAD three times gave 10:26:44, 10:27:26, 10:28:08 — 42 seconds apart, twice. Something in there runs git fetch on a 42-second cadence.

THE MECHANISM. A process that only polls neither edits a file nor touches the index, so the two clocks a sweep naturally reaches for never move. But a fetch is a write, and it lands in exactly one place: FETCH_HEAD, which is PER-WORKTREE ($GIT_DIR for a linked worktree is .git/worktrees/<name>, so a fetch run from the mayor checkout writes .git/FETCH_HEAD and never the worktree's). That per-worktree property is what makes it usable as a liveness probe.

THE CONTROLS MAKE IT A DISCRIMINATOR RATHER THAN AN OBSERVATION. Every worker worktree HAS a FETCH_HEAD — hotzone 08-21 09:37:38, repoint 08-21 09:15:58, specsize 08-22 00:29:33 — each frozen at the moment that worker died. Only the live one moves. Worktrees created by a different harness had none at all. So the file's PRESENCE says nothing; two reads a minute apart say everything.

WHY IT MATTERS AND IN WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILS. The blind spot makes a LIVE process look STOPPED, which is the direction that authorises reaping. The existing guidance gets you to the right suspicion and then stops one step short: it says a worker that is only READING touches nothing. A poller is not merely reading — it writes, once per interval, to a file the sweep was not looking at.

HOW TO RUN IT: stat .git/worktrees/<name>/FETCH_HEAD twice, 30-60 seconds apart. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration. Absence of movement is still not proof of death — it only restores the situation the older clocks described.

FOOTNOTE ON THE TWO OLDER CLOCKS, since they disagree and both are real: .git/worktrees/<n>/index moves when the worker stages or commits; the file tree moves when it edits or checks out. Neither is wrong, they answer different questions, and the earlier sweeps' recorded numbers were the index clock.

THE HEAD==origin/main VERIFICATION CAN READ A STALE origin/main FOR SEVERAL COMMANDS RUNNING, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE DIVERGENCE (2026-08-16 01:44).

WHAT I SAW. The merge sweep's closing check printed 'local==origin: NO' with local=e56fc00ccb and origin/main=401bd15991. I then ran, in order: rev-parse both refs (same mismatch), 'git fetch origin main -q', rev-parse both again (SAME mismatch), 'git pull --ff-only origin main' which printed 'Already up to date' and exited 0, and rev-parse a third time (STILL the same mismatch). Three consecutive reads agreed that the refs differed.

THEY DID NOT DIFFER. A fourth check resolved it: git rev-parse HEAD and git rev-parse origin/main both returned e56fc00ccb75a3f4f8098a5b62a515a6d1f9832d, merge-base --is-ancestor answered YES in BOTH directions, and rev-list --count was 0 both ways. The refs were identical the whole time and the SHORT read was showing a stale remote-tracking ref.

THE MECHANISM: 'git fetch origin main' and 'git pull origin main' NAME A BRANCH, so git writes FETCH_HEAD and does not necessarily update refs/remotes/origin/main. The pull can therefore be genuinely up to date while the tracking ref a later rev-parse reads still holds the previous tick's value. CLAUDE.md's rule to NAME THE REMOTE AND BRANCH on the pull is right for the pull itself — it stops the bare form no-opping against a racing audit push — but it is exactly what leaves the tracking ref behind for the verification that follows.

WHY IT MATTERS: the mayor's post-merge verification IS 'git rev-parse HEAD must equal git rev-parse origin/main'. If that comparison can read a stale ref for several commands in a row, a clean tree reports as divergence, and the remedies for real divergence — pull --rebase, force-with-lease, resetting — are all destructive against a tree that was never wrong.

WHAT SAVED IT is already written in CLAUDE.md and I nearly did not apply it: 'one mismatch is not yet evidence either ... read both refs again before believing it.' I read them a fourth time with the FULL SHAs and ancestry rather than the short form, and the phantom vanished. Note the rule says read AGAIN, not read TWICE — here it took four.

THE RELIABLE CHECK, and use this rather than repeating reads: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/main' AND the reverse, or 'git rev-list --count' both ways. Ancestry resolves the objects rather than trusting a possibly-stale ref label, and it answers the question the mayor actually has — is the checkout the same tree as the remote — instead of the question the short SHAs answer, which is whether two ref labels happen to print the same characters right now.

TO FORCE THE TRACKING REF FORWARD when you do want it current: 'git fetch origin' with NO branch name, or an explicit refspec ('git fetch origin refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main'), which is the form already used in this session for worker branches and which does update the ref.

MERGE-LOOP HAZARD: the draft interlock does NOT protect a fix worker. The method has workers publish as a draft and mark ready as their last act, so the merge loop cannot merge out from under a live author. A FIX worker dispatched onto an EXISTING branch inherits a PR that is already marked ready — by its original author, who has finished — so nothing in the rollup or the PR state says a second worker is currently inside that branch. The merge criterion tests the change, the change goes green, and the merge lands while the fix worker is still running.

Observed 2026-09-01: PR #8873 was merged on a clean five-clause pass while its fix worker (dispatched ~34 min earlier onto worker/routing-encoding-j3tud) was still live and had not reported done. Nothing was lost — its commits were what went green and they landed — but that was luck about timing, not a guarantee: had it been mid-way through a second commit, the merge would have taken a partial change.

THE ASYMMETRY TO REMEMBER: for an ordinary dispatch, draft/ready is a reliable liveness signal. For a fix dispatch, it is stale by construction and says nothing. The mayor holds the only live-worker knowledge (the dispatch ledger and the agent listing), so on a PR that has a fix worker assigned, check the agent is finished before merging rather than trusting the PR state. Candidate method-doc gap; raise at the next method-reread rather than acting on it here.

FLAKE PROOF — a run count is not always the right evidence; sometimes a MARGIN is. I briefed rf2-ybqse to prove stability with 20+ consecutive runs. Its worker (2026-07-18) correctly pushed back: focused runs could not exercise that flake at all (the bug lived in the gap between namespace LOAD and render, which a focused run collapses), and full-suite runs cost ~4 min each. It ran 20 focused + 3 full and supplied the better proof — the measured margin between the fixture's :stale-at and the render-time clock: +30461ms pre-fix (29.5s of a 60s horizon already burned), -13700ms when deliberately shrunk to falsify (reproducing the reported failure string verbatim), +60000ms post-fix. At a constant 60000ms the failure is UNREACHABLE rather than merely unobserved. RULE FOR BRIEFS: ask for proof the failure is unreachable, and let the worker choose the instrument. Repeated green runs prove absence-of-observation; a margin, an invariant, or a falsification run can prove absence-of-possibility. Demanding N runs can also mislead — N greens on a test that structurally cannot fail in that mode is a false-green about a false-green. ALSO: this class of flake (wall-clock captured in a top-level def, compared against a render-time clock) is invisible in isolation and only appears when a bundle loads all namespaces before executing any.

FREEHAND API-MANIFEST IS A SERIAL LANE for public-verb beads — the biggest merge-friction in the Freehand build wave (2026-07-23). re-frame.freehand is a FULLY-ROWED manifest surface: adding ANY public verb requires FIVE co-edited files in ONE PR — implementation/freehand/src/re_frame/freehand.cljc (facade block), spec/api-manifest.edn (REGENERATE, never hand-edit), spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (classification row), spec/API.md (roster row + remove the declared-vacancy prose), docs/api/re-frame.freehand.md (member heading + remove vacancy prose). FOUR gates enforce it: the api-manifest gen --check entry point, api-md-check, doc-api-check, and the CLJS manifest probe under npm run test:cljs.

THE TRAP THAT COST THREE REBASES (presence PR 6713, measured — the most important part): git rebase AUTO-MERGES the generated spec/api-manifest.edn with NO conflict markers, merging the var ROWS correctly while leaving a STALE :var-count HEADER (observed 517 against a set of 519). The file looks cleanly merged and is SELF-INCONSISTENT. The drift gate then reds with "var set identical; :meta or formatting differs — regenerate", which READS LIKE a formatting or toolchain problem and sends you hunting the wrong cause. IT IS NOT A TOOLCHAIN TRAP. Cure: run the plain generator (no --check flag) to overwrite byte-exact, then --check must exit 0 AND git diff spec/api-manifest.edn must be EMPTY after that fresh run — the empty diff is the proof the committed file equals the generator output.

RULE: for a GENERATED file, a clean auto-merge is NOT evidence of correctness. Treat every rebase touching api-manifest.edn as resolve-by-REGENERATE whether or not git reported a conflict.

OTHER OPERATIONAL FACTS: (a) verb-adders are a SERIAL LANE — merge one, rebase the next onto it, and HOLD the lane still for the worker you are waiting on or it rebases forever against a moving main. (b) doc-api-check requires a member heading in docs/api for every new advanced or front-porch var. (c) the CLJS manifest probe CACHES the metadata namespace across a metadata-only edit — clear .shadow-cljs to re-verify locally. (d) INTERNAL-only beads (manifests/elision, the checker, the test surface, cell/shell correctness fixes) do NOT touch this surface and parallelize freely — dispatch those alongside verb work to keep saturation without lane contention.

MAYOR PLAYBOOK: brief every verb-adding bead with "add your metadata row, REGENERATE the manifest, add the API.md row and the docs/api member IN THE SAME PR or the gate reds", treat it as a serial-lane occupant, and hold the lane still while it rebases. This tax is real ceremony, flagged to Mike as a candidate is-this-over-engineering review — do NOT weaken the gates unilaterally, it is his call.

`node implementation/freehand`, one of them at
docs/design/hicasso/studio/a-control-that-differences-the-constant-away.md:378 — a
reproduce instruction whose FLAG had just been correctly updated while its dead PATH was
left. Updating the flag and not the path is the tell that a reader treated it as prose.

SO THE PARTITION IS THREE-WAY, NOT TWO. Executable references that resolve a dead path
(none here); LIVE INSTRUCTIONS a reader is meant to run (real residue, ~40 lines, owned by

mechanically rewrite provenance ... Preserve paths that identify the object measured at a
pinned revision").

THE GENERAL RULE, CORRECTED. When a residue census is proposed after a tree is retired,
partition by WHAT ACTS ON THE PATH before counting any of it as work — and remember the
actor can be a PERSON, not only the build. "Nothing resolves it" answers the machine half
only. The discriminating question for prose is TENSE AND MOOD: an imperative a reader is
meant to obey is live; a past-tense report of a run already taken is a record.

RESOLVED 2026-07-23 by PR #6700 — the fixture-cache warning is NO LONGER needed in Freehand worker briefs. Freehand conformance fixtures are now a shadow-cljs build dependency, so a fixture-only edit invalidates the cache and the compiled test sees the new expectations.

WHAT THE BUG WAS, kept because the shape recurs: re-frame.freehand.conformance/fixture inlined its .edn at MACRO-EXPANSION time, and shadow-cljs had no dependency edge from a test namespace to the fixture it inlined. A fixture-only edit therefore did not invalidate the build cache, and the compiled test kept asserting the PREVIOUS expectations. A green CLJS or browser conformance run after a fixture change was worthless. The JVM side was never affected.

MEASURED TWICE, INDEPENDENTLY, by two workers with no stake in each other's finding — which is why it was believed rather than argued about. The route-link slice mutated a fixture and got 484 tests / 2746 assertions / 0 failures, green on a fixture that MUST fail; its probe passed TWICE before it cleared the cache. The CI-classifier slice separately flipped FH-CALL-001 :predicates :view? true->false and saw a warm cache recompile 1 file and report 0 failures, versus 124 files and 1 failure after clearing.

⚠️ THE GENERAL LESSON, WHICH OUTLIVES THIS FIX AND IS WHY THIS MEMORY SURVIVES: a table-driven gate whose expectations are INLINED AT COMPILE TIME can silently decouple from its data. Whenever test expectations live in a separate file that a macro reads, ASK WHETHER THE BUILD SYSTEM KNOWS ABOUT THAT EDGE — and prove it the only way that counts: mutate the data WITHOUT clearing any cache and require RED. A fix verified only after a cache clear proves nothing, because that is the broken state's own behaviour.

TWO SEPARATE HOLES EXISTED ON THIS PATH; both are now closed and neither alone sufficed. rf2-drpa3.66 (#6699) made the CI jobs RUN on a fixture change — the classifier had no route for spec/conformance/freehand/fixtures/** so both newly-required host jobs skipped. rf2-drpa3.65 (#6700) made the compiled test SEE the change. THE PASTE-IT-WHOLE RULE ASSUMES THE SCARCE RESOURCE IS WORKER SLOTS. LATE IN A LONG SESSION IT IS THE MAYOR'S REMAINING CONTEXT (measured 2026-08-13, third instance).

mayor-dispatch.md line 23 says paste the gate-mechanics block whole. My earlier fix for compressing it was 'dispatch fewer workers at once' - the block costs 156 lines plus 43 for the boundary block, so three parallel briefs cost over 550 lines of boilerplate.

I THEN DISPATCHED EXACTLY ONE WORKER AND STILL COMPRESSED. The measurement-window brief dropped the wedge paragraph, the read-the-clock paragraph, the artefact-naming rationale, and the hash-proves-source-not-runtime caution. Worker count was one. The remedy I had recorded did not apply.

THE ACTUAL CONSTRAINT IS THE MAYOR'S CONTEXT BUDGET, and it tightens monotonically across a session while the block stays the same size. Early ticks can afford the whole block; late ticks cannot afford it at all. So the compression is not a discipline failure that willpower fixes - it is a resource curve, and it will recur in every long session at roughly the same point.

TWO THINGS FOLLOW.

1. WHAT I DROPPED WAS NOT RANDOM, AND THAT IS THE ONE MITIGATION AVAILABLE. Each time, the load-bearing ordering survived - the arithmetic, 'detaching is CORRECT', 'do not apologise'. What went were mechanism paragraphs. If a brief must be trimmed, trim toward what the WORKER'S SITUATION cannot reach: a solo measurement window genuinely cannot hit the two-workers-wedge case, so dropping that paragraph there costs less than dropping it from a brief sent while three workers run. Say in the brief that it was trimmed and why.

2. THIS IS WORTH TELLING THE OPERATOR, because it bounds how long a mayor session runs at full fidelity. It is not a bug in the rule; the rule is right about what a worker needs. It is a limit on the mayor, and the honest response is to name it rather than to keep promising the whole block and delivering most of it.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY PROPOSING READ-BY-REFERENCE. mayor-dispatch.md already ruled that question and gave its reason: a worker told to read a file may not, and the block's ordering is what a summary destroys.

GATE EXIT-CODE TRAP, SECOND VARIANT (2026-07-25, found by the rf2-kqxe6.20 worker): a BACKGROUNDED or compound gate invocation can report 'exit code 0' while its log says FAIL. The worker's first scripts/test-fast-pr.sh run was reported exit 0 while the log read 'FAIL CLJS node integration' — the 0 belonged to a TRAILING ECHO in the compound command, not to the runner. This is distinct from the known pipe variant (piping a gate through tail/grep returns the PIPE's status). So the rule needs both halves in briefs: (a) never pipe a gate through tail/grep; (b) never read the exit status of a compound or backgrounded command as the runner's — capture the runner's own status immediately into a variable (rc=$?) on the line after the runner, echo THAT, and cross-check it against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines before believing either. A gate that reports success while its log says FAIL is the single most dangerous failure mode available to a worker, because it produces a confident false green.

RELATED ROOT CAUSE worth briefing alongside it: a FRESH worker worktree has no node_modules, so shadow-cljs is not on PATH and any CLJS/node arm dies for environmental reasons that look like test failures. Fix is 'npm ci' under implementation/ inside the worktree (NOT a junction into the mayor tree — a junction makes git worktree remove destroy the mayor's real node_modules). Multiple workers hit this today. Also observed: rewrite-local-root-coord and 'implementation JS harness helpers' flake on Git-Bash fork exhaustion (0xC0000142, 'fork: Resource temporarily unavailable') when several JVMs are live, then pass uncontended — load-sensitive, not a real failure.

A GATE THAT DERIVES REACHABILITY FROM RAW YAML COUNTS COMMENTS AS EXECUTION — and 92% of the workflow corpus is comments (2026-08-06, rf2-6ckzl).

THE DEFECT. scripts/check_gate_scheduling.py answers "is this gate scheduled to run in CI?" by searching the workflow YAML. It searched the RAW file. test.yml carries paragraph-long job comments that NAME the commands they explain, so A COMMENT MENTIONING A COMMAND MARKED THAT GATE AS SCHEDULED. Measured: only 39,567 of 511,152 chars of the workflow corpus is executable — 8%. The gate was reading its answer out of the other 92%.

THE SHARPEST INSTANCE, and it is the reason this is worth a memory rather than a bug report: the test:mcp-conformance disposition pinned its ci-runs-it-directly probe on the JOB ID mcp-conformance-re-frame2-pair, which appears 8 TIMES IN RAW YAML AND ZERO TIMES IN ANY run: VALUE. Its premise had never once been confirmed by anything CI executes. A scheduling claim resting entirely on prose, in the checker whose whole job is to verify scheduling claims.

THE FIX SHAPE: derive reachability from run: VALUES ONLY - inline, block/folded scalars, and the "- run:" first-key form - excluding name:, if:, with:, the defaults: run: mapping, and comments at every level. Transitive closure preserved, no new dependency, still pure-static.

THE LOAD-BEARING VERIFICATION: identical counts before and after on the live tree (40 gates / 34 scheduled / 6 declared). That is what proves nothing real was leaning on prose, so the tightening cannot red main. A tightening that CHANGES the live counts is telling you something was depending on the loophole - read it before shipping.

WHY THIS GENERALISES. This project has found the "a comment justifying an omission is an unverified assertion" pattern five times. THIS IS THAT PATTERN ONE LEVEL UP: not a human trusting a comment, but a MACHINE CHECK trusting one. Any checker that greps a file containing both executable content and prose has this defect available to it. Ask of every static checker: WHAT SUBSET OF THE FILE IS IT ENTITLED TO READ, and is it reading only that?

TWO PROBE TRAPS CONFIRMED IN THE SAME RUN: (1) a SUBSTRING probe was satisfied by a sibling step whose name merely extended it (...-live-overflow matching ...-live) - require complete-token match; (2) a mutation that FAILED TO APPLY (Python rejected a POSIX path form) produced two "green" verdicts the worker nearly read as results. TWO GATE FACTS THAT CORRECT MY OWN BRIEFS (2026-08-11, rf2-5i4e worker, PR #7833).

1. check_doc_slugs.py DOES NOT OPEN REPO-ROOT MARKDOWN — INCLUDING CLAUDE.md. Its own docstring (rf2-znup0) says repo-root markdown is out of scope and it "exits 0 on a broken link in any of them". CORRECTED BRIEF WORDING, add one clause: "then READ THE .exit FILE and quote that number — not the exit code the harness reports for the command line, which is the echo's."

THE COMMON SHAPE, third instance tonight after my sweep conflating FAILURE with CANCELLED and my own piped `||` fallback: an instrument that is correct for the question it was built for, reused for a question it cannot answer. Name the scope, and read the artefact rather than the wrapper.

gh pr diff <n> -- <path> IS A LOUD FAILURE THAT A PIPELINE TURNS SILENT — use git diff for any path-scoped PR diff (2026-08-15 13:02 AUSEST; CORRECTED from an earlier wrong version of this record).

WHAT I FIRST RECORDED, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG. I wrote that gh 'accepts the pathspec, exits 0, and prints nothing. NO ERROR, NO WARNING.' A worker (rf2-g76j3, PR #8280) checked that premise and refuted it. I RE-VERIFIED MYSELF:
  gh pr diff 8279 -- .github/workflows/test.yml   -> EXIT 1, stdout 0 lines,
                                                     stderr 'accepts at most 1 arg(s), received 2'
gh does NOT accept a pathspec at all. It rejects the command loudly.

THE REAL FAILURE MODE IS THE PIPELINE, NOT THE TOOL. What I actually ran was
  gh pr diff <n> -- <path> 2>/dev/null | grep -cE '...'
and that construction destroys both halves of the evidence: 2>/dev/null discards the error message, and the pipe makes the exit status GREP's rather than gh's. grep succeeds on empty input and prints 0. So a loud, correct refusal is laundered into a confident, wrong zero.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT THE GATE RULES ALREADY NAME — 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its last command's.' I have that rule in every worker brief and broke it in my own merge check. The rule is not about test runners specifically; it is about any command whose exit code carries the answer.

THE CORRECT FORM for a path-scoped diff of somebody's branch:
  git diff origin/main...worker/<branch> -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'
Two leading spaces, because job keys nest under jobs: — see job-key-test-needs-two-space-indent.

MEASURED ON THE KNOWN-NONZERO CASE, which is what made the disagreement visible: PR #8279 adds job key hicasso-naming-census. git returns 1; gh-with-pathspec returns 0; gh without a pathspec returns 238 lines and exit 1... no, exit 0 for the plain form. The plain form works; only the pathspec form is rejected.

THE DURABLE LESSONS, in order of value:
 1. A COMMAND THAT FAILS LOUDLY BECOMES SILENT THE MOMENT YOU PIPE IT AND REDIRECT ITS STDERR. Check exit codes on the producing command, not on the pipeline.
 2. A DISCRIMINATOR ONLY EVER TESTED ON ZERO-ANSWERS IS UNTESTED. Both defects in this one-line test — the unindented regex and this — survived because every case they had been asked genuinely had the answer zero.
 3. MY OWN DURABLE RECORDS ARE CLAIMS TOO. This one asserted a mechanism I had not isolated, and a worker refuted it in one command. Record what was MEASURED, and say which part is inference.

gh pr merge CAN FAIL SILENTLY WITH "Base branch was modified" (2026-07-26). The command returned, my script read state and got OPEN, and nothing in the summary line said why. Running the merge again WITHOUT redirecting stderr showed it: GraphQL: Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again. (mergePullRequest).

CAUSE: main moved between the check-reading and the merge call — in this case by my own preceding merge in the same sweep. The PR was MERGEABLE / mergeStateStatus CLEAN with 72 pass / 0 fail / 0 pending, so it was genuinely green; only the base had advanced.

FIX: retry. It succeeded immediately on the second attempt. This is NOT an --admin candidate and not a gate problem.

TWO LOOP LESSONS: (1) my sweep already verifies state == MERGED after every merge, which is what caught this — keep that, and never delete a branch on the assumption a merge succeeded (a memory already records that deleting a branch pre-merge auto-closes the PR). (2) I was discarding stderr with >/dev/null 2>&1 on the merge call, which hid the reason. Send merge output somewhere readable, or re-run the merge verbatim when the state check says OPEN — the error message is the diagnosis and it costs one call.

EXPECT THIS MORE when merging several PRs in one sweep: each merge invalidates the base for the ones after it, so later merges in a batch are the likely victims. Retrying in the same pass is fine.

gh pr merge can fail with 'Pull Request has merge conflicts' AFTER the monitor reports GREEN (checks green ≠ mergeable — a sibling merge can conflict it in the gap). NEVER chain merge+cleanup in one command: verify state==MERGED before any branch/worktree deletion. Recovery if violated: the deletion output prints the tip sha — git branch <name> <sha>, push, gh pr reopen, rebase, resolve, force-with-lease.

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION FAILS CLOSED ON A CASE MISMATCH BETWEEN TWO gh COMMANDS (2026-08-13).

gh pr checks --json state returns UPPERCASE: SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS.
gh run list --json status returns lowercase: completed, queued, in_progress.

mayor-merge.md clause 4 said 'runs whose status is all COMPLETED'. A literal test of .status != "COMPLETED" therefore counts every FINISHED run as nonterminal. It reported all six open PRs as blocked (runs@sha=5 nonterminal=5, identically) when all five runs on each were completed/success. Caught only by dumping the raw JSON.

USE (.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED".

TWO THINGS WORTH KEEPING. First, the direction: unlike every other trap in the merge criterion this one fails CLOSED, so it never ships a bad merge and never announces itself either - it presents as a CI queue that will not drain, which is entirely believable and can burn ticks indefinitely. The identical reading across all six PRs was the tell; real CI does not stall six branches in lockstep.

Second, the neighbouring fail-OPEN version of the same clause: --commit takes the FULL 40-char headRefOid. An abbreviated sha matches nothing and returns [], which reads as 'no live runs' and passes clause 4 vacuously. Same clause, one argument away, opposite direction.

THE TWO gh COMMANDS IN THE MERGE CRITERION USE OPPOSITE CASE VOCABULARIES, AND A FILTER WRITTEN FOR ONE SILENTLY MISCLASSIFIES THE OTHER (2026-08-10).

  gh pr checks <pr> --json state    -> UPPERCASE:  SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS
  gh run list --commit <sha> --json status -> lowercase: completed, in_progress

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION USES THE SECOND ONE. I wrote its check as
`select(.status != "COMPLETED") | length` — copying the case from clause 2's vocabulary —
so it matched NOTHING and counted EVERY run as nonterminal. On PR #7774 it reported
"clause4 not-COMPLETED: 5" for a PR whose five runs were all `completed/success`.

THIS ONE FAILED CLOSED, WHICH IS WHY IT COST ONLY A MINUTE. An over-blocking clause 4
refuses a green PR; the method already names that failure ("a guard that blocks forever is
not safe, it is differently wrong") but it is far cheaper than the fail-open direction.
Had I written the inverse test — count runs EQUAL to "COMPLETED" and require the count to
match the total — the same typo would have passed a branch with live runs on it.

WHAT SAVED THE EARLIER MERGES. I printed the run list and read the statuses BY EYE for
every merge before this one, and lowercase `completed` reads correctly to a human. The
defect only bit when I switched from printing to counting. So: a filter you cannot eyeball
is exactly where a vocabulary mismatch hides.

THE FIX: compare case-insensitively — `select((.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED")` — or
print the values alongside the verdict so the two can never silently disagree. Prefer
printing: the criterion is read by a human every tick anyway.

THE GENERAL RULE, which this repo keeps rediscovering in its own instruments: when one
check joins two data sources, the join is where the vocabularies must be proved equal. Do
not assume a tool speaks one language because two of its subcommands describe the same
domain.

A BRANCH WITH NO *OPEN* PR IS NOT A STRAND — query --state all before calling it one (2026-08-15 14:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED TODAY. worker/settled-10lyy reported worker/rung3-hic033 as 'a stranded branch (merge-base 2026-08-12, no PR, clean worktree) carrying an unmerged budgets.md diff — live hygiene for the mayor'. Every observable it listed was true. The conclusion was wrong.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..worker/rung3-hic033   -> 5   (looks unmerged)
  gh pr list --head worker/rung3-hic033 --state all       -> #7953 MERGED
  its commit subject located in origin/main               -> present

IT IS A REBASE-MERGED GHOST. The five 'unmerged' commits are the PRE-REBASE versions of work that IS on main under different hashes. A rebase-merge rewrites commits, so the original objects stay reachable from the branch ref forever and every count-based test reports them as outstanding.

THE TWO TESTS THAT SEPARATE GHOST FROM STRAND, and both are cheap:
  1. gh pr list --head <branch> --state ALL  — the default is open-only, which is exactly how a merged PR reads as 'no PR'.
  2. locate the branch tip's commit SUBJECT in origin/main — survives the hash rewrite that defeats every sha comparison.

WHY THE ERROR IS ASYMMETRIC AND WHICH WAY IT COSTS: calling a ghost a strand wastes a dispatch re-doing landed work, or worse, revives a diff main has since moved past — the conflict-resolution-reverts-a-refactor failure. Calling a strand a ghost loses real work. So run BOTH tests rather than picking one.

THIS IS THE PR-STATE HALF OF THE FENCE RULE DOING ITS JOB — mayor-dispatch.md already says the diff alone cannot separate a live unpushed worker from a merged leftover whose fork point predates its own merge. Multiple workers have now hit it from the other side: one found FOUR branches holding a file it wanted and every one was a merged leftover; another found five, same answer; a third found three of nine. GHOSTS ARE THE COMMON CASE ON THIS REPO — roughly 70 worktrees exist and almost all are dead.

DISPOSITION FOR rung3-hic033 SPECIFICALLY: reapable branch, hygiene-loop work, nothing to salvage.

'git branch -d' IS NOT A GUARD AGAINST DELETING UNMERGED WORK — IT COUNTS 'MERGED TO ITS UPSTREAM' AS MERGED, SO A PUSHED BRANCH DELETES AS READILY UNDER -d AS UNDER -D (measured this session, 2026-08-23).

WHAT HAPPENED. Reaching for -d as the safe form, I deleted worker/receipts-hic081. It carried THREE commits that exist nowhere else — 'git cherry origin/main' reads +3 new — and -d deleted it without a murmur, because the branch was fully merged to its OWN upstream, which is all that refusal tests. Nothing was lost only because the commits were on origin; the branch was restored at ae14841ab3 and its upstream re-set, verified equal.

THE REAL LESSON IS NOT ABOUT THE FLAG. Ten minutes earlier I had declined to test a removal script's dry-run against a live worktree, on exactly the reasoning that an experiment on live state is not free. Then I ran an experiment on a branch because a branch felt cheap. The category was the same and only the object differed.

THE GUARD THAT ACTUALLY WORKS is patch-equivalence against the TRUNK, computed yourself before deleting anything: 'git cherry origin/main <branch>', where a leading + is a commit genuinely not in main and a leading - is one already contained. This repo merges by REBASE, which is why ancestry and ahead-count are both wrong here, in opposite directions — and why -d's own notion of merged is wrong a third way.

A RELATED TRAP LIVES IN THE SAME CONFIG. A local branch keeps its branch.<name>.merge upstream setting after the remote branch is gone and the remote-tracking ref has been pruned. Three worker branches are in that state right now. A dangling upstream silently changes what -d compares against, so the flag's behaviour depends on repository state you cannot see from the command line.

AND NOTE WHICH TEST APPLIES TO WHAT: merge state is the test for a BRANCH, never for a worktree. A worktree is reaped only on its worker's own quotable completion report.

TO ASK 'DOES THIS BRANCH CARRY ANYTHING MAIN DOES NOT HAVE?', USE git cherry — NOT git rev-list --count (2026-08-13, third rev-list miss in one session).

I escalated to Mike that two guide-rewrite branches were COMPETING WHOLESALE REWRITES that conflicted and needed him to pick one. They were not competing. They had landed as a deliberate SEQUENCE, and every branch tip was PATCH-EQUIVALENT to main.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..BRANCH   read 1     <- misleading
  git cherry main BRANCH                     prints '-' <- already landed

A rebase-merge leaves the ORIGINAL commit object unreachable from main while its PATCH is fully present. rev-list counts OBJECTS; the question is about CONTENT. git cherry marks '-' for patch-equivalent and '+' for genuinely unlanded.

THE PATTERN IS BIGGER THAN THIS ONE COMMAND. A rev-list count misled three separate times in one session:
  1. liveness  - the ahead count is INVARIANT UNDER REBASE, so a working worker read as stalled (rf2-0vvw)
  2. the check band - a mid-run rollup total is a FLOOR, not a count; 92 became 93 when it settled
  3. unlanded work - object reachability is not patch equivalence (this one)

Each time the number was real and the QUESTION IT ANSWERED was not the question I was asking. Before quoting a count, say out loud what set it counts and whether that is the set you care about.

COST HERE: a false P2 escalation to the operator, a bead held at 'needs Mike' for several ticks, and three further beads fenced behind it that were never actually blocked.

A `$` ANCHOR PLACED DIRECTLY AFTER LITERAL TEXT RETURNS A FALSE ZERO IN `git grep` ON THIS CHECKOUT, AND EVERY MAYOR GOVERNING FILE IS CRLF (measured 2026-08-20).

MECHANISM. The files are stored and checked out with CRLF terminators, so a `\r` sits between the last literal character and end-of-line. `git grep` matches against that `\r`; `^` is unaffected, and `.*$` is unaffected because `.` matches the `\r`. Only literal-text-then-`$` fails, and it fails SILENTLY as "no matches".

MEASURED, on `.claude/commands/mayor-posture.md`:
  leading `^` only ........................ 1 hit
  `.*$` .................................... 1 hit
  full literal line + `$` .................. 0 hits  <-- FALSE
  same literal line, no `$` ................ 1 hit

SPREAD, and this is why it matters rather than being a curiosity: `file -b` reports CRLF for ALL of `docs/the-mayor-method/{dispatch-prompt-template,loops,bootstrap}.md`, ALL of `.claude/commands/mayor-{merge,dispatch,posture,hygiene,method-reread}.md`, and `CLAUDE.md`. `dispatch-prompt-template.md` is 900 of 900 lines CRLF. The entire surface the method-reread loop audits is affected.

HOW IT BIT. The method-reread loop's duplicate-block check ran `git grep -l "^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$"` and returned EMPTY — for a heading that demonstrably exists at `dispatch-prompt-template.md:478`. Unanchored, it returns exactly 1 file, which is the correct answer. Had a second copy of that block existed, the check would have reported clean.

WHY NO DISPATCH WAS EVER HARMED. The block extraction uses `sed`, not `git grep`, and `sed` on this Git Bash STRIPS the `\r` on read — `sed -n '/^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$/,/^```$/p'` still returns its 51 lines, and the extracted text is clean LF. So the paste path is sound and only the VERIFICATION path was blind. Do not "fix" the extraction.

THE RULE: never end a `git grep` pattern with a `$` straight after literal text on this repo. Drop the `$`, or use `.*$`. And this is the standing "a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed" rule biting the mayor's own audit — run a positive control on any census whose zero you are about to believe.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. An anchored hook-call-site census over implementation/hicasso/src read 14 with 'git grep -E' and 16 with rg, against a tree that was BYTE-IDENTICAL across the rebase (verified). The worker recorded the correction on its published page rather than absorbing it silently, which is the only reason it is knowable.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TOOL PREFERENCE. Every census on this programme is a published NUMBER that later work cites — native-share, retained-tooling, mutable-globals, public-surface, allocation. A census run with git grep can be low and internally consistent, and nothing downstream can tell. A census is not reproducible unless it records the tool as well as the pattern.

THE RULE: use rg for any census whose number gets published, and RECORD THE TOOL alongside the pattern and the count. If a census must use git grep (for example to restrict to tracked files), cross-check the total with rg and say both numbers.

A SECOND TRAP FROM THE SAME BEAD, and it is Clojure-specific: A PREDICATE NAME ENDS IN '?', WHICH IS ALSO A REGEX QUANTIFIER. The worker's grep '\bscope?\b' matched 'scop' followed by an optional 'e', so it reported two LIVE evidence vars as dead code. Escape the '?' or use a fixed-string search whenever a Clojure symbol ends in '?' or '*' or '+'. In a dead-code census this fails in the dangerous direction: it deletes live code.

BOTH TRAPS SHARE ONE SHAPE — a census that is wrong reads exactly like a census that is right, because the only evidence is the number itself. That is why a positive control (seed something the census must catch, confirm it is named, remove it) is now standard on this programme's censuses.

git rm --cached DOES NOT PROTECT FILES FROM A LATER CHECKOUT — and this will bite rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 at 85 files. Found by the ai/decisions untracking worker (#6424) on 2026-07-19, in its own worktree.

THE HAZARD: `git rm --cached` leaves the file on disk IN THE BRANCH WHERE IT RUNS — but the COMMIT RECORDS A DELETION. Any later rebase, checkout, or `git reset --hard` ACROSS that commit removes the working-tree copies too, silently and with no warning. The worker rebased onto post-#6422 main and its four dossiers vanished from disk; it caught this only on a final on-disk verification and restored them.
⚠️ THE SAME THING HAPPENS IN EVERY OTHER CHECKOUT WHEN THE COMMIT MERGES. The mayor loop `git reset --hard origin/main` after a merge will delete the operator working copies. On 2026-07-19 I backed the four dossiers up to the scratchpad BEFORE merging #6424 and restored them after, so they end up UNTRACKED BUT PRESENT — which is what "should not be tracked" means. "Untrack" is not "delete".

⚠️ rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 WILL HIT THIS AT 85 FILES (ai/findings/new-substrate-synthesis + new-substrate-codex). Its brief MUST carry:
  1. Back up the full tracked ai/ set to a location OUTSIDE the repo before the untracking commit.
  2. A POST-REBASE ON-DISK RE-VERIFICATION step — after any rebase or checkout, confirm the files are still present, not just that the index is right.
  3. The same restore step in the mayor merge sequence, or the operator local working material disappears from every checkout that pulls.
  4. State explicitly whether the operator wants them KEPT on disk or genuinely DELETED — do not infer. Mike instruction was "this path should NOT be tracked", which is about the index, not the filesystem.

GENERAL FORM: an index-only operation still produces a tree-changing commit. Whenever you `git rm --cached` anything a human is still using as working material, the deletion propagates to every working tree that later checks out that commit. Back it up first; verify on disk afterwards; and say plainly to the operator that the files will vanish from their checkout unless restored.

GREPPING A GATE LOG FOR 'FAIL' HITS ITS OWN SELF-TEST CONTROL LINES — count them against a known-good run before believing a failure (2026-08-15 20:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/release-gra70 (rf2-gra70, PR #8314). Its fast-PR spine log contained 35 matches for FAIL while the run exited 0. Those 35 are CONTROL LINES of the form 'PASS ... FAILS' — a self-test asserting that a deliberately-broken input fails. The worker's discriminator was simple and right: THE SAME COUNT APPEARED IN A RUN THAT EXITED 0, so 35 is the baseline rather than a signal.

WHY THIS MATTERS: the standing rule is already 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's'. This is the mirror failure — reading the LOG instead of the exit code, and being misled in the opposite direction. One makes a failure look like a pass; the other makes a pass look like a failure. THE EXIT CODE FROM THE RUNNER'S OWN LINE IS THE VERDICT. A log grep is at best corroboration, and only against a known baseline.

GREP -F COMBINED WITH -i SILENTLY RETURNS ZERO ON THIS PROJECT'S GREP BUILD (measured 2026-09-03 by the xray-b worker, and its CONTROL is the only reason it was caught).

MEASURED, same needle, same tree, same invocation shape:
  grep -ri  <needle> -> 43 hits
  grep -rFi <needle> ->  0 hits

No error, no warning, exit status of an ordinary no-match. So a census written with -F for literal safety AND -i for case-insensitivity reports ZERO and looks exactly like a clean tree.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG: -F is the flag careful people add. It is the correct instinct — a needle containing regex metacharacters (a dot, a question mark, brackets, and this repo is full of names like machine-has-tag? and :rf.error/...) must be matched literally. So the census that combines -F and -i is the one written BY the person being careful, and it is the one that lies. The reward for care is a false zero.

THE DEFENCE IS A CONTROL THAT BITES, AND NOTHING ELSE. A search returning zero is not a check that passed. Every census in this project must be run alongside a needle KNOWN to be present, drawn from the same pipeline with the same flags; if the control also reads zero, the instrument is broken, not the tree. The xray-b worker had exactly that control at 43 and caught its own broken census on the first read. A worker without one would have reported 'premise does not hold, zero carriers' with complete confidence.

RELATED FAILURES OF THE SAME FAMILY ALREADY RECORDED HERE: bd --json emitting CRLF so grep -F matches nothing (fixed with tr -d '\r'); a whitespace-collapsed pass and a line-oriented pass disagreeing 97 vs 117 with neither a superset; a punctuation-final needle missed by a word-boundary pattern. The generalisation is one sentence: A CENSUS IS AN INSTRUMENT, AND AN INSTRUMENT IS NOT TRUSTED UNTIL IT HAS BEEN SEEN TO MOVE.

grep -iF ABORTS and grep -oiF SILENTLY RETURNS ZERO on this Windows/Git-Bash build — measured 2026-09-02 by the setupskill-a worker, whose first flattened census returned zero FOR EVERYTHING INCLUDING ITS OWN CONTROL.

WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY TOOL BUG: the method's standing defence against a false zero is 'run the search once against something it should find'. That defence assumes the control and the target go through a WORKING instrument. Here the instrument was broken, so the control returned zero too — and a reader who checks only 'did my census return zero?' sees a confirmed premise. The worker caught it because it noticed the CONTROL had also failed, which is the only signal available. A zero control is not a weak result; it is evidence the instrument is broken, and it must never be read as 'the control does not apply here'.

THE REMEDY THAT WORKED: re-run the census in Python, once line-oriented and once flattened. Do not reach for another grep flag combination.

BOUNDS: measured on this repo's Git-Bash on Windows 11. The -F (fixed-string) flag is implicated in both failures; plain grep and rg were not observed failing this way. Re-measure before asserting the scope is wider.

THIS IS THE SECOND INSTRUMENT IN ONE DAY that answered 'nothing here' while broken — the other was the surface classifier, which reports every surface unaffected when handed revisions where it wants PATHS (hit by three separate workers). Same class, different tool: any instrument that can answer 'nothing here' gives that answer when misused, and raises no error.

HOW I GOT THE WRONG NUMBER, because the mistake is instructive: I ran a COMPOUND pattern

control the sweep against the SPECIFIC file you believe carries the claim, not merely against

CASE 1, rf2-6o5lx. I sent worker ceilinf a status check that ALSO named a defect and asked it to handle it. It did, and opened a PR. Minutes later I dispatched a second worker at the same file under the same bead. My outbox was the dispatch source I failed to read.

CASE 2, rf2-xc0bw, AND THIS ONE IS WORSE BECAUSE THE RECORD WAS ALREADY ON DISK. I dispatched ledgerdrv to build a per-frame driver. That driver had ALREADY LANDED as PR #8605 from worker framedrv, merged hours earlier. ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv carried the line "framedrv <agentId> 2026-08-21 05:45:21 rf2-xc0bw" -- I had written that bead id myself, at dispatch, exactly as the hygiene rule prescribes. I never grepped it. The bead's description was stale against the tree and I briefed from it.

THE FILE HAS A BEAD COLUMN AND I ONLY EVER WRITE TO IT. Its documented purpose is recovering a completion report across a /clear. But the same line answers a second question for free: HAS THIS BEAD ALREADY BEEN DISPATCHED? Nothing else answers that -- bd ready still lists such a bead, its status still reads open because dispatches do not claim beads, and gh pr list shows nothing once the earlier PR has merged.

THE CHECK, AND IT IS ONE COMMAND BEFORE EVERY DISPATCH:
  grep <bead-id> ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv
A hit means a worker has already been sent at this bead. That is not automatically a refusal -- work legitimately continues across PRs -- but it means READ THAT PR AND THE TREE BEFORE BRIEFING, because the bead description is now presumed stale.

WHY THE EXISTING RULES DID NOT CATCH IT. The file-ownership fence derives from open PRs, worktrees and working trees. All four sources are blind to a MERGED PR whose worktree has been reaped -- which is precisely the state a completed predecessor is in. The premises-are-claims rule would have caught it had I applied it to the bead's central premise ("topo has no driver", "the slice has no per-frame driver") rather than to its file paths. I checked paths and not the claim.

BOTH WORKERS HANDLED IT CORRECTLY AND THAT IS NOT THE POINT. ledgerdrv refused to build a second driver, said the tree governed over the brief, and landed the one item genuinely still owed. The waste was a full dispatch cycle, and the near-miss was a second driver landing beside the first.

GUARD REGIONS — a document-wide census cannot see WHERE a claim sits, and that is a false-green generator. rf2-vxcl7 (#6348, 2026-07-18) proved it in situ: deleting ONLY spec/004's Abstract sentence while leaving the body correct kept the document-wide test GREEN; only a region-bound guard (section-text slice of the Abstract) went red. RULE: when a guard pins a claim that must hold in a SPECIFIC place, bind the region, not the document. Also: vxcl7 found the existing rows were blind because they keyed on the noun 'AST' while the retired formulation said 'template representation', and its quantifier sat outside the emitter alternation — so when adding a census row, check the row matches the WORDING you are retiring, not just the concept. It surfaced only because subs-on-nil THROWS; an extractor returning an empty region instead would have made every row VACUOUSLY GREEN on the LF CI runner and nowhere else. Normalize line endings inside any section-slicing helper.

THE HARNESS'S OWN COMPLETION NOTICE CAN REPORT "exit code 0" FOR A COMMAND THAT FAILED (2026-08-10).

WHAT HAPPENED. The rf2-2rtt6.143 worker ran sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh as part of a compound command ending in a grep. The spine FAILED - its own $? was 1, on "CLJS node integration: Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js". The harness's completion notice for that run reported EXIT CODE 0, because the status it surfaced was the trailing grep's, not the script's. The worker caught it only because it read $? directly, as briefed.

THIS IS THE PIPELINE-EXIT-CODE TRAP ONE LEVEL UP. Every brief in this repo says "never pipe a gate through tail/head/grep - a pipeline's exit status is its last command's, so a red run reads green". That rule is usually explained as a risk to the WORKER. It is also a risk to the MAYOR: the tool result I read can carry the same lie. A green-looking completion notice is not evidence a gate passed.

THE ONLY TRUSTWORTHY FORM: run the gate alone, redirect to a worktree-local log, and echo $? into its own file on the very next command.
    sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > gate-spine.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > gate-spine.exit
Then read gate-spine.exit. Never append a filter to the same command line as the gate, not even to shorten output for a report.

A SECOND TRAP IN THE SAME INCIDENT, worth as much as the first. The worker's EARLIER spine run had genuinely passed - because cljs_node_test was FALSE and that whole tier was SKIPPED. Touching the classifier is what armed the tier, which is what exposed the missing implementation/node_modules in a fresh worktree. So a green spine in a worker worktree can mean "the tier that would have failed did not run". When a diff changes what CI selects, every prior gate result on that branch is stale - re-run after the classifier change, not before.

THE HARNESS EXIT-CODE DISCREPANCY HAS A MECHANISM, AND IT IS NOT A BUG (2026-08-14, rf2-5gka worker).

ALL DAY workers reported the harness saying exit 0 while their captured value said 1 — five consecutive runs for one worker, all three red runs for another, a spine run for a third. I recorded it as a harness defect and briefed workers to distrust the harness number. The mechanism is simpler and it is our own doing:

  THE TRAILING `echo "EXIT=$?"` OWNS THE SHELL'S STATUS.

Every brief in this repository tells workers to redirect a gate to a log and echo the runner's exit code on ONE command line. That trailing echo succeeds, so the SHELL exits 0 — and the harness reports the shell's status, correctly. The gate's own status was captured into the log by `$?` a microsecond earlier.

So the harness is not lying. It is reporting the last command in the pipeline, which is the echo we asked for. Both numbers are true about different things.

THE RULE IS UNCHANGED BUT ITS REASON IS NOW CORRECT: for any redirected gate, the harness number is MEANINGLESS — not wrong, just answering a different question. Quote the captured one. And do not go looking for a harness bug: there isn't one to find, and workers have spent time wondering.

WORTH SAYING IN BRIEFS AS THE REASON RATHER THAN THE RULE, because a worker who understands why will apply it correctly to shapes we have not anticipated — a pipeline ending in `tee`, a compound command ending in a cleanup, anything where the last command is not the gate.

THE HARNESS HARD-KILLS A FOREGROUND COMMAND AT 10 MINUTES — so 'run the gate in the foreground to completion' is UNSATISFIABLE for the fast-PR spine (2026-08-11, measured by the catalogrows-vkle worker).

ITS WORDS: 'a foreground run is not achievable here — the harness hard-kills foreground commands at 10 minutes, and my first foreground attempt died exactly there (exit 143, mid-JVM tier).' What matters is not foreground-ness — it is (a) unpiped output, (b) the exit code captured on the SAME command line into a file, (c) the gate root line checked against the worker's own worktree, and (d) THE WORKER STAYING IN ITS TURN, polling the log and .exit file until it exits, rather than ending the turn to wait for a notification that may never arrive.

The catalogrows worker did exactly this and said so plainly: 'The run is detached only so it can finish; the output is unpiped and the exit code is captured the way you specified, and I am waiting on it rather than reporting around it.' That is the correct shape.

A COMMITTED FILE WHOSE CONTENT HASH IS CITED MUST BE PINNED `text eol=lf` IN .gitattributes, OR THE RETENTION VERIFIES WRONG ON WINDOWS. Found by the rf2-rguy1 worker, 2026-08-08, and the audit that commissioned the work did not name it.

THE MECHANISM. This box runs core.autocrlf=true. An unpinned .json is CRLF-rewritten ON CHECKOUT, so the bytes in a Windows working tree are not the bytes that were committed. A reader who recomputes the digest to check the page's claim gets a DIFFERENT hash and concludes the evidence is corrupt — or, worse, a later pass "corrects" the published digest to the CRLF one and the Linux/CI reader then disagrees instead. Either way the retention looks done and verifies wrong.

WHY IT IS THE NASTY CLASS. The whole point of retaining evidence and citing its hash is that a fresh clone can verify a claim WITHOUT trusting the page. A silently platform-dependent digest defeats exactly that property while leaving every visible sign of success: file present, size right, page cites a hash, gates green. It is the same shape as a gate that exits 0 having verified nothing.

THE FIX, and it must be tested rather than assumed:
  1. Pin the path in .gitattributes: `path/to/*.json text eol=lf`
  2. Round-trip it: delete the file, `git checkout -- <path>`, re-hash, confirm the digest is unchanged and the file carries zero CR bytes.
Copying with `cp` and comparing with `cmp` is NOT sufficient — that tests the copy, not the checkout. Re-verify out of the git index: `git cat-file blob <rev>:<path> | sha256sum`.

WHERE IT APPLIES BEYOND THIS CASE: any committed artefact whose bytes are load-bearing — retained benchmark datasets, golden files, fixtures a test hashes, provenance sidecars. If a doc anywhere cites its sha256, it needs the pin.

RELATED, from the same worker: bind evidence to its inputs at BOTH ends. Forward, the producer should hash what it actually feeds the browser (the dist bundle the server hands out) before launching Chromium, and refuse a stale or absent dist rather than measuring it. Backward, a retained run gets a provenance sidecar whose digests are RE-HASHED FROM THE SURVIVING ARTEFACTS, never copied from the prose they are meant to corroborate.

I HAVE NOW TWICE READ A TRUNCATED OUTPUT AND REPORTED THE TRUNCATION AS THE ANSWER (2026-08-18/19). Same defect, two different tools, and the second time was WHILE CORRECTING SOMEONE ELSE FOR THE SAME KIND OF ERROR.

INSTANCE 1 — the tracker. Reading beads with "bd show <id> | head -N" gave me the DESCRIPTION, which is the oldest text, and I briefed two workers from it. Both beads newest comments said the work had already landed. Recorded as never-read-a-bead-with-head.

INSTANCE 2 — a census. Slice 2 of a retirement sweep reported two donor hits in implementation/shadow-cljs.edn. I re-derived and announced a CORRECTION to five, writing it onto the bead as a mayor count-correction so the worker would not brief from the smaller number. My command was:
    grep -nF "freehand" implementation/shadow-cljs.edn | head -5
The real count is ELEVEN. Lines 923-934 are an entire second block. I did not miss them through a bad pattern - the pattern was right and I truncated its output to five lines, then published "FIVE" as a measurement. The worker found eleven with the same command minus the head.

THE SHAPE, AND IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY MISCOUNT. head -N returns exactly N lines whenever there are at least N matches, so the output LOOKS complete at precisely the moment it is not. A truncated census is indistinguishable from a full one by inspection, and the number N is one you chose rather than one the tree gave you. It fails silently and it fails toward under-counting, which is the direction that sends a worker to fix part of a problem and report it closed.

THE RULE: NEVER PIPE A COUNT OR A CENSUS THROUGH head. If the output is long, that is information - use grep -c for the number, or read all of it. head is for glancing at a file, never for measuring anything you will assert. Where the number underwrites a brief or a bead comment, take it with -c and quote the command.

THE SECOND-ORDER LESSON, which is the one I keep having to learn: a MAYOR CORRECTING A WORKER IS STILL MAKING A CLAIM. Announcing "the count is five, not two" reads as authority and gets believed - the worker had to spend effort disproving my correction as well as the original. A correction deserves MORE verification than the thing it corrects, not less, precisely because it arrives with the weight of a second opinion.

Incident 2026-06-10 (commit 7aea52459): a mayor-loop heartbeat 'git add .beads/issues.jsonl; commit' caught the file MID dolt-re-export (transiently EMPTY/truncated) and committed+pushed a 0-line issues.jsonl to main (numstat tell: 'N deletions(-), 0 insertions' where N=full file size + working-tree still shows full content = staged blob is empty). Dolt DB was intact (bd reads fine); only the git-tracked jsonl export was truncated. RECOVERY: bd re-exports the full jsonl into the working tree; re-add + commit it. GUARD (now mandatory in the heartbeat): before committing .beads, (1) wc -l .beads/issues.jsonl must be > a sane floor (e.g. >1000), AND (2) after 'git add', verify the STAGED blob non-empty via 'git show :.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l' BEFORE 'git commit' — abort the commit if either is empty. Authoritative integrity check = git cat-file -p <commit>:.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -lc (NOT 'git show origin/main:path' which can mis-resolve transiently).

A BASH HEREDOC ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP STRIPS BACKSLASHES, SO A REGEX INSIDE `python - <<'PY'` SILENTLY BECOMES A DIFFERENT REGEX AND RETURNS A FALSE ANSWER (2026-08-10).

REPORTED BY THE rf2-re0m WORKER after it nearly published a wrong number. It ran a
throwaway `python - <<'PY' ... PY` script to count Markdown links inside fenced regions.
The heredoc ate the backslashes in its patterns, so the pattern that should have matched
`](` matched nothing, and the script reported ZERO fenced links — on a tree that had seven.
It caught the discrepancy, re-ran everything from WRITTEN SCRIPT FILES, and got the true
counts.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE BACKSLASH BUG ALREADY ON RECORD. The known form is
`git worktree add` and `cmd /c mklink` losing path separators — those FAIL, loudly and
immediately, and you go fix the quoting. This form SUCCEEDS. Python compiles the mangled
pattern happily, the script exits 0, and you get a plausible number that is wrong in the
safe-looking direction: zero findings, nothing to do, ship it. A verification tool that
misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch.

THE RULE: never put a regex, or any backslash-bearing text, through a heredoc in the Bash
tool on this setup. Write the script to a file and run the file. If a throwaway script
reports a suspiciously clean result — zero findings where you expected some — re-run it from
a file BEFORE believing it.

AND THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is the reason to remember it: an ad-hoc verification script is
itself unverified. When its answer is the evidence for a claim, the script needs the same
red-first discipline as a test — prove it can report a non-zero count on known-bad input
before trusting its zero.

SHARED-BUILD-ID CACHE TRAPS SELF-HEAL — every trial must start COLD (rf2-2rtt6.20).

The hicasso P0 lane runs N different programs under ONE shadow-cljs build id
(:hicasso-bench via --config-merge), so they share one build cache entry. Shadow
derives the cache dir from the build id alone, fixed in `new-build` BEFORE
--config-merge is applied, so --config-merge can NEVER reach :cache-root.

CARRIER is `shadow-js/` (npm-conversion cache), NOT the Closure name-stability
maps. `convert-sources-simple` invalidates its index on SHADOW-CACHE-KEY /
cache-affecting-options and never on the set of npm modules the build needs.
Reagent arms cache 14 modules with no react/jsx-runtime; a UIx arm built over
that index compiles clean and dies at first execution with "Cannot read
properties of undefined (reading 'd')".

TWO METHODOLOGY TRAPS worth remembering:
1. THE TRAP SELF-HEALS. Once the shadow-js index has accumulated every arm's
   modules, replaying the poisoning builds cannot take them back out. A control
   run from a WARM cache came back ALIVE and was meaningless. Every trial must
   rm -rf .shadow-cljs/builds/<id> first. A positive result without a DEAD
   control proves nothing.
2. DON'T BLOCK A/B COMPARISONS. Running all of main's reps then all of the
   branch's confounds the variable with box load drift — the same
   block-vs-interleave fault order_guard exists to catch. REFLECT the order.
   Blocked it looked like the branch caused an M2 guard refusal (main 0,0,0 /
   branch 2,0,0); reflected, MAIN refused and BRANCH passed in the same round.

When the harness clears the cache before every rep, a "clear the cache" fix is a
literal NO-OP in that comparison: both sides emit a byte-identical bundle
(sha256-verified), so any difference is variance BY CONSTRUCTION. That logical
argument beats statistics.

COST: clearing the whole per-build cache entry is ~free — warm 34s/26s vs
cleared 33s/37s. Time is JVM start + classpath + the Closure :advanced pass, not
the CLJS compile the cache holds. "It costs a full recompile" does not survive
measurement. Bonus: always-cleared builds are byte-DETERMINISTIC.

THE ASSERTION MESSAGE ITSELF RAISED THE ERROR UNDER TEST — the error-path-throws defect reappearing INSIDE the harness written to catch it (2026-08-06, rf2-q9q9y).

WHAT HAPPENED: the suite's outcome map recorded a :returned slot. check-key! returns its key, so for that site the slot held THE CYCLIC FIXTURE. When the assertion failed and cljs.test built its message, it pr-str'd the outcome map - and raised the very RangeError under test, FROM THE ASSERTION. The result is a red indistinguishable from the real bug.

THE FIX IS THE SHAPE, NOT THE CASE: record :returned? as a BOOLEAN, so the outcome map is safe to print BY CONSTRUCTION. Any harness that captures a subject value and then prints it in a failure message has this defect; the subject is by definition the hostile input.

PROPAGATE IT. The worker flagged this for the sibling suites - ssr diagnostic-cycle, ui semantic-cycle, and the hash foreign-value suite all use the same outcome-map shape and may capture values the same way. Whoever touches them next should check whether any slot holds the fixture rather than a fact about it.

WHY IT IS WORTH A MEMORY: this is the THIRD nesting of one idea in one session. First a probe that recorded a crash as a rejection. Then a validator that rejected correctly but exploded while explaining why. Now a TEST for that validator whose own failure message explodes on the same input. Each layer was written by someone who had just internalised the layer below - and still reproduced it one level up. The generalisation is not "check your diagnostics"; it is that ANY CODE HANDLING A HOSTILE VALUE MUST TREAT ITS OWN REPORTING PATH AS HANDLING THAT VALUE TOO.

THE METHOD DEFINES A HUSK PRECISELY: a partial removal, where the tool deregistered the worktree and deleted its metadata, then hit a lock and stopped. Its signature is four things -- it no longer appears in the worktree listing, pruning has nothing to clear, a status check inside it FAILS AND PRINTS NOTHING, and because of that a clean/dirty test reads it as CLEAN.

MY THREE FAIL ALL FOUR, and on the decisive axis they are the exact inverse: they are LISTED, their metadata directory is PRESENT, status works fine, and it reports them DIRTY (one staged file each). They are ordinary registered stale worktrees.

WHY THE WORD MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING LOOSE VOCABULARY: "husk" ROUTES TO A DIFFERENT REMEDY. The method says the ordinary removal path refuses a husk forever and that you must reach for the tool's acknowledged-husk path, which disarms links before deleting. Someone reading my sweep reports -- me, after a context roll -- would reach for that special path for trees where the ordinary path is the correct one, and would skip the ordinary path on the belief it cannot work.

THE OUTCOME HAPPENS NOT TO CHANGE, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG. They stay either way. But the REASON differs, and the reason is what a later decision keys on: they stay because they are DIRTY and carry no completion report, not because they are unremovable-by-construction. Dirty is a state waiting never clears; husk is a state retrying never clears. Different remedies, different escalations.

I DESTROYED A LIVE WORKER WORKTREE (2026-07-19) — deterministic branch names collide with HISTORICAL merged PRs.

WHAT HAPPENED: my deferred-cleanup loop removes a worktree when `gh pr list --head worker/<name> --state all` reports MERGED. I derive branch names deterministically from the bead id, so I dispatched rf2-vxgfnd.195 onto `worker/shadow-host-gates-195` — the SAME name a previous session had used for the same bead, whose PR #6030 merged on 2026-07-16. The cleanup matched that historical PR, and removed the live worktree plus the branch (local AND origin) while the worker was mid-run. Work lost, worker orphaned.

WHY THE OBVIOUS GUARDS DID NOT CATCH IT: the worktree was clean (worker had not committed yet) so the dirty-check passed; the PR state was genuinely MERGED so the state-check passed; `--state all` is what made a long-closed PR visible. Every individual condition was satisfied. This is the SECOND time I have removed a running worker worktree (the first was k8l1m), and the deferred-cleanup pattern I adopted after that incident did not prevent this one, because it addressed timing rather than identity.

TWO FIXES, USE BOTH:
1. MAINTAIN AN EXPLICIT LIVE-WORKER SKIP LIST. I dispatch the workers, so I know their worktree names — skip every one still running, unconditionally, before any state check. This is the reliable guard; the PR-state heuristic is the unreliable one.
2. REQUIRE THE MERGED PR TO BE *THIS* WORKTREE WORK, not merely same-named: compare `git -C <worktree> rev-parse HEAD` against the PR `headRefOid` (`gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid`), or require `mergedAt` to be LATER than the worktree creation. A name match alone proves nothing — bead ids are stable across sessions, so a re-dispatch of any partially-delivered bead reproduces the collision exactly.

GENERAL LESSON: a deterministic naming scheme makes names non-unique ACROSS TIME. Any cleanup keyed on a name will eventually match a historical artefact. Key destructive operations on identity (a SHA, a creation time), never on a name.

ALSO NOTE: a bead can stay legitimately OPEN after a PR citing it merges — #6030 delivered part of rf2-vxgfnd.195 (the final_schedule probe harness) while its four synthetic arms remained. So "a merged PR names this bead" does NOT mean the bead is done, and must never be used to infer cleanup safety either.

I FABRICATE BEAD IDS IN BRIEFS — FOUR-PLUS INSTANCES, AND A RECORDED NOTE HAS NOT STOPPED IT (2026-07-26). Mechanical fix below; stop relying on intent.

THE INSTANCES: rf2-t1nnf written into THREE audit briefs (real: rf2-ods8n); rf2-1i2fx (real: rf2-mom1g); rf2-zxa0j quoted in a status report for a bead I had just created and never captured the id of (real: rf2-8jbpe); and rf2-vqe8n briefed to a worker (real: rf2-yvy9x — it found the truth with bd search branch-error and told me). Every time the id LOOKED plausible, which is exactly why it survives review.

ROOT CAUSE: I compose a brief from context and reach for the id from recall, or I run bd create, do not capture the id it printed, and then refer to the bead later as though I know its id. bd create output ends with Priority/Status lines and I have repeatedly not scrolled to the id.

THE MECHANICAL FIX, which is the only thing that will work: never type a bead id into a brief, a report, or a bd command from recall. Resolve it in the SAME shell invocation that uses it — bd list --status=open --limit 0 | grep -iE <distinctive title words>, or bd search <token>. If a brief must name an id, paste it from a command run seconds earlier in that same turn. And after every bd create, immediately echo the created id (or grep it back by title) BEFORE referring to the bead again.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a wrong id in a brief sends a worker to bd show on a nonexistent bead. Three audit workers hit that and had to be corrected mid-flight. Worse, a plausible-but-wrong id could resolve to a REAL DIFFERENT bead and silently redirect work — that has not happened yet and is the failure I am actually guarding against.

THIS IS THE SAME CLASS AS MY OTHER THIRTEEN WRONG MEASUREMENTS: reaching for a cheap proxy (recall) instead of the real lookup. The worker that caught this one also caught that my brief line numbers had drifted (mkdocs.yml 251/272, not 251/268) — same lesson, different field. Verify, do not transcribe.
