I OVERRODE A RECORDED DEFERRAL WITHOUT ACKNOWLEDGING IT — SECOND TIME TODAY — AND THE WORK TURNED OUT JUSTIFIED FOR A REASON NEITHER I NOR THE DEFERRAL KNEW (2026-07-26).

rf2-jl7gz carried a note from the #7051 audit: "STAYS DEFERRED — measured zero corpus exposure". I dispatched it anyway, in a brief that never mentioned the deferral. The worker built it and FLAGGED the override rather than silently complying — same shape as rf2-n4by4 earlier the same day, where the bead said "ENFORCEMENT NEEDS A RULING, do not pick one silently" and my brief silently picked one. Two instances in one session of the same defect: I read beads for FACTS and miss their RECORDED DISPOSITIONS. A deferral, a reserved ruling and a held decision are all instructions addressed TO ME, and a brief that overrides one without saying so leaves the tracker unable to distinguish a considered reversal from an oversight.

BUT THE DISPATCH WAS RIGHT, AND THE REASON IS THE GENERALISABLE PART: THE DEFERRAL WAS MEASURED ON ONE DIRECTION OF A BIDIRECTIONAL GATE. "Zero corpus exposure" meant no FALSE GREEN was reachable today — no bad row passing. The worker found the same miscount was ALSO COSTING EVIDENCE: the `~#js [fx]` unquote island and the reader-conditional arm pairing were ALREADY DROPPING REAL EDGES, so the FALSE-RED direction was live and had never been measured. In its words, the miscount "was costing evidence as well as inventing it".

SO THE RULE: A DEFERRAL MEASURED ON ONE DIRECTION OF A TWO-DIRECTION CHECK IS NOT A DEFERRAL. Before honouring "zero exposure" on any gate that can be wrong in both directions — a census, a redaction, a refusal, a roster — ask which direction was measured. Under-matching and over-matching have different corpora and only one of them is usually counted.

THE OTHER THING WORTH KEEPING, because it is the cleanest instance yet of a probe that cannot discriminate: the bead own axis-2 case (`#_#?(:clj (def fx …))`) REDS UNDER THE OLD READER TOO, measured not assumed. Read short it does leave `(:clj (def fx …))` standing exactly as the bead describes — but `_DEFINER_RE` is anchored to a top-level form HEAD and the survivor head is `:clj`, not `def`, so no binding registers and the row reds either way. The wrapper the miscount leaves is INERT. A TAG target discriminates because there the survivor IS the form: `#_#js (def fx …)` leaves the `def` at top level to bind the fixture, giving a silent green. The worker kept the `#?` case but RELABELLED it as a regression guard on the anchoring rather than as evidence. That is the right disposal for a case that cannot fail for the reason it was written.

AND A SELF-CAUGHT REGRESSION WORTH THE SWEEP: `##NaN` is written straight into the adapter suites, and the first draft read the second `#` as a tag over `NaN`, turning `##Inf` into `##Inf 3`. Its own extent table caught it. When extending a reader rule, enumerate the OTHER `#`-prefixed forms — `#(`, `#{`, `#"`, `#=`, `#!`, `##`, and namespaced maps `#:ns{…}` — and say which need the rule and which do not.

I BROKE THE PIPELINE-EXIT-CODE RULE I BRIEF WORKERS ABOUT, IN MY OWN MERGE LOOP (2026-08-11).

WHAT I WROTE, trying to be defensive about the known post-merge pull abort:

  git pull --ff-only origin main 2>&1 | tail -1 || git pull --rebase origin main 2>&1 | tail -2

THE `||` NEVER FIRED. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, and `tail` succeeds whatever it is fed. So the fallback was unreachable, and both merges left the checkout diverged (1/2 then 2/9) with the reassuring line "fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting." printed and ignored. No damage — I noticed on the ref comparison and rebased cleanly — but the guard I wrote was decorative.

WHY IT IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN JUST FIXING: this is the SAME defect class the method documents for gate runners, and I have put it in every worker brief tonight — "never pipe a gate through tail/head/grep, a pipeline's exit status is its last command's". I then wrote exactly that pattern into my own control flow, because I was thinking about the OUTPUT (I only wanted the last line) and not about the EXIT CODE. The trap is that piping for brevity and branching on success look independent and are not.

THE CORRECTED SHAPE, for any command I want to both trim and branch on:

  git pull --ff-only origin main > /tmp/pull.log 2>&1; rc=$?; tail -1 /tmp/pull.log
  [ "$rc" -eq 0 ] || git pull --rebase origin main > /tmp/pull.log 2>&1

Redirect to a file, capture the code, THEN trim for display. Never let a display filter sit between a command and a branch that reads its result.

MAYOR-SPECIFIC: the post-merge pull now aborts routinely, because the audit hook pushes to main asynchronously and my own beads checkpoint commits locally. So the fallback is the COMMON path, not the exception — which makes an unreachable fallback exactly as bad as no fallback. Verify the outcome by comparing HEAD to origin/main rather than trusting either the printed line or a branch that may not have run.

I PRESCRIBED AN UNSOUND FIX AND A WORKER CAUGHT IT BY MEASURING (2026-08-01, rf2-8vvdo / PR #7336). Record the lesson, not the incident.

WHAT HAPPENED. A core test reddened under load because it asserted a PROCESS-WIDE weak-map count for strict equality; the diagnosing worker filed rf2-8vvdo proposing (<= (.size m) baseline) as a STRONGER replacement, and I briefed that fix as-is while telling the implementing worker 'the fix must be stronger, never weaker' and 'prove it still catches the original defect'.

THE IMPLEMENTING WORKER REFUSED IT AND WAS RIGHT. (<= (.size m) baseline) cures the false RED by buying a false GREEN under the same load: a SIBLING entry expunging in our entry's place satisfies it while OUR entry is still leaked. It did not argue this — it MEASURED it, with a probe of (and (<= (.size m) baseline) (.containsKey m our-key)) that PASSED, i.e. the proposed assertion held with the leaked entry still in the map, before the throwable was even released. That is precisely the fail-open class my own brief forbade.

THE CORRECT SHAPE, which the bead itself had offered as an alternative: assert THE ENTRY'S OWN ABSENCE, not a population count. (= (inc baseline) (.size m)) -> (= 1 (count our-keys)); (= baseline (.size m)) -> (not (.containsKey m our-key)). It also found the bead had diagnosed only ONE of the two assertions — the sibling assertion carried the identical defect and would have left the test load-sensitive.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is mine: WHEN A BEAD PROPOSES A SPECIFIC FIX, THE BRIEF MUST TREAT IT AS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT A SPECIFICATION. I passed a diagnosing worker's proposed patch through to an implementing worker with my authority attached, which converts a suggestion into an instruction and invites compliance over judgement. Correct form: state the DEFECT and the ACCEPTANCE CRITERION (here: 'the assertion must fail when this entry leaks, whatever else the process is doing'), cite the bead's proposal as one candidate, and say explicitly that a better shape is welcome and a refusal with evidence is a complete answer.

SECOND-ORDER POINT WORTH KEEPING: an assertion about a SHARED, PROCESS-WIDE quantity can almost never state a claim about ONE participant. Prefer identity over population whenever the property is about a specific object — count-based proxies fail open under concurrency in both directions.

I REPEATED THE gh --jq --arg BUG AFTER RECORDING IT (2026-07-26). gh accepts the jq PROGRAM as the argument to --jq, so writing "gh pr list --json ... --jq --arg B \"$b\" \x27<program>\x27" makes --arg the program and the real program a stray argument. The query returns EMPTY, not an error. I hit this once on a hygiene sweep where every PR read as pr=none, recorded it, and then wrote the identical construction again on the next hygiene sweep.

THE FIX: fetch once to a file with gh --json, then pipe/read that file with the jq BINARY, where --arg is valid: gh pr list --json number,state,headRefName > /tmp/prs.json, then jq -r --arg B "$b" \x27...\x27 /tmp/prs.json.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE TYPO: both times, the broken query fed a DESTRUCTIVE decision — branch deletion gated on "is this PR merged?". Both times the gate FAILED SAFE and refused, because an empty result does not match *MERGED. That is the only reason a broken query did not delete a live branch. Design destructive gates so the empty/unknown case refuses; do not rely on the query being right.

TWELFTH WRONG MEASUREMENT THIS SESSION, and the first outright repeat. The others were varied (loose greps matching comments, row-count as a proxy for content, diffing a worktree against moved main, reading a file before the pull landed, --is-ancestor after a rebase-merge). This one I had already written down. Recording a trap is not the same as building the habit that avoids it — for shell constructions specifically, the habit that works is: never put --arg on a gh command line.

MY RECURRING BRIEF DEFECT IS OVERSTATING A GATE'S OR A FENCE'S SCOPE — TWICE IN ONE SESSION, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS (2026-08-21, found by the method-reread loop grading its own briefs).

INSTANCE 1 — THE HOT ZONE. I wrote 'spec/ is HOT ZONE and single-toucher' into a brief and carried it generally. CLAUDE.md's hot-zone bullet is an ENUMERATION of 8 named spec pages, and git ls-files 'spec/*.md' returns 52. A blanket fence covers 44 pages the tree never asked to serialise. Cost direction: COVERAGE — a worker warned off a file nobody holds declines work it was free to take, and nothing on screen says so. See [hot-zone-names-eight-spec-pages-not-the-spec-tree].

INSTANCE 2 — THE FENCED-LINK RULE. I pasted into EVERY brief this session: 'Both gates strip fenced code blocks before they read a single link... if your edit lands inside a fence, neither gate is your gate.' That is FALSE for docs/design/hicasso/ and docs/the-mayor-method/, which is where nearly every worker this session was editing. scripts/check_doc_slugs.py:1708 sets FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES = ('docs/design/hicasso', 'docs/the-mayor-method'), and its own header says: 'In the trees listed in FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES a markdown doc link inside a fence is itself reported. Everywhere else it is SILENTLY skipped.' CLAUDE.md states the exception correctly; my boilerplate dropped it.

THE SHARED SHAPE, and it is what makes this one lesson rather than two: BOTH ERRORS TOOK A GENERAL RULE AND DROPPED ITS CARVE-OUT. The hot-zone rule has a list; I used a glob. The fence rule has an exception roster; I used the general case. In each the general half is memorable and the carve-out is not, which is the same failure mode the PROJECT STANCE paraphrase has — the lenses survive a summary and the when-to-stop clauses do not.

WHICH DIRECTION EACH RUNS, because they differ and both are quiet. Instance 1 understates what a worker MAY TOUCH. Instance 2 understates what a gate COVERS, so the worker hand-checks (harmless) and then MISREPORTS coverage in its PR body — the same both-directions misreporting the fast-spine-gap clause already warns about. Neither produces an error message.

THE FIX THAT GENERALISES: when a brief states a gate's or a fence's scope, NAME THE CONSTANT OR THE LIST IN THE TREE rather than paraphrasing it — FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES, DEFAULT_ROOTS, CLAUDE.md's hot-zone bullet. A prose list drifts and this repository has been bitten by exactly that before (rf2-yxuta, rf2-8pb5k). Naming today's value alongside the constant is useful; presenting it AS the definition is the defect.

WHERE THE FIX LANDED: .claude/commands/mayor-dispatch.md, which governs how a dispatch brief is written and may name repository paths and script names freely. NOT docs/the-mayor-method/**, which is generic by design and carries no repo specifics — putting it there would be the layering error the method-reread loop exists to catch.

ANY BEAD THAT ADDS AN `:rf.error/*` ID IS A FORCED spec/009 TOUCH, SO IT IS NEVER HOT-ZONE-FREE (2026-08-10, found by the rf2-hic-007 worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched rf2-hic-007 with the surface fenced to "the macro and error
files only" and treated it as parallel-safe against five other live workers. The worker
decided, correctly by my fence, to REPORT spec-drift rather than edit a hot-zone file — and
then the fast-PR spine failed it. `check_keyword_catalogue_drift` CHECK A reds on a new
`:rf.error/*` id unless spec/009-Instrumentation.md is edited IN THE SAME PR. It is an
explicit same-PR co-edit invariant, not a nightly reconciliation.

So the edit was mandatory, and the bead was hot-zone work that neither the bead nor my
brief had classified as such.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR DISPATCH, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. spec/* is on the fixed hot-zone
list: sequential, never parallel. If two beads that each mint a diagnostic id run
concurrently, both are forced into spec/009 and they collide — and neither one's stated
surface says "spec/". The collision is invisible at dispatch time unless you ask the extra
question.

THE RULE: before dispatching, ask whether the bead can plausibly MINT A NEW DIAGNOSTIC ID.
If yes, treat it as touching spec/009 and sequence it against every other id-minting bead,
regardless of what its Surface line says. Beads that obviously qualify: a new refusal, a new
error shape, a complaint-catalogue entry, anything the guide teaches as "refuses with ...".
rf2-hic-021 (the complaint catalogue) is the clearest future instance — it mints ids by
definition.

AND THE GENERAL SHAPE: a bead's stated Surface line is what its AUTHOR expected to touch,
not what the gates will force. A repo-wide co-edit invariant can drag any bead into a hot
file. Where a gate enforces "change X and Y together", X's owners inherit Y's contention.

identical? ON A KEYWORD LITERAL IS JVM-SOUND AND CLJS-UNSOUND — it silently makes a sentinel check unreachable on CLJS. Found by the rf2-6t6qk/rf2-uoy6m worker (#6452), 2026-07-19, while making the trace deferral seam cross-platform.

THE BUG: deferred-continue marked "baseline unread" with a ::unread KEYWORD and compared it with identical?. On the JVM keywords are interned so identical? works. ON CLJS KEYWORD LITERALS ARE NOT GUARANTEED REFERENCE-EQUAL, so the check never matched — every call fell through to level-testing the LIVE predicate instead. Consequence: a cascaded :rf.event/dispatched envelope whose target-live? was unbound post-drain read FALSE and THE EVENT WAS SILENTLY DROPPED. Not an exception — a dropped event.

THE META-LESSON, the important half: this was the CLJS-ONLY FACE of rf2-eaxnai REGRESSION 1. The JVM cure shipped in PR #6365 and looked complete; the CLJS half of the same defect survived undetected because no CLJS test exercised the path. A cross-host .cljc fix is NOT done when the JVM suite is green. It surfaced here only because making the seam cross-platform FORCED the CLJS gate to run it (4 cofx_cljs_test failures), and the worker instrumented the flush to diagnose rather than working around it. Fix was a dedicated OBJECT sentinel, not a keyword.

RULE: in .cljc, never use identical? against a keyword/string/number literal as a sentinel — use a dedicated object value. And when a .cljc correctness fix ships green on ONE host, ASK EXPLICITLY whether the other host exercises the same path; if no test does, that is a GAP, not a pass. Cross-ref rf2-eaxnai REGRESSION 1, PR #6365 (JVM-only cure), PR #6452 (cross-host fix).

ALSO FROM #6452 — JVM GATE TIMEOUTS ON THIS BOX ARE RESOURCE CONTENTION, NOT HANGS. Repeated 10-minute harness timeouts on implementation/core clojure -M:test were environmental: jstack showed the JVMs actively inside clojure.test with NO Java-level deadlock and no "waiting to lock". Cause: multiple agents running JVMs concurrently, AND each timed-out run ORPHANS a ~1.8 GB JVM that compounds contention. Worker guidance: if a JVM gate times out, jstack before concluding hang, kill YOUR OWN orphaned JVMs only, re-run. Mayor guidance: saturating 6 workers that each run a full JVM suite is a real resource ceiling on this machine — a timing-out gate is a signal to check concurrency, not to assume a stuck worker.

A CLJS GUARD WRITTEN WITH identical? ON KEYWORD LITERALS IS ALWAYS FALSE IN A DEV BUILD, AND AN ABSENCE-ASSERTING SUITE STAYS GREEN OVER IT (2026-08-19).

Measured by rf2-oaksj (PR #8508). The first implementation of the client-only adoption trace used identical? to compare keyword literals. identical? is reference equality, and a DEV build emits no shared constants table, so the two literals are distinct objects and the guard never fired. Nothing was ever emitted.

WHY IT SURVIVED ITS OWN TEST SUITE, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING. Every row of the first suite asserted an ABSENCE — no event here, no event there, at most once. A mechanism that emits NOTHING AT ALL satisfies every absence assertion perfectly. So the suite was GREEN OVER DEAD CODE, and it would have stayed green forever. This is the hollow-gate shape exactly: the control could not catch its own case, and the proof of coverage was the blind spot.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: a sabotage run that came back GREEN. The worker interrogated the control instead of believing it. That is the method rule "a green sabotage run is a reason to stop, not to proceed" paying for itself on a real defect rather than a hypothetical.

TWO RULES:
1. In CLJS, compare keywords with = , not identical?. Under :advanced a shared constants table can make identical? appear to work, so this defect PASSES IN PRODUCTION AND FAILS IN DEV — the opposite of the usual direction, and it will not reproduce in a release-build check.
2. A test suite for an emitter must prove the POSITIVE case. If every assertion is an absence, the suite cannot distinguish "correctly silent" from "structurally incapable of speaking". Add at least one row that fails when nothing is emitted.

The fix taken was to switch to booleans, which REMOVES the failure mode rather than repairing the comparison — the right shape, per the rule that a hollow control is replaced rather than patched.

IN_PROGRESS IS A BLIND SPOT IN THE DISPATCH LOOP — audit it every few ticks, not just bd ready. On 2026-07-19 I found rf2-kxkag (P2) and rf2-lgeron (P3) sitting IN_PROGRESS with every stated blocker long since cleared: kxkag waited on rf2-74vlo (CLOSED), lgeron on rf2-sy7zr (CLOSED), rf2-vxgfnd.96.3 (CLOSED) and four surfaces that were all free. Both were fully dispatchable and INVISIBLE, because `bd ready` does not list in-progress beads and every saturation check I run reads from `bd ready`. They would have sat indefinitely.
SAME SHAPE AS the epic-child undercount (see backlog-counting-bd-list-status-open-excludes-epic): a whole CLASS invisible to the count in use. Different mechanism, identical consequence — I under-dispatched while believing the pool was drained.
THE CHECK: `bd list --status=in_progress --limit 0`, then for each, confirm a worker is ACTUALLY live. If none is, read the NOTES: it is either (a) a stale claim for shipped work -> close with evidence, (b) a PARTIAL delivery whose blockers may have cleared -> re-verify each blocker and DISPATCH, or (c) genuinely held on an operator ruling -> leave.

⚠️ AND THE TRAP THAT ALMOST BIT: my first instinct was to close all three as delivered, because their commits ARE in main. TWO CARRIED EXPLICIT "PARTIAL" MARKERS — one written by me: "PARTIAL in #6310 — DO NOT CLOSE ON THAT MERGE." A merged PR citing a bead does NOT mean the bead is done. Precedents this session: #6030 merged a FIFTH arm of rf2-vxgfnd.195 while all four DESCRIPTION arms remained; rf2-84173 shipped its second arm while AC1 and AC3-arm-1 stayed undelivered. CLOSING WOULD HAVE BURIED THE REMAINDER PERMANENTLY — a closed bead never resurfaces in any count.
RULE: before closing any bead on a merged PR, grep its NOTES for PARTIAL / remain / not delivered / arm N / AC-N. If the marker is there, the bead stays open and the remainder gets dispatched.

ENUMERATING THE BLOCKING STATUSES IS FAIL-OPEN. INVERT IT (2026-08-10).

FOUND BY THE rf2-vfsrd WORKER against the live CLI, not by reading docs. The merge criterion said "zero QUEUED and zero IN_PROGRESS". The GitHub CLI also returns REQUESTED, WAITING and PENDING. A check in any of those three is neither QUEUED nor IN_PROGRESS, so a blocklist of two names reads it as absent and the PR looks settled.

THE CORRECT FORM IS POSITIVE: every run at the CURRENT HEAD SHA must be COMPLETED. Then an unanticipated status blocks instead of vanishing - the same inversion the provenance-pins gate needed when its trailing-character blacklist accepted %3F, : and & (rf2-styo). Twice in one day, the same defect shape: enumerate what is bad and the unimagined case defaults to accepted.

MY OWN SWEEP SURVIVED ONLY BY ACCIDENT. I count total, ok, skip, canc, fail, q, inprog and I check that ok+skip == total. That sum catches a REQUESTED check, because it would be inside total and outside every named bucket. But the arithmetic was doing work I had not consciously assigned it. State the rule as: ok+skip must EQUAL total, and separately every run must be COMPLETED. Do not rely on q==0 and inprog==0 alone.

THE COMMAND MUST ALSO BE ABLE TO PERFORM ITS OWN JOIN, and the prescribed one could not. `gh run list`'s table has NO headSha column and `gh pr checks` has NO conclusion field, so the documented spelling could not key runs to the head SHA at all. The worker verified both against the live CLI and wrote an executable form: gh pr view --json headRefName,headRefOid, then gh pr checks --json name,state,bucket, then gh run list --branch <head> --commit <oid> --json status,headSha,name.

LESSON BEYOND THE CRITERION: a documented command is not a verified command. If a rule prescribes a check, run the check once and confirm the fields it names actually exist.

"IS THROWN?" IS NOT A WITNESS. A SABOTAGE PROVED IT GREEN (2026-08-10).

WHAT HAPPENED. The rf2-hic-011 worker built the I7 ambient-read legality matrix and ran the bead's own named sabotage: remove read-key!'s nil-frame guard. It expected the escaped-read rows to red. THE READS STILL THREW - from subscribe-once, with :rf.error/no-frame-context instead of :rf.error/hicasso-sub-outside-render. So a row written as (is (thrown? ...)) would have stayed GREEN under the exact perturbation the bead named as its acceptance sabotage.

THE POINT GENERALISES BEYOND THIS SUITE. A throw assertion proves that SOMETHING failed, not that the guard under test failed, and not that it failed for the reason claimed. Any second defence downstream keeps the test green while the mechanism it names is gone. In a layered runtime there is almost always a second defence.

WHAT TO DEMAND IN A BRIEF INSTEAD: assert the exact error identity - the id and the payload as an exact map - not merely that an exception occurred. That worker asserted :rf.error/hicasso-sub-outside-render, the emitting function, the phase and the query as one map, so a different throw from a different layer reds.

THE SAME REPORT CARRIED A SECOND INSTANCE OF THE FAMILY. Its P2 control caught a defect in its own suite: a timer row's follow-up body re-read a key the enclosing body had also read, so accumulation was swallowed by the row's own expected set. Only the perturbation exposed it. Three other workers tonight found defects in their own tests the same way - a StrictMode row that could not see additivity, a passive-effect race where four rows passed by luck, a coverage floor that survived deleting the sections it guarded.

SO THE RULE FOR EVERY WITNESS BEAD: perturb, confirm red, restore, confirm green - and when it does NOT red, that is the finding. Do not adjust the control until the witness is understood. Half of tonight's most valuable results came from a control refusing to red.

THE 'DID THIS WORKFLOW CHANGE MOVE THE CHECK SET?' TEST NEEDS TWO LEADING SPACES, AND THE UNINDENTED FORM FAILS OPEN (2026-08-15 02:07 AUSEST).

THE TEST'S PURPOSE. Merge clause 5 asks whether a PR's check set was computed against the CURRENT workflow matrix. The operational question is whether the check SET moved, not whether the FILE moved: a STEP added to an existing job changes .github/workflows/* without adding any row to any PR's rollup, so nothing behind it needs gh pr update-branch. The discriminator is whether a new top-level JOB KEY appeared.

THE BROKEN FORM I USED ALL SESSION:
  git diff <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:$'
It requires a lowercase letter IMMEDIATELY after the '+'. But job keys are nested TWO-SPACE INDENTED under 'jobs:', so this pattern matches NO job key in this repository at all. It is a constant zero, not a discriminator.

THE CORRECT FORM:
  git diff <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'
THE TWO LEADING SPACES ARE THE TEST.

MEASURED BY worker/clause5-byoxk over the last 20 .github/workflows commits, parsing job-key sets inside the jobs: block at rev^ and rev: the broken form read 0 on ALL TWENTY and MISSED ALL FIVE commits that genuinely added a job. The indented form matched ground truth 20/20 with zero false positives. All 129 job keys across 13 workflow files are lowercase-start and bare, so the pattern is exact for this repo.

I VERIFIED IT MYSELF before recording: on 366e4fca79 — the commit that added provenance-pins-corpus and moved the band 97 -> 98 — the unindented form reads 0 and the indented form reads 1.

WHY NO HARM CAME OF IT, AND WHY THAT IS NOT REASSURING. I used the broken form before merging #8256, #8258, #8270, #8271, #8272 and #8274. Every one was a step addition, so ZERO WAS THE RIGHT ANSWER — reached for the wrong reason. The one real job addition this session (#8264) was caught by a DIFFERENT signal entirely: its total read 98 while its sibling #8265 read 97 on the same tree. So the count discriminated and the regex contributed nothing. A test that has only ever been asked questions whose answer is zero cannot be distinguished from a working one by its results.

IT FAILS IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION. Reading a real job addition as 'no matrix change' skips update-branch on PRs computed against a superseded matrix — precisely the bad merge clause 5 exists to prevent. Over-counting would cost one needless CI restart; under-counting reaches the merge.

THE CORRECTION LANDED in .claude/commands/mayor-merge.md via PR #8276 (rf2-byoxk), WITH a sentence recording that the unindented form fails open — because the broken form survives in rf2-byoxk's own bead text and in PR #8273's body, where a future reader will meet it.

GENERAL LESSON, worth more than the regex: A GATE THAT HAS ONLY EVER RETURNED THE EXPECTED ANSWER IS UNTESTED. This is the same defect class as the architecture census matching mutable globals by bare name, whose positive control passed because it seeded a UNIQUE name; and as a sentinel that is green on a real leak. Before trusting a discriminator, run it against a case whose answer you know is NON-zero.

A CONTENT PROBE RUN IMMEDIATELY AFTER 'bd update --append-notes' READS THE PRE-APPEND EXPORT AND LOOKS LIKE A FAILED WRITE (observed twice, 2026-08-23).

WHAT HAPPENS: bd update returns success, but .beads/issues.jsonl has not been rewritten yet. A python/grep probe against the file in the SAME command block reports the old notes length and zero hits for the new text. Both times this read as 'the append did not land'. Both times it had landed.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: re-read the export in a LATER command block. Both times the second read showed the full append (rf2-hic-090 5496->7529, rf2-hic-064 9642->11452) and the subsequent checkpoint had committed the post-append export.

DO NOT 'FIX' IT BY RE-RUNNING THE UPDATE. A second --append-notes on a write that already landed duplicates the note silently; nothing errors and the damage is only visible on a later read.

ALSO: 'bd show' is NOT a substitute probe. It wraps long lines, so a grep for a phrase that spans a wrap returns 0 on text that is present. The export is the authority on notes content; bd show is for status and headers.

Junction detection via `cmd /c dir /AL <path>` DOES NOT WORK from the Bash tool on this Windows setup - it prints only the cmd banner and no listing, so every directory reports 'no junction'. A hygiene brief that keys 'rmdir the junction first' on that command silently degrades to 'treat everything as a real directory' (or, with a fail-closed rule, 'treat everything as a junction'). Working replacement: compare file identity with `fsutil file queryfileid` - a junction shares the target's id, a real directory has its own - validated against a deliberately-created control junction. Belt-and-braces: a NON-FOLLOWING `Directory.Delete(path, recursive:false)` before `git worktree remove` unlinks a junction and fails harmlessly on a populated real directory. Related: [[junction-safe-worktree-cleanup]].

Junction-rmdir trap (RECURRED 2x, 2026-06-10): a worktree's implementation/node_modules is often a JUNCTION to the mayor checkout's real node_modules (workers npm-install/junction it to run node gates). 'git worktree remove --force' on such a worktree DELETES THROUGH the junction into the mayor's REAL node_modules (emptying it to 0) UNLESS the junction link is removed FIRST. THE BREAKING BUG (hit twice): building the rmdir path via bash sed inside a nested powershell double-quoted string — e.g. cmd /c rmdir '$(echo $p|sed 's#/#\#g')' — the sed errors 'unterminated s command' (nested-quote mangling), rmdir gets a broken path + fails ('syntax of the command is incorrect'), the junction survives, and worktree-remove nukes the target. CORRECT junction removal (PowerShell-native, NO bash sed, NO backslash conversion): powershell -NoProfile -Command "$p='<FORWARD-slash path>'; $i=Get-Item $p -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; if($i -and $i.LinkType){ [System.IO.Directory]::Delete($p,$false) }; Test-Path $p"  — [System.IO.Directory]::Delete(path,$false) removes the reparse point WITHOUT recursing into the target; forward-slashes work fine in .NET; VERIFY Test-Path returns False BEFORE git worktree remove. RECOVERY when nuked: npm ci --prefix <mayor>/implementation. Supersedes the prior trap note.

A JUNCTION INTO SHARED node_modules IS WRITABLE THROUGH THE LINK, so any installer a gate runs in the worktree rewrites the MAYOR's real tree (2026-08-29). What happened: a worker junctioned tools/mcp-conformance/node_modules at the mayor's real one (as its brief said, for a gate that needed it); the mcp-conformance runner invokes 'npm ci', which deletes node_modules and reinstalls INTO the junction target - the mayor's tree read 0 entries afterwards, while the worker's tree (post-unlink, real install) read 92. implementation/node_modules and pair-mcp were untouched because no gate ran an installer there. The existing rule (unlink before removal so cleanup does not delete THROUGH the link) covers deletion, not write-through. RULE: junction shared dependencies only for trees no nominated gate reinstalls; where a gate runs npm ci/npm install, the worker installs its OWN node_modules in the worktree (npm ci from the lockfile) and never links. Remedy when it happens: 'npm ci' in the mayor checkout's own directory from its lockfile - no data is lost, only time. Check every tools/*/node_modules count after a worker that ran an MCP/conformance gate.

JVM alloc bench: escape analysis makes a retired arm bimodal by arm order. In read_attribution.clj (rf2-a8bw0, PR #7157) the eager-payload arm S1-EAGER read 136.0 B/call in every FORWARD round and 72.0 in every REVERSED round — a clean 64 B step, not noise. 64 B is the two-entry PersistentArrayMap; the JIT scalar-replaces it when the arm runs earlier in the plan and require-current-frame! inlines into it. So on the JVM an arm that ALLOCATES-THEN-DISCARDS can read its own cost or zero depending on position, while an arm that never evaluates the expression reads flat. Two consequences: (1) always run both arm orders and quote the RANGE for any arm whose object does not escape — a mean hides a JIT decision; (2) the SHIPPED (deferred) arm being flat across all rounds is the stronger evidence, because it has nothing for EA to remove. Separately: a thread-bound dynamic Var deref costs 32 B/read on the JVM (Var.getThreadBinding -> PersistentHashMap.entryAt allocates a MapEntry) — this is the floor under every *current-frame* read and it does NOT exist in CLJS.

JVM ALLOCATION PROFILES CAN MIS-RANK A CLJS TARGET, AND THIS PROJECT'S BROWSER SUBSTRATE IS A CLJS TARGET. Measuring `subscribe` on a cache hit (rf2-j8ls2), the LARGEST single term — ~760 B of ~1,800, 41% — was the JVM's dynamic `binding`. It DOES NOT EXIST IN CLOJURESCRIPT: CLJS `binding` expands through `with-redefs` to `let` + `set!` + `try`/`finally` restore (confirmed in cljs/core.cljc, clojurescript-1.12.145), allocating ZERO. Proof in the same run: the same fn with a nil target, binding nothing, measured 16-40 B against 752-808 B bound.
CONSEQUENCE: any bead RANKED off a JVM allocation profile may be ranked wrong for the browser. Three were, and needed re-ranking (rf2-x0fe2, P1). `ThreadMXBean/getThreadAllocatedBytes` is JVM-only and there is no equivalent CLJS instrument, so this is not a gap you can close by re-running.
WHAT SURVIVES: a RATIO between two arms that BOTH pay the JVM-only term (e.g. Freehand's port vs a Reagent view body, both bound) is much more robust than either absolute — removing the term moved that comparison only 97.4% -> 94.9%. WHAT DOES NOT: absolute B/call, and any ordering of terms.
RULE: state the runtime beside every allocation figure, and before ranking work off one, ask which terms are runtime-specific.

clojure -M:test IN tools/xray CANNOT LOAD A .cljs FILE — it passes a CLJS sabotage GREEN with byte-identical counts (2026-08-15 17:18 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/xrayroster-wtznc (rf2-wtznc, PR #8310). I nominated 'clojure -M:test in tools/xray' as the gate for a change to tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/mount.cljs. The worker planted a real fault — removing :rf.adapter/uix, the exact entry its PR documents — and that runner came back GREEN with test and assertion counts identical to the control. It is a JVM runner; mount.cljs is CLJS; the file is never loaded.

THE LANE THAT ACTUALLY REACHES mount.cljs IS npm run test:cljs. Under it the same plant failed at exactly one test — mount-cljs-test/open!-on-react-element-substrate-refuses-cleanly — which is what makes the claim test-pinned rather than prose.

SO: FOR A tools/* ARTEFACT, MATCH THE RUNNER TO THE FILE EXTENSION. A .clj/.cljc change is the JVM runner's; a .cljs change needs the CLJS lane. A .cljc file is reachable by both and each sees a different half. Nominating the JVM runner for a CLJS file produces a confident green over a file it never opened.

THIS IS THE FIFTH GATE TODAY FOUND REPORTING SUCCESS WHILE VERIFYING LESS THAN THE READER ASSUMED, and the pattern is now the finding rather than any single instance:
  mkdocs --strict            does not cover docs/design/**
  the warnings-fatal compile does not police cross-namespace private-var access
  check_doc_slugs.py         does not open root markdown (DEFAULT_ROOTS)
  check_naming_census.py     could not see a name minted by (h/defview ...)
  clojure -M:test            cannot load a .cljs file
ALL FIVE FAIL GREEN. That is why none announces itself, and why every one was found by a plant rather than by reading. THE ONLY RELIABLE TEST OF A GATE IS THE RED IT PRODUCES ON A PLANTED FAULT. A gate that cannot be made to fail has not been shown to work.

MY OWN SHARE: I nominated the wrong gate in the brief. The worker checked it at source and reported it rather than trusting me — the premises-are-claims sentence earning its place again.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT FINDING FROM THE SAME RUN, worth its own guard: a KILLED background run reported 'exit 0' while its .exit file was NEVER WRITTEN. The captured artefact caught it because absence is checkable; the harness's number was not. Worse, the kill left a CORRUPT .shadow-cljs cache that then produced SEVEN PHANTOM ReferenceError FAILURES IN UNRELATED NAMESPACES. Clearing .shadow-cljs and recompiling all 2391 files returned 0/0. In the worker's words, that failure 'wears the costume of a real regression'. So: after killing a shadow-cljs run, CLEAR .shadow-cljs BEFORE believing the next run's failures.

THE JVM WEAK-REFERENCE GC TEST IS THIS REPOSITORY LOAD-FLAKE SIGNATURE — confirmed end to end on 2026-08-14.

THE INSTANCE. PR #8183 (operator-authored, arming the classifier gates) went red on "JVM core under the production gate (-Dre-frame.debug=false)" with ONE failure in 1986: jvm-weak-node-record-does-not-strong-pin-its-abandoned-reaction. The rollup check "All required checks passed" also read FAILURE, which is that job blocking the merge rather than a second defect — do not count it as two.

THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT RESOLVED IT, and it is the general one. (a) CAN THE DIFF REACH THE SURFACE? That PR touched .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh and implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs — CI classifier files that cannot influence whether a garbage collector reclaims a weakly-held record. (b) IS TRUNK GREEN? The last four test.yml runs on main were success. Both true means flake; re-run the job.

CONFIRMED BY OUTCOME: the job came back green with no change to the branch, and the PR merged on the full 93-check band.

WHY THIS TEST SPECIFICALLY. A weak-reference assertion depends on the GC actually collecting inside the test window. Under six concurrent workers, three browser engines and a shadow-cljs compile, it sometimes does not. The test is not wrong; it is timing-coupled to machine load in a way the rest of the JVM suite is not.

DO NOT FIX IT BY LOOSENING THE ASSERTION. It guards against an abandoned reaction being strong-pinned, which is a real memory-leak guard. The flake is environmental. If it becomes frequent enough to cost real time, the repair is to force collection deterministically or isolate the test from the loaded lane — file that rather than weakening the guard.

RELATED AND ALREADY RECORDED: skill-versus-MCP-drift and JVM-epoch gates flake under heavy concurrency by the same mechanism. The classifier arming that #8183 landed makes MORE PRs run the JVM tier, so expect this flake more often rather than less.

LARGE-BEAD WORKER PATIENCE: a big facade/refactor bead touching ~100 files (e.g. csbbwu, m90brg) legitimately runs 40+ min at '99 modified / 0 commits' — it commits ONCE at the very end after a long tail of call-site fixes + a heavy gate suite (test:cljs 8000+ tests, JVM core, bundle-isolation, adapter-smokes, mkdocs, manifest, skills-check, drift). Do NOT mistake 'no commits across several ticks' for a STALL on a large bead. Observed 2026-07-08: I prematurely TaskStop'd m90brg — the kill-reveal showed its last action was 'rerun core JVM tests to confirm this fixes all 3 errors' (actively debugging, not hung). DISTINGUISH stall-vs-working by the worker's LAST ACTION (a SendMessage status-ping, or the kill-reveal line), NOT by commit count. For a large-bead worker: send a status-ping first; only stop if it (a) confirms stuck, (b) doesn't respond across 2 pings, or (c) its last-action shows a tight retry loop on one gate (the mkdocs-stall pattern). WIP survives a stop (uncommitted files remain), so recovery = re-dispatch a finish-worker to the SAME worktree to continue from the WIP.

npm run lint:js LIVES IN A SEPARATE ROOT npm PROJECT, SO A WORKER WITH ONLY implementation/node_modules CANNOT RUN IT — AND THE FAILURE DOES NOT LOOK LIKE A LINT FAILURE (2026-08-06, rf2-t4j7c).

THE MECHANISM: lint:js belongs to the root package (re-frame2-lint), not to implementation/. A worker that runs `npm ci` inside implementation/ — which is the standard advice for a fresh worktree, because that is where the CLJS/node tiers need it — does NOT get eslint. Invoking the gate then fails with "eslint is not recognized", which reads as a broken environment rather than as a gate that never ran. The gate is SILENTLY UNRUNNABLE, and a worker can honestly report every other gate green while lint has never executed once.

THAT IS EXACTLY HOW PR #7609 REACHED CI RED. The worker ran test:script-helpers and node --check ×4 and reported them all 0; lint was the one gate it could not run and did not notice it could not run.

THE BRIEF LINE TO ADD FOR ANY JS-TOUCHING BEAD: run `npm ci` at the REPO ROOT as well as under implementation/, and report lint:jss own exit code. An "is not recognized" error from a gate is NOT an environment excuse — it is the gate telling you it did not run, which is the same class as the mkdocs soft-skip and the killed-wrapper exit 0.

AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN BRIEF, in the repos favour: I told the worker the tree was at ONE live ESLint suppression with rf2-kvsm1 open to retire it. It is at ZERO — kvsm1 already retired the last directive, and eslint.config.mjs records it ("the suppression went with the code it guarded"). So a disable there would have been the ONLY one in the tree, not the second. My constraint was stale in the direction that made the wrong answer look cheaper.

THE FIX IT CHOSE, AND THE REASONING THAT MAKES IT MORE THAN A LINT SILENCER: the negative fixture requires the module and never calls it, which trips no-unused-vars. It dropped the BINDING (`require(./lane_cache.cjs);` with nothing bound) rather than suppressing. That is not quieter, it is STRONGER — a refactor that deletes the clear leaves one of two shapes, and they are not equally dangerous. If the binding SURVIVES, no-unused-vars reports the orphan and lint catches that driver a gate earlier. If the binding GOES TOO, nothing in the lint path can see anything wrong: the file parses, every name is used, and only the missing CALL separates it from a correct driver. THE SECOND VARIANT IS THE ONE NO OTHER GATE OWNS, so it is the one worth modelling. Proved rather than asserted: with a comment-only rider in the discovery directory, lint:js exits 0 while the gate exits 1 on the same file.

IT ALSO DECLINED AN IGNORES ENTRY on the configs own stated terms — that list is for trees that are GENERATED and can carry JS, "not when a file in it happens to have complained". These fixtures are hand-authored, and keeping them in the lint path is what stops them drifting into shapes no real driver could take.

LINTER DIAGNOSTIC CODES GET RENUMBERED — pin the fix against the runner version AND a newer one. On 2026-07-19 the rf2-lsp1i CI fix found shellcheck reports the same finding under two codes: 0.9.0 (what ubuntu-24.04 ships) emits SC2317 on the rm line; 0.10+ emits SC2329 on the function line. Disabling only SC2317 passes TODAY and goes red silently the moment the runner image updates; disabling only SC2329 leaves CI red now. The fix names BOTH, verified that 0.9.0 tolerates the unknown SC2329 silently. RULE: when suppressing a linter diagnostic, install the EXACT version CI runs (reproduce the failure byte-for-byte first) AND at least one newer version, then satisfy both. A suppression validated only against the current runner is a time bomb. DIAGNOSIS TECHNIQUE WORTH COPYING: the worker established the cause by BISECTION, not assertion — a minimal trap-cleanup script lints clean; truncating the real script at one line is clean and at another reproduces; deleting only the trailing `exit 0` makes the diagnostic vanish. That isolated the real trigger ("shellcheck models the EXIT trap as the fall-through ending, and every path here exits explicitly") rather than accepting the message at face value. SCOPE RULE: the disable was FUNCTION-scoped with a comment stating why the code is reachable — never file-level, never blanket. Removing the trap handler instead would have leaked three temp files per run.

A LOCAL GATE RUN CAN PASS FOR AN ENVIRONMENT REASON AND TELL YOU NOTHING ABOUT CI — measured 2026-08-18, PR #8477.

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker added scripts/check_workflow_job_timeouts.py, wired it into the verify-skill-mcp-drift job, and verified it by running it locally: captured exit 0, self-test exit 0, live run exit 0 over 117 jobs. Every rule about capturing your own exit code was followed correctly. The PR still went red in CI, both steps exiting 3:

    NOT CHECKED: workflow job timeouts. PyYAML is not importable on this
    interpreter, so nothing here examined .github/workflows/. This is NOT a pass.

THE CHECKER WAS RIGHT AND THE VERIFICATION METHOD WAS WRONG. This machine carries PyYAML 6.0.2; the CI job installs no pip packages by deliberate design. So the local green was an artefact of the developer environment, and it was indistinguishable from a real pass by every test the worker applied.

THE GENERAL RULE, which is NOT covered by 'quote the number you captured': that rule protects against a number that is present and wrong, and against one that was never written. THIS is a third case — a number that is present, correct, and ABOUT A DIFFERENT ENVIRONMENT. When a gate's behaviour depends on the interpreter, the installed packages, the OS or the shell, a local run is evidence about YOUR box and not about the runner. Ask explicitly: WHAT DOES THIS CHECK DEPEND ON THAT THE RUNNER MIGHT NOT HAVE? An import, a binary on PATH, a locale, a line ending, a case-insensitive filesystem.

THE CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR: read the JOB the check will run in, not just the check. Does it install anything? Does it check out with fetch-depth 0? The dependency question is answered in the workflow file, and reading it costs one look.

WHAT MADE THIS RECOVERABLE IN ONE RUN rather than several: the checker REFUSED loudly instead of failing open. It could have caught ImportError and skipped, and then it would have vouched for 117 jobs it never opened, forever, on every PR. A checker that cannot do its job must say so and exit non-zero. That is the same principle as 'a search that returns zero is not a check that passed', applied to the tool's own preconditions.

AND THE MAYOR'S HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG, which is worth keeping: I briefed the fix worker that a step-counting meta-gate had probably been armed by the new steps. It had not — every sibling meta-gate was green throughout. I labelled it a hypothesis rather than a finding and told the worker to believe the log over me, and it did. Label speculation as speculation and the cost of being wrong is nearly zero.

"MAIN IS GREEN" IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT A BRANCH CAUSED A FAILURE — the failing job may be SURFACE-GATED AND SKIPPED ON MAIN (2026-08-12, PR #7945).

WHAT I DID. A node-test row reddened on a branch. I checked `gh run list --branch main` for the `tests` workflow, saw `success`, and concluded the branch caused it. I dispatched a fix-worker on that basis and told it so in the brief.

WHY IT WAS WRONG. `tests` reported success on main, but THE NODE-TEST JOB INSIDE IT WAS SKIPPED — surface-gated on paths the main commit did not touch. Run 31540419223 at the merge-base 5ac9d4aa17 never ran the job that was failing. A green workflow whose relevant JOB never executed is the same fail-open class this repo hunts everywhere else: it verifies the absence of bad news rather than the presence of good news.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT SETTLES THIS CLASS IN ONE STEP, from the worker:
  gh run list --workflow tests --limit 40 --json databaseId,headBranch,conclusion
then diff the FAIL line across branches. If an UNRELATED branch fails the identical assertion, the defect is pre-existing and no fix-worker should be pointed at the branch. Here a DOCS-ONLY branch (worker/cbident-hic029, two markdown files) had failed the same row four hours earlier with `actual: (not (= 4 1))`.

THREE MORE OF MY PREMISES FAILED IN THE SAME CALL, all from reading the rollup rather than the runs:
  - "Two CI failures" was ONE RUN, TWO ATTEMPTS. `gh pr checks` cannot show that; `gh run view` can.
  - "Identical numbers, so not a flake" holds PER RUNNER only. The same assertion gave 4→2 on one runner and 4→1 on another. FAILURE COUNTS WERE A STEP FUNCTION OF RUNNER SPEED, which is the signature of a wall-clock race, not of determinism.
  - So "deterministic numbers ⇒ not a flake" is a bad rule. The right question is whether the numbers are stable ACROSS RUNNERS.

THE ACTUAL MECHANISM, for the record: `arm-entry-reaper!` armed `setTimeout(…, 4)` at each entry's own minting inside `render-body`, while `lane/settle!` is `setTimeout(…, 0)` armed after ALL renders. Node drains one duration's timer list per pass, so the row turned on `settle-armed − first-mint < 3 ms` — and the harvest itself takes 1.2-2.0 ms. The test's own setup wall-clock was being charged against React's commit margin. Pre-existing on main; it only stops hitting other PRs once the fix merges.

THE RULE: before dispatching a fix-worker for a red on a branch, establish that the failing JOB actually RAN and PASSED somewhere the branch is not. A workflow-level "success" is not that. And sweep other branches for the same FAIL line first — it costs one command and it is the difference between fixing a defect and sending a worker to hunt one that is not there.

MY MATRIX COLUMN IS A PROXY FOR CLAUSE 5, AND IT OVER-BLOCKS (2026-08-11, PR #7835).

WHAT I COMPUTE: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <latest .github/workflows commit> <pr base>` — "does this PR's base contain the newest workflow commit?" When it says NO I have been treating clause 5 as failed.

WHAT CLAUSE 5 ACTUALLY SAYS: when a merge CHANGES THE WORKFLOW MATRIX — a new required job, a changed classifier, a re-scoped path filter — the PRs behind it WHOSE SURFACE THAT CHANGE COVERS do not inherit its verdict. The trigger is a changed MATRIX, not a moved FILE.

THE CASE: #7835 showed matrix=NO because two workflow commits landed after its base — a comment reword in lint.yml (rf2-93u6) and the GATE_PREFIXES widening plus prose corrections (rf2-rbdc). NEITHER ADDS, REMOVES OR RE-SCOPES A JOB. I measured it instead of assuming: diffing the check-name sets between #7835 and the last PR that reached 91/91 showed exactly ONE difference — "All required checks passed", the AGGREGATOR, which attaches only once the jobs it waits on finish. The job set is otherwise identical, so the matrix is unchanged and clause 5 is satisfied.

THE 90-vs-91 BAND DIFFERENCE WAS ALSO THE AGGREGATOR, not a missing job. Reading a short total as "a job never ran" is the same over-blocking error one field over.

THE REFINEMENT: when matrix=NO, do not stop — DIFF THE CHECK-NAME SETS against a recently-merged PR. If they match (modulo the pending aggregator), the matrix did not change and the PR is not stale in the sense clause 5 means. If they differ, name the job that appeared or vanished and THEN require the update-branch.

WHY THIS MATTERS BOTH WAYS: the method already warns that this guard fails in both directions — keyed too loosely it lets a PR through against a superseded matrix; keyed too tightly it blocks forever on a base that is merely older. A guard that blocks forever is not safe, it is differently wrong. My proxy is the second failure, and update-branching on it costs a full CI cycle and can introduce a conflict for nothing.

SISTER LESSON: my-sweep-conflates-failure-and-cancelled. Same root — a cheap summary reused as if it were the criterion.

MAYOR CI-merge gotcha: gh's statusCheckRollup includes STALE entries from superseded commits — when a worker force-pushes a fix, the prior commit's in-progress checks become conclusion=CANCELLED and its aggregates (e.g. 'Lint required','All required checks passed') linger as FAILURE in the rollup. A naive 'any conclusion!=SUCCESS' filter reads these as failures. For the merge decision use the DEDUPED latest-per-check view: 'gh pr checks <PR>' (pass/pending/fail/skipping per check). Merge only on 0 fail AND 0 pending there. Confirm ambiguity by checking a specific check has both a CANCELLED and a SUCCESS entry (latest wins).

A HARD SERIALISATION RULE DELEGATED TO A WORKER AS A CONDITIONAL CHECK BECOMES A SOFT ONE (2026-08-18).

WHAT I DID. The command file says "never dispatch two bench-class workers concurrently EVEN WITH NO WINDOW IN FLIGHT ... it is contention for the MACHINE". I dispatched an adapter-build worker that needed a shadow-cljs release build to measure a bundle delta, while a bench-class worker was live, and wrote into its brief: "if you need a release build, check first whether a bench window is live and say what you found". I turned a prohibition into an instruction to look.

WHY THAT FAILS, and it is not about the worker being careless. A WORKER CANNOT EVALUATE THAT CONDITION. It sees its own worktree and whatever it can derive from open PRs and branches; it cannot see what I am about to dispatch in the next minute, and it has no way to know that a peer whose branch looks idle is thirty seconds from starting a heavyweight run. The fleet-wide view is the mayor s and only the mayor s. Handing the worker the decision hands it to the party with the least information.

IT ALSO FAILS SILENTLY IN THE WORST WAY. Two heavyweight runs WEDGE rather than fail — no progress, no exit file, no error, several gigabytes each. So a worker that checks, sees nothing, and proceeds does not get a clean error; it gets a hang that looks like its own change misbehaving, and it will spend its context debugging the wrong thing.

THE RULE: WHERE A CONSTRAINT IS ABOUT A SHARED RESOURCE, THE MAYOR HOLDS IT ABSOLUTELY AND STATES IT AS A PROHIBITION. Never "check whether X is live", always "do not run X". If the work genuinely needs the resource, either sequence it behind the current holder or dispatch it as its own bead once the resource is free — and say in the brief that reporting the measurement as NOT TAKEN is a correct deliverable, so the worker does not substitute an estimate to fill the hole.

THE TELL that I am about to make this mistake: I find myself writing a conditional into a brief about something outside that worker s worktree. Anything outside its worktree is mine to decide.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT CATCH IT. The method already says "grep for the alleged broken symbol before DISPATCHING" and "an audit finding is a CLAIM, not automatically work". Both are aimed at the dispatch decision. Neither fires at the FILING decision, and filing is where the claim becomes durable: a bead description outlives the worker, the chat and the mayor, and the next reader has no way to tell a verified premise from a relayed one. A false premise in a bead is worse than a false premise in a message, because it looks like a finding.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS CHEAP TO FIX. Verifying costs one grep or one file read at filing time. Not verifying costs a worker's whole investigation — and it is a worker who is under a fence, on someone else's evidence, spending its context proving the mayor wrong before it can start.

THE PRACTICE:
- Before filing a bead from someone else's report, open the file at the named path and line. If the claim is about absence ("X does not exist", "nothing records Y"), run the search yourself — absence claims are the ones that fail, because the reporter searched for what they expected rather than what is there.
- If you cannot verify it in the moment, FILE IT AS A CLAIM IN THOSE WORDS: "reported by <worker>, NOT verified at source — verify before acting". That is honest and costs nothing.
- The two claim shapes that failed here are both worth naming in any brief you build on them: a FREEZE or manifest constraint (read the manifest; they shrink as things retire), and a NEVER-RECORDED / UNCITED claim (search the docs tree, not just the code).
- Tell the receiving worker explicitly that the bead text is yours and may be wrong. The line "my bead text is a claim, not a fact — verify every path, line number and structural claim before acting on it, and report anything that did not hold" turned both of these into corrections instead of wasted work.

THE SYSTEM WORKED, WHICH IS THE POINT. Both workers read the source, contradicted the bead, recorded the correction, and reached a better disposition than the one I framed. That is the bead-governs-over-brief rule running in the direction nobody designs for: protecting the worker from the mayor.

COROLLARY worth remembering: a rollup can show ONE check while four workflows sit queued on the same sha, because a queued run's checks are not yet attached to the commit. total==1 with 'no live runs' is therefore not 'this PR has one check' — it is 'look again, properly'.

But that checkout DISCARDS the bd auto-export of any close a worker performed since the last commit — and a later 'bd import' of the reverted file resurrects the bead as open/in_progress. Observed: rf2-kqxe6.17 and rf2-b617w both closed by their worker on PR #6895, both back to in_progress after the post-merge checkout; misdiagnosable as a reviewer reopen. MITIGATION: after every merge+pull, re-verify the merged PR's beads with 'bd show' and re-close any that reverted, citing the merge commit. Better: commit the .beads export BEFORE merging rather than checking it out — commit-before-pull, never checkout-before-pull, when a worker has just closed something. DISTINGUISH FROM A REAL REVIEWER REOPEN: a genuine reopen carries a MERGED-PR AUDIT / AUDIT-REOPEN note naming an unmet defect at a code site; a checkout-race revert has NO such note and the bead simply reads in_progress with its pre-close state.

MERGE-LOOP: NEVER "git checkout HEAD -- .beads" — IT HAS NOW DESTROYED NINE BEAD CLOSES (2026-07-25). The mayor merge routine says: after each merge, "git checkout HEAD -- .beads" then "git pull --ff-only". That checkout DISCARDS the bd auto-export of every close performed since the last commit, and bd tracked post-checkout/post-merge hooks then RE-IMPORT the stale file into the Dolt DB, so the close is undone in the database itself, not merely in the working file. CONFIRMED VICTIMS this session: rf2-a32r7 (three times), rf2-kqxe6.17, rf2-drpa3.178, rf2-8ewl1, rf2-zt65l, rf2-vxgfnd.99.4, rf2-qwsmv. Each showed ZERO AUDIT-REOPEN notes, which is the discriminator: a genuine reviewer reopen always carries a MERGED-PR AUDIT / AUDIT-REOPEN note naming an unmet defect at a code site. CORRECT MERGE SEQUENCE — export, commit, THEN pull; never checkout: (1) bd export --all -o .beads/issues.jsonl  (2) guard wc -l >= 2000  (3) git add + git commit  (4) git pull --ff-only (or rebase)  (5) merge the next PR. The reason the checkout was in the routine at all is that an UNCOMMITTED issues.jsonl aborts a pull — committing it first solves that without destroying anything. WHY THIS KEPT RECURRING: I fixed the CHECKPOINT flow early and left the MERGE flow alone, because the loop prompt literally instructs the checkout. Deviating from that literal instruction is correct — it demonstrably destroys tracker state — and the deviation must be applied in the merge path too, not only at checkpoint time. AFTER EVERY MERGE, re-verify the merged PR beads with bd show and re-close any that reverted, citing the merge commit.

MERGE-ORDER BEATS --admin ON THE BAKED LANE: when two PRs both rebuild docs/cljs/playground-rf2.js, a PUSH by one cannot invalidate the other — only a MERGE can. So the escape from the rebase-deadlock is to control MERGE ORDER (let A finish CI and merge, then merge B, which rebases once onto A), NOT to --admin past pending checks. I merged rf2-qg98y (#6302) past 4 pending checks on 2026-07-18 to break a 5-cycle deadlock; it worked and main stayed green, but sequencing would have achieved the same without the risk. Rule going forward: on the baked lane, hold every candidate, merge strictly one at a time on GENUINE green, and tell the next worker it is sole occupant so it rebases exactly once. Root fix is rf2-tzy13 (stop committing the bundle, build in CI).

MERGE-TIME RULE (post #6677 contamination): before merging ANY worker PR, eyeball its file list for .beads/ — a worker-worktree commit of .beads/issues.jsonl is a stale full-DB snapshot that time-travels the tracker (reopens closed beads, deletes new ones, replaces memories). Reject/strip it; never --theirs/--ours on .beads — resolve-then-regenerate. Standing until rf2-ia8o7's guards land.

Merged-PR audit posture and presentation:
- Pre-alpha: pursue elegance, power, and a masterpiece-quality SPA library.
- Trust the programmer; optimize for their and their AI's productivity through a minimal ergonomic API, excellent tools, and low friction.
- Audit material completeness, correctness, and implementation quality without over-engineering, gold-plating, litigating every fine detail, or drowning in minutiae.
- Keep concise, useful commentary visible.
- Minimize transcript noise: aggressively batch tool operations, cap/suppress routine outputs, avoid redundant inspection calls, and surface only evidence or exceptions that materially affect the audit. Tool rendering is client-controlled, so target the fewest practical calls per cycle.

MERGED PR AUDIT POLL TIMEZONE LAW (2026-08-02): In PowerShell, do not compare GitHub mergedAt values produced by ConvertFrom-Json with `[datetime]'...Z'`. The cursor becomes Local while mergedAt remains Utc and tick comparison can hide merges inside the local UTC offset; this hid PR #7382 from the gh fallback. Compare both as DateTimeOffset (for example `[datetimeoffset]$_.mergedAt.ToString('o') -gt [datetimeoffset]$cursor`) or compare an equivalent UTC epoch.

MERGING ON GREEN CAN LAND A BRANCH STATE OLDER THAN ITS TIP (2026-07-25). Twice today a PR merged while its worker was still pushing, so the merge captured an EARLIER commit than the branch's tip: #6975 landed one commit short (the worker opened #6982 to carry the remainder), and #6973 landed the v/html code half while its worker was still writing the acceptance suites (which then landed as #6980).

MECHANISM: the merge sweep reads 'fail=0 pend=0' and merges. Between that read and the merge, a live worker can push. GitHub merges the ref as it stood, so the delta silently becomes a follow-up PR — or worse, is briefly absent from main while the bead reads closed.

NEITHER CASE LOST WORK, and the reason is worth keeping: both workers were pushing as they went and both noticed, so each opened a follow-up rather than assuming its work had landed. Push-as-you-go plus a worker that verifies its own merge is what made this benign.

WHAT IT IS NOT: a reason to stop merging on green. Waiting for workers to declare done would idle the pipeline, and a green partial genuinely is worth more than a perfect whole later — that policy is correct and stays.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD: (1) when merging a PR whose worker has NOT reported terminal, expect a follow-up PR and do not treat the bead as discharged on that merge alone — read the worker's eventual report; (2) tell workers in the brief that a merge may land a state older than their tip, so if their last push is not in the merge commit they should open a follow-up rather than assume it landed (both workers did this unprompted — make it explicit so it is not luck); (3) when a merged PR's beads stay open or in_progress, that is often this, not a partial delivery — ask before inferring.

RELATED, SAME ROOT: three times today I pruned a worktree from under a live worker because the merge sweep had 'PR merged' in hand while terminality lived in task notifications. The pattern across all four incidents is the same — the merge sweep is where mayor actions and live worker state collide, so every destructive or finalising step inside it needs a liveness signal read rather than inferred.

MERGING ON GREEN LANDED A STALE TIP AGAIN -- THIRD INSTANCE, AND I NOW HAVE A ONE-COMMAND MITIGATION (2026-07-26). PR #7091 merged at c67fe52a91 while the worker branch tip was aa824a27b5. Five of six commits rebase-landed; the sixth (the FH-CTRL-018 browser row) did not, leaving the slice INCOMPLETE ON MAIN while the PR read merged. Prior instances: #6975 landed one commit short, #6973 landed the v/html code half while its acceptance suites were still being written.

WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING: the merge sweep reads fail=0 pend=0 and merges. Between that read and the merge call, a live worker can push. GitHub merges the ref as it stood. The policy of merging on green is CORRECT and stays -- waiting for workers to declare done would idle the pipeline, and a green partial is worth more than a perfect whole later.

THE MITIGATION, cheap enough that there is no excuse: before merging a PR whose worker has NOT sent a terminal report, compare the PR head against the remote branch tip --
  gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid   vs   git ls-remote --heads origin <branch>
If they differ, the PR object is stale: re-read it and merge the current head. This is the same identity-not-name discipline that governs worktree pruning -- read the tip, do not assume the PR object is current.

WHAT MADE ALL THREE BENIGN, and it is the thing to keep briefing: every worker was pushing as it went AND checked whether its own work was in the merge commit. Each opened a follow-up PR rather than assuming it had landed. So the brief line "a merge may land a state older than your tip; if your last push is not in the merge commit, open a follow-up rather than assume it landed" is doing real work -- keep it, and note that all three workers did it UNPROMPTED before it was in the brief.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a merged PR beads stay open or in_progress, suspect THIS before inferring a partial delivery or a worker error. And do not close a bead on a merge whose worker has not reported -- read the file list, not the title.

MIKE'S PHASE ORDER FOR FINISHING HICASSO — stated 2026-08-14, governs all dispatch sequencing from here.

THE SEQUENCE, in his words and in order:
  1. COMPLETE hicasso.
  2. Ensure it is CORRECT.
  3. Ensure it is GOOD QUALITY CODE.
  4. Ensure the DOCS are complete, correct, and quality.
  5. Ensure the associated SKILLS are complete, correct, and quality.
  6. Ensure the XRAY INTEGRATION is complete, correct, and quality.
  7. Ensure the COMMENTS are complete, correct, and quality.

AND THEN, OR IN PARALLEL: remove Freehand and re-frame2.ui.

HOW TO READ IT. Each stage has the SAME THREE TESTS — complete, correct, quality — applied to a different artefact. The stages are ORDERED: do not polish the prose of a feature that does not exist yet, and do not tune code quality before the behaviour is right.

THE RETIREMENT IS NOT THE PRIORITY — IT IS THE PARALLEL TRACK. I drove it hard for a whole session as though it were the main line. Mike's ordering puts it alongside, not ahead. It stays dispatchable because its surfaces are largely disjoint from hicasso's — test tooling, docs trees, tree deletions — so it parallelises without contending. But WHEN A SLOT IS SCARCE, HICASSO WORK TAKES IT.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT DISPATCH. Sort by stage first, priority second. A P3 in stage 1 outranks a P1 in stage 4. Retirement beads fill spare capacity rather than leading.

CONCRETE CONSEQUENCES:
  Docs beads WAIT until the code is complete, correct and clean — otherwise they document a moving target and go stale before they merge.
  Comments come LAST. A comment describing code about to change is worse than no comment.
  Xray integration comes AFTER skills, later than its bead priorities suggest.

WHAT IT DOES NOT CHANGE. A correctness defect found at any stage is stage-2 work and jumps the queue. The order governs PLANNED work, not discovered defects.

AND IT PAIRS WITH THE STANCE RATHER THAN OVERRIDING IT: 'complete' still means complete, not gold-plated. A stage is done when its three tests pass, not when nothing further could conceivably be added.

CORRECTED 2026-08-05: A BARE LOCAL mkdocs build --strict DOES COVER spec/** IN THIS REPO. My earlier claim was wrong and I told several workers to work around a problem that does not exist.

WHAT I HAD RECORDED: that mkdocs reads docs/ and not spec/, that docs.yml's cp -r spec docs/spec is what makes the coverage real, and therefore that a bare local run exits 0 over a tree not containing the edited file.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, verified by the rf2-2rtt6.125 worker and confirmed by reading mkdocs_hooks.py: ON_PRE_BUILD MIRRORS spec/ INTO docs/spec/ ITSELF, idempotently, on every build - it rmtree's and copytree's. So a bare local mkdocs build --strict DOES see a spec edit. docs.yml's cp -r is belt-and-braces, not the mechanism.

WHY I GOT IT WRONG: the rf2-whfte worker reported staging spec/ manually before building and said a bare run "would not have seen my file at all". That was a reasonable inference from the workflow's cp -r line, and I promoted it to a rule without checking the hook. It then went into four briefs.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE AND IS THE PART THAT MATTERS: mkdocs build --strict does NOT cover docs/design/hicasso/** - exclude_docs keeps that tree out of the site, so it exits 0 having verified nothing there. That exclusion is real and still worth stating in every brief touching the design records or the draft guide.

THE GENERAL FORM, which is the actual lesson: a gate is a claim about WHAT IT READS, and the way to establish that is to read the gate's own configuration - not to infer it from a workflow step that happens to sit near it. I inferred, and the inference survived four briefs because nobody had reason to check it.

MKDOCS GATE STALL HAZARD (Windows): 'mkdocs build --strict' can HANG/loop a worker because the system Python (3.14 observed 2026-07) has no Pillow wheel. csbbwu worked around it with an isolated Python 3.12 venv; lh9ioj's first worker got STUCK looping on it (had to be killed — its last action was retrying 'python -m mkdocs'). RULE for dispatch briefs touching docs/spec: tell the worker to try mkdocs ONCE (or once more via venv), and if it fails on a Python/Pillow ENV error (not a real anchor/link error), SKIP-with-note in PR '## Quality gates' ('mkdocs skipped — local Python lacks Pillow wheel; relying on CI') rather than loop. A skipped gate with a one-line reason is fine per the method. Do NOT let a worker burn cycles fighting the mkdocs environment — the real gate for most spec edits is the conformance/test suite, and CI runs mkdocs anyway.

mkdocs IS available in this environment. A bare "mkdocs build --strict" returns exit 127 (command not found), which is NO VERDICT -- not a pass, and NOT evidence the tool is absent. Invoke it as "python -m mkdocs build --strict", which works: measured exit 0 in ~34s on 2026-09-01. Several briefs and worker reports this session asserted "mkdocs is not installed here" purely on the bare-command 127; that inference was wrong and should stop being repeated. TWO CAUTIONS. (1) It is still NOT the anchor gate: MkDocs grades a missing heading anchor at INFO, and --strict promotes WARNING but not INFO, so scripts/check_doc_slugs.py remains the only anchor gate for pages under docs/. (2) It WRITES INTO THE CHECKOUT -- it creates site/ and stages copies at docs/spec/ and docs/migration/. All three are gitignored so git status stays clean, which means the mess is invisible; remove them afterwards. Do not run it in the mayor checkout casually.

MEASURED 2026-08-21 by worker/methodcarve-butkd on this Windows host: the bare command `mkdocs` is NOT on PATH in the Bash tool and returns EXIT 127, which is 'command not found' rather than a gate verdict. `python -m mkdocs build --strict` works and exited 0.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE: 127 is a NUMBER, and a worker following the capture-your-own-exit-code rule will faithfully quote it. A non-zero exit reads as a RED. So a brief nominating the bare name produces one of two wrong outcomes - a worker reporting the docs build as failing when it never ran, or a worker concluding the gate is unavailable and reporting no coverage where full coverage exists. Both are misreports, and the second is the understating direction rf2-butkd's carve-out sentence is about.

SO: nominate `python -m mkdocs build --strict` in every brief, never the bare `mkdocs`.

AND THE POSITIVE CONTROL THAT SETTLES A DOCS-BUILD COVERAGE CLAIM: do not infer coverage from a path's ABSENCE from mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs. Read the BUILD LOG and confirm it lists your file among the pages it processed. That worker did exactly this for docs/the-mayor-method/ - positive evidence rather than an inference from absence.

MEASURED by worker/docsguide-hic068 (rf2-hic-068, PR #8284): it REMOVED its new Troubleshooting page's nav entry and ran the gate. EXIT 0. WHAT I HAD BEEN TELLING WORKERS, wrongly, in more than one brief: 'mkdocs build --strict will FAIL on a page that is not in the nav, so your new pages need mkdocs.yml entries.' The CONCLUSION is right — new pages should be in the nav — but the REASON is false, and the reason is what a worker acts on. A worker trusting it would treat a green mkdocs run as proof its nav entries were correct. They are unrelated.

WHY --strict does not catch it: strict promotes WARNING to error. 'not included in the nav' is emitted at INFO. Verify the level rather than assuming the category.

WHAT ACTUALLY FORCES NAV CORRECTNESS: nothing automated that has been identified. So nav entries are a HAND CHECK, and a brief should say so plainly instead of naming a gate that will pass regardless.

The obvious incantation, `cmd /c mklink /J <link> <target>`, is SILENTLY MANGLED by MSYS path conversion under the Bash tool: it opens a cmd banner and RETURNS 0 WITHOUT CREATING THE LINK. Exit 0, no link, no error.

WHAT WORKS: PowerShell `New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path <link> -Target <target>`.

REMOVAL, safely: assert `(Get-Item <link>).LinkType -eq 'Junction'` first, then `[IO.Directory]::Delete(<link>, $false)` - non-recursive, so it unlinks rather than following into the mayor's real tree. Then re-count the mayor's `implementation/node_modules` (103 entries, `runner.js` present) to prove nothing was followed.

THE DOWNSTREAM SYMPTOM, which is what workers actually see: the fast-PR spine fails at the `test:cljs` tier with `Cannot find module 'shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'`. That reads like a broken diff and is really a missing junction. Two workers have now hit some form of this.

AND IT CO-OCCURRED WITH THE EXIT-CODE TRAP: the same worker's spine run exited 1 while its BACKGROUND WRAPPER exited 0. Only reading the `.exit` FILE caught it - exactly why every brief says to capture `$?` on the same command line and read the file rather than trusting the harness's reported code.

Move-aside does not simulate deletion for git-reading gates. Probing 'what breaks when we delete X' by moving X aside only tests gates that stat the filesystem. Anything reading git ls-files sees the INDEX, so it stays green through the whole move: scripts/check_donor_inventory.py held rc=0 with the entire implementation/ui tree moved out of the worktree, and only reported its 73 stale rows once the deletion was staged (git rm -r --cached, reverted with git reset -- <path>). Run BOTH halves of the probe, and restore by move-back plus 'git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no' == empty, never by git checkout.

MOVING A TREE ASIDE WITHIN THE SEARCH SPACE DOES NOT REMOVE IT — a second probe-method defect, caught by the worker before its verdict was trusted (2026-07-26).

The silent-gates worker parked a "deleted" scaffold at examples/ui/_probe-aside-... — STILL INSIDE examples/, AND STILL CARRYING shadow-cljs.edn. The gate discovers projects BY MARKER, so the supposedly-deleted project WAS STILL DISCOVERABLE and THE PROBE FALSE-GREENED. It caught this before reading the verdict.

THIS IS THE SECOND PROBE DEFECT OF THE SAME FAMILY IN ONE DAY, and the first was mine: I told a worker to simulate a deletion by moving implementation/ui/ aside, and check_donor_inventory.py held rc=0 throughout because IT READS GIT, NOT THE FILESYSTEM — the 73 stale rows only appeared once the deletion was STAGED IN THE INDEX.

SO THE RULE HAS TWO HALVES, AND BOTH ARE ABOUT MATCHING THE PROBE TO THE SEARCH:
  1. MATCH THE MEDIUM. Filesystem gate -> move the files. Git-reading gate -> stage the deletion. Marker-discovering gate -> the marker must leave the search space.
  2. MOVE IT OUT, NOT SIDEWAYS. A destination inside the tree the gate scans is not a deletion. Park probes OUTSIDE the repo, or strip the discovery marker, and VERIFY THE GATE CAN NO LONGER SEE IT before trusting any verdict.

THE SAME WORKER CAUGHT A SECOND PROBE DEFECT TOO: an rc=1 that was MODULE_NOT_FOUND from a relative path resolved against THE CHILD PROCESS cwd, not its own. MTIME ON THE WORKTREE IS NOT A QUIESCENCE SIGNAL — MY FOURTH WORKTREE-REMOVED-MID-GATE, WITH THE FIX ALREADY IN PLACE (2026-08-04).

WHAT I HAD ALREADY DONE. After three instances of reaping a worktree while its worker was still gating, I replaced "reap when the PR is MERGED" with "reap when the PR is MERGED **and** the tree has been idle >= 10 minutes", idleness read from the mtime of the worktree's implementation/ directory.

WHY IT STILL FAILED. The rf2-2rtt6.99 worker was running its SECOND fast-PR spine when I reaped. The mtime check said 34 minutes idle. It was wrong: a running spine does not necessarily touch the directory I stat. Its work goes to out/, .shadow-cljs/, a temp dir, or a detached child process, and none of that has to bump implementation/ itself. The worker's run died with "bash: ./.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh: No such file or directory" for a script that plainly exists -- the fourth false red of this exact class today, and the second whose symptom names a real file.

NOTE THE SCRIPT PARTIALLY SUCCEEDED, WHICH IS ITS OWN HAZARD. remove-worker-worktree.sh disarmed the node_modules link and DEREGISTERED the worktree, then failed to delete the directory on a Windows file lock and reported REMOVE_FAILED honestly. So the tree was already gutted -- node_modules emptied, git worktree list no longer listing it -- before the failure. A partial reap is as fatal to a running gate as a complete one.

THE RULE, and I have now been wrong three ways about it: PR STATE is not worker state; ELAPSED TIME is not worker state; DIRECTORY MTIME is not worker state. The only reliable signals are (a) the agent that owns the bead has reported completion, or (b) no process has a working directory inside that tree. Everything else is a proxy that has failed in practice.

WHAT I SHOULD DO INSTEAD: do not reap on the same tick a PR merges, and do not reap any worktree whose owning agent has not yet delivered its completion report. Those reports arrive as task notifications; until one lands for that bead, the worker may be mid-gate no matter how quiet the tree looks. Cost of waiting: a stale directory. Cost of not waiting: a red that names real files as missing, four times today, twice mistakable for a genuine regression.

WHAT THE AFFECTED WORKERS DID RIGHT, every time: discarded the exit code under the killed-gate rule rather than reporting it, said plainly which coverage was therefore unmeasured, and named the cheap substitute check.
