A FOURTH POST-MERGE PULL ABORT SHAPE, CAUSED BY CONCURRENT WORKERS SHARING FETCH_HEAD (2026-08-13).

MESSAGE: 'fatal: Cannot fast-forward to multiple branches.' Exit 128, HEAD unmoved.

This is NOT any of the three shapes mayor-merge.md documents. It is not 'local changes would be overwritten' (uncommitted tracker state) and it is not 'Not possible to fast-forward' (genuine divergence), and BOTH of those remedies are inert against it. Clearing .beads does nothing - the tree was clean. Rebasing does nothing - there was nothing to rebase.

CAUSE: linked worktrees SHARE the primary checkout's .git, and therefore share ONE FETCH_HEAD file. Three background workers had just been dispatched and each ran git fetch in its own worktree. Their multi-ref FETCH_HEAD was what the mayor's 'git pull --ff-only origin main' then read, and a FETCH_HEAD naming several branches cannot be fast-forwarded to. The mayor's own command was correct; a peer overwrote the file between its fetch and its merge.

DISCRIMINATOR: git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...origin/main. It read '0 2' - zero ahead, two behind - which is a clean fast-forward, i.e. proof this is a race and not a divergence. The two documented aborts both show a non-zero LEFT number or a dirty tree.

REMEDY: bypass FETCH_HEAD entirely by merging the remote-tracking ref, which no peer can clobber:
  git fetch origin main
  git merge --ff-only origin/main
Then verify HEAD == origin/main and the divergence count reads 0 0.

EXPECT THIS TO GET MORE COMMON, NOT LESS: it scales with fleet size, and the merge loop's own advice to dispatch immediately after merging is what puts the fetches and the pull in the same seconds.

A post-merge pull that aborts is NOT always the uncommitted .beads/issues.jsonl — that diagnosis was wrong twice in one session (2026-08-07), and the documented remedy would have found nothing both times.

THE LOOP DOCS STATE IT AS THE CAUSE: bootstrap.md and mayor-merge both say 'If the pull aborts, an uncommitted .beads/issues.jsonl is the cause: run beads-checkpoint.sh, THEN git checkout HEAD -- .beads, THEN pull.' Treat that as ONE cause of three, not the cause.

FAILURE 1 — GENUINE DIVERGENCE, NOT THE TRACKER. 'git pull --ff-only' aborted with 'Not possible to fast-forward' on a CLEAN working tree. git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD showed 2/1: the repo's post-merge hook had committed 'chore(beads): audit merged PR NNNN' locally while the rebase-merge rewrote main remotely. The remedy is 'git pull --rebase' (or fetch + rebase origin/main). Running the checkpoint dance here finds nothing to fix and leaves the pull still aborting.

FAILURE 2 — STAGED, NOT MERELY UNCOMMITTED, AND THE DOCUMENTED CHECKOUT DOES NOT CLEAR IT. A later pull failed with 'cannot pull with rebase: Your index contains uncommitted changes'. .beads/issues.jsonl was STAGED with 3 insertions/2 deletions: bd auto-stages, and it had re-staged the file BETWEEN my 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' and the pull. 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' does not reliably leave the index clean when bd is re-staging behind you.

THE SEQUENCE THAT ACTUALLY WORKS, and it must stay in this order (checkpoint FIRST so the Dolt re-export is committed before anything reverts the working file):
  sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh
  git reset -q HEAD -- .beads
  git checkout -- .beads
  git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main

DIAGNOSE BEFORE APPLYING ANY OF IT: 'git status --short' plus 'git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD' distinguishes all three cases in one look — clean tree + divergence means rebase; staged .beads means reset-then-checkout; unstaged .beads means the documented remedy. NEVER git stash in any of them: stashes are repo-global and contaminate every worktree in flight.

A PYTHON SELF-TEST BUILT ON assert PROVES NOTHING UNDER -O, AND STILL PRINTS ITS SUCCESS LINE (2026-08-13, found by worker/fencecheck-t9kd).

`python -O` strips every `assert` statement. A self-test written as a run of asserts therefore executes zero checks under -O, falls through, and prints `self-test OK`. Exit 0. Nothing warns you.

WHERE IT WAS FOUND, WHICH IS THE POINT. The worker was dispatched to fix a fence checker that counted inert macro forms as live claims — a control that could not catch its own case. It then asked the generalising question of the file it was fixing and found the SAME defect class sitting in `--self-test`, i.e. in the control that was supposed to prove the fix. The instrument and the bug were the same shape.

It is family-wide here: all five hicasso sibling scripts exit 0 under -O. Filed as rf2-uyhh (P3, and the bead explicitly licenses a refusal — copying five lines into ~40 scripts may not be worth it) and rf2-df9b (P2, a related false-green in check_optional_module_reachability where `ns_of` takes the FIRST `(ns …)`, so a discarded `#_(ns …)` above the real form makes the scanner exempt the file).

THE FIX IS FIVE LINES: have `--self-test` REFUSE when assertions are disabled. Detect with `if not __debug__:` — it is False exactly when -O is in effect — and exit non-zero naming the cause. Do not try to re-enable assertions.

THE TRANSFERABLE RULE: ask of every control whether it is constructed so that it avoids the case it exists to catch. And when you fix one control, ask that question of its NEIGHBOURS in the same file before you leave — this worker found three live instances that way, and the sharpest one was in the file it had already opened.

Related: the hollow-gate test (delete the signal, keep the fault — if it stays green it was proving nothing). This is that test applied to the test harness itself.

MY PROVENANCE FIX WAS UNSOUND: RE-PINNING RESTORES THE PATCH, NOT THE TREE (2026-08-06, rf2-owq6p, PR #7616).

WHAT I RULED, one pass earlier: "pin to a commit already on main — the measurement happened upstream of the documenting edit, so no merge can move it." I recorded it as a memory and put it in a brief.

WHY IT IS WRONG AS A GENERAL RULE: it holds for the SSR spike, where the run was taken on an UNMODIFIED MAIN TREE. But MOST of this evidence corpus measures the workers OWN INSTRUMENT CHANGES — so the measured tree was never on main, and NO COMMIT CARRIES IT. The landed commit sits on a LATER BASE. Re-pinning therefore restores the PATCH, not the TREE that was measured.

THE FAILURE IT CAUSES IS WORSE THAN THE DEFECT: an unresolvable pin is VISIBLY broken. A re-pinned wrong one is RESOLVABLE AND WRONG — it fails silently, which is precisely what the bead exists to prevent. Measured: for 9 of 11 pins the rebase preserved every contributed blob and re-pinning was safe; for TWO it did not (one rebase resolved conflicts in three files on the measured path, another moved the file its decomposition turns on) and those were ANNOTATED rather than re-pinned.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, which belongs in the convention rather than in judgement: RE-PIN ONLY WHERE THE REBASE PRESERVED EVERY BLOB THE COMMIT CONTRIBUTED. Otherwise the page says so.

AND THE ENFORCEABLE RULE IS NOT MINE EITHER: not "no authored heads" and not "every SHA must be on main", because several pages deliberately RETAIN the authored head alongside a blob-table fallback and a must-be-on-main gate would red them for being careful. It is "EVERY CITED AUTHORED HEAD MUST BE ACCOMPANIED BY A RESOLVABLE LANDED SHA".

SCALE, so the shape is not mistaken for an edge case: 319 unique hex tokens under docs/design/hicasso/**, of which only 77 are commits — 188 are content digests and FNV hashes that must not be treated as pins at all. 44 stranded, 79 occurrences, 24 pages, ALL reachable from no remote ref.

TWO METHOD NOTES WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX. (1) The recovery was VALIDATED BEFORE BEING TRUSTED, against three pages that already document authored->landed mappings as ground truth: stable patch-id is invariant across this repos rebase-merge, and 43/44 mapped exactly. (2) The worker caught its OWN first blob check comparing WHOLE TREES — which differ for every rebased pair, so it would have condemned everything; the correct check is the commits OWN CONTRIBUTED BLOBS.

THE PATTERN IN MY OWN ERROR, for the seventh time today: I generalised a cure that was correct for ONE case into a rule for a corpus I had not measured. Same shape as generalising the CRLF override from one file to a tree, and the git-grep hazard from one ref to all refs. A CURE THAT WORKED ONCE IS A DATA POINT, NOT A CONVENTION.

REACT CAN SWALLOW A DOM EXCEPTION SO THAT NOTHING REACHES THE CALLER — a refusal is not optional there, it is the only signal (2026-08-14, rf2-h6qm7 worker).

WHAT WAS MEASURED. A :value on a file input throws InvalidStateError inside React's setInitialProperties during commit. The obvious assumption is that the author can catch it. THEY CANNOT: React caught it inside its own commit and re-reported it via reportError, so a thrown-by probe around the flushSync returned NIL — the probe printed four nils. The author had neither an error id nor an exception to catch, only a console entry naming React internals.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE BUG. When judging whether a source-located refusal is worth minting, the usual test is "does the platform already tell the author?" Here the platform DOES throw and the author still learns nothing, because the framework intercepts it. So "React throws" is not evidence that attribution exists. CHECK WHETHER THE THROW REACHES THE CALLER, not merely whether something throws.

THE PROBE THAT SETTLES IT: wrap the mount in flushSync and assert on what thrown-by returns. Nil means the exception was intercepted and the author is blind.

AND THE SAME PASS PROVED A NEGATIVE PROPERLY, which is the reusable technique. I asserted that a sibling code path shared the defect. The worker showed it did not — by MOUNTING A REAL INPUT with setAttribute type FILE and measuring the asymmetry: attribute FILE, IDL property file, .files present, refusal fires. That row passed in BOTH the red and green states, which is what makes it evidence rather than assertion. A test that passes only after the fix cannot prove a path was already immune.

A THROW INSIDE A REACT EVENT HANDLER DOES NOT FAIL cljs.test — THE ROW READS GREEN OVER A LIVE EXCEPTION (2026-08-03, rf2-fki5d).

React does not let an exception escape dispatchEvent; it routes it to reportError. So a cljs.test deftest that dispatches a real DOM event and asserts 'nothing threw' sees 0 failures / 0 errors EVEN WHEN THE HANDLER THREW. The rf2-fki5d worker wrote exactly such a row first, and it passed while the code under test was raising InvalidStateError on every run.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: the runner's separate uncaught-pageerror gate (rf2-mwx08) failed the build FROM OUTSIDE the test. So the signal existed, but it was not attached to the assertion that claimed to cover the behaviour — the row itself was fail-open.

THE FIX, and it generalises: any row asserting 'this did not throw' inside a React event must install a window 'error' listener (and assert on it) so the row REDS BY NAME. Otherwise the only coverage of that case is a build-level gate that names no test.

DISPATCH RULE: when briefing browser/DOM work whose claim is 'no exception', require the listener explicitly and require a MUTATION PROOF — delete the fix, confirm the suite exits 1 with exactly one named failure. rf2-fki5d did this and it is what makes the row trustworthy.

RELATED CLASS (same shape, different mask): piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's exit status, not the runner's. Both are fail-open instruments that report success while the thing under test is broken. Distrust any green whose failure path you have not personally mutated.

READ A STATUS FROM THE STATUS FIELD, NEVER BY PATTERN-MATCHING A RENDERED HEADER — and
establish a history's ORDERING before walking it. Two instrument failures, measured together
2026-09-02, where the second appeared to CONFIRM the first.

WHAT HAPPENED. A closure sweep over twenty beads used
`bd show <id> | head -1 | grep -oE 'OPEN|CLOSED' | head -1`. It reported rf2-9stk0 as OPEN. It
was not: status field 'closed', closed_at set, absent from `bd list --status open` throughout.
THE BEAD'S OWN TITLE CONTAINS THE WORD — "...the inverse ... fails OPEN" — and the title
precedes the status field on that line, so the probe returned the title's word. Of the twenty
swept, it was the ONLY one whose title could poison its own status read, and it was the one
that flagged.

THE CORROBORATION FAILED TOO, WHICH IS WHAT MADE IT CONVINCING. The confirming check was a
status-transition walk over `bd history --json`, which reported "closed -> open" at the newest
index. The history is NEWEST-FIRST, so walking indices upward walks BACKWARDS IN TIME: a pair
reading closed-then-open by index is open-then-closed by TIME. The detector printed every
transition reversed, and would report a reopen on ANY bead that has ever been closed.

COST: a no-op re-close, plus a false "reverted close, third this session" finding written onto
the bead and then corrected there.

THE TWO HABITS.
  - Parse the JSON (`bd show <id> --json` -> `status`, `closed_at`), never grep the rendered
    header. An item's own text can contain the words a status probe looks for, and prose is
    where that collision lives.
  - Before trusting any walk over a history, read the timestamps at both ends and establish
    which is newest. Ordering is a property of the tool, not something to assume, and an
    ordering error inverts every answer while producing perfectly well-formed output.

GENERAL SHAPE, and the reason this is worth remembering rather than just fixing: two
independent-looking instruments can be wrong in ways that agree. loops.md section 4 already
records one instance ("Tip, fetch clock, write clock and a direct message then read as dead
TOGETHER, for one cause, which is why corroborating one with another does not help here") - the
general form is that corroboration only buys you something when the two signals cannot fail for
the same reason. Here they could: both were my own ad-hoc parses of the same tool's output.

REAGENT 2.0.1 SWALLOWS :on-recoverable-error — hydration error-capture harnesses built on reagent.dom.client/hydrate-root are VACUOUS. Found by the rf2-53lsj worker (#6407) on 2026-07-19, in its OWN test harness, before shipping. Reagent destructures :on-recoverable-error and NEVER PASSES IT to React hydrateRoot, so the callback fires for nothing: the harness captured NOTHING on either input and passed identically on broken and fixed HTML. Driving React hydrateRoot DIRECTLY, React 19 correctly reports the mismatch ("Hydration failed... + revenue / - :revenue").
RULE: to assert on hydration mismatches, call React hydrateRoot directly. Do not route through Reagent for error capture. And whatever harness you use, PROVE IT CAPTURES: feed it known-bad input and confirm it reports, before trusting a green on good input.
SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME PR, easy to get backwards: Reagent renders a keyword/symbol child via (name x), which DROPS THE NAMESPACE — :a/b renders as "b", not "a/b". A JVM emitter fix that merely strips the leading colon would emit "a/b" and leave the hosts FURTHER apart while appearing closer. Namespaced symbols diverge identically. Always diff the actual BYTES against the client, never reason about the shape.

Reagent's get-react-key (reagent2.impl.template L407) only reads :key meta from VECTORS. ^{:key k} attached to a function-call list form (e.g. ^{:key g} (group-section g …)) is lost on evaluation — the meta lives on the source list at READ time, not on the returned value. Two fixes: (a) put ^{:key k} on the vector literal returned by the function, or (b) wrap the result in (with-meta result {:key k}). Found in views_view.cljs PR #1471 fixing rf2-gphsi; same anti-pattern exists across several other panels (audit bead rf2-?? filed). Tell future test authors: a test that asserts :key meta on the rendered child reproduces the bug.

WHAT THIS MEMORY USED TO SAY, and it was measured, not guessed: `gh pr merge --rebase --delete-branch` lands the merge but cannot delete a branch that a worktree still holds, and gh abandons the REMOTE deletion along with the local one — so roughly twenty merges in one session each left an orphaned origin branch. Reaping the worktree first made the flag work completely, four for four (#7842, #7843, #7845, #7848), because the worktree pins the branch and nothing else does. The mechanism was real and the measurement stands.

WHY IT IS SUPERSEDED ANYWAY. The ordering only ever worked when the worker had already reported done — the three merges in that same session whose workers had NOT reported were correctly merged without a reap and orphaned their branches 3/3. So reap-first solved the orphan for the easy half of the cases and left the hard half untouched, while placing the reap immediately beside a merge: the exact structural condition of the catalogrows-vkle violation, where I reaped mid-gate holding the worker's own message saying it was not done. An efficiency that re-creates the shape of the worst mistake in the session is not a bargain.

Merge with `gh pr merge --rebase` — NO `--delete-branch`. Zero orphans by construction, for reported and unreported workers alike, with nothing to remember afterwards.

SO THE ORDERING IS MOOT, WHICH IS STRONGER THAN "DISCOURAGED". There is no orphan left to avoid, so reap-before-merge buys nothing and is not a reason to reap, to hurry, or to sequence anything. The never-pair rule in mayor-hygiene.md stands VERBATIM: never pair a merge with a reap, never put the reap in the merge loop. Reaping is a separate deliberate hygiene step.

THE AUTHORISATION IS UNCHANGED AND NON-NEGOTIABLE — only the agent's own report that it has FINISHED authorises a reap. Not merge state, not PR state, not elapsed time, not mtime, not cleanliness. The test is still: can I quote the sentence where this agent says it is done? See reap-requires-a-finished-report-not-just-a-message, which cost a destroyed gate run to learn.

THE ONE REMAINING MANUAL DELETE: `git push origin --delete <branch>` is now ONLY the post-MERGED fallback for a remote ref that survives the merge — head-ref branch protection, or a cross-repo PR whose head lives in a fork the server will not touch. Verify MERGED, delete that ref, and nothing else. A surviving remote ref is never grounds to reap a worktree early.

I REAPED A WORKTREE MID-GATE, AND I HAD THE WORKER'S OWN WORDS SAYING IT WAS NOT DONE (2026-08-11, catalogrows-vkle / PR #7813).

WHAT HAPPENED. The worker sent two interim messages. The second said, verbatim: "Holding for the spine — not done yet, and I won't report a colour I don't have." Minutes later I merged #7813 and reaped its worktree in the same breath. Its spine was in the JVM tier. git worktree list stopped showing the tree, .git went, gate.log was deleted mid-write, and the run died. The worker found gate.exit = 1 afterwards and CORRECTLY REFUSED TO REPORT IT AS A FAILURE — that 1 was written by a script whose own checkout had been deleted underneath it. My cleanup manufactured a red.

WHY I DID IT, because the mechanism matters more than the apology: I batched the reap into the merge pass. The hygiene procedure forbids exactly this — "Never pair a merge with a reap in the same breath, and never put the reap in the merge loop." A merged PR is the moment a tree LOOKS finished, which is precisely why the pull is dangerous. I had also, without noticing, promoted "the agent sent me a message" to "the agent reported done". Those are not the same thing and the difference was written in the message I was reading.

SO THE REAP CONDITION IS NARROWER THAN I HAD IT: not "the agent has spoken", but "the agent has reported that it has FINISHED". An interim status, a progress note, a partial hand-off, a PR-opened announcement — none of these are completion. A BACKGROUND GATE STILL RUNNING IS THE WORKER STILL RUNNING, even though nothing in the branch, the tree or the PR shows it.

WHY IT LOOKED SAFE, and this is the trap for next time: every proxy agreed. PR merged, branch clean, commits pushed, no junction, worker had messaged recently. All six of the forbidden proxies pointed at "done" simultaneously. That is not evidence; that is what a disciplined worker mid-gate looks like BY DESIGN, since commit-and-push-as-you-go is what every brief demands.

WHAT SAVED IT: the work was committed and pushed incrementally, so only the RUN was lost, not the diff. And CI's 90/90 on the merged PR is strictly better evidence than a local spine anyway — which is worth remembering when tempted to wait on a local gate at all.

THE RULE I AM ADDING TO MY OWN LOOP: before any reap, re-read the LAST message from that agent and find the sentence where it says it is finished. If I cannot quote that sentence, the worktree does not get reaped. Cost of waiting: one stale directory.

REBASE conflict resolution: --ours/--theirs INVERT vs merge. In a rebase, --ours = the branch you are replaying ONTO (e.g. origin/main), --theirs = the commit being replayed (the worker's own branch). So to take MAIN's version of a generated file (e.g. docs/cljs/playground-rf2.js) during a rebase, use 'git checkout --ours <file>', NOT --theirs. My earlier dispatch instructions said --theirs for this and were WRONG (caught by the rf2-ywwpx worker on #6284, 2026-07-18, which verified empirically: stage2/--ours == origin/main, stage3/--theirs == its own stale commit). Harmless for a generated file that gets regenerated afterwards, but on a NON-generated conflict the same wording silently takes the wrong side and can revert main's work. ALWAYS instruct workers to verify which stage matches origin/main (git show :2:<file> / :3:<file> and compare digests) rather than trusting the label.

Rebase-merge makes a worker branch look UNMERGED to an ancestry check. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` returns N>0 and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` fails for a branch whose PR was merged with --rebase, because the rebase rewrote the SHAs. Judging 'abandoned, holds unmerged work' from that heuristic mislabelled 7 of 9 branches in one hygiene pass (their PRs #7096-#7107 were all merged). The authoritative test is PATCH-ID containment: `git cherry origin/main origin/<branch>` counting '^+' lines == 0 means fully merged. Confirm with `gh pr view --json state` == MERGED as the second signal.

A MERGE TIMESTAMP EARLIER THAN A RUN'S START DOES NOT MEAN THE RUN'S TREE CONTAINED THAT CHANGE — this repo rebase-merges (found 2026-08-07, rf2-jv36i).

WHAT HAPPENED. A bead assumed 'the codec change is on main by then' because PR #7390 merged at 18:06:11Z and the measurement windows ran 18:14:02Z-18:21:10Z. Eight minutes clear, in wall clock. But the run was taken from a worker branch based at b4144427ec, authored BEFORE the change landed and rebase-merged AFTER. The landed history orders the commits correctly; the measured tree never contained them.

WHY IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. Under rebase-merge the branch tip that produced a measurement is not an ancestor of main at all, and its base can predate several landings that appear, in main's log, to sit before the run. Reading merge times off main and comparing them to a run's clock is exactly the wrong instrument.

HOW TO CHECK PROPERLY — any one of these settles it, and they should agree:
  - BLOB: the evidence page stamps the blob of the file under test; compare it to the change's before/after blobs. This is the strongest check because it names what was actually loaded.
  - ANCESTRY: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor <change-commit> <producing-commit>' — NO means the tree lacked it.
  - BASE: what commit the producing branch was cut from, and what that tree's relevant blob was.

RELATED, same root cause: a stranded authored head's patch-id may differ from its landed counterpart because the rebase resolved conflicts — so 'the patch landed' and 'this tree was measured' are separate questions, and provenance prose must not conflate them.

A PROVENANCE PIN NAMING AN AUTHORED SHA IS STRANDED BY REBASE-MERGE — THE PAGE LOOKS PINNED AND IS NOT (2026-08-06, rf2-zn7pj / PR #7610; scope filed as rf2-owq6p).

THE FINDING: the SSR spike witness pinned its evidence to 952a3f2024. That commit IS NOT AN ANCESTOR OF MAIN, and neither is its sibling 6f40304011. This repo REBASE-MERGES, which rewrites SHAs, so the authored head a page names is stranded the moment its PR merges. Verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` returning non-zero.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE STALE FIGURES IT WAS FILED FOR: stale figures under a RESOLVABLE pin are checkable and wrong, which is a normal defect. Figures under an UNRESOLVABLE pin are NOT CHECKABLE AT ALL — a reader cannot obtain the tree the measurement was taken on. The pages central verifiability claim fails SILENTLY, and it fails while looking rigorous. This is the evidence-corpus form of the fail-open class.

THE FIX THAT DISSOLVES IT: PIN TO A COMMIT ALREADY ON MAIN. The measurement happens upstream of the documenting edit, so no merge of the documenting PR can move it — main advanced eight commits during that pass and the pin never had to change. Do not pin to your own branch head.

AND THE REASONING THAT DECLINED A BLOB TABLE, which is the better half: a blob table pins the INSTRUMENT when the anchor cannot be pinned. Here the anchor CAN be pinned, and a resolvable whole-tree SHA pins strictly more. It would also PIN LESS THAN IT LOOKS — the clock pages magnitudes are a function of three driver files, whereas these figures are a SHA-256 over a whole document plus a boundary census, a function of corpus, entry, substrate, adapter and the pinned react-dom. A short blob table would ADVERTISE A CLOSURE IT DOES NOT HAVE. Ask what the artefact is actually a function of before choosing what to pin.

RELATED, ALREADY KNOWN: `git merge-base --is-ancestor` and `git cherry` disagree for the same reason — rebase-merge rewrites SHAs, so ancestry says "unmerged" for branches that are fully merged. Same mechanism, two different wrong conclusions: there it under-reports merge status, here it strands a citation.

A GATE CONFLATED "THE TEST FAILED" WITH "THE TEST NEVER RAN", AND THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHETHER THE RUNNER PRINTED ITS OWN COUNT (2026-08-06, rf2-v8561, PR #7608).

THE REPORTED DEFECT: three CLJS namespaces failing per-namespace isolation. It did NOT reproduce — clean worktree, fresh npm ci, fresh compile, the beads own repro command twice, exit 0 both times, and all 17 roster namespaces green alone (196 tests / 731 assertions).

THE TELL THAT CRACKED IT, and it is the kind of thing only a fresh reading finds: THE THREE REPORTED NAMESPACES ARE THE LAST THREE ROSTER ENTRIES, CONSECUTIVELY. That is not three independent fixture defects — it is a CONTIGUOUS TAIL, the signature of something collapsing partway through a sweep that spawns one node process per namespace over 276 measured seconds.

THE CAUSE: compile-node-test.cjs UNLINKS out/node-test.js before every compile, deliberately, so a failed compile leaves nothing stale (rf2-6t03c). A compile starting mid-sweep pulls the bundle out from under every run still to come. Injecting exactly that at t=225s of a 276s sweep reds EXACTLY THOSE THREE NAMESPACES, namespace for namespace. Both recorded sightings were worktrees with other builds running.

THE STRUCTURAL DISCRIMINATOR, which is the reusable part: --test=<ns> is a RUNTIME selector over a bundle that links EVERY test namespace, so A MODULE-LOAD CRASH CANNOT SINGLE A NAMESPACE OUT. Therefore: A RED CARRYING "Ran N tests containing M assertions." IS A VERDICT ABOUT THAT NAMESPACE; A RED WITHOUT ONE NEVER WAS. Three causes reach a non-zero standalone exit and the gate was reporting all three as the first — ISOLATION (real leak, fixture remedy), ROSTER (stale curated list; 9dd9633d0b and d3969eb67b are both commits fixing that AFTER the gate blamed fixtures), ENVIRONMENT (bundle vanished; the sweep is INDETERMINATE, exit 2, and ITS GREENS ARE WORTH NO MORE THAN ITS REDS).

TWO RULES TO CARRY:
1. When a gate accuses several namespaces at once, CHECK WHETHER THEY ARE CONTIGUOUS IN ITS ROSTER. Adjacency is evidence of one external event, not of N independent defects. The old gate under an unlink at t=6s accused SIXTEEN namespaces of leaking, every one MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
2. A GREEN MUST ALSO CARRY A NON-ZERO TEST COUNT. This is the same floor as the long-standing "Ran 0 tests reads as green" family, arriving from the opposite direction: there the count was zero because nothing was selected, here because nothing could load.

SIBLING TO CHECK, filed as rf2-1wyyb: check-ui-adapter-isolation.cjs has the same --self-test shape and plausibly the same conflation. Not verified — a shared filename pattern is not evidence of a shared defect.

  (B) NEW-RESIDUAL REOPENS — the close was fully evidenced and ACCEPTED, and the audit found something ELSE by examining the merged code. This is the audit working as designed and is NOT a defect in my closing. Treating it as one would push me toward defensive over-closing, which is worse.

THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is one I keep relearning: a measured finding is usually true of the subset I measured, not of the whole. My first pass looked only at gate beads and generalised. WHEN A GATE FAILED BECAUSE ITS PREDICATE WAS TOO NARROW, WIDENING THE PREDICATE REPEATS THE DEFECT (2026-08-11, rf2-hic-021 repair, PR #7813).

THE SETUP. The complaint-catalogue checker reads four file families. Its CI invocation sat inside a job gated on the changed-surface output cljs_node_test, which only implementation/hicasso/** sets true — so register-only, spec-only and guide-only edits all skipped the gate silently. The audit's bounded repair said: give it a CI path whose changed-surface inputs include every family it reads. My message to the worker repeated that framing.

THE WORKER DECLINED THE FRAMING, and it is right: "The defect being repaired IS an arm that failed to cover a checker's inputs, so A NEW ARM IS A FRESH CHANCE TO MAKE THE SAME MISTAKE and needs re-widening whenever the checker learns a new file." A widened predicate is correct exactly until the checker reads one more path — and nothing makes anyone revisit it then.

WHAT IT BUILT INSTEAD: an UNCONDITIONAL job — no needs:, no if: — listed in all-required-passed. That covers all four families and every future one BY CONSTRUCTION, with no predicate to keep in sync. It then drove all three previously-dead families red (R1, R3, R8 -> exits [1,1,1]), restored byte-identically, re-ran [0,0,0], AND drove the routing claim itself red by re-gating the job on cljs_node_test and watching the new scheduling test fail verbatim.

THE GENERAL RULE: a conditional that must be kept in sync with a growing input set is a standing liability, and the cheap fix (widen it) preserves the liability while looking like a repair. Prefer removing the condition when the job is cheap enough to always run. Ask "what makes someone update this predicate the next time the thing it guards changes?" — if the answer is "nothing", the predicate is the bug.

MAYOR NOTE: I passed the audit's remedy through verbatim. A worker that treated the bounded repair as a FLOOR rather than a CEILING produced a better answer. Brief the PROBLEM and the FENCE; do not hand over the audit's proposed mechanism as though it were settled.

THE OBVIOUS FIX TO A DEPTH-LIMITED WALK HAD ITS OWN TRAP (2026-08-14, rf2-2cu7f worker).

THE DEFECT: an artefact-root enumeration listed at depth 1, so four adapter artefacts nested one level deeper were never walked. 377 files walked, ZERO adapter files, against an independent walker's 425 including 14.

Inert under a depth-1 listing, because no top-level directory has a `src` child. Under recursion it would have swept `tools/`, `examples/` and `migration/` into two ratchets scoped to `implementation/`.

So a latent bug sat DIRECTLY BEHIND the one being fixed, invisible until the fix removed what was masking it. The worker identified the implementation root POSITIVELY instead — by the directory that carries `core/src` — rather than by relative position.

THE GENERAL FORM: WHEN A CONSTRAINT IS REMOVED, CHECK WHAT THE CONSTRAINT WAS ACCIDENTALLY PREVENTING. A depth limit, a narrow pattern, a small timeout — each may be masking something the author never considered, and the fix that removes it inherits everything it was holding back.

AND THE TWO CONSUMERS CARRIED SEPARATE COPIES OF THE ENUMERATION — under a comment claiming it was 'reused verbatim'. That comment is exactly how fixing one would have left the other broken. A CLAIM OF SHARING IS NOT SHARING; check whether the definition is actually one definition.

CORRECTED PATTERN, use this: grep -ciE "audit.?reopen|merged-pr audit|reopened|REOPEN" — case-insensitive, tolerant of hyphen/space/underscore, and including bare "REOPENED" which several audits use as the leading verb. A close is destructive to an audit obligation and cheap to defer; when the two hypotheses are "my tooling reverted it" and "a reviewer reopened it with a finding", the cost of being wrong is asymmetric — assume reviewer unless the notes plainly show otherwise. THE UNDERLYING LESSON, which recurs: a negative grep result is weak evidence. It proves your PATTERN did not match, never that the THING is absent. Same class as "grep -c beads <file> || echo NO HOOK" (grep exits 1 on zero count, not only on a missing file) and the "&& / ||" precedence bug that truncated issues.jsonl. THE statusCheckRollup LAGS THE BRANCH IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — THE BRANCH QUERY IS GROUND TRUTH (observed twice, 2026-08-07).

DIRECTION 1, too OPTIMISTIC: the rollup reported ok=78 canc=0 fail=0 pend=0 total=78 — settled by every field it exposes — while "gh run list --branch" showed TWO runs QUEUED. A queued run has no checks attached to the head commit yet, so the rollup does not know they are coming. Merging there ships a PR two workflows short.

DIRECTION 2, too PESSIMISTIC: the rollup reported two checks IN_PROGRESS ("CLJS (shadow-cljs :node-test)" and "JVM tools/template") while "gh run list --branch" showed ALL FIVE workflows completed/success at that exact head sha. Here the rollup holds stale entries from a superseded run; the work is done and the PR is genuinely green.

SO: clause 3 (zero QUEUED/IN_PROGRESS in the rollup) is NOT sufficient and NOT necessary on its own. The authoritative question is always the branch, keyed to the CURRENT head sha:
  gh run list --branch <headRefName> --limit 25 --json workflowName,status,conclusion,headSha
and then: every workflow at that sha is completed with conclusion success (or a deliberate skip), and none is queued or in_progress.

WHEN THEY DISAGREE, BELIEVE THE BRANCH — but say in the report that they disagreed and which way, because a reader checking later will see only one of them. Do not merge on a rollup that is more optimistic than the branch; do not block forever on a rollup that is more pessimistic than it.

This is the same lesson as everything else in this family: a summary that is derived, cached or lagged is not the fact. Go to the thing that ran.

statusCheckRollup CAN REPORT ZERO PENDING WHILE WORKFLOW RUNS ARE STILL QUEUED (observed 2026-08-07, PR #7630).

WHAT HAPPENED: 'gh pr list --json statusCheckRollup' reported ok=78, cancelled=0, failed=0, PENDING=0, total=78 — a fully concluded rollup by every field it exposes. 'gh run list --branch worker/navkeys-jr0tg' at the same instant showed TWO runs with status=queued (docs, portability). A queued run's checks are not yet attached to the head commit's rollup, so the rollup does not know they are coming and reports the PR as settled.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS: it is indistinguishable from genuinely complete. The total even LOOKS plausible — 78 against an expected band of ~82-86 — because a re-run had replaced earlier entries and shrunk the count. Merging there ships a PR two workflows short, which is exactly how PR #7628 reached main unverified.

THIS IS THE THIRD DISGUISE OF ONE DEFECT IN A SINGLE SESSION. (1) An EMPTY rollup satisfies '0 fail and 0 pending'. (2) Counting status==COMPLETED as passed silently counts CANCELLED as green. (3) pending==0 while runs are queued. All three report the absence of bad news as the presence of good news.

THE MERGE CRITERION, all four clauses, none sufficient alone:
  - total is non-empty and in the band the repo actually produces (~86 here; verify with 'gh pr checks' on recent merged PRs, do not assume)
  - every conclusion is SUCCESS or SKIPPED — CANCELLED is NOT passed
  - zero QUEUED or IN_PROGRESS entries in the rollup
  - AND 'gh run list --branch <head>' shows no run with status queued or in_progress
The last clause is the one that catches this case, and it needs a second API call. Make it; a merge is not the place to save a round trip.

ENUMERATING GRAMMAR SHAPES IS NOT ENOUGH — EACH ROW MUST BE DISCRIMINATING (2026-08-11, AUDIT #7818 on rf2-hic-022).

THE REFINEMENT, and it is the eighth instance tonight of claim-exceeds-coverage — this time INSIDE a witness built to my own grammar-derived instruction, which is why it matters.

I briefed: derive the witness from the GRAMMAR of the construct, not from your fix. The worker did exactly that — eight legal letfn shapes, each committed as an independent negative row. It was still insufficient.

WHY: locals-bound-by unions all names for the whole letfn, and self-call-nodes suppresses the entire form as soon as ANY arity binds the view name. Every committed multi-arity row bound THE SAME view name in BOTH arities. So recognising only the LATER arity makes every row green, and the stated property — "every parameter of every arity" — is load-bearing nowhere.

THE AUDIT PROVED IT rather than asserting it: it changed fn-locals' multi-arity source from `forms` to `(rest forms)`, skipping the first arity, and the pinned live gate STILL EXITED 0. The existing mutation only removed ALL arities, so it could not catch the narrower regression.

THE RULE TO ADD TO BRIEFS, alongside grammar-derivation rather than replacing it:

  A ROW MUST BE ABLE TO FAIL FOR THE REASON IT NAMES. For every negative row, ask: what SINGLE NARROWING of the implementation would make this row pass while the property it tests is broken? If such a narrowing exists, the row is decorative.

  Practically: bind the target in the position HARDEST TO REACH, and have another position in the same form bind a DIFFERENT name, so the row can only pass if the arm truly reads that position. Then state in the PR body, per shape, WHICH NARROWING the row would catch. That list is the evidence the rows are load-bearing — and writing it is what exposes the decorative ones.

WHY THE GRAMMAR RULE ALONE FAILS: shape coverage answers "did I test this form?" It does not answer "can this test tell the difference?" A row can exercise a legal shape and still be satisfied by a wrong implementation, because the shape and the discriminator are different questions. Both are needed.

SISTER RULES: witness-derived-from-fix-inherits-its-blind-spots (the origin of the grammar instruction) and sweep-generator-defines-reachable-failure-directions (a generator's excluded shapes make an error DIRECTION unreachable). All three are the same disease at different scales — coverage is defined by what the instrument can DISTINGUISH, not by how much of it you ran.

MAYOR NOTE: the mutation self-test is the place this gets caught. A mutation that removes a capability WHOLESALE proves less than one that narrows it. Prefer narrowing mutations, and prefer several small ones to one large one.

A RULING CAN BE RIGHT ABOUT THE DECISION AND WRONG ABOUT THE SITE — AND ONLY MEASUREMENT SEPARATES THEM (2026-08-06, rf2-nqj22).

MY RULING said: refuse a mismatched carried stamp inside a substrate render extent, and "require-current-frame! raises when tier 1 answers something else". The DECISION was right. The SITE was wrong, and I stated it as though it were part of the ruling.

WHY IT IS WRONG: require-current-frame! is NOT the single funnel the Spec 009 row describes. subs/subscribes 1-arity deliberately INLINES (or (frame/resolve-current-frame) (frame/require-current-frame! ...)) so its error payload stays off the per-read fast path — rf2-a8bw0 records "Do NOT collapse this back". So AN AMBIENT SUBSCRIBE WITH A STAMP IN SCOPE NEVER REACHES THE REQUIRING PRIMITIVE. A check placed there leaves the LARGEST ambient door unguarded while every test exercising the smaller doors passes.

HOW IT WAS FOUND: the worker implemented exactly what I ruled, and its own new test went RED on the subscribe arm with the read silently succeeding. Not by reading the code — by building the thing and watching the one door it could not reach. It then moved the check to resolve-current-frame, where the reader answers nil for a stamp the extent will not accept, which fixes every reader-first caller BY CONSTRUCTION and leaves the optimisation intact.

THE RULE FOR MY RULINGS: rule the DECISION and the ACCEPTANCE, and mark any implementation site as a suggestion to verify. I have no measured basis for naming a site, and naming one with the authority of a ruling invites a worker to implement it and stop. Say "I believe the natural site is X — check whether every door actually passes through it" rather than asserting the mechanism.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is the ninth instance this session of one class: A FUNNEL THAT IS DOCUMENTED AS THE SINGLE PATH IS AN ASSERTION TO TEST. Spec 009s own row says "every ambient resolution goes through require-current-frame!" — false, and now filed as rf2-ur3ey. A performance optimisation that inlines a call is exactly what turns a documented funnel into a bypassed one, so wherever a hot path has been deliberately specialised, expect the guard placed at the general site to miss it.

AND THE ACCEPTANCE CHECK EARNED ITS PLACE: I made the ruling explicitly conditional on a-carried-with-frame-still-carries-inside-a-body staying green, and told the worker to RUN it rather than assume, and to stop rather than bend it. It ran green alone under the fix, and mutation M2 reds it — so it is load-bearing rather than a passenger. A conditional ruling with a named falsifier is worth more than a confident one.

RUNNING THE LANE AN AUDIT COULD NOT RUN OVERTURNED THE AUDIT ITSELF (2026-07-26, rf2-drpa3.182.4 defect 3).

MERGED-PR AUDIT #7095 found that controls/composing? ORs three independent signals — event.isComposing, keyCode == 229, nativeEvent.isComposing — while press-enter! set BOTH isComposing true AND keyCode 229 on one event, so an implementation reading only isComposing stayed green and the Chromium fallback was never exercised. Its prescribed fix: make each of the three OR branches independently falsifiable. The audit stated plainly that it COULD NOT RERUN THE BROWSER LANE because shadow-cljs was not installed in its environment, so its finding was reasoned from the test event and the shipped OR.

THE WORKER RAN THAT LANE, AND THE THREE-BRANCH PREMISE WAS WRONG. Disabling (.-isComposing e) on the SYNTHETIC event reds NOTHING — React does not forward the flag — while disabling the nativeEvent read withholds nothing. So the OR named TWO COORDINATE SIGNALS, one of them UNREACHABLE under every shipped Freehand host, because the substrate is React-only.

THE HONEST FIX WAS THEREFORE NOT THREE FALSIFIABLE BRANCHES. It is ONE SIGNAL WITH TWO SURFACES — nativeEvent for a React host, the event itself for a raw DOM one — plus the keyCode sentinel. Truth value unchanged for every input; the docstring now describes what the code can actually observe. Each remaining signal IS independently falsifiable, proved one at a time: disabling the standard flag reds only the flag row, disabling the 229 sentinel reds only the fallback row, one failure each.

THE GENERAL RULE, and it is the sharpest form of verify-the-verifier this artefact has produced: AN AUDIT THAT NAMES ITS OWN UNRUN GATE IS TELLING YOU WHICH PART OF ITS FINDING IS INFERENCE. Read that admission as a pointer, not as a caveat. Where an audit says "I could not run X, so this follows from reading the code", the FIRST thing the fixing worker should do is run X — because the reading can be right about the defect and wrong about its shape, which is exactly what happened: the vacuous-test finding was real, the three-branch model was not.

COROLLARY FOR MY BRIEFS: when I dispatch an audit residual whose audit records an unrun gate, say so explicitly and instruct the worker to run it FIRST. I did tell this worker "you should actually run it" and that instruction is what produced the correction. Keep it.

PROCESS NOTE WORTH KEEPING: the same worker also proved defect 1 by reverting a predicate to contains? and observing 6 failures ALL NAMING ITS OWN NEW TEST and NOTHING ELSE IN A 1207-TEST SUITE — which is the direct measurement of the audit claim that prior coverage was blind. A mutation that reds only your new test is how you prove the gap was real rather than asserted.

THE BEST SABOTAGE CONTROL IS A SHIPPED DOOR CALLED IN THE WRONG PLACE, NOT A MOCK (2026-08-11, rf2-1mmn).

WHAT THE WORKER FOUND, and it did not expect it either. Kernel risk row 2 — "independent roots and SSR requests cannot reset, adopt, dirty or release one another's state" — turned out controllable WITH NO MOCK, NO SEAM AND NO REDEFINITION. The pre-fix behaviour still ships under an honest name: `impl.mount/release!` is `unmount!` plus container removal plus `collector/reset-runtime!`, which is exactly the meaning rf2-31xm took OFF the public facade and KEPT as the fixture door. `reset-runtime!`'s own docstring states the defect it would cause: "calling it to tear a root down empties the runtime under every other root on the page too."

So the sabotage is simply THE SHIPPED PAGE-WIDE DOOR CALLED WHERE THE ROOT-SCOPED ONE BELONGS. That is a far stronger control than a mock: it exercises real code on the real path, and it cannot drift away from the runtime the way a hand-written stub does.

LOOK FOR THIS SHAPE FIRST when a risk row needs a control. A repo that has REMOVED a dangerous door from its public surface has usually kept it somewhere for fixtures, and its docstring often names the hazard verbatim — which is both the control and its documentation.

TWO TRAPS THE SAME WORKER HIT, worth carrying into any sabotage brief:

1. **DO NOT REPLACE A FUNCTION THAT IS A REACT HOOK.** Its first plant replaced `adopting-here?` outright and dropped a `useContext`, so the tray rendered 3 hooks where the shipped code renders 4. Disarming then raised "rendered more hooks than during the previous render" — A RED THAT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE THING UNDER TEST. The fix: the replacement CALLS THE ORIGINAL FIRST, let-bound so an `or` cannot short-circuit past the hook. Any sabotage inside a component must preserve hook count and order.

2. **RUN BOTH HALVES OF THE CONSTRUCTION IN THE CONTROL.** Each of its controls reds if the runtime regresses AND if the sabotage quietly becomes a no-op. That second half is what stops a control decaying into a green that proves nothing — the exact fail-open shape this project keeps finding.

AND ONE REFUSAL WORTH KEEPING: it declined to make one mutation executable because the outcome depends on the ordering of one root's closer versus another's recoverable-error callback, WHICH REACT DOES NOT LET A CALLER CHOOSE. An executing version would go green or red on the scheduler. It recorded that in the comment and named the PR and commit instead. A control whose verdict is decided by scheduling is worse than a documented absence.

RECOVERING A LOST PR REFERENCE: this repo REBASE-merges, so a commit sha does not carry its PR. `gh api repos/day8/re-frame2/commits/<sha>/pulls` resolves it. That is how every "the PR body records it" comment — which named no PR at all — was turned into a real citation.

THE SAME UNLINK MECHANISM PRODUCED TWO DIFFERENT DEFECTS AT TWO DIFFERENT TIME SCALES — TENS OF SECONDS AND TWO SYSCALLS (2026-08-06, rf2-v8561 then rf2-1wyyb).

THE SHARED CAUSE: compile-node-test.cjs UNLINKS its :output-to before every compile, deliberately, so a failed compile leaves nothing stale (rf2-6t03c). Anything reading that bundle while a compile starts loses it.

MANIFESTATION 1, over ~276 SECONDS (rf2-v8561): check-per-ns-isolation.cjs spawns one node process PER NAMESPACE over a shared bundle. A compile landing mid-sweep pulled the bundle from under every run still to come, and the gate accused the LAST THREE ROSTER ENTRIES, CONSECUTIVELY, of fixture leaks. Contiguity was the tell — three independent defects do not arrive adjacent.

MANIFESTATION 2, over TWO SYSCALLS (rf2-1wyyb): check-ui-adapter-isolation.cjs probed existsSync then readFileSync. A compile landing in THAT gap made readFileSync throw ENOENT uncaught, and node exits 1 — the exact code this gate reserves for a real wrapper leak. A classic TOCTOU, and an ENVIRONMENT cause wearing the ISOLATION verdicts exit code.

THE LESSON: when a shared resource can vanish, ASK WHAT ELSE READS IT, and do not assume the window has to be large to matter. A two-syscall gap and a four-minute sweep are the same bug class; only the odds differ. Both were found by INJECTING the fault rather than by reading — the second one specifically by asking "does the sibling share this defect?" and fault-injecting even after concluding it did not.

AND THE MODEL ANSWER TO A "DOES THIS SIBLING SHARE THE DEFECT?" CHECK: it does NOT, and the reason is structural rather than incidental. The sibling spawns nothing per namespace — arm 1 reads the bundle ONCE AS TEXT and executes no test, arm 2 spawns one clojure -Stree. No roster, no sweep, no runtime selector, so THE DISCRIMINATOR HAS NO REFERENT. Driving main() through each cause confirmed the three-way split was already present and correct. Note the failure DIRECTION also differs: a stale denylist there is a false GREEN, not a misattributed red. Answering "no" with a structural reason plus fault injection is worth more than answering "yes" and copying a fix across.

I FILED THAT CHECK EXPLICITLY AS "a shared filename pattern is not evidence of a shared defect", and that framing is what produced a real finding instead of a copied patch.

SCALE THE BRIEF HAZARD SECTION TO THE SURFACE, NOT TO EVERYTHING I KNOW (2026-07-26, posture applied to my own dispatches).

MY BRIEFS GREW to nine false-green classes plus four recurring patterns plus two live CI conditions, repeated near-verbatim into every dispatch — including a five-line alias change. That is uniform maximum effort regardless of what the task warrants, which is the shape of gold-plating the standing posture rules out. Long briefs also bury the two or three warnings that actually apply.

THE HAZARDS THAT DEMONSTRABLY EARN THEIR PLACE, by worker reports rather than my own citations: (1) test-fast-pr.sh soft-skips its own mkdocs step and still exits 0 — workers hit this repeatedly and said so verbatim; (2) never junction node_modules to the mayor tree — this one stopped a git worktree remove from emptying the real directory; (3) a canned value/fixture can assert what the producer cannot emit while every suite passes; (4) capture rc immediately and cross-check the log, since a wrapper-reported exit 0 has disagreed with a captured rc more than once.
