  3. implementation/hicasso/test/.../reincarnation_seams_cljs_test.cljs:39-40 — a test docstring.
Every individual repair was bounded and correct. The PROCESS was wrong: three round-trips of mayor, worker and CI for what one `git grep` would have closed.

THE PRACTICE: when a bead corrects a stale factual claim, the brief says SWEEP EVERY CARRIER. `git grep` the exact wording over TRACKED files, read every hit, dispose of each in the one PR, and list in the PR body what was changed and what was left correct. "Bounded repair" should bound the CHANGE, not the SEARCH.

TWO CAUTIONS THAT MAKE THE SWEEP HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, both earned here:
  - THE PHRASE IS OFTEN CORRECT ELSEWHERE. invariants.md L150's timer-callback row says "one macrotask later" and is RIGHT, because a timer callback is a macrotask. The React-controlled deferral under rf2-hic-014 is also correctly a macrotask, and its repair is unreachable by this one. `git grep "macrotask later"` also hits core/substrate/spine.cljs, the react_shared_suite and two arm1 bench tests. Reading every hit is the work; the grep is only the index.
  - NAME THE DISCRIMINATOR IN THE BRIEF, or the worker cannot tell the stale hits from the correct ones. Here it is WHO SCHEDULES THE DEFERRAL: the runtime's own collector (repaired to a microtask) versus React or a timer (still a macrotask). Without that sentence a sweep either under-corrects or breaks correct prose.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS AS THE CENSUS'S THIRD SPECIES — text that matches the search and is not about the subject — and as the "confident sentence outliving its behaviour" shape the Checkpoint 1 review named. All three are one thing: a claim and its carriers drift apart, and only an exhaustive read reunites them.

A SWEEP'S GENERATOR DEFINES WHICH FAILURE DIRECTIONS IT CAN EVER FIND (2026-08-11, rf2-skpf worker, PR #7811).

THE CASE. PR #7803 swept 1,728 quoted-fence prefix triples against the real MkDocs renderer to characterise a docs-gate defect, and its numbers held up. But EVERY shape that generator emits has BALANCED backtick runs on lines 1 and 3. So the inline-masking defect could only ever manifest there as pairing that should not happen — a FALSE POSITIVE. The false-negative half needs an ODD backtick-run count either side of a boundary, a shape the fence-triple generator CANNOT EMIT BY CONSTRUCTION.

Result: in that domain the defect was 188/188 false positives and its expensive half was invisible. Not because 1,728 was too few — because the generator excluded the direction. Running 17,280 would have found nothing more.

THE LESSON, in the worker's words: 'a sweep generator defines its reachable failure directions, and the direction it excludes is invisible no matter how many shapes you run.' A sweep's SIZE is not its coverage; its GENERATOR is. So a big clean sweep is not evidence of absence outside the directions its generator can express — and the false-negative direction is usually the expensive one, because it is the one where a checker stays silent.

THE COUNTERMEASURE THAT WORKED: two probes over the same boundary, each mapping the disagreement onto the OPPOSITE error direction (a mask probe and a wrap probe over the same middle line), so neither direction can hide. When commissioning or reading a sweep, ask: what shapes can this generator NOT produce, and which error direction does that make unreachable? Put the answer in the report.

MAYOR APPLICATION: when a worker reports 'N shapes swept, zero disagreements', that is a claim about the generator, not about the surface. Ask for the generator's excluded shapes before treating it as clearance.

AFTER A CONTEXT CLEAR, PRIOR-SESSION AGENTS STAY ALIVE BUT GO INVISIBLE TO TaskList — AND I USED TaskList AS THE LIVENESS SOURCE (2026-08-10).

WHAT I DID WRONG. Recovering from a /clear, the handoff said the rf2-vsgq worker on worker/hmrbrowser-vsgq was "live and resumed". I called TaskList; it returned "No tasks found". I trusted the tool over the handoff, concluded the agent was dead, and dispatched a fresh fix-worker into that SAME worktree on that SAME branch. Two executors then ran on one branch — the exact thing "no concurrent workers same branch" forbids.

HOW IT SURFACED. Not from any check of mine. The original agent's own completion report flagged it: "A commit I did not author appeared on my branch at 15:50 — 13e9750dc9 ... it may be a second executor in this worktree." It was mine.

NO HARM, BUT ONLY BY LUCK. Both agents happened to fix different halves of the same red gate (one renamespaced the :dev-http build id, the other added the README build->port row), the commits did not conflict, and PR #7768 merged green. Nothing about that outcome was guaranteed.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS A TOOL BOUNDARY, NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL. TaskList reports the CURRENT session's task registry. A /clear starts a new registry. Agents spawned before the clear keep running and keep pushing commits, but they are absent from it. An empty TaskList after a clear therefore means "this session has spawned nothing yet", NEVER "no workers are running". It also returned empty immediately after I spawned six agents, so it is not a reliable liveness source in this harness at all.

WHAT TO USE INSTEAD, in order:
  1. The worktree list under the re-frame2-worktrees sibling — a live worker owns a worktree, and a finished one removes its own.
  2. Whether the branch's commit count has MOVED since the last tick. bootstrap.md already names this as the cheap reliable discriminator; a moved count says alive. A still count says nothing and never authorises a reap.
  3. Whether SendMessage finds a live task to deliver to.

A HANDOFF DOCUMENT OUTRANKS AN EMPTY TaskList. The handoff was written by the session that spawned those agents and it was right; the tool was answering a narrower question than the one I asked it.

AND THE SAFE MOVE WAS AVAILABLE AND CHEAP: SendMessage to resume the existing worker keeps its full context and cannot create a second executor. Never re-dispatch a fresh worker over one that may still be live — resume it.

TENTH FALSE-GREEN VARIANT: report-changed-surfaces.sh TAKES PATHS, NOT REFS, AND SILENTLY REPORTS NOTHING CHANGED (2026-07-26, hit by the scaffold-floor worker on itself).

Invoking scripts/.../report-changed-surfaces.sh origin/main treats "origin/main" as a literal FILE PATH. No such path changed, so it prints every surface false and exits successfully — i.e. "your diff touches nothing, no gate needs to run." Re-run on the real changed paths, it correctly armed examples_compile=true. There is no error, no usage message, and no hint that the argument was misread.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE INVOCATION: this is the classifier that decides which CI jobs arm. A caller who passes a ref gets a confident all-false answer, which is exactly the answer that means "skip everything". It is the same failure direction as check-beads-pr-boundary.sh exiting 0 with no base ref — a gate-adjacent script that cannot understand its input and reports the benign case rather than refusing.

DIRECTLY RELEVANT RIGHT NOW: the ci-arming worker is editing this very script to add JVM arms for tools/machines-viz and tools/testbed-support. It must pass real paths when testing its own arms, or it will see all-false and conclude its arm does not work — or worse, conclude the arm works when it has not exercised it.

GENERAL RULE, now with two instances: a script in the gate path that accepts an argument should refuse an argument it cannot interpret, not fall through to the empty result. When touching either of these, prefer making the misuse loud over documenting the correct usage.

TENTH INSTRUMENT FAULT CLASS: A LARGE-OBJECT ARM INFLATES ITS SUCCESSOR BY 2x, REPRODUCIBLY. Measuring narrow-write allocation (rf2-jr76s), an SMI control read 16.1052 B/slot in FORWARD order and 8.0027 B/slot (+0.03% against prediction) in REVERSED order — the only difference being whether an 87 KB arm ran immediately before it. When testing dispatch captures via with-redefs: rf/dispatch is a MACRO that expands to rf/dispatch* (adds :rf.trace/call-site). TEST-RUNNER FALSE GREEN: from implementation/, 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' WITHOUT '-d <dir>' makes the Cognitect runner default to a non-existent ./test and silently report 'Ran 0 tests, 0 assertions' — which READS AS GREEN. Correct form is 'clojure -M:test -d core/test -n <ns>' (adjust the -d dir per artefact). Found by the rf2-8sc64 worker on #6308, 2026-07-18. THIS AFFECTS MAYOR BRIEFS: I have repeatedly written focused-ns gate commands as 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' — any worker that ran exactly that and reported a small/zero test count may have proven nothing. When a worker reports a focused-ns run, CHECK THE TEST COUNT IS NON-ZERO and plausible for the ns; 'Ran 0 tests' or an implausibly small count is a red flag, not a pass. The 'already landed' grep has a BLIND SPOT: work fixed under a SIBLING bead's id. `git log --grep=<bead-id> origin/main` catches 'this bead was fixed and left open', but NOT 'another bead's PR captured this bead's substance'. rf2-xu6rx (interpreter memo caches -> js/Map) returned nothing for its own id, yet the swap had already merged ~12h earlier in PR #7077 under rf2-lnecd. THE BASH TOOL SILENTLY STRIPS BACKSLASHES FROM HEREDOC STRINGS ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP (2026-07-26).

Found by the checker-residuals worker while probing a char-literal guard: a heredoc probe string lost its backslashes, so the probe read as a FALSE NEGATIVE — the guard looked broken when the input had been mangled before it arrived. It rewrote every probe as a FILE under its own worktree and the results reversed.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE KNOWN git worktree add BACKSLASH STRIPPING, which is already recorded, but the surface is different and more insidious: a worktree path failing is loud, whereas a mangled PROBE STRING silently changes what you are testing. Any probe involving backslashes, char literals, regex escapes or line continuations must be written to a FILE, not passed through a heredoc.

AND IT COST A REAL VERDICT IN THE SAME SESSION, in a second form: that worker plant C did not apply because of a LINE-CONTINUATION BACKSLASH in the anchor, and the self-test returned rc=0 — INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT MISSED THE DEFECT. Only the mandated "confirm the diff applied before reading the verdict" protocol caught it. That is the twelfth false-signal class firing in the wild and being caught by the exact rule written for it.

SO THE RULE COMPOUNDS: for any mutation or probe whose payload contains a backslash, (1) write it to a file rather than a heredoc, and (2) confirm it applied by git diff --stat AND by grepping the token back out. Either check alone would have missed one of the two failures above.

A THIRD FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, unrelated but worth the same memory: a PRIME-SUFFIXED SYMBOL (db-prime, tags-prime) reads as a QUOTE to the bijection walker regex — 352 occurrences in the tree, the same class the existing backslash-quote lookbehind was written for, and a FALSE-GREEN direction. Latent rather than live because all 352 sit inside binding vectors the walk cannot reach. Closed with one lookbehind. The lesson: when a regex already has a lookbehind for one lookalike, ASK WHAT ELSE LOOKS LIKE THAT — the second instance is usually already in the tree.

The core JVM suite (implementation/core clojure -M:test) runs ~10min under concurrent worker/mayor JVM load — right at the 600s foreground tool limit. This is the ROOT of the 'workers strand on backgrounded gates' pattern: a worker can't reliably foreground it when the machine is contended, so it backgrounds the gate + ends its turn with work uncommitted + no PR. Mitigation: briefs must say 'run gates FOREGROUND, do not background; if the core JVM suite risks the 600s limit run a FOCUSED namespace subset (clojure -M:test :only <ns>) not the whole suite'; recover a stranded worker by SendMessage-resume telling it to finish foreground in one turn.

THE CROSS-BASE CHECK: TWO PRs EACH GREEN AGAINST A BASE LACKING THE OTHER CAN STILL BREAK IN COMBINATION (2026-07-26).

A worker did this unprompted and it is the practice I most want to adopt. Its work and PR #7081 were EACH GREEN against a base that did not contain the other. Rather than assume the combination was fine, it built a THROWAWAY WORKTREE AT origin/main WITH BOTH MERGED and ran the suite: freehand JVM 1156/7707, 0F 0E. Then removed the worktree.

WHY THIS MATTERS AT SATURATION: I run up to six workers, each rebasing onto a moving main, and I merge on green. Every green I act on was measured against a base THAT NO LONGER EXISTS by the time I merge. Nineteen PRs today merged a state older than the worker tip; several pairs touched adjacent surfaces. THE MERGE LOOP HAS NO CROSS-BASE SIGNAL AT ALL — CI re-runs on the merge commit, but I do not wait for it.

WHEN TO REQUIRE IT: when two live PRs touch the SAME artefact or adjacent seams — for example one editing implementation/freehand/src and another editing implementation/freehand/test, or two both moving spec/009 rows. It is cheap: one throwaway worktree at origin/main, both branches merged, the ONE suite that spans both surfaces. Not the whole spine.

WHEN NOT TO: disjoint surfaces. Most of the time the fence system already guarantees it, and this would be ceremony.

A SECOND, SMALLER FINDING FROM THE SAME REPORT — a worker inherited MY STALE CANARY. It reported "mayor node_modules canary: 101 before and after". 101 IS THE OLD TOP-LEVEL DIRECTORY COUNT, which I retired hours ago after finding it nearly blind to the hazard it guards: the junction-follow deletes FILES, and 103 directories with emptied contents reads identically to 103 healthy ones. THE LIVE FIGURE IS 2933 FILES. It got the number from an older brief of mine. THE "git grep <ref> -- <dir>/ RETURNS FALSE-EMPTY" HAZARD IS NOT REAL, AND I HAVE BEEN PUTTING IT IN EVERY BRIEF (2026-07-26).

TESTED TODAY, three ways, same answer: git grep -l defhost HEAD -- implementation/freehand/src/ returns 7; without the ref, 7; plain recursive grep on the worktree, 7. NO DISCREPANCY.

AND THE ORIGINAL OBSERVATION WAS ALMOST CERTAINLY A CORRECT EMPTY MISREAD AS A FALSE ONE. At an older ref c6f3c3b8ed the directory implementation/freehand/src EXISTS, and git grep for defhost there returns 0 — BECAUSE v/defhost DID NOT EXIST YET AT THAT COMMIT. That is the right answer. WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A WRONG NUMBER: the instruction did not merely mislead, IT DEGRADED THE WORK. I told workers to use `git show <ref>:<file> | grep` INSTEAD — which is per-file, has no directory recursion, and requires knowing every filename in advance. Workers have been doing by-hand file enumeration for a whole session to route around a hazard that does not exist. At least one reported a "targeted grep" workaround because of it.

THIS IS THE THIRD STANDING INSTRUCTION OF MINE PROVEN WRONG TODAY, all three boilerplate I repeated without re-testing: (1) "sample coverage unchanged at 113 of 136 proves an edit fell outside a digest fence" — the census is insensitive to block text BY CONSTRUCTION; (2) "simulate a deletion by moving the tree aside" — blind for git-reading gates, and a sibling then showed moving it aside WITHIN the search space is not a deletion either; (3) this one.

THE RULE FOR MYSELF: BOILERPLATE IS THE LEAST-AUDITED TEXT I PRODUCE, BECAUSE IT IS COPIED RATHER THAN COMPOSED. Every standing instruction is a claim, and a claim repeated forty times without re-testing is forty chances to be wrong at scale. RE-TEST ONE BOILERPLATE CLAIM PER RETROSPECTIVE, cheaply, against the actual repo — today that took two commands and killed a hazard that had been costing real worker time all session.

WHAT STAYS VERIFIED, tested in the same pass: test-fast-pr.sh DOES soft-skip mkdocs when it is not on PATH — its own header says so at lines 12-13, 37 and 82, and it is not on PATH here. That instruction is sound and should remain.

THE IN_PROGRESS BLIND SPOT BIT AGAIN, AT SCALE — 13 BEADS INVISIBLE AT ONCE (2026-07-26). Audited in_progress against live worktrees and found THIRTEEN beads claimed by workers that no longer exist, every one with real outstanding work and NONE of them visible to bd ready, which excludes in_progress by construction. Flipping them to open took the ready pool from 26 to 38 — so I had been reporting a 26-bead pool while the real dispatchable count was half again as large. That is the third recurrence of this exact failure and by far the biggest.

WHY IT ACCUMULATED THIS TIME: an API outage killed a dozen workers in two hours. Each had claimed its bead, so each claim outlived its worker. A crash or outage therefore produces stale claims IN PROPORTION TO THE FLEET SIZE, which is precisely when the pool most needs to be accurate.

THE AUDIT, and it is cheap: for each in_progress bead, ask whether a live worktree holds it — parse `git worktree list --porcelain` for branch names, never construct them. If no worktree AND no open PR, no worker holds it. Then read the notes and classify: (a) stale claim for shipped work -> close with evidence; (b) PARTIAL delivery -> flip to OPEN so it is dispatchable again; (c) genuinely held on an operator ruling -> leave and record the hold ON THE BEAD.

A MEASUREMENT ERROR I MADE INSIDE THIS VERY AUDIT, which is the reusable part: my first matcher tested whether the branch name contained the bead id `rf2-7gth0`. Branch names carry the BARE id — `worker/xray-schema4-7gth0` — so the match failed and a bead with a perfectly live worktree was reported as a stale claim. Strip the `rf2-` prefix before matching. Same family as every other name-derivation bug here: a worktree directory name, a branch name and a bead id are three different strings, and deriving any from another eventually matches the wrong thing or nothing.

AND A NEGATIVE GREP IS STILL WEAK EVIDENCE. Two of the thirteen showed zero partial/reopen markers and looked closable. Reading them showed BOTH had complete analysis and a pending fix — and both hinge on the same open question, whether the thing they would fix retires with the donor at F6e, in which case recording that is the honest fix rather than building a check for rows about to vanish. THE MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN DESTRUCTIVELY OVERWRITE A BEAD'S ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (2026-07-25, found by EP-0037 review gate 2). This is a process defect in a process I do not control, and it silently destroys the only record of what a slice promised.

WHAT HAPPENED: R1's and R2's slice acceptance criteria were REWRITTEN — both the title AND the description — into the audit's follow-through text. PRs #6875/#6877 name rf2-kqxe6.5/.6 as the slice owners; their original criteria no longer exist anywhere. By contrast the audits of .3 and .7 APPENDED their findings, leaving the criteria intact. That difference is exactly why an independent completeness review could verify .3 and .7 and could NOT verify .5 and .6. Named casualty: the R2 tooling clause ended up with no bead at all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE EPIC: acceptance criteria are the only durable record of what was promised. A merged-PR audit's job is to record what it found, and it is very good at that — it caught a keyword-as-Var false green, a load-order privacy defect, a declared-:on-* classification defect and a census extent bug. But an audit that overwrites the promise it is auditing removes the ability to check completeness later, and the loss is invisible: the bead still reads coherently, just as the audit's narrative rather than as the slice's contract.

MAYOR ACTIONS: (1) treat audit notes as APPEND-ONLY when I write them myself, and say so in briefs — findings go in notes, never over a description; (2) when a bead's description reads as audit narrative rather than as acceptance criteria, suspect this and check git history of .beads for the original; (3) rf2-twpp6 tracks the append-only repair for the two affected beads; (4) when commissioning a completeness review, tell it that a bead whose criteria were overwritten is UNVERIFIABLE and should be reported as such rather than passed — gate 2 worked this out unprompted and it is the reason its verdict is trustworthy.

GENERALISABLE FORM: any automated process that writes into the tracker can destroy the state a later reviewer needs. Prefer append. If a tool overwrites, the tracker's git history is the only recovery path — which is another reason the .beads export must keep being committed on the heartbeat.

THE MID-WRITE RACE ACTUALLY FIRED TODAY AND AN EMPTY EXPORT REACHED main (2026-07-26).

WHAT HAPPENED: commit 4d8042d80d ("chore(beads): audit merged PR #7063") committed .beads/issues.jsonl AT ZERO ROWS. The previous commit d1c49b1164 had 2573. The working tree, the index and HEAD were all empty and git status was CLEAN, so nothing looked wrong — the file simply was not there any more.

THE DATABASE WAS NEVER AT RISK. Dolt is the source of truth; bd list returned every bead normally throughout. Recovery was one command: scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, which runs bd export and REGENERATES from Dolt rather than trusting the working file, then refuses an empty or badly shrunken result. It committed 2576 rows over a HEAD of 0. That refusal-plus-regenerate design is exactly why the script exists instead of a hand-rolled git add.

THE MECHANISM, now observed rather than theorised: a process ran git add on the export WHILE a bd operation was rewriting it, and snapshotted the zero-length intermediate. I hit the same window myself twenty minutes earlier — read the export as 0 rows with bd.exe alive — and did NOT commit, which is the only reason my own pass was clean. The audit process hit it and did commit.

TWO RULES THAT FOLLOW, and the first is cheap enough to be unconditional:
  1. GUARD EVERY CHECKPOINT ON A ROW COUNT. Never commit the export without asserting it is above a floor (2000+ here). The checkpoint script already does this; anything else that touches the file must too.
  2. AN EMPTY EXPORT IS NOT A DATA LOSS EVENT — IT IS A REGENERATION EVENT. Do not panic-restore from git history: git checkout of an older export would TIME-TRAVEL THE TRACKER, reopening closed beads and vanishing new ones. Always regenerate from Dolt.

AND A DETECTION NOTE: I nearly reported "0 open beads" as a real number. The tell was that it disagreed with the previous pass by 49. WHEN A COUNT MOVES TO ZERO, SUSPECT THE INSTRUMENT BEFORE THE WORLD — that is the tenth measurement error of this class I have caught today, and the only one that would have been consequential.

THE REOPEN TAXONOMY HAS A THIRD CLASS, AND I MISSED IT TWICE (2026-07-26).

I recorded two classes: (A) WEAK-CLOSE reopens, where the close said the job was ARMED rather than CATCHING and the audit had nothing to verify against — mine to prevent; and (B) NEW-RESIDUAL reopens, where a fully-evidenced close was accepted and the audit found something ELSE in the merged code — the audit working as designed.

THE REOPENS WORKER FOUND A THIRD, and it is distinct from both: (C) THE CLOSE ITSELF INTRODUCED THE DEFECT. rf2-12g5z was reopened against PR #7028 OWN NEW TEXT — spec/Privacy.md claimed "every production error record shipped off-box carries one too", which is false because error_emit.cljc:216 returns nil for three shapes and the emitter conditionally assocs the slot. The audit ACCEPTED the original finding and objected to the prose the fix added. In the worker words: "neither residual missed nor original re-asserted".

WHY C MATTERS SEPARATELY: A is a discipline failure I can fix by writing better close reasons. B is discovery I cannot reduce. C IS A REVIEW GAP — the fix was right and its accompanying claim was wrong, which no amount of close-reason rigour catches, because the close reason is describing a fix that IS correct. The remedy is different again: when a fix adds NEW PROSE asserting a general property, that prose needs the same evidence standard as the code. A sentence like "every production record carries X" is a UNIVERSAL CLAIM and should be checked against the conditional that emits X.

AND A FOURTH BUCKET THAT IS NOT A REOPEN AT ALL: rf2-ia904 reads like a reopen of rf2-2z9u3 but was FILED NEW by the #7042 audit. rf2-2z9u3 stays correctly closed. So "the bead is open again" has at least four causes and only one of them is my fault. Before treating an open-looking bead as a reopen, ASK WHICH OF THE FOUR IT IS — the worker did this per bead and it changed what each one owed.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THE BACKLOG NUMBER: I have been reporting roughly one reopen per merged PR as partly my defect. The honest split is now: A is mine, B and D are the system working, and C is a review gap that belongs to whoever wrote the accompanying prose. Only A responds to better closing.

The skill↔MCP drift gate has TWO distinct failure modes — do NOT assume flake (learned 2026-07-18, rf2-92dlh). (1) The TRANSIENT flake: 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' fails under concurrent-PR load; structurally impossible when the diff has 0 skills/MCP files → --admin-justifiable. (2) A REAL main-red drift: when a PR adds/changes MCP server tools WITHOUT reconciling the consumer skills' allowed-tools + the retro drift-set, check_skill_mcp_drift.py --ci reports real findings and the gate is RED ON MAIN — every subsequent PR inherits that red. I conflated the two: rf2-vxgfnd.95.8 added 5 re-frame2-pair MCP tools (explain-render/read-view-*) without updating skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md allowed-tools + scripts/check_skill_mcp_drift.py's re-frame2-pair-retro intentional_server_only set, so main's drift gate went REAL-red — and I kept --admin-ing PRs past it as 'the flake' for many merges until .95.10's spine run surfaced it (rf2-92dlh). FIX GOING FORWARD: when the drift gate is red, VERIFY main's own drift state — run/check  (or check main's gate run). If it exits non-zero (real findings), it is NOT a flake — file/dispatch a fix (allow-list the new tools in SKILL.md + the retro drift-set) instead of --admin-ing PRs past it. Only --admin when main's drift gate is GREEN and the PR's red is the load flake (0 skills/MCP diff).

⚠️ AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FLAKE HEURISTIC: I diagnosed this as a CI flake because "the diff touches 0 files under implementation/core/ and JVM core is green on main." THAT REASONING IS WRONG for cross-artefact conformance tests. The real touched surface was spec/009-Instrumentation.md (the catalogue), which the PR DID touch; a CORE test parses that shared spec file and compares it to a literal. So "diff has no core SOURCE files" does NOT imply "core gate cannot be affected" — a gate in artefact A can read a shared artefact-agnostic file (spec/009, Spec-Schemas, Conventions) that the diff edited. THE LOAD-BEARING TYPE MUTANT IS THE ONE THAT IS VALID IN A SIBLING CATEGORY (2026-08-06, rf2-am6qs, PR #7605).

Tightening three `:where` slots from `:any` to `:symbol`, the worker mutated four types at each slot — string, number, map, and a BARE KEYWORD. It named the keyword as the load-bearing one, and the reason is the generalisable part: OTHER CATEGORIES IN THE SAME CORPUS GENUINELY CARRY `:where :event`, `:where :flow-eval`, `:where :reactive`. So `:any` was not admitting arbitrary garbage — IT WAS ADMITTING A SPELLING THAT IS CORRECT ONE ROW OVER.

WHY THAT MATTERS FOR HOW YOU CHOOSE MUTANTS: a string/number/map mutant proves the slot rejects nonsense, which nobody was going to write. The keyword mutant proves it rejects THE MISTAKE SOMEONE WILL ACTUALLY MAKE — copying a neighbouring row. When picking negative cases for a schema slot, look for a value that is VALID IN AN ADJACENT DECLARATION and use that; the plainly-absurd mutants are the cheap ones and prove the least.

CONTROL SHAPE WORTH COPYING: each mutant had to be REJECTED by the shipped `:symbol` AND ACCEPTED by an `:any` control rebuilt from that slots OWN shipped schema, with a minimal base so only the `:where` type can be under test. Without the acceptance half you have not shown the TIGHTENING is what did the work rather than something else in the base.

AND THE CENSUS DID NOT TRANSFER, which is why it had to be redone per slot: the brief told the worker not to assume the previous slots answer carried, and the beads own call-site list was INCOMPLETE. Beyond the four sites it named there were five more through `require-frame-provider-target!` — `re-frame.freehand.substrate/frame-provider`, `v/->react`, `re-frame.ui/frame-provider` (twice, once via `require-scope-frame!`) and `re-frame.ui/->react`. A bead enumerating call sites is a starting point, never the population.

RESULT: all three tightened, no `:where` slot in Spec-Schemas.md is `:any` any more, and spec/009 needed NO edit because no row disagreed.

`git diff origin/main...<branch>` IS NOT A CONTAINMENT TEST, and it is tempting precisely
because it looks like a stronger one than `git cherry` (measured 2026-09-02, hygiene loop).

WHAT IT ACTUALLY ANSWERS: three-dot diffs from the MERGE BASE to the branch, so it reports
"what this branch changed since it forked" - not "does the trunk already have it". Under a
rebase-merge workflow those are entirely different questions, because the branch's commits land
on the trunk under NEW shas while the branch's own merge base stays where it was.

MEASURED, same eight branches, two instruments:
  - `git cherry origin/main <b>` read unmerged=0 (fully contained) for adapterswitch-oz7wr,
    twosmall-uuqek, http-issuance-rsv2n, wsreply-tb442 and xrayseam-7htk7 - all five with
    MERGED PRs.
  - `git diff origin/main...<b> --stat` returned large non-empty diffs for every one of those
    five: 242, 28, 253, 317 and 475 insertions respectively, xrayseam also showing 4717
    deletions.
A non-empty answer for a branch that is provably contained. Nothing errors; the numbers are
real; they are about the wrong question.

WHY IT MATTERS: the failure is fail-DANGEROUS in the useful direction. It never says "contained"
when a branch is not, so it cannot cause a wrong delete - but it says "not contained" for
branches that are, which keeps merged branches forever and, worse, makes a reader distrust the
cherry result that was right. I reached for it as a "secondary check that could clear a branch
honestly" and it would have done the opposite.

THE RULE STANDS UNCHANGED: patch-equivalence via `git cherry` is the containment test.
`-` is proof of containment; `+` is only the ABSENCE of proof, because patch identity is computed
over the diff INCLUDING context lines, so a sibling landing in neighbouring lines changes your
commit's identity. Keeping a `+` branch costs nothing; deleting a genuinely unmerged one costs
work. docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md section 5 "Branches" already states all of this correctly -
this memory is about the WRONG instrument I reached for, which that section does not name and
does not need to.

GENERAL SHAPE: an instrument can be right and answer a different question from the one you asked,
and the well-formed plausible number is what stops you noticing. Exercise a containment probe
against a branch you KNOW is merged before believing what it says about one you do not.

THE THREE-POINT CONTROL'S REFUSAL IS A DENOMINATOR-CLASS FAULT, NOT A ROW-CLASS ONE — diagnosed 2026-08-07 from 42 refused runs across two ensembles (rf2-8a746).

TWO INDEPENDENTLY FATAL HALVES.
(1) THE PREDICTION IS WRONG. 2.0101x is the statistic's expectation only if T is AFFINE in the dirty set over [1,200]. On the published TaskDuration clock it is not: marginal cost is 12.6 us/cell over [1,100] and 6.8 over [100,200]. True centre is 1.55x, which sits 2.6% above the band's own rejection edge of 1.5076 — so half of every run's blocks fall out the bottom ON A PERFECTLY QUIET BOX.
(2) THE STATISTIC IS ILL-CONDITIONED. Differencing away the constant also throws away the PEDESTAL that made relative noise look small, leaving a denominator of 1.25 ms carrying 0.60 ms of dispersion — 2.09 sigma from zero. Even with the centre corrected only ~60% of blocks land in band, and a strict every-one-of-18 rule turns that into P(pass) ~ 1e-4.

THE DECISIVE CONTROL EXPERIMENT: ctl3Layout — the SAME statistic on LayoutDuration over the IDENTICAL blocks and samples — reads 1.9681 / 1.9801 with marginals affine to 5% and no sign-gate firing in 756 blocks. So the arithmetic, door, tare and aggregation are all sound; the PAGE is not affine on the counter the row is published on. The non-layout half carries it: 7.13 -> 1.83 us/cell, a 3.9x collapse.

WHY ctl-2x SURVIVES AND ctl3 DOES NOT — this is the transferable lesson: ctl-2x's denominator is a LEVEL (the floor's whole tared reading, ~4.5 ms) carrying the same ~0.4 ms of estimator error, so 9% relative against ctl3's 48%; and its centre sits 20% above the edge against ctl3's 4%. Distance-above-edge and per-block scatter, raised to the strict-rule exponent, reproduce every pass rate in the programme. A DIFFERENCE-OF-DIFFERENCES DENOMINATOR IS THE FAULT. The invariance argument ('an additive constant cancels in each difference') is true of the LEVEL and is not the problem; what destroys it is the error in each arm's ESTIMATE of that level, which is independent between arms and ADDS. Measured corr(T(1),T(100)) = 0.43, so differencing removes only 40% of the denominator's variance where the argument assumes nearly all.

THE DEGENERATES ARE THE SAME FAULT, NOT A SECOND ONE: den=+0.019 ms -> 86x, den=+0.026 ms -> 114x, and in 9 of the 10 worst blocks T(1) is elevated — it enters BOTH differences, so it drives the smaller one to zero first.

RE-SITING THE POINTS DOES NOT RESCUE IT. Re-adjudicating the same committed blocks at 100/200/300 (above the knee) gives 1.9975 / 2.0777 against a prediction of 2.0000 — the affine premise holds there — but den halves to 0.70 ms while its IQR does not, and in-band blocks FALL from 47% to 33%. Span the knee and the centre is wrong; avoid it and the denominator is gone.

THE ONLY CONSTRUCTION THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS has a denominator that is a LEVEL rather than a difference. That is a decision about what the lane measures and belongs to the operator.

THE HARNESS DOES NOT SIGNAL A CAPPED TOOL CALL — IT BACKGROUNDS IT, AND THE GATE KEEPS RUNNING (measured 2026-08-07 on rf2-ketqy, PR #7642). CORRECTED: an earlier version of this memory said the harness kills the parent and orphans the child. That model was wrong and the fix built on it would not have worked.

MEASURED, not inferred. Capped at 90s, a backgrounded 'sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' kept running after the tool returned — its log grew 41822 to 49220 bytes and two more stages completed. TaskStop behaves identically: reports success, kills nothing, fires no trap. So there is no signal, and a signal handler alone can never see this case.

TWO FURTHER MEASUREMENTS THAT KILL THE OBVIOUS FIXES:
- 'kill the child PROCESS GROUP' would kill the CALLER. Every child shares the caller's PGID under Git Bash.
- bash DEFERS a trapped signal until the foreground child returns — measured at 22 seconds (SIGTERM at t+3s to a script running 'sleep 25'; handler ran at t+25s). So even when a signal IS delivered, a trap is late.
- 'taskkill /F /T' is silently mangled by Git Bash into 'taskkill F:/ ...'. Behind the customary '|| true' it is a NO-OP that looks like it worked. Needs MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 and MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*'; Cygwin ignores both.

THE DAMAGE the orphan does: it keeps writing to the SAME log as the relaunch (two writers, NUL-riddled output), and its 'npm run test:cljs' unlinks out/node-test.js underneath the next run's per-namespace isolation sweep, which then reds with 'the bundle changed on disk during the sweep' and MODULE_NOT_FOUND. That red is the sweep working correctly and is indistinguishable from an isolation regression in the worker's own diff. The culprit java.exe is invisible to 'ps -ef' entirely.

THE SHIPPED REMEDY (PR #7642): a trap for the genuinely-signalled cases PLUS the same reap invoked at the START of the next run — the only moment it can act, because the path that actually bites delivers no signal. Not a lock: the second run never waits or refuses.

DISCRIMINATORS, unchanged and still the useful part: LAUNCH failure ('Command failed:') = spawn contention. 'changed on disk during the sweep' = a live orphan; kill it and re-run quiet. ASSERTION mismatch = real.

GATE LOGS MUST NOT GO TO /tmp UNDER MULTI-AGENT LOAD — /tmp is SHARED across concurrently running worker agents on this box, so one worker gate log silently OVERWRITES another. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.112 SSR worker, which nearly shipped a false green.

THE MECHANISM: worker A runs "npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate-browser.log 2>&1". Worker B, running concurrently in a DIFFERENT worktree, writes the same path. A then reads a log that is really B run. In the observed case the log EXIT=0 and reported "0 failures" — every number looked right. The ONLY tell was the shadow-cljs banner naming the WRONG worktree (pilot-react-interop-46 instead of the reader own).

WHY THIS IS NASTY: it defeats the standard exit-code discipline. The capture-to-a-file-and-echo-the-exit-code rule was adopted precisely because piping into tail/grep discards the runner exit status. But if the FILE ITSELF belongs to another agent, the captured exit code is ALSO another agent — a correct technique reading the wrong evidence. Both the summary AND the exit code agree, and both are about someone else run.

THE FIX, now standard in every dispatch brief: write gate logs to the SESSION SCRATCHPAD or a worktree-local path, never a bare /tmp name. e.g.
  <gate> > "$WT/gate-<name>.log" 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -30 "$WT/gate-<name>.log"
And VERIFY OWNERSHIP: the shadow-cljs "config:" banner line names the worktree whose build ran. Grep it and confirm it is YOURS before believing any number in that file. That is the cheap proof.

MAYOR NOTE: my own standing gate-discipline boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log". That instruction is now known-unsafe whenever more than one worker runs at a time, which is the normal case at saturation. Update the boilerplate; do not keep handing workers a colliding path.

GENERAL FORM: this joins the roster of ways green has meant nothing-was-measured here. The others are about a check that could not fail; this one is about a check that MEASURED SOMEBODY ELSE. When an assertion rests on an artefact OUTSIDE your process (a shared temp file, a shared port, a shared cache), ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read.

THE TRACKER CONTENDS WITH THE FLEET, AND THE MAYOR IS ONE OF THE CONTENDERS (2026-09-01, mayor session 9a).

WHAT HAPPENED: at six concurrent workers, three of the mayors own tracker commands hit the two-minute harness ceiling in one tick -- a beads-checkpoint export, a combined ready-plus-JSON listing, and a plain bd ready. The same commands take seconds when the fleet is idle. Nothing was broken; the Dolt database was simply serving six workers running bd show, bd history --json and bd close while the mayor asked for a full listing.

WHY IT MISLEADS: a timeout on a tracker read presents exactly like a tracker fault. The temptation is to re-run harder, or to conclude the export is stuck and reach for a recovery that rewrites state. Both are wrong and the second is dangerous. The checkpoint that appeared to hang had in fact COMPLETED -- exit 0, confirmed later -- and the state was already consistent.

THE CHEAP VERIFICATION THAT DOES NOT TOUCH THE DATABASE: compare row counts. git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl piped to wc -l against wc -l on the working file. Equal counts plus a clean git status means the export is consistent and no checkpoint is owed, and neither read costs the database anything. That answered in one second what a re-run could not answer in three minutes.

PRACTICAL RULES: (1) at saturation, ask the tracker for ONE thing per command -- a combined listing plus a JSON dump in one shell is two queries and times out where each alone succeeds. (2) Treat a tracker timeout as CONTENTION until proven otherwise, never as corruption. (3) Never respond to an apparently-hung checkpoint by restoring an older export from git history: the Dolt database is the source of truth and that would time-travel the tracker.

GENERAL FORM: this is the gate-mechanics wedge rule -- a gate heavy enough that two cannot coexist wedges rather than fails -- applied to the TRACKER rather than to a build, and with the mayor as one of the competing processes rather than an observer of them. Saturating the fleet slows the instrument the mayor uses to decide what to dispatch next.

THE TRACKER SILENTLY REVERTS CLOSURES TO OPEN, REPEATEDLY, AND ONLY A PER-TICK AUDIT CATCHES IT (observed twice on 2026-08-07: 2 beads, then 5).

WHAT HAPPENS. Beads closed with a verified reason read OPEN again a few ticks later, with no action of mine in between. First occurrence reverted rf2-2rtt6.56 and rf2-2rtt6.62. Second reverted rf2-kqac1, rf2-drpa3.182.12, rf2-2rtt6.103, rf2-ketqy and rf2-cvvb7 — every one of which had a PR I could verify MERGED at the moment of re-closing.

WHY VERIFYING AT CLOSE TIME IS NOT ENOUGH. I verified each of these CLOSED immediately after closing. They reverted anyway. So the audit has to run EVERY tick against the full list of everything closed this session, not just the recent ones — the second wave included beads closed many ticks earlier.

HOW TO AUDIT SO THE AUDIT ITSELF DOES NOT LIE: key on the STABLE BEAD ID, never an internal row UUID (a re-import regenerates UUIDs and a UUID-keyed diff reports phantom losses), and read the STATUS FIELD rather than grepping the whole record (the word 'open' appears inside titles). 'bd show <id> | head -1 | grep -oE CLOSED|OPEN|DEFERRED' is enough.

WHAT MAKES RE-CLOSING CHEAP: the close REASON is the durable artefact. If it names the PR number and the concrete evidence, re-closing is a thirty-second job of verifying 'gh pr view <n> --json state' still reads MERGED and pasting the reason back. If the original close said only 'done', a revert costs a full re-investigation. Write close reasons for the revert you have not had yet.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE PROJECT KEEPS FINDING IN ITS OWN INSTRUMENTS: a state that reports success while the underlying fact has moved. Treat the tracker as untrusted for closure state, exactly as you treat a statusCheckRollup.

CHECKING WHETHER A WORKER COMMITTED .beads: a TREE diff manufactures a false positive. Ask the commit, not the trees. Measured 2026-08-22.

WHAT HAPPENED. Worker sliceclock's branch read "git diff --stat origin/main f77316d601" -> ".beads/issues.jsonl | 7 +----". My first reading was a durability violation: the one thing a worker must never commit, with a whole CLAUDE.md section and two recorded incidents behind it.

IT WAS BASE DRIFT. The worker branched at cc563fd8fb and origin/main had moved 2 commits ahead -- my own bead checkpoints. "git diff A B" compares TREES, so it reports the worker's older .beads snapshot as a difference the worker introduced. The commit touched ONE file, a 329-line pre-registration doc.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, run both directions on the same sha:
    git diff --stat origin/main SHA -- .beads/   -> 7 lines (3+/4-)   WRONG QUESTION
    git show --stat SHA -- .beads/               -> empty             RIGHT QUESTION

WHY THIS IS MORE THAN ORDINARY GIT LITERACY: the false positive fires on EVERY worker branch once the mayor has checkpointed twice, which is every branch older than about twenty minutes. So the natural check is not merely imprecise, it is reliably wrong IN THE ACCUSING DIRECTION -- and repeated false accusations train you to stop reading the one signal that catches the real thing.

SAME FAMILY AS the ahead-count trap the hygiene loop names: this repo rebases, so ancestry and ahead-count are both wrong, and patch-equivalence via git cherry is the fix. Both are TREE-COMPARISON answers to a question about AUTHORSHIP. When the question is "what did this commit do", ask the commit.

TRUE-CONCLUSION-DEAD-REASONING — a documented defect class, seen twice on 2026-07-19 and subtler than plain drift.

DEFINITION: a document states a correct conclusion resting on an inference that has since been invalidated. Nothing looks wrong — the conclusion checks out — so a reviewer confirms the conclusion and moves on. But the NEXT reader follows the stated reason, finds it false, and "corrects" the conclusion in the wrong direction. The rot is in the justification, not the claim.

INSTANCE 1 (rf2-0qsp5, #6386): spec/005-StateMachines.md derived :rf.machine/join-dispatch target protection FROM its REJECT-tier membership. Worker verdict: "The conclusion is true; the inference is precisely what the split invalidated." Preserving the reasoning would have re-merged the two fx policies the next time anyone extended it.

INSTANCE 2 (rf2-vxgfnd.188, #6391, worse): the canonical W1 rule table declared SEVEN verbs unavailable — ui/adapter, local, effect, ui/event, ui/handler, ui/render-fn, ui/dispatch-fn. ALL SEVEN SHIP, exported from ui.cljc. MIG-16/17/18 "this gates" conclusions stayed TRUE, but the reason inverted: from "the verb has not shipped yet" to "the decision belongs to the human". Retiering alone would have let the next reader check whether S3 shipped, find it had, and UNGATE RULES THAT MUST STAY GATED. The worker rewrote the reasons and left the tiers.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when reconciling a document against code, verify the DERIVATION, not just the conclusion. Ask "if the stated reason were false, would the conclusion change?" If yes and the reason IS false, the conclusion is correct by luck and the next edit will break it.
HOW TO FIX IT: rewrite the reason, keep the conclusion. Do NOT retier/restate/delete the conclusion just because its stated basis collapsed.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY: a bead PREDICTION can be wrong too. rf2-vxgfnd.188 own preliminary map predicted six rule retirements; ALL SIX were refuted against shipped code (one, R-X7, had NO DETECTOR AT ALL and became a new rule; R-S3 was missing the cursor WRITE side). A worker trusting the bead analysis would have deleted six live rules. The bead is authoritative about WHAT TO DO, never about WHAT IS TRUE — always re-verify its factual claims against the code.

DC-09 TWO-CLOCK ENVELOPE, MEASURED (rf2-drpa3.182.12, PR #7179, HeadlessChrome 147, dev build :optimizations :none goog.DEBUG true). Sustained semantic rate ~190/s at 0 dirty siblings, ~49/s at 200. 60 Hz crossing is comfortable to 50 siblings and breaks between 50 and 200; 120 Hz never clears p95 in a dev build; 240 Hz is unreachable because the BROWSER stops offering first, not because the framework refuses.

THREE STRUCTURAL FACTS worth reusing before re-measuring anything on this surface:
1. PEAK BACKLOG IS 1, at every offered rate and both sibling loads, with rf/dispatch (async). The setInterval callback IS the main thread, so overload manifests as OFFER LOSS at the host, never as a growing queue; latency stays bounded at one crossing and the settlement tail stayed <=5.4 ms even at 240 Hz requested against a 20 ms crossing. This is why no throttle/debounce/coalesce verb is warranted — the browser already back-pressures. CAVEAT: measured with a TIMER. Coalesced pointermove / pointerrawupdate bursts can deliver several events to one task and are the only shape that could exceed backlog 1; do not quote this for raw-pointer bursts without re-measuring.
2. THE EVENT HALF IS FLAT, THE COMMIT HALF SCALES. Splitting the window at the instant dispatch-sync returns: :event-ms (router, interceptors, reducer, app-db install, 300 subscription notifications) is 3-4 ms whether 1 or 201 cells moved; :commit-ms goes 0.4 -> 17.5 ms at ~0.085 ms per dirtied cell. An expensive crossing is expensive in React, not in re-frame — attribute before optimising.
3. WHERE YOU READ THE SUB COSTS MORE THAN HOW MUCH CHANGED. Reading a high-rate value in a view that ALSO builds a collection costs a CONSTANT 40-44 ms more than reading it one boundary down — independent of payload size (Vega 96 leaves 45.6->5.0 ms, Spread 900 leaves 63->18.8 ms) — while moving THREE FEWER DOM nodes. Same 'one leaf of app-db changed', 8-19x apart. Guidance: if a high-rate value must cross into app-db, read its subscription at the boundary that USES it.

EQUALITY IS FREE AND FREEHAND ALREADY ELIDES. Fresh-but-rf=-equal is indistinguishable from stable-reference (0.2-0.3 ms at 96 leaves, 0.4-0.6 at 900) and repaints nothing; a full structural walk of a 900-leaf map is under a millisecond. Behavior :update ran exactly 52 times for 52 changed crossings and ZERO times for stable or fresh-equal ones — elision is VALUE-based (rf=), not identity-based. Proved by counting, not by reading the runtime. No equality hook is warranted.

INSTRUMENT NOTES for the next perf bead in a browser:
* A COMPUTED-DURATION POSITIVE CONTROL DOUBLES AS A CONTENTION METER. A busy-wait of exactly 4.00 ms riding in every cell read p50 4.0 with overshoot never above 0.3 ms — which is what let the numbers be published without the usual 'other agents were running' caveat. On a loaded box it would have said so in every table simultaneously. Cheap, and it retires the standing wall-clock-is-unreliable worry per-run instead of per-repo.
* A COMPUTED-SIZE CONTROL CATCHES A KNOB THAT DOES NOT TURN. Predicted DOM mutation counts (host-only 1, fresh-equal 0, one-leaf k+1) matched measured at all 15 mode x rung combinations, and the driven arm independently reproduced exactly 201.0 per crossing. MutationObserver.takeRecords() answers SYNCHRONOUSLY, which is the only reason it can be read inside a flushSync-bracketed window.
* AN ARM WHOSE POINT IS THAT NOTHING CHANGES CANNOT BE VERIFIED BY NOTHING CHANGING. The fresh-equal arm is verified at the STORE (reference moved AND value equal), because an arm that silently did nothing would otherwise be the fastest arm in the table.
* ROTATING ARM ORDER FOUND A REAL FAULT: the first equality arm built its config from a FIXED generation, so a fresh-equal crossing following a one-leaf one was equal to nothing and failed its own read-back in 7 of every 10 samples. Build the comparison value from WHATEVER IS CURRENTLY IN THE STORE, and build it OUTSIDE the timed window.
* BOTH LADDER ORDERS: the only non-overlapping range tracked a monotonic round-1-to-4 warm-up present at EVERY rung in BOTH orders — drift, not order. Three warm-up samples per cell did not fully absorb first-round JIT.
* prov/result REFUSES a record with no revision, and the :browser-test lane has none. Do not route around it: catch the refusal and publish :d021 :not-release-evidence with the reason, so the same rows can run in the ordinary gate AND in the focused bench build with RF2_REVISION set.
* Chrome clamps performance.now() to 100 us. A sub-0.1 ms arm reads 0.0 and its honest report is 'under 0.1 ms', never 'free'.

TWO FREEHAND ADAPTER FACTS the rf2-vo8fb conformance found that reading could not (PR #6948, 2026-07-25):

1. A CLJS NAMESPACE AND A VAR CANNOT SHARE A JS PATH. The bead specified an internal ns 're-frame.freehand.adapter' alongside the published var 'v/adapter'. The compiler emits :ns-var-clash and ONE OF THE TWO SILENTLY READS nil — observed live: v/adapter installed fine while the test namespace's own reference read nil, so the fixture installed nothing and every assertion failed for the wrong reason. Homed at re-frame.freehand.substrate instead (the same split the donor arrived at). The ruled AUTHORING name is unaffected. Generalise: never name an internal namespace the same as a published var in its parent ns.

2. ADAPTER DISPOSAL MUST BE REFERENCE-RELEASE, NOT FRAME DESTROY, and the bug was CLASSPATH-DEPENDENT. Core's claim-installed-for-dispose! sets :disposing? and closes public delegation BEFORE calling the adapter's :dispose-adapter!, so every read-container inside that window raises :rf.error/adapter-disposed — and a frame's destroy recipe reads the runtime-db container. On a classpath WITHOUT the machines artefact that read IS the fallback path, so the defect was latent for some apps and fatal for others. Correct shape: drain-live-roots! releases claims + the frame REFERENCE + the ViewCells, while v/unmount! on a live adapter still destroys a root-owned frame; both share one tear-down-root! differing only in that function. The drain is the safety net for a FORGOTTEN root outliving the adapter, not a substitute for orderly teardown. Conformance carries two rows of different strength rather than one overclaiming row.

TWO GENERALISABLE FINDINGS FROM THE CI-COVERAGE WORK (2026-07-26, PR #7068).

1. WHEN AN INCLUSIVE PATH FILTER WOULD BE THE WHOLE REPOSITORY, DELETE THE FILTER — DO NOT EXTEND IT. rf2-kx06s asked to add two omitted files to a workflow push-path filter. THE GENERAL RULE: before adding a path to a filter, ask WHAT THE JOB ACTUALLY READS. If the read universe is unbounded, the filter is not incomplete — it is WRONG IN KIND, and every future addition to it is a false sense of coverage. THE 'TWO HEAVY GATES CANNOT COEXIST' RULE APPLIES TO YOUR OWN CONCURRENT RUNS, NOT ONLY TO PEER WORKERS (2026-08-15 18:52 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/retire-unwire (rf2-0yp7w.3/.5, PR #8308, merged). Its spine died in 'CLJS node integration' with NO TEST SUMMARY — a clean build followed by a bare crash. Cause: it ran npm run test:script-helpers CONCURRENTLY WITH THE SPINE, and those bench-clock tests spawn their own shadow-cljs lane builds against the SAME .shadow-cljs and out/. Two shadow-cljs processes, one cache.

Run alone: 13918 tests / 70176 assertions / 0 failures, PASS fast PR spine, captured exit 0.

ITS OWN WORDS, and this is the correction to my briefing: 'The two heavy gates cannot coexist rule applies to the spine itself, not just to peer workers — I'd been applying it only to other people's runs.' I brief that rule as a fence against PEERS. It is really a fence against CONCURRENCY, whoever owns it. A worker running two of its own gates in parallel to save wall-clock produces exactly the same corruption, and the failure is a bare crash with no summary — indistinguishable from a real regression until you re-run serially.

SO THE BRIEFED RULE SHOULD READ: run heavy gates ONE AT A TIME, including your own. If a run dies with no summary line, suspect cache contention before suspecting the change. This composes with the already-recorded rule that a killed shadow-cljs run leaves a CORRUPT .shadow-cljs producing phantom ReferenceErrors in unrelated namespaces — same cache, two ways to poison it.

A SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME TASK, worth its own line: A REBASE FORCE-PUSH MAKES THE SURFACE CLASSIFIER FALL BACK TO RUNNING EVERYTHING. The CI log reads 'base ref dead0000... does not resolve to a commit. Classifying as --all ... Usual cause: a force-push'. The fallback is FAIL-SAFE and correct — it errs toward more coverage — but it widens exposure to unrelated flaky jobs. So after a force-push, expect jobs your diff cannot reach, and DISCRIMINATE before treating one as yours.

HOW THAT WORKER DISCRIMINATED, which is the model: JS harness self-tests was red on clock_exit_path.test.cjs, a bench-clock witness in implementation/hicasso/ that its branch never touches. It changed NOTHING, on four independent confirmations — (1) the diff cannot reach the file, grep returns 0; (2) the eight most recent test.yml runs on main are green; (3) green locally on its branch, captured exit 0; (4) green under the exact npm script CI ran. A re-run confirmed: 83 SUCCESS / 17 SKIPPED / 0 failures. FOUR CONFIRMATIONS BEFORE DECLARING A FAILURE FOREIGN is the right bar; one is not.

TWO MAYOR ERRORS THE rf2-n4by4 WORKER CAUGHT, BOTH ABOUT MY BRIEFS (2026-07-26).

ERROR 1 — I SILENTLY RESOLVED A RULING THE BEAD HAD EXPLICITLY RESERVED. rf2-n4by4 said in as many words: "ENFORCEMENT NEEDS A RULING — do not pick one silently", and listed (a) mark-and-refuse versus (b) leave it to the spec. My brief supplied (a) as though it were settled. The worker followed the brief and FLAGGED THE DIVERGENCE, noting that per my own standing instruction the bead is authoritative over the brief.

That is the sharpest form of a mistake I make often: I put "the bead is authoritative over this brief, and tell me if they disagree" into every dispatch, which is right — and then write briefs that quietly overwrite the bead. The instruction only works if I read the bead for RESERVED QUESTIONS before writing the brief, not just for facts. A bead that says "needs a ruling" is addressed TO ME, and the honest brief either states the ruling AS a ruling ("I am ruling (a), here is why") or asks the worker to return the options. Silently picking one means the tracker never records that a decision was made, and the next reader cannot tell a considered choice from an oversight.

THE RULING ITSELF STANDS, and the reason is worth keeping: the failure is SILENT — :className arriving as :class is a DIFFERENT React prop, so the component gets no class and nothing reports it. Guard warranted. And the cost turned out near zero: the author spelling rides in METADATA, refused at one seam, with =, hash and pr-str all ignoring it, so the legal element use pays nothing. But I could not have known the cost when I ruled, which is exactly why the ruling should have been visible.

ERROR 2 — MY COLLISION WARNING WAS A GREP, AND TWO OF FOUR HITS WERE FALSE POSITIVES. I warned that four test files contained both "spread" and "defhost" and might pin the accepting behaviour, so the flips had to ride in the same PR. NONE of the four pinned it. Two matched on "SPREADSHEET" and "SPREADJS". One already asserted the CORRECT behaviour (an earlier PR had landed that flip). The fourth was the digest gate, whose spread-forms row points at an element-level fixture.

So a plausible-sounding hazard cost the worker a verification pass it did not need. The mutually-invalidating-test rule is real and has reddened the trunk before — but a bare token grep is not evidence FOR it. Before warning about a witness collision, check whether the match is the CONSTRUCT or merely the SUBSTRING, and whether the assertion pins the old behaviour or the new. Sixteenth instance this session of the same underlying error: a cheap proxy standing in for the real question.

AND THE FINDING MY BRIEF SHOULD HAVE CARRIED, which the worker found instead: THE REFUSAL MUST RUN BEFORE THE EXACTNESS LAW. A spread canonicalises "class" into the keyword :class, so inexact-host-prop-names sees a CLEAN call — exactness would PASS and the corruption would be the answer. Ordering, not presence, is what makes that guard work. Generalise: when adding a check to a pipeline of checks, ask what the earlier checks NORMALISE, because a normaliser upstream can launder exactly the defect you are trying to catch.

TWO DIFFERENT NUMBERS ARE BOTH CALLED "THE BAND" AND I CONFLATED THEM IN A BRIEF (2026-08-14).

THE TWO:
  1. THE PR CHECK COUNT — what `gh pr checks <n>` returns. Measured settled values today: 92, 93, 94, 95. It VARIES WITH THE DIFF'S SURFACE because most jobs are surface-gated. This is what clause 1 of the merge criterion means by "this repo's band", and it is a RANGE, not a value.
  2. THE FAST-SPINE GAP — what `scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py --list` reports: required CI checks the local fast spine does not decide. Measured 96 all day. This is what every dispatch brief quotes.

I wrote "the band is 95" into a brief meaning number 1, and the worker measured number 2 and found 96. Neither of us was wrong about our own number; the WORD was ambiguous. From now on: say PR CHECK COUNT or FAST-SPINE GAP, never "the band".

AND THE WORKER'S ACTUAL FINDING IS BETTER THAN EITHER NUMBER. My brief asserted "adding a job takes the gap N to N+1". THAT IS FALSE AS A RULE. A job whose checker the SPINE ALREADY RUNS through an npm chain adds NO new gap — the gap counts what the spine cannot decide, and the spine already decides it. So the figure holds at 96 across the addition.

BUT IT HOLDS ONLY IF THE SPINE_LANES ENTRY LANDS WITH THE JOB. The worker proved that entry load-bearing by rebuilding the map with the lane removed in memory: WITH the lane 96, WITHOUT it 98 — because the job has TWO steps, not one. The same is true of the three sibling jobs, which is why none of them moved the figure either.

SO THE RULE TO BRIEF IS: adding a CI job changes the fast-spine gap only if the spine cannot already decide its checker. If it can, add the SPINE_LANES entry in the same PR and the figure is unchanged — and if you omit that entry the figure rises by the job's STEP COUNT, not by one.

TWO VACUOUS-PASS TRAPS WHEN MOVING TESTS UNDER A PRODUCTION GATE (rf2-d2841, PR #7142). Both make a suite report GREEN while proving nothing, and neither is visible in a passing run. (1) A NEGATIVE trace assertion — `empty?` / `not-any?` over a trace ring — passes automatically under `-Dre-frame.debug=false` because the ring is empty BY DESIGN. It must move INSIDE the dev-only guard with the positive assertions, not be left outside as 'posture-independent'. Same for any 'no :rf.error/... was emitted' read. (2) A namespace that is 100% dev instrumentation (trace-listener-*, trace-test, db-pending-trace-test, sub-dispose-trace-test) has NO semantic residue: guarding it wholesale and removing its exclusion-roster line makes the lane report green for a namespace that EXECUTED NOTHING. Those need a var-level tag (`-e :requires-debug`) so the runner skips them explicitly rather than running an empty shell. GENERAL RULE: when a gate's whole point is that instrumentation is absent, any assertion whose subject is that same absence is worthless in that posture — check what each assertion would do if its subject simply never existed.

A TWO-VALUED PROBE CONFLATES 'REJECTED' WITH 'CRASHED', SO TWO VALIDATORS THAT BOTH EXPLODE AGREE (rf2-dhl4d, 2026-08-03).

THE MECHANISM, and it is the best fail-open diagnosis this project has produced. A viz<->engine parity ratchet compared two validators by asking each "do you accept this definition?" — a BOOLEAN. On CLJS, engine-accepts? wrapped the call in (catch :default ... false). So when the engine raised a host ClassCastException on a non-Named key, the probe recorded FALSE — indistinguishable from a clean, documented rejection. The viz side crashed the same way. TWO VALIDATORS THAT BOTH EXPLODE AGREE, and the ratchet stayed green over a live crash in a security gate.

THE FIX IS THE SHAPE, NOT THE CASE: make the probe THREE-VALUED — :accept / :reject / :host-throw — plus a definition-validation-is-total assertion. Proof it now sees the divergence: (engine :reject, viz :host-throw).

GENERALISE IT. Any comparison harness that reduces its subjects to a boolean, or that catches broadly and maps the catch onto one of the two legitimate outcomes, is fail-open BY CONSTRUCTION — parity ratchets, differential tests, golden-file comparators, A/B benchmark agreement checks. Ask of every such harness: WHAT DOES IT RECORD WHEN THE SUBJECT CRASHES? If the answer is "the same thing as one of the normal outcomes", it cannot see the failure class it exists to catch.

ALSO FROM THE SAME BEAD, a distinct defect class worth naming separately: THE ERROR PATH ITSELF THREW. A (pr-str offending) in the diagnostic message reached an arbitrary object's toString, so a throwing-toString key DESTROYED THE FAILURE BEING DESCRIBED. A validator that rejects correctly but explodes while explaining why is still broken on hostile input. Exercise the diagnostic path with the same forged corpus as the validation path.

AND: the bead named ONE defect site; there were TWO (an inline copy elsewhere in the same file). A worker fixing only the cited line would have shipped a half-fix that passed its own new test. Grep for the PATTERN, not the line number.

MECHANICAL NOTE FOR WHOEVER WRITES THE NEXT MEMORY: do not pass prose containing backticks to bd through a shell double-quoted string — bash runs the backticked spans as command substitution and silently mangles the text. Write the body to a file and pass it with "$(cat file)", or avoid backticks entirely. I did exactly this while recording this memory, and a worker hit the same trap earlier the same day leaving a stray file in the mayor checkout.

THE RULE: WHEN A BLOCKER CLEARS, RE-DERIVE THE BLOCKED BEAD'S ANSWER FROM THE POST-BLOCKER TREE. A bead blocked on a decision was, by construction, written BEFORE that decision. The likeliest thing the decision changed is the very thing the bead was waiting to record. Treat 'unblocked' as 'now re-plannable', never as 'now executable as written'.

COROLLARY FOR BRIEFS: never paraphrase a technical clause out of a bead into a brief as if it were established. Either quote it as the bead's CLAIM and require verification, or verify it yourself first. My paraphrase inherited the bead's staleness and amplified it, because a brief reads as the mayor's instruction rather than as a bead's assertion.

Untracking a gitignored-but-force-added path via 'git rm --cached' in a SEPARATE worker worktree then merging to main DELETES the files from the mayor checkout's disk on pull — because the resulting commit is a plain file-deletion, and 'git pull' removes working-tree copies of files a commit deletes (the --cached keep-on-disk only protected the worker's tree, which didn't have the files). Recovery: 'git show <pre-untrack-sha>:<path> > <path>' to restore each file as untracked local content (they're gitignored so git ignores them). Better approach next time: do the 'git rm --cached' + commit in the SAME checkout that holds the files (but the mayor hook forbids that), OR restore the files immediately after the untrack merge.

BACKLOG DISCIPLINE (mayor): validating an item against its own text, its dependencies, or a sibling ruling is NOT validating it. Check the TREE. Measured 2026-09-01, twice in one session, both caught by a worker rather than by me:

THE CHEAP SWEEP that finds this class in one command, worth running in the backlog-reread loop rather than per-item:

It surfaced NINE open beads with merged commits citing them in one pass.

BUT A COMMIT-SUBJECT MATCH IS NOT A CLOSE. It is a pointer to go and read the tree. Some hits are partial work, and some are the very change the item was filed AGAINST — rf2-0o5dx has a merged commit citing it while its title says the defect STILL stands, so closing on the match would repeat the original error one level up. Related: a bead's stated GATES can be wrong — all three tools/{xray,machines-viz,story} :test aliases are JVM (re-frame.test-quiet.runner) and cover no .cljs file; the deciding lanes are npm run test:cljs and test:browser from implementation/.

VERIFY A CONFLICT RESOLUTION STRUCTURALLY, NOT BY EYE — prove the prefix relationship (2026-08-14, rf2-guidepin worker).

THE SITUATION. Two branches both appended a checker to the same npm chain in implementation/package.json. Either wholesale resolution shipped a real defect: --theirs silently un-gates the incoming worker's whole deliverable, --ours drops a gate that now has a required CI job and reds main. Both changes were correct and independent.

THE TECHNIQUE THAT MADE THE MERGE PROVABLE rather than plausible:

  main chain: 12 commands   resolved: 14 commands
  resolved.startswith(main) == True
  delta == the two commands I added, and nothing else

That is a PROOF that nothing of main's was dropped. On a fourteen-command single line, "looks right" is not evidence — the eye cannot reliably diff a long shell chain, and that is exactly the shape where a wholesale resolution hides.

GENERALISE IT: after resolving any conflict in a LIST — an npm chain, a needs: array, a roster, a require block, a nav section — assert the relationship rather than reading it. Either side's content must appear in the result; compute the set difference and check it is exactly what you intended to add. A resolution you can state as an equation is one you can defend.

TWO COMPANION CHECKS FROM THE SAME PASS, both cheap and both catching real risk:
  - `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD | grep ^.github/` returning EMPTY proved the branch never touched workflows, which made a whole class of suspected conflict structurally impossible. Establish what your branch CANNOT have conflicted on before hunting for what it did.
  - It confirmed main had NOT touched the guide tree, so its 188 digest rows were still valid. A guide edit on main would have staled every one of them silently. After a rebase, re-check the inputs your gate pins, not just that your gate passes.

AND RE-RUN GATES AFTER RESOLVING, INCLUDING THE DISCRIMINATION. A green taken on a tree that no longer exists is not evidence. That worker re-proved its digest gate by inserting one character and taking a red naming the block, then hash-verifying the restore.

VERIFY A SABOTAGE RESTORE WITH git hash-object, NOT sha256sum - CRLF TRANSLATION MAKES A CORRECT RESTORE LOOK FAILED (2026-08-13, found by the navfence-cluster worker).

The method's rule is right: verify a restore by hashing the bytes, never by reading git diff, because 'unchanged' and 'never applied' produce the same diff. But the INSTRUMENT matters and sha256sum is the wrong one on this checkout.

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker planted a fault, ran the gate red, restored, and 'sha256sum -c' FAILED on a restore that was actually correct. Git's LF->CRLF conversion rewrote the working file during a rebase checkout AFTER the baseline hash was taken. The bytes on disk genuinely differed; the CONTENT did not.

USE git hash-object against the committed blob instead. It normalises line endings the same way git does, so it compares what git compares. Both reads agreed at c37e900... where sha256sum had disagreed.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a false 'restore failed' is not merely noise. The worker's next move is to re-apply the restore, or to doubt the whole sabotage result - and the sabotage result is the deliverable. An instrument that misreports is the same defect class as the hollow gate it was being used to prove.

Pair it with the other half already recorded: a hash proves the SOURCE changed, not that the RUNTIME saw it. A fault outside the build's module graph compiles into nothing and the sabotage run comes back green for an unrelated reason.

A STATUS AUDIT KEYED ON A BARE ID STRING READS ANOTHER RECORD'S STATUS (2026-08-13, my own tool misreporting).

WHAT HAPPENED: verifying that five beads had really been deferred, I grepped the committed export for the bead id in quotes:

  grep '"rf2-hic-092"' .beads/issues.jsonl | grep -o '"status":"[a-z]*"' | head -1

It reported rf2-hic-092 as CLOSED. The bead was in fact DEFERRED - bd show said so, with the deferral date. The grep had matched the FIRST LINE CONTAINING that id string, which was a DIFFERENT bead whose dependency list or note text mentions rf2-hic-092. I then read that other record's status as this bead's.

Four of the five happened to be right, which is worse than all five being wrong: a spot-check would have passed.

THE FIX IS ONE CHARACTER OF PRECISION - key on the id FIELD:

  grep '"id":"rf2-hic-092"'

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE METHOD ALREADY NAMES. mayor-hygiene.md warns that gh pr list --search 'head:<branch>' substring-matches and returns a SIBLING branch's PR, so you must ask for headRefName and compare equality yourself. This is that rule in a second place. The general form: AN ID IS NOT A SEARCH TERM. Any tracker, VCS or CI query that accepts a bare string will substring-match it, and the record it returns will look entirely plausible because it is a real record - just not yours.

AND NOTE WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILED. It reported a live bead as closed, i.e. it manufactured a false alarm rather than hiding a real one. Reversed - reporting a closed bead as open - it would have sent a worker at finished work. Both are available from the same bug.

THE DISCIPLINE: a verification tool that misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch. Cross-check the export against the database (bd show) rather than trusting either alone; here the disagreement between the two is what exposed the grep.

WHAT HAPPENED, and it is a two-layer miss. rf2-r7zq blocked rf2-5gka on a "target-side advance-clock!".
  - LAYER 1, which a previous mayor got wrong: closing the bead because SOMETHING named advance-clock! had landed. It had — three of them — but all were the wrong KIND (a test-kit harness facility, plus two other substrates' runtimes). That mayor recorded afterwards that "the property I verified and praised is exactly what makes it unusable".
  - LAYER 2, which I then got wrong: I verified the kind carefully, avoided layer 1, wrote a detailed note proving none of the three served — AND NEVER ASKED WHETHER THE REQUIREMENT STILL STOOD.
