title: bug(machines-viz): SCXML import turns executable-content elements into fake states
description:
## Scope

Correct only the `tools/machines-viz` SCXML import boundary so non-state SCXML children cannot become re-frame2 `:states` entries and `scxml->spec` never returns a structurally invalid machine definition. Preserve the public `spec->scxml` / `scxml->spec` signatures, the supported topology mapping, the existing regex-reader posture, the id codec, and exporter round-trips.

## Correctness finding

`scxml->spec` silently turns ordinary SCXML executable-content elements into fake machine states. `group-children-by-state` says it pairs only `<state>` / `<final>` blocks, but after special-casing `<transition>` its `:self` and `:start` branches accept every tag. `consume-transitions` leaves non-transition elements such as `<onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<datamodel>`, `<data>`, `<invoke>`, and `<log>` in `:children-tokens`; `parse-state-block` then feeds them to that broad grouper and maps every resulting block through `parse-state-block`. An element with no `id` becomes a state keyed by `nil` (`id-string->abs-path nil` -> `[nil]` -> local key `nil`). Multiple such elements can also overwrite one another in the resulting map.

The import path has no final canonical grammar check. `spec->scxml` validates with `grammar/valid-definition?` at `scxml.cljc:840-863`, and share/AI/Mermaid use the same projectability boundary, but `scxml->spec` returns its assembled map directly at lines 1462-1602. Thus the public importer can report success with a definition that `reg-machine`, `MachineChart`, every sibling emitter, and `grammar/valid-definition?` reject.

## Reproduction

A conforming SCXML 1.0 state may contain `<onentry>`; an empty `<onentry/>` is enough:

```clojure
(def xml
  "<scxml xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml' version='1.0' initial='idle'><state id='idle'><onentry/></state></scxml>")
(let [spec (scxml/scxml->spec xml)]
  {:spec spec
   :valid? (grammar/valid-definition? spec)
   :defect (grammar/definition-defect spec)})
```

Measured on current HEAD:

```clojure
{:spec {:states {:idle {:states {nil {}}}}, :initial :idle},
 :valid? false,
 :defect {:category :rf.error/machine-compound-state-missing-initial,
          :path [:idle]}}
```

A second measured case with `<onentry><log .../></onentry>` and a real `:go -> :done` transition preserved the transition but returned nested `{nil {:states {nil {}}}}`, proving this is not merely an empty-document edge.

W3C SCXML 1.0 section 3.3 explicitly permits `<onentry>` under `<state>`; the importer advertises interchange with external SCXML tooling and says unsupported executable bodies are lossy. Lossy/ignored is coherent. Inventing an occupiable nil-id state and returning an unusable definition is not.

## Evidence

- `tools/machines-viz/src/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/scxml.cljc:1253-1314`: the child grouper's contract names `<state>` / `<final>`, but all non-transition `:self` / `:start` tokens are collected.
- `scxml.cljc:1137-1248`: only direct `<transition>` tokens are consumed/removed; other SCXML child elements remain for the broad grouper.
- `scxml.cljc:1340-1391`: `parse-state-block` derives every block's key from optional `id`, recursively treats grouped blocks as child states, and never checks the tag.
- `scxml.cljc:1462-1602`: `scxml->spec` checks non-string, missing root, unclosed containers, and empty top-level states, but never validates the returned definition.
- The public docstring at lines 1473-1478 says missing required structure throws `:scxml/invalid-spec`; returning invalid structure contradicts that error boundary.
- `tools/machines-viz/spec/API.md:2200-2231,2343-2354` presents `scxml->spec` as the inverse import and the canonical recursive grammar gate as the invalid-spec boundary.
- `tools/machines-viz/test/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/scxml_cljs_test.cljc` heavily covers emitter-owned round-trips plus non-string/missing-root failures, but contains no `<onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<datamodel>`, `<invoke>`, or unknown-element import case; emitter output never creates the triggering tokens.
- W3C authority: https://www.w3.org/TR/scxml/#state — `<onentry>` and `<onexit>` are valid `<state>` children.
- History: `git blame` attributes the broad grouper and return shape to the initial SCXML implementation, commit `1403ca5a69e` (2026-05-21). Later grammar and SCXML fixes hardened export, ids, action comments, history, and root-parallel transitions, but no history entry filters imported state children or validates the completed import.

## Impact

A programmer importing a normal external SCXML document can receive a plausible-looking EDN map that is unusable by the library. Failure is displaced to later registration/render/export, where it reports a misleading compound-state error about a state the programmer never authored. This defeats the ergonomic value of the interop seam and is especially hostile to AI/tooling pipelines, which reasonably trust `scxml->spec` success as its postcondition.

## Recommended bounded repair

1. Make the direct-child block collector classify only the tags the re-frame2 importer actually models (`state`, `final`, and `history`). Skip an unsupported self-closing element, and skip an unsupported open element together with its whole subtree so nested markup cannot be promoted accidentally. Continue handling direct transitions through the existing transition consumer.
2. Before returning from `scxml->spec`, validate the assembled definition with the existing `grammar/valid-definition?`. If parser output is not projectable, throw the documented `:scxml/invalid-spec` through the existing error builder with a value-free `grammar/definition-summary`; never return malformed data and never include the raw XML.
3. State the narrow import behavior in API/docs: unsupported executable/datamodel/invoke content is ignored/lossy; it is not reinterpreted as topology.

This is one tag allowlist at the existing collection boundary plus one shared postcondition check, not a new XML framework.

## Posture fit

This removes surprising behavior at a public conversion seam and reuses machinery already present. SPA programmers and agents get a simple law: successful import yields a machine the rest of re-frame2 accepts. No new public options, compatibility modes, AST, schema system, or abstraction is needed.

## Non-goals

- No execution or round-trip support for SCXML `<onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<script>`, `<assign>`, `<log>`, `<datamodel>`, `<invoke>`, or other executable/data-model constructs.
- No replacement of the deliberately small regex reader with a full XML/SCXML processor.
- No expansion to XState JSON/Stately formats, nested-parallel semantics, or arbitrary namespace handling.
- No W3C omitted-`initial` defaulting or `<initial>`-element implementation in this task; preserve the currently documented requirement/rejection rather than broadening this repair.
- No change to export syntax, id encoding, action-comment lifting, or supported round-trip equality.

## Related / duplicate search

Tracked `.beads/issues.jsonl` searches for `SCXML default initial`, `SCXML first child`, `SCXML <initial>`, `group-children-by-state`, `fake/bogus nil state`, `non-state child`, `unknown XML element`, `SCXML onentry`, and `SCXML datamodel` found no relevant bead; no current issue title contains `SCXML`. Closed `rf2-sxw06` is the distinct one-click Mermaid workflow and closed `rf2-x19xi` is stale ELK arbitration. Historical SCXML commits (`rf2-mnp93.*`, `rf2-qgtcvy`, `rf2-j538f7.18`) address id/action/export/grammar issues, not this import classification.

## Uncertainty

The parser explicitly promises best-effort behavior for unsupported XML, so either ignore or a controlled parse error could be defensible for some foreign tags. The hard invariant is not ambiguous: success must never invent topology or return a definition the canonical grammar rejects. Ignoring standard executable/data-model children best matches the existing lossy contract and preserves useful topology import.
acceptance_criteria:
- A JVM+CLJS regression imports the conforming `<scxml ...><state id='idle'><onentry/></state></scxml>` fixture and produces no nil/phantom state; the returned definition passes `grammar/valid-definition?`.
- A fixture with `<onentry><log/></onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<datamodel><data/></datamodel>`, and `<invoke>` around otherwise supported states/transitions proves each unsupported subtree is ignored wholesale while the real state ids and transitions remain exact.
- An unsupported element containing a nested `<state>` does not promote that nested element into the parent's re-frame2 `:states`; only direct recognized state/history children are collected.
- Every successful `scxml->spec` result passes the canonical recursive grammar gate. Parser output that cannot be represented as a valid re-frame2 definition throws `:scxml/invalid-spec` with a value-free definition summary and no raw XML/content.
- Existing flat/compound/parallel/history/action/reenter/id-codec round-trips remain byte/value-equivalent, and malformed-root/unclosed-input error ids remain unchanged.
- Negative control: restoring the current catch-all self/start branches makes the new onentry fixture produce a nil-key state and fail the validity assertion.
- API/ns prose accurately describes unsupported SCXML child content as lossy/ignored and does not imply executable semantics were added.

title: Fail closed when a Node renderer's 200 omits x-rf-ssr-build
description:
## Problem

`re-frame.ssr.ring.node/renderer` requires `:build-id`, sends it to the sidecar, and promises an answer-side build-skew check before Node-rendered bytes enter the JVM-owned document. But the 200 arm of `interpret-response!` in `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/node.clj` (currently lines 347-356) checks only `(and serving (not= serving build-id))`. If `x-rf-ssr-build` is absent, `serving` is nil, the check is skipped, and the response is accepted as `{:body-html ... :render-hash nil}`.

Absence is not a verifiable match. It can happen with a malformed/impostor service or a proxy that strips the response header. Because this adapter deliberately returns `:render-hash nil` for native roots, the structural hydration-hash channel does not provide a second check: unverified body bytes can be wrapped with the JVM hydration payload and shipped as a successful SPA document.

## Evidence and verified impact

A focused, no-edit JVM probe reused the existing `with-stub-sidecar`, `node-renderer`, and `handler` fixtures in `implementation/ssr-ring/test/re_frame/ssr/ring/node_crossing_test.clj`. The stub answered HTTP 200 with `{}` headers and `<main>impostor</main>`. After the canonical test runtime reset, the observed result was exactly:

`{:status 200, :impostor-shipped? true, :payload-shipped? true}`

The sibling test `build-skew-arm-a-200-from-the-wrong-build-is-refused-on-the-jvm` (currently lines 415-427) covers only a PRESENT but different `x-rf-ssr-build`. It proves that case projects a 500 and suppresses the impostor body; there is no missing-header row. The `node.clj` namespace contract says the 200 answer is checked defensively, and the real sidecar advertises `x-rf-ssr-build` on render responses, so accepting absence weakens the exact deployment invariant the required `:build-id` exists to enforce.

History confirms the gap dates to the crossing's introduction: commit `25685ab2e4` (`feat(ssr-ring): re-frame.ssr.ring.node — the JVM->Node adapter and the JVM->Node->JVM crossing witness (rf2-8arzr.4)`) introduced both the truthy-header guard and the present-wrong test. The later naming-only commit did not change the condition.

## Bounded recommendation

In `interpret-response!`, accept a 200 only when `x-rf-ssr-build` is present and exactly equals the configured `:build-id`. Route both an absent header and a different value through the existing `:rf.error/ssr-node-build-skew` render-failure projection before returning body bytes. Keep the existing error id and projected-5xx path unless evidence requires a smaller internal reason tag; do not add a new handshake or public protocol surface.

Extend `node_crossing_test.clj` at the existing stub-sidecar build-skew cluster with the missing-header case. Pin that it returns the projected 5xx, never ships the stub body or `__rf_payload`, emits exactly the existing build-skew id with the configured expectation and an honest missing-serving representation, and tears down the request frame. Preserve the present-wrong row as the companion discriminator.

## Non-goals and posture

Do not add health preflights, retries, proxy detection, new pools, a second build-id option, or broad response-header validation. Do not constrain the documented non-loopback endpoint escape hatch: the programmer still owns where the sidecar runs. This is one cheap equality boundary on the response that already claims to carry the identity, closing a silent wrong-build success without adding ceremony to the normal SPA path.

## Duplicate and landed-work search

All-status tracker searches for `build skew`, `x-rf-ssr-build`, `missing build`, `absent build`, `build identity`, `missing header`, and `impostor` found only the CLOSED originating programme items `rf2-8arzr` / `rf2-8arzr.4`; neither owns an absent-success-header follow-up. Path history and `git log -S"x-rf-ssr-build"` found only the landed introduction commit above. Current source still contains the truthy guard, and the focused probe demonstrates the defect at the reviewed tip.

## Uncertainty

The smallest error-data spelling for absence is open: retaining `:serving nil` is sufficient and avoids surface growth; an internal closed `:reason` may improve diagnostics if the existing error-shape conventions demand it. The official sidecar currently supplies the header, so this is a defensive deployment failure rather than a happy-path fault, but answer-side defense is the stated purpose of this check and the consequence is silent successful delivery of unverified native-root bytes.
acceptance_criteria:
- A stub HTTP 200 with no `x-rf-ssr-build` is rejected before its body enters the Ring document and follows the existing projected-5xx / `:rf.error/ssr-node-build-skew` path.
- The response contains neither the stub's body marker nor `__rf_payload`, and the per-request frame is destroyed.
- The existing present-but-different build-header case remains rejected, while a present exact match remains successful.
- Focused tests name all three 200-answer cases (matching, different, absent) without requiring a real Node process for the two stub cases; the ordinary ssr-ring test lane and the dedicated crossing lane remain green.
- No new handshake, retry, endpoint restriction, or public error category is introduced.

title: ssr-node: render exceptions can leak application data and spoof refusal status
description:
## Evidence

- The package states the response law repeatedly: README.md:275 and :668 say Node returns body markup and nothing else; test/egress.test.cjs:31-37 tightens that to “nothing the render module authored” outside chunk HTML and says a refusal must not carry the payload through the error channel.
- The success/return-value door enforces that law, but the exception door does not. In src/worker.cjs:221-225 the render catch copies application-authored error.code, error.message, and error.detail into the worker error message. src/isolate.cjs:200-208 preserves the code/message and spreads detail into the public Refusal. src/http.cjs:67-76 serializes that Refusal to JSON and statusFor maps the copied code to HTTP status.
- A read-only worker probe loaded an in-memory render module whose render threw an Error built from allowlisted request state. The module set message to "message:state-secret-7b2", detail to {echo:"state-secret-7b2"}, and no custom code. The actual worker output was:
  {"t":"error","id":7,"code":":rf.ssr-node/render-threw","message":"message:state-secret-7b2","detail":{"echo":"state-secret-7b2"},"afterChunks":0}
  This proves the state sentinel crosses both live fields; it is not inferred from source alone.
- The repository's own throws fixture provides the HTTP half without a synthetic file: POSTing app/before returned HTTP 500 with JSON message "fell over immediately", the exact string authored at test/fixtures/throws.cjs:20.
- error.code is the same untrusted path. A render module can set it to a known protocol member such as :rf.ssr-node/unknown-entry, service-saturated, or render-timeout; statusFor will then present an application render bug as HTTP 400, 503, or 504 instead of the documented render-threw 500. It can also emit an arbitrary refusal-code string.
- The green egress row at test/egress.test.cjs:311-323 exercises only a module that returns a payload. It does not throw an Error carrying code/message/detail, so the package gate remains green (108 rows, 9 suites) while the second channel is live.
- History localizes the gap: git log -S "err.detail" attributes the pass-through to the initial service commit b2b35bf6e9. The later response-egress hardening (67d4d9338a, b34fe600fa) closed returned values but did not touch this catch.

## Impact

A routine renderer exception can put server-only render state, environment-derived data, or other application values into the in-process Refusal and the sidecar's HTTP JSON response. The JVM consumer then retains the sidecar message/detail on its internal ssr-node-refused error. Independently, application code can spoof the closed refusal taxonomy and its caller-fault/deadline/saturation status, sending operators and retry policy down the wrong path. This is a correctness and boundary failure, not a request from hostile code: error messages that interpolate the value being processed are ordinary.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use a valid module with an app/root entry and an allowlisted :secret state key.
2. In render, construct an Error whose code, message, and nested detail are derived from state[":secret"], then throw it before emit.
3. Call Service.renderFrames or POST /render.
4. Observe the module's message/detail in the Refusal/JSON. If code is set to a known non-render member, observe the corresponding non-500 HTTP status.

The read-only probe above establishes steps 1-3 at the worker boundary, and the checked-in throws fixture establishes the message-to-HTTP leg.

## Recommended bounded repair

Close the exception path at src/worker.cjs, the first boundary that can enforce it. A caught render-module exception should always cross as CODE.RENDER_THREW with service-owned wording and a small service-owned detail shape (for example entry plus the existing afterChunks fact); do not copy error.code, error.message, error.detail, or other module properties. Preserve the existing pre-chunk refusal versus post-chunk torn-response behavior. If retaining full diagnostics locally is required, keep that as a sidecar-local logging decision rather than putting application-authored values on the response protocol.

Add the focused adversarial case to test/egress.test.cjs with a fixture that demonstrably throws distinct sentinels in code, message, and nested detail, and check both the in-process Refusal and HTTP response.

## Posture rationale

This is one missing closure on an existing boundary, not a new subsystem. The ergonomic rule should be simple for SPA authors: throw from a renderer and get one honest render-threw failure; never learn a redaction DSL or remember which Error properties are safe. A fixed service-owned refusal is smaller, safer, and easier for people and AI-generated integration code to reason about than configurable projection.

## Non-goals

- No new refusal code, public option, redaction framework, safe-key registry, or exception wrapper API.
- No change to successful chunk/complete frames, request validation, allowlists, timeout, pool replacement, or JVM/browser error projection.
- No redesign of sidecar logging or observability; local diagnostics may be decided separately.
- Do not broaden this into boot-error handling. Module boot fails before the service listens and has different operator-diagnostic needs.
- Do not terminate a healthy isolate merely because application render code threw; current reuse semantics are separate.

## Related and duplicate search

Searched all 935 tracker records, including closed/deferred, across title, description, notes, and close reason for ssr-node, body markup, egress, render-threw, err.code/err.detail, render exception message/detail, diagnostic-shaped leak, refusal-code spoofing, and application-authored error data. No issue owns this exception pass-through. Closest is closed rf2-6r9j.77, which removed worker stack fields because receivers discarded them; this finding is distinct because code/message/detail are live and serialized. Closed rf2-6r9j.70-.74/.84/.86 and .176-.179 cover boot-test validity, envelope scope, selector/residue cleanup, and naming. The crossing parent rf2-8arzr and success-egress commits establish the law but do not close this path.

## Uncertainties

The repair must choose the exact service-owned message/detail wording and whether the original exception is logged only on sidecar stderr. Those choices do not alter the required boundary: no application-authored exception property may enter a public Refusal or HTTP frame. The JVM host sanitizes what reaches the browser, but that is downstream defense and does not repair the Node service's own public in-process and HTTP contracts.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A controlled render module throws an Error whose code, message, and nested detail each carry distinct sentinels sourced from request state; a direct fixture control proves all sentinels really exist before the service handles it.
2. Service.renderFrames/renderToString rejects that render with exactly :rf.ssr-node/render-threw, service-owned wording, correct afterChunks, and no sentinel anywhere in the public Refusal (code, message, detail, stack serialization).
3. The same request over HTTP returns 500 with x-rf-ssr-refusal :rf.ssr-node/render-threw; its JSON body and headers contain no sentinel. Choosing known 400/503/504 protocol codes in the thrown Error cannot change that outcome.
4. Both pre-emit and post-emit exceptions are covered: pre-emit is a clean refusal; post-emit remains a torn response and streaming HTTP destroys rather than completes the socket.
5. A negative control restoring any code/message/detail pass-through makes the new egress test fail.
6. Existing successful rendering, ordinary throw, return-value egress, timeout, byte-fidelity, and all ssr-node suites remain green.

title: hic: RULING — a bead id in the design corpus is provenance, not a live pointer (rf2-wx96 census)
description:
Filed by rf2-wx96's census (2026-09-04, main@cf4a98a084). The census is taken; what is left is one ruling on (a) versus (b), which rf2-wx96 says is Mike's call.

THE CENSUS, across docs/design/. 86 distinct rf2-hic-NNN ids in 1,181 citations. FIVE resolve in the tracker: rf2-hic-051, -063, -064, -088, -090 (four closed, rf2-hic-063 open). Probed both ways: bd show rf2-hic-038 returns "no issue found", bd show rf2-hic-064 resolves. Two of the 86 - rf2-hic-9001 and rf2-hic-9002 - are correction-ledger.md's deliberately fictional worked-example ids and were never beads.

THE MEASUREMENT rf2-wx96 DID NOT HAVE, AND IT CHANGES THE QUESTION. The ids were REAL and the citations were VALID when written. The tracker export at 63a3d44086 (2026-08-16) carries NINETY rf2-hic-NNN values as .id. The drop is between 1246e4e422 (2026-08-31, still 90) and dc88bc6aae (2026-09-02, 5).

AND IT IS NOT SPECIFIC TO THIS CORPUS. Comparing the whole id set at 1246e4e422 against tip: 1,145 ids then, 935 now, 848 gone - of which 85 are rf2-hic-* and 763 are not. So this is a general tracker compaction with a visible face in the hicasso corpus, not a hicasso bookkeeping defect, and EVERY closed bead id cited anywhere in the repository is subject to the same disappearance.

WHY THAT DECIDES (a) VERSUS (b) ON THE EVIDENCE. Option (b), "live owner references needing a mapping", cannot be sustained: it would require the design corpus to track a tracker that compacts, and the mapping would be 848 ids wide rather than 60. The surviving convention already reads the other way - the derivative beads that outlive a programme item carry hic-NNN in their TITLE and an ordinary rf2-<slug> id of their own (rf2-w01c is "hic-036 clock driver: ...", rf2-85og2 is "hic-071 remainder: ..."), and the five ids that DO resolve are all titled "hic-NNN - <name>", so id and title-prefix agree only where the bead survives.

RECOMMENDED RULING (a): a bead id in a design record is a PROVENANCE CITATION - the name of the bead under which a change was made - and not a resolvable pointer. Consequences if ruled: requirements-mine.md's "How to read a row" defines Owner as "the bead accountable for carrying the answer to done", which reads as resolvable and would need one sentence saying it need not be; the maintenance rules gain a rule for what a dead owner-id means; and the passes stop treating ids as look-ups, so a dead id is not a finding. What stays a finding is a row asserting a STATUS the tracker contradicts, which only binds ids the tracker still holds.

title: Lifecycle-verb law: the closed roster has no verb for install-*/remove-*/register-*, which three live re-frame.core facade exports use (found by the rf2-2hpxo facade sweep)
description:
Found while classifying the 103 re-frame.core facade rows for rf2-2hpxo (slice 1 of the retrospective facade audit). Recorded as keep-with-uncertainty on each row's :justification rather than renamed, because the law itself says what to do here.

THE GAP. spec/Conventions.md $Lifecycle-verb law is a CLOSED verb roster: clear-* / unregister-* / destroy-* / reset-* / unsubscribe / watch-* / attach!-detach! / mount!-unmount! / open!-close! / configure!. Three live re-frame.core facade exports use verbs that are not in it:

  install-adapter!                  (:advanced, owner 006)
  install-revalidation-listeners!   (:advanced, owner 016)
  remove-revalidation-listeners!    (:advanced, owner 016)

The nearest roster entry is attach! / detach! -- 'Add / remove a listener to an existing thing' -- which is a good literal fit for the revalidation pair (they install and remove host focus/reconnect listeners) and a poor one for install-adapter!, which installs a whole substrate adapter rather than a listener.

A FOURTH, WEAKER CASE. register-listener! uses register-*, which is also not in the roster -- but its partner unregister-listener! is the roster's own NAMED EXEMPLAR of the unregister-* row, so the pair reads as sanctioned even though only half of it is written down. Worth settling in the same pass.

WHY THIS IS NOT A RENAME BEAD. The law's own closing sentence: 'a surface that fits none of these is evidence the law is missing a verb -- file a bead against this section rather than coining dispose- / teardown- / shutdown- / a fresh un-*. Adding a verb is a Spec change to this table, not a per-author call.' So the question is whether the roster gains an install-* / remove-* row (or an explicit note that attach!/detach! covers listener installs and install-* covers subsystem installs), NOT whether these three vars get renamed on a worker's initiative.

API.md $Tier taxonomy names install-adapter! as a canonical :advanced example, so a rename would ripple into that table, docs/api, the skills corpus and every consumer -- which is exactly why it needs a ruling rather than a sweep.

NOT a tag blocker: rf2-2hpxo recorded these keep-with-uncertainty and does not hold the PR or rf2-kmqx3 on them.

title: hic: the design corpus cites ~60 rf2-hic-NNN ids that no longer resolve in the tracker
description:
Found by rf2-j77q's pass 3 on docs/design/hicasso/product/requirements-mine.md (2026-09-04, main@bd61169475), and recorded on that page rather than repaired there.

THE MEASUREMENT. The ledger rows of requirements-mine.md cite roughly sixty rf2-hic-NNN bead ids as owners and as evidence. Only FIVE rf2-hic-* ids exist in the tracker at all: rf2-hic-051, -063, -064, -088, -090. 'bd show rf2-hic-007' returns 'no issue found'; the same command resolves rf2-hic-064, so the probe was exercised in both directions and this is a real absence rather than a bad search. 'jq -r .id .beads/issues.jsonl | rg -F rf2-hic-' returns the same five.

WHY IT MATTERS AND WHY IT IS A DIFFERENT CLASS. requirements-mine.md's passes were built to catch two failures: a dead PATH (a witness a reader cannot open) and a stale STATUS (a row asserting open where the tracker says closed). This is a third: a dead ID, an owner a reader cannot look up. No maintenance rule on the page covers it, and the page's own acceptance criterion — 'no row states a bead status the tracker contradicts' — is vacuously satisfied by an id the tracker has never heard of.

SCOPE IS NOT JUST THIS PAGE. requirements-mine.md is where it was measured, but rf2-hic-NNN ids are cited across docs/design/hicasso/ (dispositions.md, the checkpoints, correction-ledger.md, the lanes). A census across that tree is the first step.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS NOT. It is NOT 'repoint sixty ids'. The derivative beads that survive carry hic-NNN in their TITLES rather than their ids (rf2-w01c is 'hic-036 clock driver: ...'), and only some do, so a mechanical repoint would be guesswork. The decision to take first is whether these citations are (a) historical provenance that is allowed to name a retired id, in which case the maintenance rules should say so and the passes should stop treating ids as resolvable, or (b) live owner references, in which case they need a mapping. Mike's call.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a census of rf2-hic-NNN citations across docs/design/hicasso/ against 'bd list --limit 0', plus one ruling on (a) versus (b).
close_reason:
PR #9189. The census the bead asks for is taken and recorded on requirements-mine.md; the ruling on (a) versus (b) is filed for Mike as rf2-3w7t. NO ID IS REPOINTED - the bead rules that out as guesswork and the measurement below makes it worse, not better.

THE CENSUS, two axes, across docs/design/. Axis one, the id form rf2-hic-NNN: 86 distinct ids in 1,181 citations. Axis two, bare hic-NNN not preceded by rf2-: finds the form the surviving derivative beads actually use, in their TITLES. FIVE ids resolve - rf2-hic-051, -063, -064, -088, -090 (four closed, -063 open) - confirmed against the export and probed both ways (bd show rf2-hic-038 returns "no issue found"; bd show rf2-hic-064 resolves). Two of the 86, rf2-hic-9001 and rf2-hic-9002, are correction-ledger.md's deliberately fictional worked-example ids and were never beads.

THE MEASUREMENT THE BEAD DID NOT HAVE, AND IT CHANGES THE QUESTION. The ids were REAL and these citations were VALID when written. The tracker export at 63a3d44086 (2026-08-16) carries NINETY rf2-hic-NNN values as .id. The drop is between 1246e4e422 (2026-08-31, still 90) and dc88bc6aae (2026-09-02, 5).

AND IT IS NOT A DEFECT OF THIS CORPUS. Comparing whole id sets at 1246e4e422 against tip - 1,145 ids then, 935 now - 848 ids are gone, of which 85 are rf2-hic-* and 763 are NOT. So this is a general tracker compaction with a visible face in the hicasso corpus, and EVERY closed bead id cited anywhere in the repository is subject to the same disappearance. That is why (b) cannot be sustained: a mapping would be 848 ids wide and would require the design corpus to track a tracker that compacts.

The page's acceptance criterion - no row states a bead status the tracker contradicts - then binds only ids the tracker still holds, which is what makes a dead id not a finding.

  reg-resource   + clear-resource    both on the facade
  reg-mutation   + clear-mutation    both on the facade
  reg-http-interceptor + clear-http-interceptor  both on the facade
  reg-resource-scope + clear-resource-scope      both on the facade
  reg-flow       + (no clear-flow)   registrar ONLY

rf2-wad2fl (the front-porch shrink) moved clear-flow to re-frame.flows and kept reg-flow on the facade. Every other registrar/clear pair kept both halves together. So either the flows pair should be reunited (add clear-flow back to the facade as a late-bind wrapper -- the wrapper already exists in implementation/core/src/re_frame/core_flows.cljc and is simply not re-exported), or the OTHER seven pairs are the anomaly and rf2-wad2fl's reasoning should extend to them.

EVIDENCE THE FIRST READING IS RIGHT: the defwrapper for clear-flow is already written and live -- it is one of the 51 wrappers in implementation/core/src/re_frame/*.cljc -- so restoring the export is a re-export line, not new machinery. But this is pre-alpha and the surface is deliberately small, so it is Mike's call which direction to make consistent, not a worker's.

P4: a coherence nit, not a correctness one. Not a tag blocker; rf2-2hpxo does not hold on it.

title: surface-review(examples-machines): clear stale login errors when leaving :error-shown
description:
## Scope

Correct the error lifecycle in `examples/capabilities/machines/state_machine_walkthrough/**` and strengthen its existing out-of-tree headless coverage. Keep the three-attempt lockout, managed-HTTP stub, draft slice, tag-driven view, and test-free examples policy. This is a small correctness/teaching repair, not a redesign of machines or forms.

## Finding

The walkthrough records each failed reply into machine `:data :error`, but neither transition out of `:error-shown` clears it:

- `:walkthrough.login/dismiss -> :idle` has only a target.
- `:walkthrough.login/submit -> :submitting` has only a target.

The view renders the error row whenever `err` is non-nil and the machine is not locked; it does not condition the row on `:error-shown`. Consequently, clicking the visible **Dismiss** button changes the banner to `idle` but leaves the same error and Dismiss button on screen. Further Dismiss clicks are unhandled no-ops in `:idle`. Submitting directly from `:error-shown` likewise carries the old error into the new `:submitting` request. The initial `:idle -> :submitting` transition does run `:clear-error`, but that is too late to make Dismiss dismiss anything and does not cover direct retry.

This is exactly the kind of copyable SPA pattern an example must get right: status and error data disagree, and a control named Dismiss has no visible effect.

## Evidence

- `examples/capabilities/machines/state_machine_walkthrough/core.cljc:74-75` already defines the minimal reusable `:clear-error` action as `{:data {:error nil}}`.
- `core.cljc:98-101` writes the failure message into `:data :error`.
- `core.cljc:126-128` declares both exits from `:error-shown` without `:clear-error`.
- `views.cljs:44-45,69-76` subscribes to the error and renders the row/button solely from `(and err (not locked?))`; after Dismiss, `locked?` is false and `err` is unchanged.
- Spec 005, `Action effect map — {:data :fx}` (`spec/005-StateMachines.md:737-755`), says `:data` is merged into existing machine data. Reusing `:clear-error` therefore preserves `:attempts`; no custom reset/event/sub is needed. The implementation performs that merge at `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc:2025-2029`.
- The current guide's corresponding full transition (`docs/machines/tutorial.md:193-197`, repeated at 435-439) does clear the error on direct retry. The walkthrough's namespace says to read it beside the guide and its README calls this the chapter flow, so this is behavioral drift, not an intentional alternate policy. The guide view hides errors by exact state; the walkthrough intentionally does not, making Dismiss's missing clear observable here.
- Existing out-of-tree coverage misses it: `implementation/core/test/re_frame/examples_test.clj:906-922` dispatches Dismiss twice but asserts only the eventual `:locked-out` state. It never reads `:walkthrough.login/error` after Dismiss or inspects a direct retry snapshot.
- The runnable build is correctly declared at `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn:1723-1730`, but `npm run test:examples-compile` is compile/warning coverage only (`examples/TESTING.md:15-23`; `implementation/scripts/check-examples-compile.cjs:57-82`), so it cannot detect this state/data mismatch.
- History explains why it survived. The original browser spec (introduced by `58adfc02e7`) clicked Dismiss and asserted only that the banner said `idle`, never that the error row disappeared. Per-example browser specs were intentionally removed by `2d2f4aff53`; the present framework test inherited the same narrow assertion. The June 26 draft-slice refactor `2dc95699af` retained the data-only error render. The Aug 13 guide rewrite `6012a7b21a` added `:clear-error` to direct retry but did not update this example.

## Recommended bounded fix

Reuse the existing machine-local `:clear-error` action on both transitions that leave `:error-shown`: Dismiss to `:idle`, and Submit to `:submitting`. This is two table entries, preserves `:attempts` by the documented merge rule, and makes the current view truthful without adding a state predicate, another tag, another subscription, or view-local cleanup.

Extend the existing `state-machine-walkthrough-runs-headless` test in `implementation/core/test/re_frame/examples_test.clj` with focused transition assertions for both exits. Briefly align the example prose/comments with the now-explicit lifecycle. Keep tests outside `examples/`.

## Acceptance criteria

- Starting from `{:state :error-shown :data {:attempts 1 :error "bad creds"}}`, a Dismiss transition produces `:idle`, sets `:error` to nil, and preserves `:attempts` at 1; therefore the existing error-row predicate becomes false.
- From that same failed snapshot, a direct Submit transition produces `:submitting`, clears `:error`, preserves `:attempts`, and still emits exactly the existing `:rf.http/managed` request effect through `:submitting` entry.
- The browser-facing Dismiss control no longer remains visible after it is clicked; a fresh request never carries a stale visible failure.
- Existing lockout behavior is unchanged: first two failures remain retryable, the third reaches `:locked-out`, attempts becomes 3, and the terminal failure message is retained for the locked snapshot.
- The existing out-of-tree JVM example test covers both clear paths; no `*.spec.cjs` or test file is added under `examples/`.
- The focused core JVM test namespace and the existing example compile gate pass.

## Non-goals

- No machine runtime/API/spec changes.
- No new error tag/subscription, state-specific rendering branch, form framework, schema, or validation.
- No change to retry count, draft preservation, HTTP reply shape/stub timing, final/resting-state semantics, or locked panel.
- No resurrection of per-example Playwright tests and no broad cleanup of the related `examples/core/login` feature.

## Duplicate search

All-status `rg` over `.beads/issues.jsonl` used `state_machine_walkthrough`, `state-machine-walkthrough`, `walkthrough.login`, `login-dismiss`, `dismiss`, `clear-error`, `stale error`, `error-shown`, and retry/error combinations. The only beads naming this example are closed `rf2-ujdn0` (copyable capability launch recipes) and closed `rf2-wuten` (the skill's example catalogue); neither owns runtime error lifecycle or Dismiss behavior. No relevant open, deferred, or closed duplicate was found.

## Uncertainty / witness

Per the review brief, no runtime gate or browser launch was executed during research. The result follows directly from the transition table, documented/implemented merge semantics, subscription, and render predicate. The implementer should first add the two focused assertions against the current table and capture the expected red (error remains `"bad creds"`), then make the two action changes and turn them green.

title: bug(template): prove the optimized release boots for every emitted substrate
description:
## Problem

The generated scaffold gives Reagent and UIx users the same release command and says the resulting resources/public directory is deployable, while the template contract says each substrate is exercised end-to-end and builds an advanced release. The behavioral tier does not enforce that contract: it boots only the development bundle, runs shadow release only for Reagent, and checks the optimized output only for process exit plus a non-empty main.js. UIx's release command is never executed, and neither optimized bundle is loaded in a browser.

## Evidence

- tools/template/resources/day8/re_frame2_template/root/README.md:26-33 tells every generated project to run npm run release and serve resources/public.
- tools/template/resources/day8/re_frame2_template/_shared/package.json maps release to shadow-cljs release app for both substrates.
- tools/template/spec/000-Vision.md:25-30 says the generated SPA can be run, tested, and released.
- tools/template/spec/Principles.md:149-178 says each Reagent/UIx substrate is exercised end-to-end and that the behavioral layer builds the advanced release.
- tools/template/test/day8/re_frame2_template/emitted_test_run_test.clj:351-376 and :457-461 boot the development output before release.
- The release arm at emitted_test_run_test.clj:481-500 asserts only command exit and a non-empty main.js.
- Reagent enables that arm at :516-527; UIx passes an empty option map at :529-539, so its advertised release command never runs.
- The rationale at :424-428 calls the module/export shape substrate-invariant, but the product contract deliberately swaps deps.edn, core.cljs, and views.cljs per substrate (spec/000-Vision.md:33-36), which is source and dependency surface Closure compiles.
- Commit adf2f47322 added the existing Chromium proof after a real emitted page compiled successfully but booted blank under its own CSP. That history demonstrates that compile success is not a page-boot proof. Release currently overwrites the proven dev bundle and the driver is not rerun.
- Closed bead rf2-zq34m acceptance criterion 4 required each substrate to build an advanced release and open the real page. Its implementation note records advanced release on Reagent, matching the residual in current code.

## Impact

A UIx-specific advanced-compilation failure can reach users without CI executing the documented command. For both substrates, a non-empty optimized JavaScript file can still throw at load or paint a blank page, so the deployable release path is materially weaker than the first-run path. This is a narrow scaffold correctness gap, not a request for general production infrastructure.

## Posture fit

The template is the front door to a small SPA and release is one of its three documented commands. Reusing the browser proof already paid for keeps the fix simple and outcome-focused: prove the generated app users deploy, without adding options, policy, or framework machinery.

## Duplicate result

A targeted rg search over .beads/issues.jsonl for template/scaffold with advanced, optimized, release bundle, and npm run release found only closed rf2-zq34m and deferred rf2-8urba. rf2-zq34m is the original contract but was closed after the Reagent-only implementation landed; no open bead owns this residual. rf2-8urba is the future Hicasso substrate and is unrelated. Also checked rf2-pygpw (closed pre-publish generator coordinates), rf2-fo4ng (deferred Maven coordinate rename), and rf2-fgb1 (post-tag documentation flip); each has a distinct center.

## Uncertainty

This review did not execute a UIx optimized build because it was explicitly read-only and prohibited node_modules links. It does not claim today's UIx output is observed broken. The objective defect is the unexercised per-substrate release contract and the absence of a browser verdict for both optimized outputs.
design:
## Bounded fix

- In the existing opt-in behavioral tier, execute shadow-cljs release app for both Reagent and UIx.
- Immediately after each successful release, reuse the existing browser driver against the overwritten resources/public directory and require the same heading, counter 0 to 1, and zero-pageerror verdict. Make driver labels mode-neutral if needed; do not add a second browser harness.
- Keep package-completeness and development-page proof before release because the development build has distinct chunk/eval behavior.
- Keep the existing broken-mount witness as the browser driver's non-vacuity proof.
- Align Principles and test descriptions with the executable per-substrate behavior.

## Non-goals

- No generated API, source, or dependency changes unless the new proof exposes a real fault.
- No new build mode, deployment provider, CSP or hosting policy, performance or bundle-size work, npm-install matrix, substrate selector, or bespoke production driver.
- No expansion into publication-coordinate or repository-split work.
acceptance_criteria:
1. With RF2_TEMPLATE_RUN_EMITTED_TESTS=1, both Reagent and UIx emissions execute shadow release app and assert exit 0 plus a non-empty optimized output.
2. After each release, the exact emitted index.html and optimized js/main.js are served through the existing driver; the heading paints, the value starts at 0, clicking +1 reaches 1, and Chromium reports zero uncaught pageerrors.
3. The existing development-bundle proof still runs before release for both substrates, and package completeness still reads the development manifest before release overwrites it.
4. Test output and assertions distinguish development and optimized boot so neither verdict can be supplied by the other; the existing broken-mount witness remains red and restores its input byte-for-byte.
5. Principles and test prose state the same per-substrate release contract the executable tier enforces.

title: Seven GUIs Timer counts delayed callbacks instead of elapsed time
description:
## Correctness finding

The runnable Seven GUIs Timer advances `:elapsed-ms` by the configured 100 ms sampling interval each time a delayed callback happens, rather than by the time that actually elapsed. `:dispatch-later` promises “not before this delay”, not an exact clock pulse. Any late callback therefore makes the timer permanently slow: if the main thread is blocked for 5 seconds, the next callback moves the display by only 100 ms and schedules the following callback from that late point. Browser throttling, a busy event loop, or a suspended tab can make the nominal 10-second timer take arbitrarily longer.

That is the classic timer mistake in the example whose stated purpose is to teach concurrent time/user interactions. It can mislead both a programmer and an AI into copying a callback-counter as an elapsed-time clock.

## Exact evidence

- `examples/core/seven_guis/timer/core.cljs:31-34` defines `tick-ms` as 100. `:timer/initialise` schedules `[:timer/tick 0]` after that delay at lines 81-88. The live tick at lines 90-103 computes `next-elapsed` as `(min (+ elapsed-ms tick-ms) duration-ms)` and only then schedules another 100 ms callback. No event timestamp or clock sample participates.
- The runtime does not promise periodic precision. `implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc:275-344` arms each `:dispatch-later` using `rf.interop/set-timeout!`; the CLJS implementation is exactly `js/setTimeout` at `implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.cljs:141-149`. The HTML Living Standard explicitly says timer callbacks are not guaranteed to run exactly on schedule and delays from CPU load or other tasks are expected: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/timers-and-user-prompts.html#timers .
- The canonical 7GUIs task describes a gauge and label for elapsed time, and names concurrency, competing user/signal interactions, and responsiveness as the challenge: https://eugenkiss.github.io/7guis/tasks/#timer . Its cited FrTime source computes elapsed as current time minus the reset/start time, rather than counting wakeups (`Crossing State Lines`, pp. 3-4): https://cs.brown.edu/~sk/Publications/Papers/Published/ick-adapt-oo-fwk-frp/paper.pdf .
- re-frame2 already has the small, replay-honest input this example needs. The router stamps every dispatch (including a fresh `:dispatch-later` child) with recordable `:rf/time-ms` at `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc:122-152`; a handler opts in with `:rf.cofx/requires [:rf/time-ms]` and receives the value flat. `docs/core/coeffects.md:22-53,87-95` teaches exactly that contract. No ambient `Date.now`, new scheduler, or public API is needed.
- The only focused Timer behavior test positively pins the wrong model. `implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_generation_guard_cljs_test.cljs:97-105` dispatches a live tick and requires `elapsed-ms` to become `before + timer/tick-ms`. The test replaces `:dispatch-later` with a capture function (lines 28-33, 75-78), so it proves generation-chain ownership but cannot observe a late host callback. `example_frame_scoping_cljs_test.cljs` only covers schema registration, and `test:examples-compile` only compiles declared builds. Repository search found no browser-level Timer behavior test.
- History shows the fixed-step accounting dates to the initial example import. `e296c072b3` correctly added the generation token for Reset races, `e0e7a5aaec` correctly re-armed after raising a completed timer's duration, and `be375bc4c8` later added the generation-guard test; none changed elapsed accounting. The current test consequently protects the cancellation/re-arm idea and the callback-counter together even though only the former is correct.

## Impact

A user can open this ordinary 10-second example, switch tabs or make the main thread busy, return well after the duration, and still see a timer far from complete. More importantly, this is a canonical teaching example: it currently says time lives honestly inside the event pipeline while demonstrating that callback count equals time. Real SPAs routinely experience delayed tasks. Copying this pattern into cooldowns, progress indicators, session timers, or polling UX produces clocks that drift under exactly the load where correctness matters.

The fix is valuable because it showcases re-frame2's intended ergonomic answer: scheduling decides when to sample; a declared recordable coeffect says what time it was when the sample entered the pipeline. That keeps handlers pure, replay deterministic, and the API minimal.

## Bounded recommendation

Keep the 100 ms `:dispatch-later` chain as the display sampling cadence and keep the existing generation guard. Change only elapsed accounting:

1. Add a durable last-sample/reset timestamp to `TimerState` (or an equivalent minimal anchor).
2. Declare `:rf/time-ms` on the handlers that establish or consume the anchor. On a live tick, advance by the non-negative observed delta since the prior live sample, clamp at `duration-ms`, store the new anchor, and schedule at most one next tick. A stale-generation tick must still be a complete no-op.
3. Reset should zero elapsed, bump the generation, and establish the new time baseline. When increasing a completed timer re-arms it, establish the baseline at that user event so time spent stopped is not charged after restart.
4. Rewrite the focused example test to inject explicit `:rf.cofx {:rf/time-ms ...}` values. Keep its exact-one-chain/stale-generation teeth, but prove a 450 ms late tick advances by 450 ms rather than 100 ms and a tick beyond the deadline clamps once and stops.
5. Make the comments/Seven GUIs README distinguish the 100 ms sampling cadence from elapsed-time measurement.

An equivalent anchor-based formulation is fine; the invariant is that elapsed state follows recorded causal time, not callback count.

## Non-goals

- No new timer, cancellation, clock, or public framework API.
- Do not replace the event pipeline with `requestAnimationFrame`, a component-local interval, or direct mutation.
- Do not remove or redesign the generation token, post-completion duration re-arm, slider, subscriptions, or view.
- No attempt to provide a general pause/resume/countdown library or define every possible wall-clock adjustment policy.
- Do not broaden this into a review of machine `:after`, resource timers, or other examples.

## Posture fit

This is a small honesty repair to a high-leverage example, not gold plating. One built-in coeffect and one timestamp make the happy path correct under ordinary browser behavior while teaching the library's elegant existing time boundary. It reduces surprise and gives programmers/agents a pattern worth copying without adding machinery.

## Duplicate search

All-status `rg` searches over `.beads/issues.jsonl` covered the exact path and namespace, `:timer/tick`, `tick-ms`, callback/elapsed combinations, fixed-tick and timer drift, browser/background/hidden throttling, callback counting, and `:rf/time-ms` with Timer. I also enumerated every issue title containing “timer”. No issue owns this example outcome. The timer-titled beads concern machines hydration/cancellation, Hicasso reaper coalescing, a schemas fixture rewrite, and skill prose; all are distinct.

## Uncertainty

I did not compile or run a browser in this review because the assigned worktree intentionally had no `node_modules` link and the task forbade creating one. The defect is source-level and does not depend on timing luck: the handler unconditionally adds 100 for one callback, while the production effect delegates to `setTimeout`, whose late-fire behavior is explicit. `:rf/time-ms` is epoch wall time rather than a monotonic duration clock, so the minimal implementation should clamp negative deltas to zero; inventing a new monotonic recordable clock would be disproportionate to this example.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The Timer's live elapsed value is derived from recorded `:rf/time-ms` deltas (or an equivalent recorded time anchor), never from “one callback equals `tick-ms`”. There is no direct ambient clock read in an event handler.
2. A deterministic focused CLJS test supplies an initial timestamp and a live tick 450 ms later; elapsed becomes 450 ms (the current implementation must fail this control by producing 100 ms). A later timestamp beyond the duration clamps elapsed exactly to the duration and schedules no further tick.
3. The existing generation semantics remain pinned: a stale-generation tick changes neither db nor scheduling, Reset produces observable zero, bumps the generation, establishes a fresh time baseline, and arms exactly one chain.
4. Raising duration after completion still re-arms exactly one chain, and the first resumed tick counts from the re-arm event rather than including time spent stopped.
5. The 100 ms value remains only the sampling/scheduling cadence; comments and the Seven GUIs teaching prose no longer describe fixed callbacks as elapsed time.
6. The example schema/frame-scoping test, focused generation/timing test, consolidated CLJS Node lane, and all-example compile gate pass. A temporary mutation back to `(+ elapsed-ms tick-ms)` makes the delayed-timestamp assertion red and is restored before handoff.
7. No new public API, general timer abstraction, component-local timer state, or changes outside the Timer example and its existing focused test/teaching row are introduced.

title: Spec 016 SSR: state the shipped projection-metadata contract at :1609 (framework computes, host records, no trace op) + projection-metadata docstring clock caveat
description:

The api-manifest gate does not pin docstrings (verified). CRLF: plain add; confirm git diff --stat shows a handful of lines, not the whole file.

ACCEPTANCE: (1) 016:1609's clause states the framework computes the projection metadata and does not record or trace it, recording being the host's per :1595, with no capitalised modal added or removed and no trace op named; (2) projection-metadata's docstring carries the clock caveat; (3) grep for any new rf.resource keyword (e.g. ssr-projected) across implementation/ spec/ tools/ returns nothing; (4) both doc gates green, resources JVM and CLJS suites green; (5) PR body quotes the spec wording, states prose was checked by hand, and states the tree is executable-identical.
