GATE COVERAGE, stated rather than assumed: the edit is prose in a paragraph and NOT inside a fenced block, so both link gates genuinely apply to it. Neither gate validates prose, anchors added (none), or tables (none touched) - all hand-checked and said so in the PR body. check_doc_slugs.py was proved to be reading this branch's tree rather than passing vacuously: a broken link planted on the edited line turned it red naming spec/016-Resources.md:1609, and the file was restored and verified byte-identical by blob hash before the green run.

BRIEF/BEAD DIVERGENCE, recorded because the bead governed: the dispatch brief listed FOUR files in scope, adding spec/009-Instrumentation.md ("touch only if the no-trace-op half genuinely requires a catalogue statement") and implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr.cljc. This bead's description forbids both explicitly - 009 as a hot-zone one-toucher not part of this work, and ssr.cljc:404 as an error-only listener not to be wired into. The bead governed: neither was touched, and neither needed to be. The "no trace op" half needs no catalogue statement precisely BECAUSE no op is minted - there is nothing to catalogue, and adding a 009 row saying an op does not exist would be the gold plating the ruling rejected. The brief also framed commit 866e452d37 as "A RULING MIKE MADE HIMSELF"; the ruling note on rf2-6r9j.53 corrects exactly that misattribution (it is PR #9097's rebase commit from branch worker/falsegreen-a, authored as Mike by the no-AI-attribution convention). The brief's "tension to resolve" between "no spec change to make" and this bead's reword is likewise already resolved on the bead, under "WHY B AND NOT 'LEAVE THE SENTENCE AS IS'": no rewrite is REQUIRED because no MUST is unmet, and the sentence is still reworded because four readers took it two ways. The reword makes an accurate-but-under-explicit contract explicit; it changes no obligation.

title: surface-review(examples-patterns): make Nine States managed loads newest-intent-wins
description:
## Slice reviewed

`examples/patterns/**`: boot, long-running work, nine states, and websocket, including their runnable build entries, adapter tests, governing pattern/spec text, and introducing history. This is the single cohesive correctness/teaching issue selected from that review.

## Correctness finding

The canonical Nine States example starts every data load with a direct `:rf.http/managed` effect but gives none of those requests a stable `:request-id`. That makes overlapping user intents first-settle-wins instead of newest-intent-wins.

The control panel leaves every Empty/One/Some/Too Many/error load button enabled whenever the page is not archived, including while the data region is already `:loading`. A second click therefore starts a second unkeyed request. The `:loading` state has no `:fetch-started` transition, so both requests remain in flight while the region stays at `:loading`. It accepts whichever `:fetch-succeeded` or `:fetch-failed` arrives first and immediately leaves `:loading`; its bucket/error states do not accept a completion. Thus an older request that was nearly finished can settle after a newer intent was issued, choose the visible bucket or error, and cause the newer request's eventual result to be ignored.

Concrete sequence: issue A for 25 rows, then issue B for 1 row before A settles. If A completes first, the page lands at `:too-many`; B later completes into a state that has no `:fetch-succeeded` handler, so the requested `:one` result never appears. The same ownership hole crosses success/failure: a nearly-complete old failing request can put the page in `:error` while a newer success is still in flight, then discard that success.

This is exactly the stale-reply case the governing pattern calls out. `spec/Pattern-NineStates.md` says a fresh load must prevent the previous reply from landing and demonstrates a stable `:request-id`; managed HTTP already gives the minimal mechanism: issuing the same id supersedes the old attempt and suppresses its app reply. The example omitted that one field.

## Evidence

- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:463-488`: both `:nine-states.demo/load` and `:nine-states.demo/load-with-failure` broadcast `:fetch-started` and issue `:rf.http/managed`; neither args map has `:request-id`.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:490-502`: every success/failure callback is forwarded unconditionally as a machine completion, with no ownership token or stale check.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:339-385`: only `:loading` consumes `:fetch-succeeded` / `:fetch-failed`; `:loading` itself does not consume another `:fetch-started`, and the settled bucket/error states consume only a future `:fetch-started` or reset. This makes the first completion decisive.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:756-782`: load controls are disabled only by `:mode/read-only`, not by `:data/loading`, so overlap is a supported interaction, not merely a fabricated internal event.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/stories.cljs:116-159`: the Story twins reproduce the same managed-request envelopes without a request id. Their canned fxs are synchronous, so the omission is visually hidden there too.
- `spec/Pattern-NineStates.md:289-313`: the canonical direct-managed-HTTP handler includes `:request-id :counter/load`.
- `spec/Pattern-NineStates.md:342-359`: direct effects do not get actor-lifetime cancellation; the stale-detection section says a fresh load while a previous request is live must not admit the previous reply, and names stable same-id supersession as the common-case mechanism.
- `docs/async/http.md:24-37`: public managed-HTTP reference defines `:request-id` as the stable id whose reuse supersedes the old request.
- `implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_cljs_test.cljs:1503-1547`: the CLJS transport regression proves same-id supersession delivers no app reply from the superseded request.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/nine_states_cljs_test.cljs:80-132`: the example suite routes HTTP to the synchronous demo stub; it even has to manufacture `:loading` by dispatching `:fetch-started` alone. These one-at-a-time rows cannot exercise overlap.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/nine_states_cljs_test.cljs:260-283`: the only stale-completion test resets to `:nothing` and sends a completion while still at `:nothing`, where it is trivially ignored. It does not exercise reset-then-reload or two live attempts, where the region is back at `:loading` and will accept the old completion.

## History

`1392aa0d1e` (2026-05-11) introduced the current load handlers without request ids. `git log -S":request-id" -- examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs` returns no commit: this path has never owned one. Sixteen minutes after the example rewrite, `a385d1aaba` added the managed-HTTP integration to `Pattern-NineStates`, including the stable request id and the explicit stale/supersession rationale. Later edits improved replies, schemas, reset semantics, frames, and prose, but never reconciled this executable companion with that requirement.

## Bounded recommendation

Define one clearly named stable request id for the Nine States data-load lane and put it on both live request shapes (`load` and `load-with-failure`), so any newer load intent supersedes either kind of older attempt. Carry the same field in the Story twins so the teaching envelopes remain faithful even though canned stubs do not model a real in-flight registry. Add a short adjacent explanation: the id expresses ownership of one replaceable page-load slot; it is not incidental tracing metadata.

Add one deterministic single-frame CLJS composition regression with a controlled/deferred transport: issue A, issue B before A settles, prove A's app target is suppressed, then settle B and prove only B's exact items/failure choose the machine state. Include a cross-kind row or table case so `load` and `load-with-failure` cannot accidentally drift onto separate ids.

This is the pre-alpha ergonomic fix: one existing field, one shared constant, one behavioral witness. It trusts the programmer and keeps all concurrency policy in readable data instead of disabling buttons or building a coordinator abstraction.

## Non-goals

- Do not redesign the parallel machine, cardinality cascade, render-priority table, or reply handlers.
- Do not add a request manager, sequence counter, promise layer, or generic remote-data abstraction.
- Do not disable load controls while loading; that only hides the race from mouse users and leaves programmatic intents incorrect.
- Do not move this example to the `:rf.http/managed` machine wrapper solely for this fix.
- Do not add a connection/page epoch to this non-routed, single-frame demo unless a separate lifecycle case proves it necessary. Stable same-id supersession closes the demonstrated overlap and reset-then-reload window.
- Do not change managed HTTP, canned-stub semantics, or the other three pattern examples.

## Duplicate search

Immediately before creation I searched all statuses in `.beads/issues.jsonl` with targeted `rg` combinations for Nine States/nine_states plus `request-id`, `stale`, `supersession`, `first-settle`, `newest`, `overlap`, and `demo/load`. No issue owns this example-level omission.

Closest open issue `rf2-o8ek` concerns the HTTP implementation's process-global registry colliding when two different frames reuse the same raw request id. It is complementary, not duplicate: this bead is a single-frame caller that supplies no id at all, so it cannot get supersession even after `rf2-o8ek` lands. The proposed regression is intentionally single-frame. Closed `rf2-iyjae` concerns websocket inbound correlation/validation, a different example and transport boundary.

## Uncertainty

Per review dispatch, I did not run a browser/runtime or external network. The verdict is derived from the executable transition tables, request envelopes, synchronous-test setup, current managed-HTTP contract, and its existing CLJS supersession regression. The exact controlled-fetch helper can follow the HTTP suite's established harness rather than inventing a new one. The canned demo resolves synchronously, so the current clickable app may not visibly reproduce the race until its override is replaced by the real asynchronous transport—the exact copy/adaptation moment this canonical example is meant to guide.
design: Use one stable keyword/constant for the replaceable Nine States data-load slot and attach it to every request producer in this example. Keep stale arbitration in the existing managed-HTTP boundary: same-id issue supersedes the previous attempt and the old app reply is suppressed before the page handler can broadcast it into the machine. Do not add local sequence bookkeeping. Test through a real controlled managed-HTTP lifecycle in one frame, because the canned effect intentionally has no in-flight lifecycle and cannot prove supersession.
acceptance_criteria:
- `:nine-states.demo/load` and `:nine-states.demo/load-with-failure` issue `:rf.http/managed` with the same stable, namespaced request id; the two Story request twins carry that same ownership field for envelope fidelity.
- A deterministic CLJS test in one frame holds request A open, issues request B through the shipped example event before A settles, and proves A's later success or failure dispatch reaches no app target and cannot move or mutate the Nine States machine.
- Settling B produces exactly B's expected `:items`/`:error`, data-region state/tag, and `:ui/render` result. At least one table row crosses request kind (old success versus new failure, or old failure versus new success) so both producer events are proven to share one replacement lane.
- A reset-then-new-load sequence cannot be overwritten by the pre-reset attempt; either cover it directly or make the overlap test's same-id suppression mechanism and existing reset test jointly explicit.
- The regression uses the real managed-HTTP supersession path or an existing controlled transport seam, not only the synchronous canned stub and not a hand-dispatched `:fetch-succeeded` event. A negative control removing/changing the shared request id makes the new overlap witness fail.
- Existing nine-state, reset, Story lifecycle, example compile/asset, and relevant managed-HTTP CLJS tests remain green. Reader-facing prose near the request explains newest-intent ownership in a few lines without adding a new abstraction.

title: examples(resources-ssr): client boot never acquires the route-free resource
description:
## Slice

`examples/capabilities/ssr/resources_ssr/**`, checked against the Resources/SSR implementation, Specs 011/016, the runnable Shadow build, example tests, tracker, and focused git history.

## Correctness finding

The route-free resource SSR example never causes its resource on the browser side. Its only `:rf.resource/ensure` is emitted by `:rf/server-init`, whose registration is server-only. Browser `run` creates the client frame, calls `rf.ssr/hydrate!`, and immediately renders `:app/root`; that view only dereferences the intentionally passive `[:rf/resource ...]` subscription. There is no client `ensure`/`refetch`, no live client owner, and no matching client release lifecycle.

Hydration cannot supply that missing liveness. The resource reconcile deliberately drops the baked `[:ssr request-id nav-token]` owner because it belongs to the completed server request. It computes/emits a hydration refetch plan, but does not issue those requests itself; the contract leaves issuance to a still-live route/consumer. This example explicitly has no route.

The result has three user-visible/semantic failures hidden behind one omission:

1. A client-only/no-payload load leaves the resource absent. `hydrate!` returns nil without seeding; the passive subscription projects the absent entry as `:idle`; `articles-page` falls through to an empty `<ul>`; nothing ever fetches.
2. The checked-in forever-fresh payload initially renders, but after hydration its SSR owner is removed and no client owner replaces it. The entry is not an active consumer: tag invalidation and focus/reconnect revalidation leave it stale instead of refetching, and the client ownership/GC lifecycle is never established.
3. A stale/no-data hydration disposition is only classified in `hydrate-refetch-plan`; this route-free boot never causes the load. The README nevertheless says stale/redacted/omitted entries refetch and that the client reconcile + refetch plan run end to end.

This is a teaching correctness bug, not a request for subscription-driven fetching. A programmer or AI copying the example learns that `hydrate!` plus a passive read is sufficient to acquire and keep a resource live, precisely opposite to the library's causal-command model.

## Evidence

- `examples/capabilities/ssr/resources_ssr/core.cljc:112-119` registers `:articles/list`.
- `core.cljc:136-148` is the only acquisition: server-only `:rf/server-init` dispatches `:rf.resource/ensure` under an SSR owner.
- `core.cljc:154-182` correctly says the view is passive; `core.cljc:395-413` hydrates and mounts without any client resource command while claiming an absent entry refetches.
- `README.md:99-110` claims fresh avoids a double-fetch and stale/redacted/omitted refetch; `README.md:122-125` says the refetch plan runs end to end.
- `index.html:69-90` bakes a `:loaded`, `:stale-at nil` entry with only an SSR owner. That deliberately easy fixture makes the documented run command look correct while avoiding every failing branch.
- `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/subs.cljc:1-14` states subscriptions are pure passive reads; `:332-347` projects a missing entry as `:idle` with no loading/fetching signal.
- `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/boot.cljc:154-163,323-327` skips hydration when no payload exists.
- `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/ssr.cljc:1324-1431` drops SSR owners; `:1495-1503,1626-1633,2311-2319` computes the refetch plan and says a live route issues it.
- `spec/016-Resources.md:303-306` defines attach/hold/release/GC; `:1187,1197` says stale hydration refetches on mount and that the client ensure/fresh-skip re-establishes ownership; `:1597,1603-1607` conditions hydration refetch on a resource the route still needs.
- `docs/api/re-frame.resources.md:310,614,708-710` states passive reads never fetch and only active-owner entries refetch on focus/reconnect or invalidation.
- `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn:1794-1804` runs this browser entrypoint against the static pre-baked page.
- `implementation/core/test/re_frame/examples_test.clj:677-847` tests dynamic and checked-in fresh payload hydration. It asserts the fresh plan is empty, but never executes the browser startup with no payload/stale data, never asserts a client owner, and never proves an actual refetch after invalidation.

## History

The client acquisition omission dates to the initial example. Commit `48dd1b928e` fixed the baked payload's storage key and made it permanently fresh, then added a regression that only proves fresh hydration/no immediate refetch. Commit `cd6fd08587` moved the client mount onto the adapter handle while retaining the omission and the explicit “absent one refetches” claim. This is not a new runtime regression; the static fixture and coverage have continually selected the one branch that passes without acquisition.

## Recommended bounded repair

Keep the example route-free. After hydration and before the first client render, cause one explicit client acquisition of `:articles/list` with the same global scope/params and a named app/page owner. Give that app-minted owner a matching release path. For this example's real resource:

- a fresh hydrated entry must take `ensure`'s cache-hit/fresh-skip path, attach the client owner, and issue zero transport requests;
- an absent/no-payload or stale entry must issue exactly one request;
- later invalidation must refetch because the resource now has a live client owner.

Keep views passive. Correct the prose to distinguish “hydration reconciles/classifies” from “the live client acquisition causes work.” This resource declares no sensitive/large policy, so remove the claim that this particular route-free demo executes redacted/omitted refetch unless the implementation and test actually cause those cases; linking to the normative generic contract is enough.

## Non-goals

- Do not make subscriptions fetch.
- Do not add a route/router merely to obtain an owner; route-free is a useful minimal SSR shape.
- Do not add a general hydration orchestration API or redesign resource ownership.
- Do not add mutation, GraphQL, polling, or broad resource examples here.
- Do not turn this into a full failure-matrix exercise; cover the small startup/liveness invariant.

## Duplicate audit

All-status `rg` searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` covered `resources_ssr`, `resources-ssr`, `client-only`, `no payload`, `passive`, `hydrate`, `owner`, `ensure`, `idle`, and `refetch`, including title combinations for hydrated owner/acquisition and SSR client fallback. No bead owns this outcome. Nearest hits are closed `rf2-6r9j.53` (projection metadata recording), closed `rf2-ujdn0` (copyable example run commands), and closed `rf2-ghxt` (a different RealWorld resources app-db schema boot defect).

## Uncertainty

This review was static by review-worker constraint: no runtime/browser/test execution. The documented runner always stages the forever-fresh payload, so the cold-load failure is masked in that command rather than visibly reproduced there. The causal absence is direct in source and contract, and the ownerless hydrated branch affects that documented fresh run after startup.
acceptance_criteria:
- The exact browser startup recipe (not a test-only clone) causes one post-hydration client acquisition for `:articles/list` under the same scope/params, with a documented app/page owner and matching release event/path.
- With no `__rf_payload`, startup issues exactly one managed-HTTP request, first projects loading rather than a false empty-success list, and renders the returned articles when the canned reply settles.
- With the actual checked-in fresh payload, startup issues zero managed-HTTP requests, preserves first-paint data/DOM adoption, removes the SSR owner, and attaches exactly the intended client owner via the fresh-skip/cache-hit path.
- With a focused stale/invalidated payload, startup keeps last-known-good data visible while issuing exactly one background request; after a fresh startup, `:rf.resource/invalidate-tags` refetches exactly once, proving the client owner is semantically live.
- Exercising the matching release removes that owner and leaves the entry eligible for the ordinary configured/default GC lifecycle.
- README/source comments no longer claim that a passive subscription or hydration reconciliation itself issues work, and do not claim redacted/omitted end-to-end refetch unless a test drives it.
- Existing server preload, payload projection, static-fixture hydration, and fresh no-double-fetch regressions remain green.

title: examples(routing): advertised route schema has no validator or observable effect
description:
## Finding

The canonical routing example presents its article-detail declaration as a working Malli route contract, but the app never loads the optional schemas artefact.

`examples/capabilities/routing/routing/core.cljs:49-51` declares `:params [:map [:id :string]]`; `README.md:24-28` explicitly calls out the Malli `:params` schema as a demonstrated feature. Yet the namespace requires only `re-frame.routing` and the Reagent adapter (`core.cljs:24-31`), and the `:examples/routing` build has no schema preload (`implementation/shadow-cljs.edn:1544-1548`). Having `schemas/src` on the compiler source path does not execute the namespace.

Routing deliberately does not require schemas: `implementation/routing/deps.edn:33-40` gives the production artefact only core, while `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/registry.cljc:1190-1210` documents and implements `[false nil]` when no validator hook is registered. The hook is published only when `re-frame.schemas` loads (`implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas.cljc:93,122`). The public guide is explicit that the require itself wires the validator (`docs/core/how-to/validate-with-schemas.md:20,39-41`), and Spec 010 lines 7 and 766 say schema implies validation only after requiring that artefact; omitting it is the Malli-free posture.

This instance hides the defect especially well: path captures are already strings, and routing's schema-derived coercion treats `:string` as passthrough (`registry.cljc:635-680`), so the declaration has no observable effect and the app still works. Routing can inspect other Malli-shaped metadata for limited coercion without loading schemas; the finding is specifically that validation is absent, not that every route schema is universally inert.

## Impact

This is a canonical teaching surface for programmers and coding agents, so it demonstrates a silent half-configuration as the happy path. Copying it and changing `:string` to `:int`, an enum, constraints, or a closed map can appear to work for valid input because routing derives coercions, while malformed input remains unvalidated. The registry's schema-free tests pin the revealing behavior: `?flag=maybe` and `?n=abc` remain strings (`implementation/routing/test/re_frame/routing_registry_test.clj:1257-1269`); with no validator the declared boundary does not reject them. Programmatic `route-url` validation likewise no-ops (`registry.cljc:1909-1915`). That is precisely the kind of subtle API lesson an example should not teach.

## Bounded recommendation

Keep this example minimal and routing-focused: remove the unnecessary `:params [:map [:id :string]]` from article-detail and remove the README parenthetical claiming it demonstrates Malli. The path param remains a string and visible behavior is unchanged. A terse cross-link may mention that route validation requires `[re-frame.schemas]`, but do not add that artefact merely to preserve a declaration with no visible learning payoff: Spec 010's measured matched A/B cost is +39.9 KB gzip (`spec/010-Schemas.md:726-733`). If a future example intentionally teaches route validation, it should load schemas and visibly exercise valid and invalid input; that is outside this bead.

## Non-goals

No change to routing's schemas-optional packaging, late-bind soft-pass, coercion rules, validator APIs, route IDs/URLs/navigation, article data, other examples, or a new browser/test harness. Do not make routing depend on schemas or add generic schema machinery.

## History and duplicate search

The schema line dates to initial import `8c6e5a5060` (2026-05-06); routing became its own optional artefact in `c435165251` (2026-05-09); schema-implies-validation landed in `d0b95fdc54` (2026-06-01); README's Malli claim came later in `fdecf54a1fc` (2026-06-26). The declaration survived those contract shifts untouched.

Exact `rg` searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` for this example plus schema/Malli/validation and the current `HEAD..origin/main` beads delta found no owner. Nearby but non-duplicate: `rf2-nvcp` (route-link boot failure), `rf2-ujdn0` (one-command README launcher), `rf2-g1gt` / `rf2-do50` (relative asset/deep-link hosting), and `rf2-6r9j.3` (unconsumed internal RouteAddress constant). The standalone-server history-fallback candidate was discarded because existing beads already discuss that mechanism.

## Uncertainty

No runtime was executed during this read-only review. The namespace load graph and explicit missing-hook branch are direct evidence; the recommended source/prose deletion preserves the currently observed string-param behavior.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `routing.core` no longer presents a route schema while loading only routing (preferred: article-detail metadata retains only `:doc`), and `/articles/:id` still supplies the same string `:id` to the existing detail view.
2. The routing README no longer claims this app demonstrates or carries a Malli `:params` schema; its route-table description stays accurate.
3. If a schema note is retained, it states that loading `re-frame.schemas` is required for validation; this minimal example gains no schema dependency solely for the inert `:string` declaration.
4. `:examples/routing` compiles cleanly through the existing example compile gate. No bespoke runtime suite or scanner is introduced for this two-line teaching correction.
5. No runtime, package, coercion, or other-example behavior changes.

title: surface-review(examples-substrates): keep the runnable slim-counter bundle free of its CI SSR fixture
description:
## Scope

Separate the runnable Reagent Slim counter under examples/substrates/reagent_slim/counter from the CI-only pure-CLJS-SSR bundle-isolation fixture that currently owns its only Shadow build entry. Keep the stock/slim counter comparison focused on the existing counter app and keep the adapter-owned S3-005/S3-008 isolation proof non-vacuous in a dedicated build. Limit changes to the slim counter entry/fixture seam, the paired Shadow/package/checker configuration, directly coupled staging/checker tests, and prose that describes this comparison.

## Correctness finding

The repository presents examples/counter-slim-and-fast as the runnable “same app, different package” counterpart to examples/counter, but its only build does not invoke reagent-slim.counter.core/run. It invokes reagent-slim.counter.bundle-isolation-entry/run, which executes test-only pre-mount SSR work, pulls reagent2.dom.server and its serializer into main.js, creates a throwaway frame, clears its subscription cache, and writes globalThis.counterSlimPrerender.

This is not just extra source beside the example. Both documented launch paths compile and serve that same contaminated build, so the runnable artifact and the bundle a reader is invited to compare against stock contain and execute a CI harness that the stock app does not. The comparison therefore changes two variables at once: substrate/package and an SSR fixture. It undermines the folder’s central teaching claim that the app is held constant, especially because the catalogue explicitly says the interest is what the bundle does not contain.

## Evidence

- implementation/shadow-cljs.edn:1259-1270 declares :examples/counter-slim-and-fast and points its :init-fn at reagent-slim.counter.bundle-isolation-entry/run, explicitly not reagent-slim.counter.core/run.
- examples/substrates/reagent_slim/counter/bundle_isolation_entry.cljs:1-29 says it is gate plumbing, is the build’s init-fn, and passes prove-pure-cljs-ssr! into the app boot before mounting.
- examples/substrates/reagent_slim/counter/bundle_isolation_fixture.cljs:1-54 requires reagent2.dom.server, calls render-to-static-markup, writes counterSlimPrerender on globalThis to defeat advanced DCE, and clears the transient subscription cache.
- examples/substrates/reagent_slim/counter/core.cljs:96-126 exposes an optional on-frame boot arity and a with-new-frame branch whose only caller is that fixture. The supposedly plain teaching file therefore still carries a public-looking harness seam even though its zero-arity run does not use it.
- examples/substrates/reagent_slim/counter/README.md:13-22 says the meaningful diff from stock is only the package/import and adapter, calls core.cljs the plain idiomatic example, labels both sibling fixture files “not app practice”, then at lines 49-55 tells the reader to launch the build whose init-fn is the fixture entry.
- examples/substrates/README.md:7-15 defines the track as “same authoring language, different package”, says each example changes exactly one place, and says the interest is what the bundle does not contain. Lines 84-95 route the slim command through the same build.
- examples/README.md:163 repeats that the interest is what the bundle does not contain.
- implementation/package.json:46 makes test:reagent-slim:bundle-isolation release examples/counter-slim-and-fast, while line 53 routes dev:example through the normal standalone runner. examples/scripts/serve-example.cjs:149-210 resolves the selected build and compiles it unchanged; there is no teaching-entry substitution.
- implementation/scripts/check-reagent-slim-bundle-isolation.cjs:135-182 defines counterSlimPrerender and a reagent2.dom.server-only literal as required positive sentinels. Lines 275-364 read out/examples/counter-slim-and-fast and require those SSR sentinels in that bundle, confirming the contamination is load-bearing for the gate rather than dead source.
- Git history identifies the incomplete separation. Commit b2ae161b17 (rf2-vyl0vt, “prune scaffolding from Reagent-family examples”) moved the fixture out of core.cljs so the source looked clean, but deliberately repointed the one example build to the new gate entry. It separated files, not the runnable artifact or core’s fixture-only boot seam.

## Failure scenario / impact

A programmer or coding agent follows the catalogue and compares the release outputs of examples/counter and examples/counter-slim-and-fast to understand the substrate cost. The stock bundle contains the counter client. The slim bundle contains the counter client plus a forced server serializer, a DCE anchor and fixture orchestration, and it performs an unrelated static render/global write before mounting. Any size, reachability, startup, or “what ships” conclusion attributes fixture-only differences to Reagent Slim.

The same problem appears without bundle analysis: running the advertised slim example executes code every comment calls CI-only and “not app practice”. Reading core/run is not enough to discover what the official page actually boots; the authoritative build config chooses a different entry. The invariant for a comparison example is simple: its documented runnable build must boot the code it teaches, and gate-only work must not be reachable from that runnable entry.

## Recommended minimal fix

Restore :examples/counter-slim-and-fast to reagent-slim.counter.core/run. Give bundle_isolation_entry and bundle_isolation_fixture a dedicated, non-runnable Shadow build with a separate output directory, and make test:reagent-slim:bundle-isolation release and inspect that output. Keep the existing stock build as the methodology control and retain all six isolation contracts, including the two positive SSR sentinels that make S3-005 non-vacuous.

Move the fixture-only orchestration out of core’s optional on-frame boot arity so the teaching boot is the same small install-then-mount shape readers actually run. Update the checker diagnostics, targeted Shadow/staging/script-policy tests, and the few comparison paragraphs that currently conflate the runnable example and gate fixture. Use an existing local convention for the dedicated check build id; do not introduce a build registry or generalized harness framework.

## Non-goals

- No change to Reagent Slim, stock Reagent, core frame, rendering, SSR, or adapter APIs.
- No removal or weakening of the pure-CLJS-SSR non-vacuity proof, stock-Reagent absence proof, react-dom/server absence proof, or mirror slim-absence proof.
- No bundle-size threshold or performance claim.
- No new browser/Playwright example matrix; examples remain test-free learning surfaces and adapter behavior remains adapter-testbed-owned.
- No extraction or redesign of the counter’s events, subscriptions, views, frame id, or mount lifecycle.
- No cross-product of examples across every substrate and no general example-manifest redesign.
- No effort to make the dedicated gate fixture user-runnable or to teach its orchestration as app practice.

## Related / duplicate search

Searched all issue states in .beads/issues.jsonl with targeted rg queries for counter-slim-and-fast, bundle-isolation entry/fixture, counterSlimPrerender, reagent-slim bundle isolation, teaching build, runnable fixture, and same-app bundle. No issue owns this separation.

Closest records are not duplicates:
- rf2-fmns2 (closed) owns the three-view-layer login comparison and its cross-runtime isolation proof, not the slim counter entry.
- rf2-k5r9t (closed) added the Reagent client-root lifecycle and migrated example mounts; it does not separate test and runnable builds.
- rf2-vyl0vt is represented by commit b2ae161b17 and physically moved fixture code out of the teaching namespace, but intentionally kept the one runnable build pointed at the gate entry. This finding is the remaining artifact-level half of that cleanup.
- rf2-5x1xt (closed) fixes missing UIx consumer dependencies and is unrelated.
- rf2-cdoo (open) concerns Reagent Slim after-render ordering, not examples or bundle reachability.

## Uncertainty

The exact dedicated build id and output prefix should follow whichever current non-page/check-build convention best fits Shadow configuration and CI surface classification. The required outcome is not a particular spelling: the documented :examples/counter-slim-and-fast output must be fixture-free, and the isolation checker must consume a separate output that remains deliberately fixture-full. No runtime execution was needed for this review; the entrypoint and reachability contradiction is explicit in source/config and in the gate’s required sentinels.
acceptance_criteria:
1. :examples/counter-slim-and-fast uses reagent-slim.counter.core/run as its init-fn, remains listed by the standalone example runner, and both documented launch commands serve that build.
2. A focused config/staging assertion proves the runnable build resolves to core/run and does not silently regress to bundle-isolation-entry.
3. The runnable advanced main.js contains neither counterSlimPrerender nor the reagent2.dom.server-only SSR presence sentinel. The check is non-vacuous by also proving ordinary Reagent Slim client sentinels are present.
4. A separate non-runnable build owns reagent-slim.counter.bundle-isolation-entry/run and emits to a distinct output directory not staged or advertised as the counter example.
5. test:reagent-slim:bundle-isolation releases that dedicated build and the stock counter, and its checker reads the dedicated slim output.
6. The dedicated gate bundle still contains counterSlimPrerender plus the serializer-owned static-markup sentinel, contains the ordinary slim client sentinels, and contains none of the stock-Reagent or react-dom/server sentinels. The stock bundle retains its own positive controls and remains free of slim sentinels.
7. The teaching core no longer exposes an optional callback/throwaway-frame seam used only by the bundle fixture; core/run and any retained boot helper express only the runnable app lifecycle.
8. The slim README and substrate catalogues distinguish the runnable comparison from the dedicated CI fixture without teaching the fixture as application code or weakening the “same app, different package” claim.
9. Targeted checker self-tests, example staging/manifest tests, npm run test:examples-compile, and npm run test:reagent-slim:bundle-isolation pass, with a planted reachability/config regression demonstrating the new separation check fails on the old shape.

value:
NEVER PUT AN AD-HOC EXTRACTION'S OUTPUT IN A BRIEF WITHOUT A CONTROL — five distinct instrument faults in one session, every one failing toward "nothing here", and three of them reached a worker.

THE FIVE, all mine, all on this box, all in one day:

1. `sed -n '/DESCRIPTION/,/^$/p'` — bd prints a BLANK LINE immediately after the DESCRIPTION header, so the range ends at once and prints nothing. I told a worker "the description read as empty in the tracker's rendering, which is itself a signal" and instructed it to pull with --json. The description was 7,847 characters and `bd show` rendered it in full. The worker had to establish that before it could start.

2. `git log --grep=<id>` is an UNANCHORED PREFIX match, so `rf2-6r9j.24` matched `.244` and `.249` — three hits, none about the bead. Anchored, zero. Check 5 of the backlog reread acts on a hit by CLOSING, so this fails toward "looks done".

3. `jq -r` emits CRLF here, so every id looped from it carries a trailing carriage return; `bd show "rf2-aunp\r"` answers "no issue found" ON STDOUT, and a grep of that error for fence markers finds none and prints "(clear)". Fourteen of fifteen beads read as clear having never been read.

4. Flattening does not undo a renderer's MID-TOKEN line break, at hyphens AND underscores. It fails both ways: a present token reads absent, and harvesting identifiers from rendered output MINTS NAMES THAT DO NOT EXIST — `oke_dom_cljs_test.cljs` was manufactured from `per_keystroke_dom_cljs_test.cljs` and went into a dispatch brief as a real file. `mine.md` and `keystroke.md` came from the same extraction.

5. Two canary counts that both look canonical: `ls -A implementation/node_modules | wc -l` = 103, `ls ... | wc -l` = 101, differing by two dotfiles. I quoted 103 to some workers and the standing note says 101, so a worker measuring correctly reported a discrepancy that was not one. STATE WHICH INSTRUMENT with the number, or the number is not checkable.

THE SHAPE IS ALWAYS THE SAME. An extraction is misused; it raises no error; it returns empty or plausible; and empty reads as a finding. None of these five failed loudly. Positive controls catch (2), (3) and (5); only reading the RENDERED TEXT catches (1) and (4).

THE RULE, and it is cheap: BEFORE A MEASUREMENT GOES INTO A BRIEF, A BEAD OR A REPORT, EXERCISE THE COMMAND ONCE AGAINST SOMETHING IT SHOULD FIND. If it cannot find that, the zero is about the instrument. For an extraction that produces IDENTIFIERS rather than counts, add the second half: validate every path with `git ls-files <path>` — a 0 means you invented it.

AND THE ASYMMETRY IS WHY THIS MATTERS AT THE MAYOR'S DESK SPECIFICALLY. A wrong measurement in my own reasoning costs me one command to recheck. The same measurement in a BRIEF costs a worker's whole context, and the project's own method doc names briefs as where the mayor's errors concentrate. Workers caught all three that escaped, and none reached the trunk — but each cost a cycle.

title: dev:example advertises a live SPA before the first watch build exists
description:
## Scope

Make the default `npm run dev:example -- <build-id>` watch path advertise a runnable SPA only after that run's first browser bundle exists. Keep the current manifest-derived build selection, clean staging, shadow-cljs watch, loopback http-server, ownership-token handshake, and test-free examples policy. The synchronous `--no-watch` path is already ordered correctly and should remain so.

## Finding

The runner announces that an example "is live" after proving only that http-server owns the selected output directory. In the default watch path it has deliberately deleted the previous `main.js`, starts `shadow-cljs watch` asynchronously, and never waits for the first successful compile before printing the URL. On a cold or otherwise slower compile, the printed page therefore serves its host and shared assets while its required `main.js` is still absent. Opening it in that interval requests a missing script and leaves a blank/non-booted app. Because no bundle loaded, no shadow client is present to turn the later compile into recovery; the programmer has to notice the compiler finished and manually reload.

This is a small but high-leverage ergonomics defect in the catalogue's canonical one-command front door. The command's strongest status line says the SPA is live when only the static server is live.

## Independently established evidence

- `examples/scripts/serve-example.cjs:186-202` applies the correct clean-stage boundary and removes the selected output directory, including every prior `main.js`.
- The runner itself records the consequence at `serve-example.cjs:204-210`: in watch mode the cleaned directory has no `main.js` until the first compile lands.
- `serve-example.cjs:222-224` stages `index.html`, `_shared`, and declared static assets; it does not produce the compiled entrypoint.
- `serve-example.cjs:241-264` spawns `shadow-cljs watch` as a long-running asynchronous child. There is no first-build promise, emitted-file wait, or successful-compile signal in this path.
- `serve-example.cjs:275-286` then calls `startLocalHttpServer`; immediately after its `ready` result, lines 288-293 print `serve-example: <build> is live at ... (shadow-cljs watch running - edits recompile live)`.
- `implementation/scripts/lib/local-browser-harness.cjs:636-722` defines that readiness narrowly and correctly for its own purpose: publish and fetch `/.rf-harness-token` to prove the responder serves this run's root. It does not inspect or request `main.js`, so a clean staged root with only HTML/assets is `ready: true`.
- The current example inventory has 33 `index.html` / `*.index.html` host pages that load `<script src="main.js">`; `check-examples-assets.cjs` makes a live `main.js` script reference mandatory but exempts the generated file from source-tree existence checks. Thus host correctness depends on the compile product that server readiness does not cover.
- `examples/README.md:15-23` makes this runner the canonical command and says it "serves the result ... and prints the URL to open"; raw watch is explicitly contrasted with `dev:example` as compiler-only, while `dev:example` is the route to "the running app."
- The `--no-watch` branch at `serve-example.cjs:211-219` runs `shadow-cljs compile` synchronously and rejects nonzero status before staging/server startup, so the defect is confined to the default watch lifecycle.

No application, browser, build, or network operation was run during this review. The race follows from the explicit process ordering. Whether a particular warm-cache launch exposes it depends on scheduling; the cold/slow-compile case is the material witness to add.

## History and why existing coverage misses it

- Commit `a4636f853f` introduced the one-command runner with the current asynchronous watch-before-server shape.
- Commit `1d62730eb1` (`rf2-rg2tze`) fixed a worse stale-output false green by cleaning first. Its commit message and current comments explicitly say `main.js` is now visibly absent until the first compile. That is the right stale-file policy, but it exposes the remaining readiness mismatch rather than resolving it.
- Commit `3686d3ffd0` (`rf2-35lfqo`) made unexpected child failures nonzero; it does not establish first-build success while a healthy watcher is compiling or waiting after a compile error.
- Commit `0b438394dc` centralized local-server readiness around an ownership token. That helper is behaving as designed: server ownership and application-build readiness are different facts. The example runner is the layer that must compose them.
- `implementation/scripts/_examples-staging.test.cjs:411-481` proves stale `main.js` removal and call order. Its lifecycle tests cover child exit classification, not the interval between server readiness and first output. The static asset tests prove the host references `main.js`, not that the dev runner waits until it is served.

## Recommended bounded fix

Keep the existing architecture. In watch mode, distinguish two states in the runner:

1. The local server owns the staged root, but the first build is still pending. If this state is logged at all, call it "waiting for initial build," not live/openable.
2. The current run's `main.js` is present, non-empty, and retrievable from the owned server while the watch child remains alive. Only then print the existing live URL/status.

A small runner-local wait/predicate is sufficient. It may poll the selected output plus the already-owned loopback server; do not parse shadow-cljs's human log format. While waiting, retain the current long-running development behavior: a compile error may be fixed by editing source, and Ctrl+C still tears down the process tree. An unexpected watch exit must abort the wait and remain nonzero.

## Acceptance criteria

- With a fake/delayed watch child and an initially clean output directory, the runner does not emit its `is live`/open-this-URL signal while `main.js` is absent, zero-length, or not served successfully.
- When that same child publishes a valid non-empty `main.js`, the runner emits the live URL once and continues watching/serving as today.
- If the watch child exits before first-build readiness, the runner does not announce the app as live, tears down the server, and exits nonzero with a direct initial-build diagnostic.
- A compile error from a still-running watcher does not require restarting the runner: after the programmer fixes source and the first successful output lands, the URL becomes live.
- The existing ownership-token handshake remains the authority for "this server serves this run's root"; first-build readiness is composed in `serve-example`, not generalized into every local-browser harness consumer.
- `--no-watch` still compiles once before server startup and reports compile failure nonzero. `--list`, build-id normalization, staging, per-example assets, free-port selection, reload caching policy, and cleanup remain unchanged.
- Add focused script-level coverage for delayed artifact, successful first publication, and watch-before-build failure. Demonstrate the new check failing against the current ordering, then run the existing examples staging/script tests.

## Non-goals

- No new launcher, build registry, dev server, compiler wrapper, or shadow-cljs protocol.
- No parsing of compiler console text and no dependence on a particular shadow-cljs log phrase.
- No browser auto-open, page-level smoke for every example, HMR redesign, service worker, retry UI, or generalized file-watching abstraction.
- No change to example application code, public re-frame2 APIs, shared visual assets, or the test-free `examples/` policy.
- No attempt to make every later recompile atomic; this issue owns only the first truthful runnable status after a clean launch.

## Duplicate distinctions

Targeted all-status searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` covered `serve-example`, `dev:example`, `initial compile`, `first compile`, `main.js` with live/ready/404/blank, and frozen bundle; no bead owns first-build readiness.

- Historical `rf2-rg2tze` removes stale output and intentionally leaves `main.js` absent until the first compile; this finding is the remaining live-status/readiness seam.
- Closed `rf2-iacw2` and `rf2-ujdn0` correct documentation so programmers invoke `dev:example`; they do not change when that command's URL becomes runnable.
- Closed `rf2-y1kbf` requires host HTML to contain a live `<script src="main.js">`; it does not verify the generated script exists at launch time.
- Historical `rf2-35lfqo` handles watcher/server crashes. A healthy but not-yet-successful first compile is not a child-exit outcome.
- The shared ownership-token work (`rf2-slapfs`) prevents a foreign server false green and should not be broadened; it cannot prove application artifacts by design.

## Uncertainty

No cold compile was launched under the review's no-runtime constraint, so the exact user-visible duration is cache and machine dependent. A sufficiently fast warm build can land before http-server readiness and hide the race. The unsynchronized state is nevertheless explicit in source and guaranteed to be reachable whenever initial compilation takes longer than server startup. The implementer should capture that case deterministically with a fake delayed producer rather than relying on machine timing.

title: bug(realworld-http): profile replies can overwrite a newer username route
description:
## Scope

Review surface: `examples/real-apps/**`, specifically the managed-HTTP RealWorld profile page. The resources-based RealWorld variant was compared and is already keyed by canonical resource params; it is not part of the fix.

## Correctness finding

`examples/real-apps/realworld_http/profile.cljs` binds each request URL and request ID to the current `:username`, but every banner/authored/favorites reply target omits that identity and every terminal handler writes the one shared `:profile`, `:profile.articles`, or `:profile.favorites` slice unconditionally. Follow/unfollow similarly captures the route username only in the URL, then applies success or rollback to whichever profile slice is current.

Navigating Alice -> Bob leaves Alice and Bob under distinct request IDs, so managed HTTP may legally deliver both. A late Alice settle can therefore replace Bob data, statuses, errors, timestamps, or following state. It can also corrupt the current state-machine presentation.

## Evidence

- Routes `/profile/:username` and `/profile/:username/favorites` run profile plus list loads on each match: `examples/real-apps/realworld_http/routing.cljs:110-126`.
- The page has shared unkeyed slices initialized once: `examples/real-apps/realworld_http/profile.cljs:39-46,147-153`.
- Banner request ID is `[:profile/load username]`, but targets are `[:profile/loaded]` and `[:profile/load-failed]`; both handlers write unconditionally: `profile.cljs:159-198`.
- Authored requests are keyed by username but their targets omit it and their handlers write unconditionally: `profile.cljs:200-239`. Favorites repeats the defect: `profile.cljs:241-280`.
- Follow/unfollow paths use the current username, while `:profile/followed`, `:profile/unfollowed`, and rollback handlers mutate the shared current profile without issuer identity: `profile.cljs:286-331`.
- The view consumes only those shared slices (`profile.cljs:380-389,438-502`), so stale Alice can be rendered and acted upon under Bob's URL.
- This is not just a cosmetic flash. If late Alice failure arrives while Bob is loading, it can send the data machine to `:error`; a later Bob success writes DB data, but the `:error` state has no `fetch-succeeded` transition (`profile.cljs:86-121`), leaving the page stranded in an error presentation.
- Managed HTTP only supersedes an old request when a new request has the same request ID (`docs/async/http.md:312-316`; `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:1573-1580`). Alice and Bob IDs differ, so route staleness remains application-owned.
- The local canonical precedent already fixes the equivalent article defect: `examples/real-apps/realworld_http/comments.cljs:152-157,242-284,317-364` carries the slug through targets and rejects replies that do not match the active slug (closed `rf2-iy3d6`).
- The resources variant is immune by construction: identity includes canonical params (`examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/resources.cljs:13-18`), profile/list resources include username/page (`resources.cljs:172-233`), and routes plan those keyed resources (`realworld_resources/routing.cljs:206-245`).
- Existing profile coverage (`implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/realworld_cljs_test.cljs:2860-2897`) uses immediate canned replies for one username and cannot expose ordering. The same suite's held-request cross-slug tests around lines 1900-2130 provide a suitable pattern.
- History traces this shape to managed-HTTP conversion `36436af528`; the current `origin/main` profile blob is identical to this review worktree's blob.

## Impact

This canonical realistic example teaches programmers and AI that username-keyed request IDs alone provide navigation stale suppression. Under ordinary network reordering it can show or mutate the wrong user's profile, authored/favorited articles, and following state. The machine can remain in an error presentation even after current data succeeds.

## Recommended bounded fix

Use one local correlation convention, mirroring `comments.cljs`:

1. Carry the issuing username in every banner and social terminal target; carry the relevant username/page key (or equivalent generation) in list targets.
2. Record or compare the active logical key and reject stale success, failure, rollback, status, timestamp, and machine writes before mutation.
3. On username identity change, clear or hide prior-user data. Retaining data for a same-key refresh remains valid.
4. Correlate follow/unfollow settlements to their issuing profile. A stable per-profile social request ID may additionally supersede rapid same-profile toggles, but generic framework machinery is unnecessary.

## Non-goals

Do not migrate this page to resources, add a cache framework or generic remote-data abstraction, change the route/HTTP API, redesign the UI, or modify the already identity-keyed resources variant.

## Duplicate review

Searched `.beads/issues.jsonl` and the `origin/main` tracker for cross-profile/cross-username/late-profile/profile-race/wrong-profile terms, every affected handler name, request-id/profile, and out-of-order/profile. Only closed `rf2-iy3d6` matched because its article defect recorded `profile race` as a search term. Generic profile-file/page searches found closed article/comment social work (`rf2-amhpk`, `rf2-84iek`, `rf2-iy3d6`) and unrelated base-href work (`rf2-do50`). Those are precedents, not owners of profile replies. No open or closed duplicate owns this behavior.

## Uncertainty

The review is static by review-pool constraint, but the delivery branch follows directly from the documented same-ID-only suppression and the distinct username IDs. The exact internal key shape, and whether a reply after leaving and returning to the same username should be accepted, are implementation choices. The required invariant is that a settle cannot mutate a different active profile identity.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Add deterministic held-transport CLJS coverage for Alice -> Bob navigation across banner, authored, and favorites requests. Settle Bob first and then Alice success/failure; Alice cannot change Bob data, status, error, timestamps, or machine presentation.
2. Prove non-vacuity: the corresponding current-Bob success/failure is accepted. A late prior-profile failure cannot strand the current machine, and current success can present loaded data.
3. While Bob is pending, previously settled Alice banner/list data is not exposed under Bob's route. Same-identity refresh retention remains allowed.
4. Hold Alice follow/unfollow, navigate to Bob, then settle Alice. Neither success nor rollback mutates Bob; current-profile settlements still work.
5. Production reply vectors carry enough identity for every state-changing terminal path to reject stale work.
6. Demonstrate a red negative control by removing or inverting the correlation guard, then restore it and pass the focused RealWorld CLJS suite and applicable build/type gates.

title: bug(skill-setup): custom-name manual scaffolds bypass the generator's identity derivation
description:
## Problem

`re-frame2-setup` treats an author-supplied project name as a first-class zero-friction override, but its default manual route never defines how that name becomes the several identities a CLJS project needs. It says only to rename `acme` / `my-app` consistently. The generator route uses a real derivation instead: Clojure namespace, filesystem path, npm package name, output directory, `:init-fn`, headings, and requires are related but not identical strings. Therefore the two routes advertised as producing the same files are deterministic only for the fixed reference name.

A common qualified name exposes the gap. For `com.acme/my-cool-app`, the generator emits namespace `com.acme.my-cool-app`, source path `src/com/acme/my_cool_app`, and npm name `my-cool-app`. A manual textual rename can naturally produce `src/com.acme/my_cool_app`, which does not back the namespace named by `shadow-cljs.edn` and fails namespace resolution. Bare and mixed-case names have different hazards: deps-new currently doubles bare `my-app` into the almost-certainly-unintended `my-app.my-app`, while npm identity must be lowercased and validated independently.

## Evidence

- `skills/re-frame2-setup/SKILL.md:42` says an author-supplied project name overrides the default, without restricting its shape.
- `skills/re-frame2-setup/SKILL.md:55` says manual and generator routes land on the same files.
- `skills/re-frame2-setup/SKILL.md:67` and `references/first-counter.md:3` give the manual operation only as renaming `acme` / `my-app` consistently across paths and contents.
- `tools/template/src/day8/re_frame2_template/hooks.clj:119-162` defines separate `->file-path`, `->ns-form`, lowercasing, and npm-name validation; `data-fn` at lines 166-191 derives `:namespace`, `:nested-dirs`, and `:npm-name` separately.
- `tools/template/test/day8/re_frame2_template/template_test.clj:294-320` proves the nontrivial mapping `com.acme/my-cool-app` -> `com.acme.my-cool-app`, `src/com/acme/my_cool_app`, and `my-cool-app`. Lines 332-360 separately cover qualified, dotted, bare, mixed-case, and invalid npm names.
- `tools/template/spec/API.md:160` explicitly records that a bare name is accepted by deps-new but becomes doubled (`my-app.my-app`) and recommends a group-qualified name. The setup skill exposes a natural-language "project name" override without carrying that rule or choosing a different normalization.
- `skills/re-frame2-setup/tests/first_counter_derivation.clj:78-82` renders only the fixed `{:name "acme/my-app" :top "acme" :main "my-app"}` identity. The setup drift suite and `evals/evals.json` grade the reference default, empty-project merge, and generator route, but no custom-name manual result.
- History confirms the split: `18b9486664` added deterministic npm/name derivation to the generator, while `98aa4b1f5f` made the setup leaf a derivation of the one reference identity and described all custom identities only as a rename.

## Programmer and AI impact

Naming the app is one of the most ordinary scaffold requests. A programmer or AI can follow every stated setup instruction, write all twelve files, and reach the terminating compile only to discover a missing namespace or invalid npm name. Repair then requires reverse-engineering the generator's rules after the skill promised one prompt and one served SPA. Even when a capable agent guesses the CLJS path mapping correctly, route parity is accidental and untested, so model or wording changes can silently reintroduce the failure.

## Posture fit

This is not a request for a naming system. A single small identity rule removes guesswork from a high-frequency override, keeps the API ergonomic, and lets humans and agents start the SPA successfully on the first pass.

## Duplicate research

Targeted searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` for setup/custom names, dotted groups, name derivation, npm names, and manual-route naming found no issue owning this residual. Closed `rf2-zq34m` fixed generator output and npm-name validity, not the setup skill's manual override. Closed `rf2-rc0yh` established the fixed `acme/my-app` default. `rf2-h4q82` and `rf2-pygpw` concern generator location and post-emission coordinates; `rf2-0ddz3` concerns merging into a shadow-only project. Open `rf2-eiev` covers optimized release proof and `rf2-1c60` distribution metadata. None defines manual custom-name parity.

## Uncertainty

This read-only review did not execute a generated project. The concrete bad path is a permitted result of the current underspecified instruction, not a claim that every capable model will choose it. The objective defect is that the promised deterministic override has no specified derivation and no parity test, despite the adjacent generator already proving the distinctions matter.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The manual route documents or executes one unambiguous mapping from a supplied project identity to every emitted identity-bearing field; it no longer says only to rename tokens consistently.
2. `com.acme/my-cool-app` produces the same observable identity on both routes: namespace `com.acme.my-cool-app`, files under `src/com/acme/my_cool_app` and `test/com/acme/my_cool_app`, npm name/output directory `my-cool-app`, matching `:init-fn` and internal requires, and consistent human-facing labels.
3. Bare and mixed-case inputs have an explicit shared policy. An invalid npm artifact is rejected before any manual-route file is written just as the generator fails before emission; no partial scaffold remains.
4. A focused setup eval grades an explicitly named manual scaffold, including source path, namespace, package name, and successful compile/handoff rather than merely checking that the name appears in prose.
5. A deterministic test compares manual identity derivation with the template hook for the dotted, bare, mixed-case, and invalid cases. At least one non-reference qualified identity reaches the existing compile proof, or an equivalently strong namespace-to-path resolver test demonstrates that the emitted `:init-fn` can be found.
6. The zero-interview `acme/my-app` default and explicit UIx override remain unchanged, and the fix adds no new scaffold files, dependencies, selector, or user questionnaire.
design:
## Bounded fix

- Define one canonical project-identity normalization for both setup routes. At minimum, specify how a supplied coordinate yields the group/artifact, namespace, source/test directories, npm name, output directory, `:init-fn`, internal requires, README/title, and heading.
- Reuse the generator hook's current semantics as the oracle, or deliberately improve a questionable case in both places together. Do not leave manual and generator behavior different. In particular, make the bare-name policy explicit: either reject it before writing, normalize it intentionally, or document and reproduce the doubled deps-new identity; never let the routes improvise different answers.
- Put the compact rule in the normal setup path, close to the custom-name override. Keep `first-counter.md` as the one reference scaffold rather than copying twelve custom variants.
- Add a focused custom-name outcome eval and a small derivation/parity test driven by the template hook. Cover one dotted qualified name plus bare, mixed-case, and invalid-artifact boundaries. Extend the existing emitted compile fixture for one non-reference identity only if static parity cannot prove namespace/path coherence.

## Non-goals

- No naming DSL, wizard, profile system, compatibility aliases, or clarification round for the existing unqualified default.
- No change to the counter, substrate choice, dependency pins, twelve-file manifest, build/watch workflow, or publication-coordinate handling.
- No matrix of arbitrary Unicode/package-manager policy and no attempt to replace deps-new.
- No duplicated hand-maintained scaffold per project name.

title: bug(skill-reagent-migration): MIG-04/05 silently turn queued Reagent dispatches into synchronous Hicasso intents
description:
## Scope

Correct the scheduling contract taught by skills/reagent-migration/** for Reagent handler rewrites into Hicasso intents. Keep Hicasso's synchronous runtime semantics and data-first event API unchanged. The target is truthful, low-friction migration guidance: ordinary intents remain the default, while the rare ordering-sensitive handler gets one explicit preservation route.

## Correctness finding

The skill classifies its full M-tier, including MIG-04, MIG-05, MIG-06 and MIG-33 handler lifts, as unambiguous and observably identical. Its canonical rewrite turns a Reagent closure that calls rf/dispatch into a Hicasso intent vector.

Those two forms do not have the same scheduling contract. re-frame2 rf/dispatch appends to the router queue and returns immediately before the handler runs. A Hicasso intent closes over the frame API's dispatch-sync operation, drains the event and its synchronous cascade inside the browser callback's turn, and notifies the store before that turn ends. This is intentional Hicasso behavior, especially for controlled-input convergence, but it is a behavior change in an arbitrary migrated handler and the skill never names it.

## Exact evidence

- skills/reagent-migration/SKILL.md:107 calls the M-tier rewrites, expressly including dispatch lifting and keystroke maps, unambiguous and observably identical.
- skills/reagent-migration/references/catalog-mechanical.md:64-84 makes #(dispatch [:go 1]) -> [:go 1] a direct MIG-04 rewrite and performs the same lift for value/checked handlers in MIG-05. The MIG-33 rule at lines 397 onward likewise replaces conditional queued dispatch calls with a key map.
- skills/reagent-migration/evals/evals.json:38 and :51 grade the direct event-vector result. No expectation asks the agent to disclose or preserve queue ordering.
- implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc:1167-1171 defines rf/dispatch as enqueue-and-return before the handler runs. Lines 1200-1207 distinguish dispatch-sync as an end-to-end fixed-point drain for tests, REPL and bootstrap.
- implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/impl/collector.cljs:85-96 mints Hicasso's frame dispatch from the captured :dispatch-sync operation. Lines 513-522 state that the event drains synchronously inside the caller's turn and store notification occurs before the turn ends.
- implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/impl/intent.cljs:497-524 routes ordinary intent vectors through that captured dispatch.
- implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/callback_form_dom_cljs_test.cljs:8-17 and :101-108 are an existing real-browser witness: a returned intent reaches the synchronous door and produces its echo in the same turn.

## Concrete impact

A Reagent click handler that only enqueues an event returns before application handlers and effects run. After the prescribed migration, those handlers and their synchronous cascade finish before the Hicasso callback returns. Ordering can therefore reverse relative to later propagation listeners, browser default actions, imperative code outside the component, and observations made immediately after the callback. A coeffect or structural failure that used to occur during the queued drain can also surface on a different stack.

Most application events should still use the concise intent vector. The defect is not that Hicasso is synchronous; it is that the migration promises observational identity and gives an ordering-sensitive application no signal that it crossed this semantic boundary. Shadow comparisons that inspect settled DOM and intent streams can remain green while missing callback-turn ordering.

## Recommended bounded fix

1. State once in the mental model/procedure that Hicasso event intents dispatch synchronously, unlike rf/dispatch, and explain why controlled writes require same-turn convergence.
2. Remove the blanket observably-identical claim for handler-lifting rules. Keep ordinary dispatch-only closures as the idiomatic default rather than turning every handler into a decision ceremony.
3. Add one narrow detection/question for an explicitly ordering-sensitive site: code, tests or comments that require the event to remain queued until after the callback/propagation/default-action phase.
4. For that exceptional site, teach the existing preservation route: call rf/capture-frame during render, close a plain callback over the captured frame API's queued :dispatch function, and return nil. Do not call ambient rf/dispatch after the render extent; that is the separate no-frame-context failure already taught by MIG-26.
5. Add one behavioral eval that distinguishes queued-after-callback semantics from Hicasso's same-turn intent semantics and rejects an answer that calls the two observationally identical.

## Non-goals

- No Hicasso runtime change, async-intent variant, scheduler abstraction or new public API.
- No per-handler prompt, blanket refusal to use data intents, or compatibility mode.
- No weakening of synchronous controlled-input convergence.
- No redesign of event vectors, key maps, h/event, the reporter or the view migration tiers beyond the scheduling distinction.
- No attempt to enumerate every browser ordering edge; one clear invariant and one existing escape are enough.

## Duplicate and history research

Targeted all-status searches over .beads/issues.jsonl for reagent-migration, MIG-04, dispatch-lifting, Hicasso intent and dispatch-sync found no bead owning this async-to-sync migration seam. Closed rf2-90k4a covers three frame-context/refusal diagnostics, rf2-vpdrf covers SSR adapter boot, and rf2-qxca8 covers retired Hicasso read/navigation doors; none addresses event scheduling.

Git history strengthens the mismatch: the exact MIG-04 example originated in 819a2f68a7 for an earlier destination and survived the Hicasso retarget in 6cdc1979da unchanged. Hicasso's captured synchronous dispatch was established separately in 69e160e1d1. No later skill commit reconciled those two contracts.

## Uncertainty

No new runtime was launched in this review-only worker. The semantic mismatch is directly established by current public core docs, current implementation, and an existing real-browser Hicasso witness. What remains unknown is how many consumer handlers rely on callback-turn ordering; that uncertainty is why the repair should preserve the vector as the default and add one bounded exception rather than impose ceremony on every event.
acceptance_criteria:
- SKILL.md and the routed migration references no longer describe rf/dispatch-to-intent handler lifts as observationally identical without qualification.
- The skill states the exact scheduling boundary once: rf/dispatch queues and returns before the handler runs; a Hicasso vector, key-map branch, or vector returned from h/event drains synchronously inside the callback turn.
- MIG-04/05/06/33 remain concise defaults for ordinary application handlers. The guidance does not ask about every handler or introduce a new runtime form.
- The skill identifies only explicit queue-order dependencies as judgment work and gives a valid preservation spelling using a render-time rf/capture-frame and its captured queued :dispatch operation in a plain callback. It clearly distinguishes that captured operation from an ambient rf/dispatch invoked after render.
- Controlled input guidance continues to require same-turn synchronous writes and explains that this is intentional rather than accidental equivalence.
- A focused behavioral eval presents or states an ordering-sensitive Reagent handler and fails an answer that silently emits an intent while claiming equivalent timing; it passes either an informed semantic change accepted by the author or the captured queued-dispatch escape.
- Existing handler-lifting, no-frame-context, key-map and controlled-input eval expectations remain coherent; eval JSON and skill/package structural checks pass.
- No Hicasso/core runtime API or behavior changes.

title: Require-alias dialect: walk the baselined per-surface debt down to zero
description:

  python scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py --scan-path <surface>

and then lowering that surface's floor in scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn (the gate exits 1 on a surface now BELOW its floor, so a stale floor is caught rather than forgotten).

  tools                                  2294
