title: machines: compatibility reset drops spawned-actor identity and strands the live snapshot
description:
## Finding

The supported handler-entry recovery for an incompatible machine snapshot replaces the entire snapshot with the registered type's fresh initial snapshot. That is correct for authored state/data, but for a spawned actor it also deletes the runtime-owned identity envelope that makes the actor addressable. The event that discovers the incompatibility completes against the fresh definition; the next event to the same still-present actor snapshot resolves no handler and is rejected as `:rf.error/no-such-handler`.

This is a composition bug between snapshot compatibility recovery and runtime-db-derived spawned-actor liveness, not a request for a migration framework.

## Verified current behavior

I exercised the public runtime on the JVM with the machines `:test` classpath:

1. Register child type `:probe/worker` at snapshot version 1 with state `:old` and `{:n 0}`.
2. Register a parent whose transition declaratively `:spawn`s that type; capture actor id `:probe/worker#1`.
3. Re-register `:probe/worker` at snapshot version 2 with initial state `:ready`, `{:n 100}`, and a `:bump` action that increments `:n`.
4. Dispatch `:bump` twice to the actor.

Observed (process exited 0):

```clojure
{:actor :probe/worker#1
 :before-root {:state :old
               :meta #:rf{:snapshot-version 1}
               :rf/machine-type :probe/worker}
 :before-data {:n 0
               :rf/self-id :probe/worker#1
               :rf/parent-id :probe/parent
               :rf/invoke-id [:running]}
 :after-first-root {:state :ready
                    :meta #:rf{:snapshot-version 2}}
 :after-first-data {:n 101}
 :after-second-data {:n 101}
 :version-errors 1
 :no-handler-errors 1}
```

The first dispatch proves version drift is detected and the replacement definition runs. It also drops `:rf/machine-type` plus the actor lineage. The second dispatch cannot lazily resolve a handler, does not increment `:n`, and emits `:rf.error/no-such-handler`, even though the actor snapshot remains physically present in runtime-db.

## Root cause and exact surfaces

- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/registration.cljc`, `rebuild-incompatible-snapshot` (around lines 334-358), returns only `(assoc @base-initial :rf/bootstrap-pending? true)`. `prepare-machine-ctx` / `reconcile-snapshot` applies this to every existing snapshot, including spawned actors, for both `:version-mismatch` and `:state-not-in-definition`.
- That `base-initial` is derived from the current type definition. It contains authored initial data and fresh transient counters, but it cannot contain per-instance values stamped only by the spawn runtime.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/spawn.cljc`, `machine-type-ref` and `stamp-framework-data` (around lines 252-280), establish the missing envelope: root `:rf/machine-type`; data `:rf/self-id`; optional `:rf/parent-id`, `:rf/invoke-id`, and `:rf/join-child`.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/resolver.cljc`, `spec-from-snapshot` (around lines 63-82), intentionally resolves an unregistered actor instance only through root `:rf/machine-type`.
- `registration.cljc`, `resolve-actor-handler-meta` (around lines 1347-1389), returns nil when that slot is gone, handing the next dispatch back to the router's genuine no-handler path.
- `spec/005-StateMachines.md`, Snapshot shape invariants and Reserved snapshot-internal keys (around lines 58-87), calls these keys framework-owned and says `:rf/machine-type` persists and makes spawned liveness a function of runtime-db. The reset currently treats the identity envelope like disposable user data.

## Coverage gap

`implementation/machines/test/re_frame/snapshot_compat_test.clj` proves compatibility recovery for singleton/manual snapshots only. Spawned-actor lifecycle tests (including `implementation/machines/test/re_frame/actor_liveness_cljs_test.cljc`) prove spawn/destroy/restore resolution but do not compose it with handler-entry compatibility recovery. Consequently each feature's local tests pass while their combination strands the actor.

## Impact

Hot reload is an explicit pre-alpha productivity path: an author who correctly bumps `:rf/snapshot-version`, or merely removes a live state, can silently turn every affected spawned instance into an inert snapshot after its first post-reload event. The same lost lineage is also used for declarative ownership/finalization, and `:rf/join-child` carries exact-attempt completion correlation for `:spawn-all`; losing it can break parent cleanup or join completion even during the reset event. The directly reproduced impact is the actor becoming unaddressable on the next dispatch.

## Bounded recommendation

Keep the existing fresh-user-snapshot reset, but preserve or reconstruct a deliberately small, canonical spawned-actor identity envelope from the existing snapshot before bootstrap/transition processing. At minimum this includes root `:rf/machine-type` and data `:rf/self-id`; when present, retain the runtime-stamped ownership/correlation values `:rf/parent-id`, `:rf/invoke-id`, and `:rf/join-child`. Implement this through one named helper/catalogue so snapshot recovery and spawn agree on which values are durable actor identity.

Do not merge the old `:data` map wholesale: authored data and transient timer/spawn/history counters should continue to reset exactly as the current compatibility contract intends.

## Non-goals

- No general snapshot migration API or user hook.
- No per-instance handler registry or change to runtime-db-derived liveness.
- No broad merge of old user data, timer epochs, spawn counters, or history into the new definition.
- No redesign of actor ids, spawning, hot reload, or epoch restore.

## Posture rationale

This is a narrow fix with high ergonomic leverage. It makes the documented, simple action (bump the snapshot version during a pre-alpha definition change) safe for the ordinary SPA actor model. Preserving the runtime-owned envelope keeps the API minimal and trusts the programmer; it avoids both a migration subsystem and surprising zombie actors.

## Duplicate and history search

I searched the review-time tracker corpus (923 issues) across titles/descriptions/notes/close reasons and repeated `bd search` queries for `machine-type`, `snapshot-version`, `version mismatch`, `state-not-in-definition`, `compatibility`, `hot reload`, `reset-to-initial`, `rebuild-incompatible-snapshot`, `spawned actor`, `inert snapshot`, and `no-such-handler`. No issue described this reset/liveness composition. Spawn-related matches concerned mixed-prefix teardown, naming, tooling branches, cancellation docs, and websocket correlation; hot-reload matches were unrelated examples/templates/Hicasso work.

Relevant landed history shows why the gap is plausible:

- `6b445ca978` (2026-05-14), snapshot-compatibility checks, introduced `rebuild-incompatible-snapshot` with singleton-oriented tests.
- `38b5a25407` (2026-06-03), runtime-db-derived spawned-actor liveness, later made `:rf/machine-type` the dispatch authority.
- `d0ce1cd437` (2026-06-09), spawned-actor version-drift checks on epoch restore, did not exercise a subsequent handler-entry rebuild.

No later commit in the affected files adds a compatibility-reset/spawn composition test or restores the envelope.

## Uncertainty

The live reproduction exercises the version-mismatch branch for a registered `:machine-id` spawn. The state-not-in-definition branch calls the identical replacement helper, so its identity loss is source-proven but was not separately driven. Loss of subsequent handler resolution is directly observed; the additional parent/join lifecycle effects follow from the documented consumers of the erased lineage and should be pinned by focused regression tests rather than assumed beyond those paths.
acceptance_criteria:
- Add a regression test in `implementation/machines/test/re_frame/snapshot_compat_test.clj` (or a narrowly named spawned-compatibility test) that declaratively spawns a registered v1 type, re-registers it with a v2 definition, dispatches at least two events to the same actor, and proves: exactly one mismatch recovery occurs, the first event uses the fresh definition, the second event is processed, no `:rf.error/no-such-handler` occurs, and the snapshot remains handler-resolvable.
- Cover `:state-not-in-definition` as the second entry path into the same recovery behavior, either by parameterizing the regression or with one focused sibling assertion.
- Compatibility recovery still replaces authored state/data and resets transient runtime counters per the existing contract; it does not wholesale merge the old snapshot.
- The recovered spawned snapshot preserves/reconstructs the canonical runtime identity envelope: root `:rf/machine-type`, data `:rf/self-id`, and any present `:rf/parent-id`, `:rf/invoke-id`, and `:rf/join-child`. Registered keyword and inline-definition type references remain valid.
- Add one lifecycle assertion that an affected declarative child can still complete/tear down through its parent after recovery; if the implementation touches `:rf/join-child`, pin exact-attempt `:spawn-all` completion as well.
- Existing singleton compatibility behavior and trace shapes remain unchanged. Update the implementation/spec prose only where needed to state that reset replaces user state while retaining framework-owned actor identity.
close_reason:
RE-CLOSED 2026-09-04 by the mayor's backlog reread — CHECK 3, a reverted closure. THIRD instance today of the worker-close-mid-tick race, and the discrimination needed a different instrument this time.

WHY THE USUAL TEST WAS NOT AVAILABLE. For rf2-hic-064 and rf2-2hpxo the tell was a notes field unchanged across the newest snapshots. Here NOTES IS EMPTY — 0 characters in every snapshot — so "unchanged" would have been the null-hash trap: an absent field hashes constant and reports a clean walk in exactly the words a genuinely unchanged one does. Believing it would have been believing nothing.

SO I CONTROLLED AGAINST FIELDS THAT DO VARY ON THIS ITEM. The description holds at 7,847 characters and acceptance_criteria at 1,562 across the newest six snapshots, while 23 snapshots in the history DO carry status=closed — so the item was genuinely closed and the only thing that moved back is the status. Control on a bead that is closed and stayed closed (rf2-4thn) returns 19 closed snapshots by the same query, so the query discriminates.

NO AUDIT OBLIGATION. Greps for AUDIT-REOPEN, "REOPENED THIS EXACT", REOPENED, "residual" and "still owed" all return zero, against a control counting rf2- references that returns 1, so the instrument bites. Contrast rf2-c5w1 and rf2-o8ek, which reverted in the same window and DO carry REOPENED markers with residuals — those are audits and stay open. This one wrote nothing, because nothing reopened it.

THE DELIVERABLE IS ON MAIN, verified in the tree: PR #9192 reads state=MERGED, and `carry-actor-identity` resolves at tip in implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/resolver.cljc. The fix carried a real red witness — 17 assertion failures with the tests in place and the fix absent, 1244 tests / 4528 assertions green after — plus a 210-line snapshot-compat suite and the two-line spec/005 clarification at invariants 3 and 4. Nothing about this bead's output is missing.

MECHANISM, unchanged from the earlier two: the prescribed checkpoint-then-checkout ordering protects the MAYOR's own tracker mutations, because the checkpoint exports them before the checkout restores that same commit. It does not protect a WORKER's close landing between my checkpoint's export and my checkout. All three instances today fit that shape — a worker closed the bead, I verified CLOSED immediately after merging its PR, and a later tick found it open with its text intact.

STILL NOT PROPOSING A PROCESS CHANGE. Three re-closes across a session is cheaper than reordering a sequence that exists to prevent tracker time-travel, and check 3 catches every instance by design. What this one adds is the lesson that the discrimination must use a field that VARIES on the item in front of you — the notes-length test is not universal.

title: Xray: retract the dead universal value-copy affordance and its dispatcher-less copy events; correct the off-box egress inventory (B.9 lock honoured)
description:
## Finding

Xray documents a universal `⎘` value-copy affordance on every value inspector, and retains the component, CSS, event, and safe-egress contract for it, but no current inspector renders the button. The user-visible feature is unreachable and `:copy?` is now an accepted-but-ignored option.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start any current Xray build/testbed and open a panel that renders a canonical EDN inspector (for example App-DB current state or an expanded Trace value).
2. Inspect, hover, and keyboard-focus the value-inspector root.
3. Observe that no `⎘` copy control or `.rf-xray-edn-widget-copy` element is rendered, despite the README/API promise.
4. At source level, search for calls to `day8.re-frame2-xray.views.edn-widget/copy-affordance`; there are none. Passing `{:copy? true}` to the facade also has no effect because the option is ignored.

## Evidence

- `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/views/edn_widget.cljs` defines public `copy-affordance` and says it rides every widget root. Repo-wide exact symbol search finds no call to `copy-affordance`; the only occurrences are its definition, comments, and the test note that prior copy-affordance tests were deleted.
- The same facade's `inspect` doc says `:copy?` is accepted but ignored, then delegates directly to `views.edn-inspector` without rendering the affordance or forwarding that option. No current `views.edn-inspector` code contains the `.rf-xray-edn-widget-copy` class.
- `theme/global_styles.cljs` still ships hover/focus CSS for `.rf-xray-edn-widget-copy`, but the only element that applies that class is the uncalled component.
- The backend event `:rf.xray/copy-value-to-clipboard` remains registered and tested in `panels/app_db_diff_events.cljs`; those tests dispatch it directly and do not prove a UI button exists. `egress.cljs` explicitly counts the universal button as one of two live off-box sinks.
- Current public/current-state docs promise the UI: `tools/xray/spec/API.md` lists "The `⎘` copy button riding every value inspector" and `tools/xray/README.md` describes two human copy surfaces. This is therefore not merely an unused internal helper.
- Git commit `0a38534c54` migrated value rendering to the first-class data-display widget, removed the old copy-affordance assertions, and stated copy chrome was deferred to a later popup phase. Subsequent inspector rewrites retained the dead component/contract but no current renderer wired it.
- Bead title searches for `copy affordance`, `copy value clipboard`, `universal copy`, and `copy chrome`, plus description search for `copy-affordance`, found no existing issue.

## Impact

The public API/security inventory claims an off-box UI operation users cannot reach, while production ships dead component/CSS and an ignored option. Tests prove the safe backend only through direct dispatch, so a missing integration can remain green indefinitely. Any repair must also preserve frame isolation and fail-closed egress; casually reattaching the raw-value button would be a security regression.

## Proposed disposition

Resolve the contract explicitly. Preferred while the README/API promise remains: render one accessible copy affordance from the canonical `views.edn-inspector` root (or its single facade), route the click back to the frame captured at render time, and exercise the full safe-egress/clipboard path. Remove the accepted-but-ignored `:copy?` shim unless a real supported per-call opt-out is defined. If product direction instead retires universal copy, remove the dead component/CSS/no-op option/backend-only surface as appropriate and retract the README/API/egress inventory together; do not leave a phantom feature.

## Risks

Clipboard output is an off-box sink. Preserve `egress/egress-value`, sensitive/large-value elision, nil/stale-target fail-closed behavior, and per-instance frame routing. Ensure hover-only styling does not hide the control from keyboard or assistive-technology users. Avoid adding one button per recursive tree node when the contract is one affordance per inspector root.
acceptance_criteria:
- A rendered canonical value inspector has either a reachable, keyboard-accessible `⎘` control with stable test identity, or all current public promises of universal value copy are explicitly retired and the dead implementation is removed.
- If restored, an integration test clicks the rendered control (not direct-dispatch only), proves dispatch targets the surrounding frame, and verifies sensitive/large/nil-or-stale-frame values remain fail-closed before clipboard egress.
- The unused `copy-affordance` component/CSS and accepted-but-ignored `:copy?` option no longer exist as dead compatibility surface; any retained option has observable tested semantics.
- README, API, egress inventory, registry catalogue, source docs, and tests describe the same two-or-one copy-surface reality.
- Xray CLJS/browser tests and feature-gate smoke pass.
notes:
HOLD SHARPENED 2026-09-04 by the mayor (quiet merge tick, no dispatchable work). I have been holding this vaguely as 'restore or retract — a product call'. That framing was too loose to act on, and the evidence below makes the choice narrow and cheap. IT IS STILL MIKE'S CALL, but it is now a one-line call.

WHAT I ESTABLISHED AT SOURCE:

1. NOBODY DECIDED AGAINST THE FEATURE. edn_widget_cljs_test.cljs:6 records that the copy-affordance tests 'are deleted with the cljs-devtools cut-over', and the commit is 0a38534c54 'feat(xray): data-display widget PHASE 1 — core renderer + App-DB integration (drops cljs-devtools dep) (rf2-oqa60)'. So this is not a retracted feature; it is a phase-1 rewrite that left the affordance unwired at a phase boundary.

2. NO PHASE 2 WAS EVER SCOPED. rf2-oqa60 DOES NOT EXIST in the tracker —  returns nothing. So there is no record anywhere that the copy button was meant to come back, and equally none that it was meant to go. It simply fell between phases.

3. THE INFRASTRUCTURE IS ALL STILL THERE, so this is WIRING rather than BUILDING: the public  defn survives in edn_widget.cljs (1 occurrence, its own definition, 0 external callers), the CSS rides in theme/global_styles.cljs:684, and the safe-egress event contract is intact. What is missing is the call.

4. AND THIS IS THE PART THAT RAISES THE STAKES — THE SHIPPED README DOCUMENTS IT AS A SECURITY SURFACE, NOT A CONVENIENCE. tools/xray/README.md:264-265 reads: 'surfaces are the two human copy affordances (the  palette verb and the  copy button), both fail-closed with no...'. That is an ENUMERATION OF VALUE-EGRESS SURFACES for a fail-closed posture. So the defect is not a missing nice-to-have: a reader auditing where values can leave Xray is told there are two, and one of them does not exist. An egress enumeration that is wrong is worse than a feature that is absent.

THE TWO OPTIONS, both bounded:
  (a) WIRE IT. Call copy-affordance from the canonical EDN inspector and honour . The component, CSS and egress contract already exist, so the diff is small, and the README's two-surface enumeration becomes true again.
  (b) RETRACT IT. Delete copy-affordance, its CSS, the  option, and CORRECT THE README to enumerate one egress surface rather than two.

MY RECOMMENDATION IS (a), on three grounds. The stance values excellent tools and low friction, and a value-copy button is table stakes for a debugging inspector. The work is wiring, not building — everything but the call site survives. And an accepted-but-ignored  option is the worst of the three states we could be in, so either option beats today, but (a) also leaves the security enumeration correct rather than shrinking it.

WHAT MAKES THIS MIKE'S RATHER THAN MINE: (b) is a decision that a documented user-visible egress surface is unwanted, and shrinking a security enumeration is a product statement I should not make unilaterally. Either way this is a single word of instruction — 'wire it' or 'retract it' — and I will dispatch it the same tick.
CORRECTION to the note immediately above, which lost six tokens to shell command substitution — I passed the text inline with backticks in it, and the shell executed them. My own recorded hazard; the fix is a quoted heredoc, used here. Nothing else in that note is affected and no prior note was touched (--append-notes only adds). The eaten tokens, restored in order:

1. In point 2, "rf2-oqa60 DOES NOT EXIST in the tracker — ___ returns nothing" should read: the command 'bd show rf2-oqa60' returns nothing.

2. In point 3, "the public ___ defn survives" should read: the public copy-affordance defn survives.

3. In point 4, the README quote should read in full:

An exact CLJS probe on merge e5c8c81ee4 used 12 ordinary filler attrs plus authored `"data-rf-view" "author"`; expected `author`, actual emitted prop `framework` (focused run: 58 tests / 450 assertions, 1 failure). The diagnostic probe was restored after the red run; no source edit remains.
SECOND CARRIER, PR #9200 (2026-09-05). The audit's premise HOLDS at source and is now closed.

MECHANISM, verified rather than assumed. `codec/canonical-slot` IS `codec/cached-prop-name`, which is `slot/prop-name` — the shared `.cljc` rule the reagent-to-hicasso codemod holds `identical?` to. It reads a key through `name`, so the NAMESPACE is discarded, and it takes a string verbatim. The accepted spelling set for one attribute is therefore CLOSED and exactly five: `:data-rf-view`, `:any-ns/data-rf-view`, `'data-rf-view`, `'any-ns/data-rf-view`, `"data-rf-view"` — same for `data-rf2-source-coord`, both of which the `dont-camel-case` set (`#{"aria" "data"}`) passes through unchanged. camelCase spellings such as `:dataRfView` land in a DIFFERENT slot and are correctly not the framework's business. `merge` is keyed by `=`, so it kept both the author's key and the framework's; `convert-props` wrote both into one React slot and the map's iteration order picked.

value:
`grep -c $'\0' <file>` IS A SELF-DEFEATING NUL PROBE — bash strips the NUL and hands grep an EMPTY PATTERN, which matches EVERY line, so it reports the file's line count as a NUL count. Measured 2026-09-04 by two workers independently; one reported "6 NUL bytes" in a log whose real count was 0.

WHY THIS MATTERS DISPROPORTIONATELY HERE. Every worker brief in this project tells the worker to check its gate log for "a hole of NUL bytes" — the tell that a killed shell's orphan process is still writing to the `.log` and `.exit` the restarted run is using. That check is a safety property, and this bug makes it a false positive on EVERY non-empty file, so a worker that trusts it concludes a good log is corrupt.

THE MECHANISM: bash cannot put a NUL into an argument — C strings terminate there — so `$'\0'` expands to the empty string and `grep -c ''` matches every line. Nothing errors, and the number looks plausible because it is a real fact about the file.

WHAT WORKS, IN ORDER OF RELIABILITY ON THIS BOX:
  1. BYTE-COUNT DIFFERENCE — `tr -d '\0' < f | wc -c` against `wc -c < f`. Portable, no locale dependency, and the form that worked when the others did not.
  2. `od -An -tx1 f | grep -c ' 00'` — byte-level, also locale-independent.
  3. `grep -c -P '\x00' f` — CORRECT IN PRINCIPLE BUT REFUSED ON THIS BOX: a worker measured `grep -P` rejected by the local locale configuration (2026-09-04). Do not reach for it first here.

ALWAYS CONTROL IT: `printf 'a\0b' > probe` and confirm the chosen instrument reports 1 on that and 0 on a clean file. A peer measured 3 bytes vs 2 by the byte-count method, which is exactly what made the wrong answer visible.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, and it is this session's recurring one: an instrument misused returns a plausible number, raises no error, and errs in the reassuring direction. Exercise it once against something it SHOULD find before believing what it did not find.

ALSO FROM THE SAME PAIR OF WORKERS: `compile-node-test.cjs` treats its output-path argument as an ASSERTION, not a destination — passing a renamed baseline artefact makes it fail AFTER a successful compile, which reads as a compile failure and is not one.

title: reagent-slim sub-cache poison proof is vacuous: the bare js-obj is skipped, never thrown
description:
Found while landing rf2-ss8x (PR #9201).

`reagent_slim_dispose_sub_cache_walk_cljs_test.cljs`'s `dispose-adapter-walk-is-best-effort` injects `{:reaction (js-obj "not" "a reaction")}` and claims to pin 'a throwing per-entry dispose'. Nothing throws. The ratom family's claimed-generation disposer is `make-ratom-dispose-dispatch` (spine.cljs), which dispatches `re-frame.disposable/IDisposable` -> the substrate's `IDisposable` -> `:else nil`; a bare js-obj satisfies neither protocol, so the entry is SKIPPED in silence. The test therefore proves visit-and-clear only, and the per-entry failure path it was written for is never reached.

Measured directly: adding a rethrow assertion to that test returned `nil` (no throw) while the stock-Reagent equivalent, rebuilt on a reify of Reagent's real `IDisposable` (methods `dispose!` / `add-on-dispose!`), threw as expected.

Remedy: give the slim test a poison entry that really throws — reify `reagent2.ratom/IDisposable` the way rf2-ss8x's stock-Reagent witness reifies `reagent.ratom/IDisposable` — and assert both the sibling drain AND the post-drain rethrow. Left out of rf2-ss8x deliberately: that bead's non-goals fence reagent-slim redesign, and its reviewed surface is stock Reagent. The vacuity is documented in a comment in place meanwhile.

Note the same shape does NOT apply to `react_shared_suite.cljs`: the React-hook spine passes `rf.disposable/-dispose` directly rather than through the dispatch, so its poison entry genuinely throws (verified green under rf2-ss8x's rethrow assertion).

value:
`npm run test:cljs` DOES NOT CATCH `:infer-warning`s, AND THOSE BREAK SILENTLY UNDER `:advanced`. The adapter smoke's RELEASE compile is what catches them. Measured 2026-09-04 on the reagent-adapter teardown fix (rf2-ss8x, PR #9201).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker's first cut attached secondary teardown errors to a rethrown primary via a property access ClojureScript could not infer a type for. `test:cljs` — 11,180 tests, 55,782 assertions — passed with **zero compile warnings reported**. `npm run test:adapter-smokes`, which does a RELEASE compile, raised **six `:infer-warning`s**. Under `:advanced`, the Closure compiler renames an un-inferrable property access, so the attachment would have compiled, shipped, and silently lost the very data it existed to carry — in production only.

WHY THIS IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE. The failure is invisible in dev, invisible in the main test lane, and only appears in optimised output where nobody is watching. A green `test:cljs` is genuinely meaningless about it. The worker fixed it by rebuilding on two `volatile!`s plus `unchecked-set` on a string key, which needs no inference.

THE RULE: ANY CHANGE THAT TOUCHES JS INTEROP — property access on a foreign object, `js-obj`, `aset`/`goog.object`, attaching fields to an Error — MUST be compiled in a RELEASE/`:advanced` configuration before it is believed. `npm run test:adapter-smokes` is the cheap one that does this. Nominate it in the brief for any interop-touching bead; do not accept `test:cljs` alone as coverage.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, worth pairing with it: THE PRE-EXISTING "POISON" TEARDOWN PROOFS WERE VACUOUS. They passed a bare `(js-obj "not" "a reaction")` expecting the disposer to throw, but that object satisfies NEITHER disposal protocol, so the ratom disposer's `:else nil` branch skipped it silently — nothing ever threw and the per-entry catch those tests were written to pin was never reached. True in the Reagent proofs, the reagent-slim proofs, and by a different route in the shared suite. A real witness must reify Reagent's actual `IDisposable`, whose methods are `dispose!`/`add-on-dispose!` — NOT `-dispose`. The reagent-slim half is filed as rf2-vy0a.

Both findings are the same underlying lesson in different clothes: a green that inspected nothing is not evidence. RELATED: [[never-put-an-uncontrolled-extraction-in-a-brief]], [[any-new-file-under-a-zero-or-low-floor-surface-reds-the-ratchet]].

title: xray managed_http testbed: seeded handle carries no :frame, so its abort step is unreachable (rf2-o8ek fallout)
description:
The xray managed_http testbed's seed fx ignores its frame-ctx and records a
handle with no :frame stamp, so the handle keys under [nil <id>]. Since PR
#9195 the :rf.http/managed-abort fx is frame-scoped — managed-abort-handler
calls require-frame-stamp! and then abort-in-flight-in-frame! with the REAL
frame-id — so it cannot resolve a nil-frame handle at all. The testbed's
abort step (5) therefore resolves nothing.

Measured on this repo tip with a JVM registry probe reproducing the seed
shape, exit 0:

  {:keyed-under ([nil :xray/in-flight]),
   :any-frame-finds? true,
   :real-frame-finds? false,
   :managed-abort-hits? false}

Site: tools/xray/testbeds/managed_http/core.cljs — the seed fx binds
_frame-ctx (unused) and records {:url pending-url :abort-fn ...} with no
:frame; its :abort-fn also calls the one-arg clear-in-flight!, which #9195
redefined as an ANY-FRAME sweep, and its rf/dispatch carries no {:frame ...}.

The repair mirrors what examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs now
does (rf2-o8ek audit fix): bind (:frame frame-ctx), stamp it on the handle,
pass {:frame frame} to the deferred dispatch, and clean up through
registry/clear-in-flight-in-frame! rather than the one-arg sweep.

Out of the rf2-o8ek fence (tools/** is owned by another peer this wave), so
filed rather than fixed. Not covered by any gate: examples/testbeds carry no
spec.cjs for this path.

description:

RE-CLOSED 2026-09-05 by the mayor's backlog reread — CHECK 3, a reverted closure. FOURTH instance this session, and the SECOND time this particular bead has come back, which is exactly why the discrimination had to be sharpened rather than repeated.

WHY THE MARKER TEST WAS NOT ENOUGH HERE, and this is the refinement worth keeping. This bead carries a REOPENED marker — but that marker is from its FIRST reopen (the audit of PR #9184, which hicnative-a then serviced in PR #9193). A grep for reopen markers therefore returns a hit on a bead whose CURRENT transition wrote nothing. Stale evidence from an earlier round reads exactly like fresh evidence for this one. On a bead that has been through a chain, "does it carry a REOPENED marker" is the wrong question.

THE TEST THAT ACTUALLY DISCRIMINATES: compare the notes length ACROSS THE REOPEN BOUNDARY, not across the newest N snapshots. Walk the history newest-first, find the first snapshot whose status is `closed`, and compare it with its immediate newer neighbour — that pair IS the transition. For this bead: idx39=closed/notes=1045, idx38=open/notes=1045. Identical. The status moved and not one character was written. Compare rf2-r9kf, reverted in the same window, where the same probe reads idx22=closed/notes=4369 → idx21=open/notes=5521: 1152 characters added BY the reopen, which is an audit writing its reason. That one stays open and is real work.

Note also why "notes unchanged across the newest four" was insufficient: both beads read unchanged over that window, because both had settled since their transition. The window has to be anchored to the boundary, not to the head.

NO AUDIT OBLIGATION ON THIS TRANSITION. Nothing was added, so there is nothing owed. The first reopen's residual — Hicasso-native still presented as a third component-authoring route across hot-path-architecture.md, specification.md and react-compatibility-notes.md — was serviced by PR #9193 (merged): 12 files amended, every passage restated with an italic note giving its former wording, the ruling and the date, plus three live checklist rows and two stale witness citations the first pass had left. MECHANISM, unchanged across all four instances: the prescribed checkpoint-then-checkout ordering protects the MAYOR's own tracker mutations, because the checkpoint exports them before the checkout restores that same commit. It does not protect a WORKER's close landing between my checkpoint's export and my checkout.

STILL NOT PROPOSING A PROCESS CHANGE. Four re-closes across a long session is cheaper than reordering a sequence that exists to prevent tracker time-travel, and check 3 catches every instance by design. What this instance adds is the boundary-anchored test, which is now the method for any bead that has reopened more than once.

A "PR MERGED" LOOKUP KEYED ON BRANCH NAME CAN RETURN AN OLD SESSION'S PR — worker branch names are reused, so `gh pr list --head worker/<name>` matches a PR that has nothing to do with the live worker occupying that worktree. Measured 2026-09-05 during a hygiene tick, and it would have authorised destroying a RUNNING worker's tree.

WHAT HAPPENED. The hygiene enumeration printed `epoch-a  pr=#9098 MERGED`. #9098 was real and merged — on 2026-09-03, titled "refactor(epoch): retire three vestiges from the epoch surface", head `worker/epoch-a`. But the CURRENT `worker/epoch-a` was created this session from origin/main at 886c6ed061, dispatched 2026-09-05 00:39:06, agent RUNNING for two minutes with uncommitted work. Two dispatches, two sessions, one branch name. `git reflog show worker/epoch-a` confirms the branch was created fresh; the ledger carries TWO rows for that worktree path, one per dispatch.

WHY IT DID NOT BITE: the hygiene rule reaps ONLY on the agent's own quotable completion report, and explicitly names a merged PR, a clean tree, elapsed time and directory age as REFUSED PROXIES. That refusal is what saved the tree. This is the concrete case the rule was written for, and it is worth keeping precisely because the proxy looked so authoritative — a real PR, genuinely merged, correctly matching the branch name.

THE CLASS: unanchored matching, at the layer above the filesystem. The same session produced five siblings — `git log --grep=<id>` matching `.24` inside `.244`; a path regex matching `spec/004-…` inside `tools/xray/spec/004-…`; a job-name substring matching the green `JVM->Node->JVM crossing (ssr-ring …)` instead of the failing `JVM ssr-ring (clojure -M:test)`; `grep -c $'\0'` matching every line; a `sed` range collapsing at the first blank line. A NAME IS NOT AN IDENTITY.

WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU DO NEED THE PR: match on the branch's CURRENT TIP OID, not its name — `gh pr list --head <branch> --json number,state,headRefOid` and compare `headRefOid` against `git rev-parse <branch>`. A stale PR's headRefOid will not match. Also check `mergedAt` against the ledger's `dispatched` timestamp for that worktree path: a PR merged BEFORE the current dispatch cannot be the current worker's.

AND READ THE LEDGER'S LAST ROW FOR A PATH, NOT ITS FIRST. `ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv` is append-only and a reused worktree path accumulates one row per dispatch, so an `awk` that stops at the first match returns a dead agent's id. Take the last (`awk -F'\t' -v p=<path> '$1==p {a=$2} END{print a}'`), and read fields by NAME per the CLAUDE.md ledger contract, never by index.

RELATED: [[never-put-an-uncontrolled-extraction-in-a-brief]], [[nul-byte-probe-with-dollar-quote-is-self-defeating]].

`pkill -f "^find /"` DOES NOT MATCH A GIT-BASH `find` ON THIS BOX — the process's real command line starts with the full Windows path, `"C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\find.exe"`, so a pattern anchored on the bare verb matches NOTHING and exits SUCCESS. Measured 2026-09-04; it cost 63 minutes of an unnoticed whole-filesystem scan competing with peers' gates for disk I/O.

WHY IT IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE: a cleanup command that reports success and removes nothing. Identical in class to the `cmd /c` junction no-op already recorded in CLAUDE.md — exit 0, no output, no effect — and to `grep -c $'\0'` reporting a line count as a NUL count. The worker believes the runaway is dead, stops watching, and the process keeps running.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THIS PROJECT SPECIFICALLY: workers here are told to kill orphaned processes they can prove are theirs, and a heavy gate that two workers cannot coexist on WEDGES rather than fails. An orphan that survives a "successful" kill is exactly the contention source that makes the next worker's gate hang with no exit file and no error — and it is invisible, because the kill reported success.

WHAT TO DO:
  * Allow the full path in the pattern, or drop the `^` anchor: `pkill -f 'find\.exe'` or `pkill -f '/usr/bin/find'`.
  * BETTER — VERIFY BY EFFECT, NOT BY EXIT CODE. List the process afterwards and confirm it is gone. This is the same rule already recorded for junctions: verify the EFFECT, not the exit code.
  * And keep the standing constraint: never kill a process you cannot show is yours. The right proof is walking the parent chain to a DEAD root — the shell your run started and the harness killed. A peer used exactly that to kill only its own orphan while correctly leaving six foreign `node` processes alone.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS BELONGS TO: on this box, a command that reports success is not evidence it acted. Junction creation, junction removal, process kills, NUL probes and log fetches have all returned exit 0 while doing nothing. Check the world, not the status.

RELATED: [[nul-byte-probe-with-dollar-quote-is-self-defeating]], [[branch-names-are-reused-so-a-merged-pr-can-belong-to-a-dead-worker]].

USE `git diff --quiet -- <path>` AS THE GROUND TRUTH FOR "IS THIS FILE RESTORED", NOT A HASH. Hash comparison misreports in BOTH directions on this repo, and `--no-filters` is NOT the universal answer. Established 2026-09-04/05 by three workers, two of whom corrected the mayor's over-generalisation.

WHY IT MATTERS: every worker here verifies a planted-fault restore by comparing bytes rather than reading a diff, because a patch that never applied reads clean too. A phantom mismatch sends a worker chasing corruption that is not there, or makes it distrust the technique.

THE CONFIGURATION THAT DECIDES IT: this repo runs `core.autocrlf=true`, so the NORMAL case is a blob storing LF that checks out CRLF.
  * DEFAULT `git hash-object <path>` runs the clean filter (CRLF -> LF) and MATCHES the stored blob. This is the correct form for the normal case.
  * `--no-filters` hashes the CRLF working bytes against an LF blob and reports a MISMATCH on a genuinely clean tree.
  * The reverse case exists too — a blob that genuinely stores CRLF, where `--no-filters` is the matching form. One worker hit that on spec/011-SSR.md.

MEASURED, on gen.clj after a verified-clean restore: committed 5f17c3e8…, filtered 5f17c3e8… (match), `--no-filters` 501ff83e… (mismatch), with `git diff --quiet` exiting 0 as ground truth.

THE METHOD:
  1. `git diff --quiet -- <path>` — exit 0 means the working file matches HEAD. This is filter-aware, needs no guess about line endings, and is the check to rely on.
  2. If you want a hash to corroborate, run BOTH forms: a clean tree matches ONE of them, a real corruption matches NEITHER.
  3. `git show HEAD:<path> | diff --strip-trailing-cr - <path>` also works when you want to see the difference rather than a boolean.

AND THE PROCESS LESSON, which is the more important half. The mayor recorded "use --no-filters" from ONE worker's measurement on ONE file and then put that flag into FOUR subsequent briefs before two other workers measured the opposite and corrected it. A single measurement on a single file is not a rule. Briefs should say "verify with `git diff --quiet`; if you hash, run both forms and expect one to match" — naming a flag encodes a guess about a file's storage that the brief author has not made.
