description:
## Scope

Correct the stock Reagent adapter-wide teardown path, with the shared ratom-spine helper changed only where needed: `implementation/adapters/reagent/src/re_frame/adapter/reagent.cljs` (`spine-fns`, `dispose-once!`, and the adapter map), `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs` (`dispose-frame-sub-caches!`, `dispose-active-roots-and-caches!`, and `make-ratom-spine`'s `dispose-adapter!`), plus focused stock-Reagent lifecycle tests under `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/`. Keep the one shared drain rather than forking a Reagent-only copy.

## Correctness finding

The stock Reagent adapter does the good half of best-effort teardown—attempting sibling cached-Reaction disposals and sibling root unmounts—but silently discards every failure. `dispose-frame-sub-caches!` catches each disposer throw as `_` and returns `nil`; `dispose-active-roots-and-caches!` does the same for every `unmount-op`. Consequently `rf/destroy-adapter!` reports clean success even though adapter-owned cleanup failed. This directly contradicts Spec 006's current lifecycle rule: attempt all remaining cleanup, preserve and rethrow the first failure, and attach or report later failures as secondary evidence.

This is not a request to stop at the first throw. The required invariant is **drain everything, finalize ownership, then surface the original first failure**.

## Verified evidence

- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:1470-1519` documents and implements the frame sub-cache walk. Lines 1517-1518 are `(try (dispose-reaction! r) (catch :default _ nil))`; the exception is irretrievably dropped before the caller can see it.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:1521-1547` is the shared adapter drain. Lines 1542-1544 catch and drop every root-unmount failure, then lines 1545-1546 clear active-root ownership and the emitter and line 1547 returns `nil`.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:3539-3545,3657-3660` shows the stock Reagent ratom spine owns those exact cells and delegates its entire `dispose-adapter!` to that helper.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent/src/re_frame/adapter/reagent.cljs:88-113` injects guarded stock `Reaction` construction/disposal and `reagent.dom.client/unmount` into that spine. `dispose-once!` correctly preserves a throw from stock `ratom/dispose!`; the shared outer catch is what erases it.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/adapter.cljc:230-257` already provides the right process boundary: it invokes the adapter disposer in a `try/finally`, clears the claimed generation even if cleanup throws, and naturally rethrows the adapter's exact failure. The Reagent drain prevents that tested/public mechanism from ever seeing its failures.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc:2613-2624` publicly promises that `destroy-adapter!` marks the adapter disposed and then rethrows the primary cleanup failure.
- `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:320-337` requires every resource to be attempted, caches/claims to be cleared in a finally-shaped boundary, the first failure to be rethrown, and later failures to be attached or reported.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/dispose_adapter_sub_cache_walk_cljs_test.cljs:144-188` already builds the decisive stock-adapter witness: a poison cached entry throws while real reactions in the same and later frame are still disposed and both caches are cleared. Line 179 currently expects `adapter/dispose-adapter!` to return normally, so the test pins only sibling progress and accidentally codifies disappearance of the primary error.
- `implementation/core/test/re_frame/substrate/spine_dispose_cljs_test.cljs:54-76,185-209` likewise proves sibling drains but never asserts the promised post-drain rethrow. `implementation/core/test/re_frame/boot_test.clj:163-187` separately proves the core preserves exact cleanup-error identity and terminal lifecycle state when an adapter actually lets a failure escape.
- The adapter README recommends Form-3 wrappers for imperative libraries and says cleanup is mandatory (`implementation/adapters/reagent/README.md:23-42,94-101`). Silent teardown failure makes the shutdown/test-fixture boundary claim success precisely when application or host cleanup has malfunctioned.

## Impact / concrete failure scenario

A test or hot-reload fixture installs the stock Reagent adapter, creates subscriptions in multiple frames, and registers a user/framework on-dispose hook that throws. During `rf/destroy-adapter!`, the throwing Reaction is terminally marked and its error reaches `dispose-frame-sub-caches!`; other cached Reactions and roots are still attempted and ownership cells are cleared, but the original exception is dropped. The caller sees `nil`, so the fixture, reload tool, or programmer cannot distinguish clean shutdown from a failed cleanup and may continue after listeners or an imperative host resource failed to release.

The same masking exists when the injected root unmount operation throws. Whether React has already detached some host state is host-specific; the certain defect is that the adapter reports success despite the observed cleanup failure.

## Recommended bounded change

At the existing shared drain chokepoint, capture cleanup failures by **presence**, continue every Reaction and root attempt, clear each sub-cache plus `active-roots-cell` and `emitter-cell` in finally-shaped cleanup, then rethrow the first captured value unchanged. Reuse the spine's existing private `capture-none` identity sentinel (or an equally explicit sentinel), because CLJS may throw `nil` or `false`; a truthiness accumulator would recreate a silent-failure hole. Retain later failures as secondary diagnostic evidence using the project's existing diagnostic/attachment convention without replacing or wrapping the first failure.

Keep the direct zero-argument test seam compatible if it has a distinct caller contract; an optional accumulator/result between `dispose-frame-sub-caches!` and `dispose-active-roots-and-caches!` is preferable to duplicating the walk. Do not retry a consumed Reaction/root and do not add a supervisor, rollback transaction, or root registry.

## Acceptance criteria

- Update the stock-Reagent poison-entry proof so `rf/destroy-adapter!` throws the identical sentinel error **after** the real cached Reactions in the same and later frames have been disposed and every involved sub-cache is `{}`.
- Add a stock-Reagent root proof with one throwing injected `rdc/unmount` and at least one healthy sibling: every snapshot root is attempted exactly once, active-root ownership and the emitter are cleared, and the identical primary failure reaches the caller only after the drain.
- With more than one cleanup failure, the first encountered value stays the thrown primary and later failures are attached or emitted as secondary evidence; `nil`/`false` thrown values are captured by presence rather than lost.
- After either failure, `adapter/current-adapter-spec` is `nil`, `adapter/adapter-disposed?` is true, public delegation reports `:rf.error/adapter-disposed`, and a fresh `rf/init!` can install a new generation.
- Happy teardown still returns `nil`; empty frames/roots remain no-op-safe; existing stock-Reagent exactly-once Reaction disposal and client-root idempotence tests remain green.
- Non-vacuity: on the pre-fix implementation the new primary-error assertion fails because the call returns `nil`, while counters still prove sibling cleanup ran. Record that red control and then restore/apply the fix.
- Run the focused stock-Reagent CLJS adapter lifecycle lane plus the shared spine/core lifecycle tests that cover the helper and process finalization.

## Non-goals

- No change to callback registration order, the landed exactly-once marker (`rf2-rzeko`), or isolation among multiple callbacks inside one native Reagent `Reaction` disposal.
- No retry/recovery protocol for a root or Reaction whose teardown threw, no async-settlement machinery, and no new public API.
- No Reagent 1.x or React 18 compatibility work.
- No redesign of UIx, reagent-slim, Test-React, frame destruction, or application Form-3 lifecycle policy. The shared helper should remain contract-consistent for its existing callers, but this bead's regression proof and reviewed product surface are stock Reagent.

## Posture rationale

This is a small correction at an existing lifecycle chokepoint, not gold plating. Best-effort cleanup and loud failure complement each other: drain siblings for robustness, then trust the programmer with the original error so tests and tools do not claim success falsely. It preserves the minimal adapter API and removes friction from diagnosing real SPA teardown bugs.

## Duplicate and history research

Searched the complete 913-bead corpus across all statuses (title, description, notes, acceptance, and close reason) and repeated final `bd search` checks for `reagent teardown failure`, `dispose active roots`, `sub-cache cleanup error`, and `rethrow first cleanup`; no bead owns this outcome. Exact symbol/phrase searches for `dispose-active-roots-and-caches!`, `dispose-frame-sub-caches!`, `unmount ... swallow`, `cleanup failure`, `first failure`, and `secondary diagnostic` found no matching adapter-drain task. `rf2-rzeko` is closed and distinct: it made one stock Reaction's callbacks exactly-once and explicitly excluded general callback-exception isolation. `rf2-k5r9t` is closed and distinct: it added the reusable client-root lifecycle/idempotent explicit unmount, not adapter-wide failure propagation.

History confirms the defect is still live rather than already repaired: `df8aad1215` introduced per-entry swallow for the unified sub-cache walk; `1ae9c8846c` consolidated root draining with per-root swallow; `2d51830e37` then ratified terminal adapter destruction and the first-failure rule in Spec 006 while retaining both swallow catches. Later stock-Reagent disposal work (`rf2-rzeko`) changed only exactly-once behavior. Current HEAD `1ad17a77fe123bc233a88b89335dcf48196500c1` still contains both catches and the tests above still expect normal return.

## Uncertainties

- React/Reagent may have performed part or all of a particular host teardown before an unmount error escapes; do not claim rollback or infer host settlement. Surface the observed error after local ownership is finalized.
- Spec 006 intentionally permits later failures to be either attached or reported. Choose the smallest established project mechanism; do not invent a new user-facing error taxonomy solely for this fix.
- The active-root set does not promise semantic insertion order. The primary is the first failure in the actual snapshot traversal; tests should avoid depending on a different ordering contract.
notes: PR #9201 audit reopened this exact owner: the shared Reaction/active-root drain now captures and rethrows correctly, but make-dispose-adapter! still catches and discards an exception from the separately owned singleton after-render driver root at implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:1716-1719. That root is a host-specific resource outside active-roots-cell. If its unmount is the only failure, destroy-adapter! still reports clean nil; if the shared drain already failed, the driver-root failure is not attached as secondary evidence. Both violate Spec 006 lines 320-350 and contradict the PR/README claim that every teardown failure is audible. Keep one teardown transaction across the shared drain and layered cleanup, then rethrow only after the driver-root attempt and ownership resets. Add driver-root-only and shared-primary-plus-driver-secondary witnesses; preserve primary identity and continued finalization.

title: flows: direct clear-flow leaves dependent materialized outputs stale until an unrelated drain
description:
## Scope

Correct the plain/direct `re-frame.flows/clear-flow` lifecycle path when it is called outside an active event drain. Clearing a producer flow must not return with other registered flows still materialized from the producer value that was just removed. Keep the existing id/opts API, frame scoping, leaf-only vacation, and the already-correct `:rf.fx/clear-flow` behavior.

## Verified finding

At HEAD 52b2579e9b53816abddd3406f72db5a5278bed1c, a live JVM probe registered producer `:probe/a` (`[:x] -> [:a]`) and dependent `:probe/b` (`[:a] -> [:b]`), then seeded `{:x 2}`. Before clear, app-db was `{:x 2, :a 2, :b 2}`. Calling `(flows/clear-flow :probe/a {:frame :probe})` returned with `{:x 2, :b 2}`: the source slot was gone but its dependent still published the value derived from that removed slot. Only a later unrelated no-op dispatch changed it to `{:x 2, :b :absent}`. The probe exited 0 and used the package's plain-atom runtime.

This follows directly from `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc` `clear-flow` / `vacate-output-path!` (currently lines 798-891): outside a drain it writes the vacated live app-db immediately, removes the registry/cache row, and returns; no flow pass is requested. The next ordinary drain finally dirty-checks `:probe/b` against nil and repairs it.

## Impact and ergonomics

This is an observable split-brain app-db state, not a trace-only detail: a view, handler, test, or per-tenant setup reading app-db immediately after the documented synchronous function returns can trust a dependent value whose declared input no longer exists. `docs/core/flows.md` lines 325-341 explicitly advertises the plain functions for boot code, tests, and per-tenant setup, while `docs/api/re-frame.flows.md` lines 55-73 describes `clear-flow` as a synchronous deregister-and-vacate function. Requiring each such caller to invent an unrelated event to repair the dependency graph recreates the ceremony already removed from the effect route.

The existing direct-clear test, `implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_test.clj` `clear-flow-removes-from-registry-and-vacates-output-slot` (lines 102-118), checks only the cleared producer row and leaf. The stronger dependent-flow behavior exists only for the effect route in `implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_settle_on_dispatch_test.clj` `settle-runs-once-and-recomputes-dependents` (lines 85 onward), leaving the plain function gap untested.

## Bounded recommendation

After a successful out-of-drain direct clear, settle the selected frame's remaining flows through the existing private/ordinary flow-pass machinery before the synchronous call completes, so dependents observe the producer's absence without an application-authored nudge. Reuse the established settle/error semantics where practical; do not add a public settle command, option, alternate clear API, fixed-point engine, or general scheduler. Preserve in-drain behavior, where `clear-flow` already queues the vacation for the current pending-db flow pass, and preserve no-op behavior for an unknown flow or absent frame.

The precise internal bridge (for example, reusing the private settle transport after releasing the drain lock versus a smaller exact-owner helper) is intentionally left to implementation review. It must not deadlock/re-enter the current serialization gate, and it must retain the exact-incarnation fences around direct vacation and teardown.

## Posture rationale

Flows are deliberately a small convenience, so the right fix is one consistent lifecycle boundary, not more API. The effect form already guarantees cleared inputs and their dependents settle together. Making the documented plain function honor the same observable invariant removes a surprising manual drain and keeps boot/test/per-tenant use low-friction for people and generated code without broadening flows into a dataflow system.

## Duplicate and history search

Searched all tracker statuses across titles, descriptions, and notes for `flow`, `clear-flow`, `direct clear`, `outside a drain`, `dependent flow`, `initial output`, `settle`, and `unrelated event`. No issue owns this direct-clear/dependent-output boundary. Closest is closed `rf2-kh73v`, which fixed automatic settling only for `:rf.fx/reg-flow` / `:rf.fx/clear-flow`; its scope and tests are effect-specific and its non-goals explicitly exclude static/direct registration work. Closed `rf2-pt637` fixes only the cart example's hot-reload callback.

History confirms the split: `clear-flow` dates to 691c892564e; direct path vacation was added in 7e83e7c691 and later exact-owner-fenced by b5c4599df0/a3ca268cdc0/5c660f2fda. Commits 47e90cf3b4 and 7b6d1e75a3 added and ordered private settling for lifecycle effects without changing the plain direct path.

## Uncertainties

The spec currently states direct clear's deregistration/vacation but does not explicitly say whether dependent flows settle before return; the public synchronous shape and advertised outside-handler use make the current inconsistent graph the actionable defect. The fixing worker should record the chosen direct-call failure boundary if a remaining dependent's derive throws, aligning with the existing private settle semantics rather than inventing rollback behavior.
acceptance_criteria:
- A focused CLJ regression reproduces producer A -> dependent B and proves that after direct `(flows/clear-flow A {:frame frame-id})` returns: A is unregistered, A's output leaf is absent, and B has recomputed once against that absence without any unrelated/app-authored dispatch.
- The regression has a negative control: it fails against the current implementation with B retaining the pre-clear value.
- Unknown-id and absent-frame direct clears remain silent no-ops; clearing one frame does not settle or mutate a sibling frame.
- In-drain direct clear and `:rf.fx/clear-flow` keep their current one-settle/topological behavior; existing settle ordering tests remain green.
- The implementation does not expose a public settle event/function/flag, add fixed-point iteration, or change `clear-flow`'s public arities.
- Exact-incarnation loss cannot let an old direct clear or its settle tail mutate a same-id successor frame, and the implementation does not deadlock by dispatching while holding the drain lock.
- Spec/API/core guide wording states the observable direct-clear boundary and its downstream behavior; JVM and CLJS coverage is added in proportion to the cross-host `.cljc` lifecycle code.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #9204 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9204).

REPRODUCED at merge base, exactly as described: producer :probe/a ([:x]->[:a]), dependent :probe/b ([:a]->[:b]), seeded {:x 2, :a 2, :b 2}; after (flows/clear-flow :probe/a) RETURNED, app-db was {:x 2, :b 2} — :b still derived from the :a slot that same call removed.

HOW NOTHING DRAINED BETWEEN THE CLEAR AND THE OBSERVATION (the load-bearing claim):
(1) ADJACENCY — clear-flow is the SOLE call between the precondition read and the capture. No dispatch, no dispatch-sync, no manual flow pass, no other framework call. The observed db is bound to a local immediately after the clear and every assertion reads that captured value, not a re-read.
(2) PURE OBSERVATION — re-frame.core/app-db-value is a pure deref of the frame's app-db projection through the substrate adapter (core.cljc:1918 -> frame.cljc:1726 frame-slot-value); it cannot trigger a pass.
(3) DERIVE COUNTER — the dependent's :derive increments an atom. Across the window it incremented by 0 before the fix and by exactly 1 after. This separates 'settled inside the clear' from 'settled later', which an app-db read alone cannot.
(4) TRACE RECORDER over EVERY op-type — :rf.event op-type events are emitted by any dispatch and any drain, so an empty :rf.event slice across the window is affirmative evidence no event ran. In the RED run that assertion PASSED while the staleness assertion failed, i.e. the stale value was measured with nothing draining. It also pins that the settle must not be a dispatched event (it would re-enter the drain gate the call already holds).
(5) THE RECORDER'S OWN POSITIVE CONTROL, in-run — the same :rf.event slice is re-read after a deliberate dispatch and asserted non-empty, so a dead instrument (tracing compiled out, op-type renamed) cannot report the empty window slice in the same words a working one does.
(6) DRAIN-EQUIVALENCE, which states the diagnosis directly — the value captured at the clear must equal the value after a subsequent unrelated no-op dispatch. Its negative-control failure reads literally (not (= {:x 2, :b 2} {:x 2, :b nil})): the clear left :b 2, an unrelated drain changed it to :b nil. That IS the bead's phrase 'until an unrelated drain'.

NEGATIVE CONTROL: with the fix reverted to merge base and the regression kept, exit 1, 5 failures / 16 assertions, 'app-db was {:x 2, :b 2}'. Test expectations were written before the fix, corrected once against the fx-route precedent (a dependent's slot stays PUBLISHED with the recomputed value — flows-settle-on-dispatch-test pins "total=", not removal), then re-red against the reverted source to prove they were not tuned to the implementation.

FIX: out of a drain, clear-flow settles the frame's remaining flows through the ORDINARY run-flows-on-db engine before returning — routed through the existing mechanism, not a second settle implementation. Placed inside the when-let on the flow row (unknown id settles nothing), inside the exact-owner postcheck (a stale A's settle tail cannot recompute a same-id B), and inside the existing serialized region (closes the window entirely: no drain can observe the frame between the row's removal and the dependents' repair). No deadlock: call-serialized-with-drain! runs its thunk directly for a thread already owning the region rather than re-taking the non-reentrant cell, and a drainer already runs this exact engine under this exact lock. registry cannot require the facade, so the facade installs a settle seam at load. In-drain and :rf.fx/clear-flow behaviour untouched; unknown-id/absent-frame stay silent no-ops; no public settle surface; arities unchanged; one pass, not fixed-point.

CONTRACT: owning spec is spec/013-Flows.md (via spec/Ownership.md row 60). Its Sequencing section made the settle boundary NORMATIVE FOR THE FX ROUTE ONLY and was SILENT on the plain function — so the spec was silent, not contradictory, and the third outcome (propose + implement) applied. New subsection states the direct boundary and its bounds, incl. the failure boundary the bead asked to be recorded: a settling :derive throw propagates the ordinary :rf.error/flow-eval-exception to the direct caller, the clear stands (already committed, and what the caller asked for), the candidate db is discarded unwritten — reusing the existing structured failure rather than inventing rollback. spec/API.md was NOT touched: it is fenced to a peer this wave.

GATES: implementation/flows clojure -M:test exit 0, 250 tests/6102 assertions BEFORE -> 253/6119 AFTER. implementation/core clojure -M:test exit 0, 2175 tests/11142 assertions (its test classpath includes flows). python -m mkdocs build --strict exit 0. check_doc_slugs.py exit 0, proven live with a plant (exit 1 naming all three edited pages); restores verified by blob hash. npm run test:cljs NOT run — no node_modules in this worktree and the tree was deliberately not linked; named rather than implied, CI owns it. No JS interop touched, so no release compile required. Witness is *_cljs_test.cljc so the shadow-cljs :node-test build runs it on the CLJS host too.

title: epoch: lowering :depth leaves stale epochs queryable and restorable
description:
## Finding

Changing the live epoch `:depth` only updates the config atom; it does not resize the rings that already exist. The sharp case is `:depth 0`: because `record!` skips `append-record` entirely when depth is zero, retained records survive indefinitely. The public read and time-travel surfaces still consume them, so the documented “disabled ring” remains queryable and writable-through.

This is one configuration-transition defect, not a request for a new history abstraction.

## Verified reproduction

Reproduced at `52b2579e9b53816abddd3406f72db5a5278bed1c` on the JVM through the public API with the plain-atom adapter:

1. Make `:probe/frame`; dispatch `:probe/seed` to `{:n 1}` and `:probe/inc` to `{:n 2}`; save the first epoch id.
2. Before disabling, `(count (rf/epoch-history :probe/frame))` is `2` and app-db is `{:n 2}`.
3. Call `(rf/configure! {:epoch-history {:depth 0}})`.
4. Observed `(count (rf/epoch-history :probe/frame)) => 2`, then `(rf/restore-epoch! :probe/frame saved-id) => true`, and app-db rewound to `{:n 1}`. The probe exited 0.

A smaller data-level probe also recorded one row with `state/record!`, set depth to zero through `epoch/configure!`, and observed the same row from `epoch/epoch-history` afterwards.

Expected from the shipped contract: `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:118-123` says `epoch-history` is empty when depth is 0; its `configure!` doc at lines 57-63 says depth 0 disables recording and nothing lands in the ring. `spec/Tool-Pair.md:718` is explicit that setting depth 0 disables the per-frame ring and `epoch-history` returns `[]`, while listeners continue firing. The bounded-history rule at `spec/Tool-Pair.md:100` says the runtime keeps the last N epochs; lowering N should therefore make the live ring obey N, not wait for an unrelated future append.

## Cause and impact

- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/state.cljc:55-83` (`merge-config!`) validates and swaps only `config`.
- `state.cljc:192-203` (`record!`) enforces the depth cap only on a later append, and its `(when (pos? history-depth) ...)` means depth 0 never reaches the cap logic.
- `state.cljc:205-208` (`history-for`) returns the retained vector without consulting the current depth.
- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/tool_pair.cljc:409-410` and `:586-587` resolve restore/replay targets from that stale vector; `:2079-2081` projects it off-box.

Consequences are user-visible in the dev/tooling tier: the memory/retention knob does not release already-retained full frame-state and raw trace snapshots; an operator choosing “no retained history, listeners only” can still read/project old records; and old ids remain valid restore/replay inputs. Positive reductions have the same delayed behavior (the ring can exceed the new N until another record appends); zero is permanent because no append occurs to repair it.

## Bounded recommendation

Make a valid `:depth` reduction enforce the new cap against every existing per-frame ring at the configuration boundary. Preserve newest-first retention semantics: depth N keeps each frame’s newest N existing records; depth 0 drops them all. Reconcile any internal last-settled/back-fill anchors that would otherwise keep naming removed records, so disabling then re-enabling starts from a genuinely empty history rather than resurrecting or targeting an old epoch. Keep the existing depth-0 listener contract: newly assembled records still fan out raw to registered epoch listeners but are not retained.

Prefer the smallest change around `re-frame.epoch.state/merge-config!` and its storage helpers. The implementation may choose its own synchronization shape; the observable invariant is that once `configure!` returns, every ring respects the accepted depth.

## Posture rationale

This closes a broken existing knob and removes surprise from a core SPA debugging gesture. It gives people and AI tools one honest meaning for “history depth” without adding API, modes, compatibility branches, or policy. The value is correctness and low-friction ergonomics, not a more elaborate timeline system.

## Non-goals

- No branching timeline, archive/export, persistence, or new clear-history API.
- No change to listener publication at depth 0.
- No new error category and no change to normal restore/replay semantics for records that remain retained.
- No retroactive rewrite of record payloads or `:trace-events-keep` semantics beyond what is necessary to keep the accepted depth invariant.
- No unrelated cleanup of the epoch state atoms or concurrency machinery.

## Duplicate and history search

All-status bead searches were run for epoch titles and description phrases `depth 0`, `ring disabled`, `disables recording`, `lowering depth`, `stale history`, `epoch-history returns`, `epoch-history`, `trace-events-keep`, and `history-for`. No bead describes this config-transition defect. The two all-status `depth 0` description hits were unrelated: `rf2-5mr6` (malformed routing fixture) and `rf2-6ka0` (retired tools-root prose). Relevant closed work is adjacent but distinct: `rf2-gba3ou` covers leakage of the `replace-history-disabled` trace; commits `417628bdd9` / `4aec0cbfc5` reject state injection at depth 0 and pin back-fill snapshot consistency. Neither trims a pre-existing ring on configuration change.

Path history and `git blame` show `merge-config!` / `history-for` originated in the epoch cohesion split (`cd9fdb75587`); later naming and depth-0 work did not add a transition-time trim. `git log --all --grep=depth.0` and retention searches found no commit claiming this behavior.

## Uncertainties

The contract is clear for the post-return observable state, but the best internal synchronization with a JVM append racing `configure!` needs implementation-time judgment. A focused test should pin the synchronous public behavior first; add a race test only if the chosen implementation introduces a meaningful interleaving, rather than building machinery speculatively.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A public-API test records several epochs in at least two frames, lowers `:depth` to a positive N, and immediately (without another dispatch) sees only each frame’s newest N records.
2. A public-API test records an epoch, sets `:depth 0`, and immediately sees `[]` from both `rf/epoch-history` and `rf/projected-history`; the saved id can no longer be restored or replayed and frame state is unchanged by those refusals.
3. Depth 0 continues to publish newly assembled records to epoch listeners while retaining none.
4. Re-enabling a positive depth after the zero-depth interval starts with no pre-disable records; a new dispatch records normally, and post-settle back-fill cannot target a retired epoch id.
5. Existing invalid-config, ring-eviction, restore/replay, listener, and production-elision tests remain green. Add focused coverage in `implementation/epoch/test/re_frame/epoch_test.clj` and the representative CLJS epoch suite for the cross-platform public behavior.
6. No public API, error vocabulary, or compatibility alias is added.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #9205 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9205). Premise held at tip and both halves were reproduced through the public API before the fix: after {:depth 2} on a 5-record ring epoch-history still returned all five, and after {:depth 0} epoch-history/projected-history still returned the retained record, restore-epoch! returned true and rewound app-db {:n 2} -> {:n 1}, and replay-epoch! returned :ok? true (it re-drove the event). Witness suite captured exit 1 with 16 failures before the change, exit 0 after. FIX: re-frame.epoch.state/merge-config! now enforces an accepted :depth against every live ring before it returns, so the invariant is 'once configure! returns, every ring respects the accepted depth'. Config is swapped first, then the rings, so any record! beginning afterwards reads the new depth. Both back-fill anchors that name ring records are reconciled against the pruned map in the same call: last-settled-epoch (whole-frame) and mount-attribution's :epoch-id (per-render-key); left behind, either would send the post-settle splice at a nonexistent record whose epoch-index resolves nil, silently dropping the render. Only :epoch-id goes, never the learned :deps read-set (not an epoch reference, and learned at mount so unrecoverable for an already-mounted view). READERS ENUMERATED (symbol census over implementation/ and tools/ for history-for/histories, then each call site read): epoch.cljc epoch-history and the depth-exceed settle path; tool_pair.cljc restore preconditions, replay preconditions, perform-replay! and projected-history; state.cljc's back-fill splice and value-changed-epoch-for. All eight resolve through the ring vector, so pruning it closes every one; tools/ holds no reader of this store. SPEC: no contract change needed - Tool-Pair 'Bounded history' and the depth-0 bullet already mandated it; two prose sentences added to make the transition explicit rather than inferred, which is the gap that let the defect live. :trace-events-keep deliberately stays an append-time rule. No public API, error vocabulary or alias added: a retired id refuses through the existing :rf.epoch/restore-unknown-epoch and :rf.epoch/replay-unknown-epoch modes. AC1-AC6 all covered by tests in epoch_test.clj plus a cross-target test in epoch_cljs_test.cljs. Gates on the final rebased base, all captured exits: epoch JVM suite 556/7259 exit 0; epoch prod-gate lane 25/76 exit 0; npm run test:cljs 11176/55769 exit 0; mkdocs build --strict exit 0; check_doc_slugs.py exit 0 (proved live with a planted broken anchor, then reverted and verified by blob hash).

title: flows: direct reg-flow does not materialize a new flow's initial output until an unrelated drain
description:
Sibling of the fixed rf2-g1zb, found while fixing it. NOT yet reproduced with a live probe — the evidence below is source-level, so the first task is to measure it.

CLAIM (verify at source): `re-frame.flows/reg-flow` called as a plain function OUTSIDE an event drain registers the flow and returns without running a flow pass, so the new flow's INITIAL output is not materialized until some later, unrelated drain. Source evidence: `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc` `reg-flow` writes output marks, mutates the registry, drops the dirty-check row and emits traces — it contains no call to `run-flows-on-db` and no settle. That is the same shape as the clear-flow defect rf2-g1zb fixed. Its own comments note the asymmetry: a DIRECT cold `reg-flow` does not inherit the router's exact-owner predicate that the `:rf.fx/reg-flow` route does.

WHY IT IS FILED SEPARATELY AND NOT FIXED IN PR #9204: rf2-g1zb's scope and bounded recommendation were explicitly clear-flow-only, and its acceptance criteria named no reg-flow arm. PR #9204's spec wording therefore says in terms that the new Spec 013 subsection governs clear-flow only and that reg-flow's direct path is out of scope, so symmetry is NOT read into it — see spec/013-Flows.md, the subsection 'The same boundary for a direct clear-flow'. That sentence is what this bead would revisit.

WHAT IS ALREADY SPECIFIED: Spec 013 §Sequencing is NORMATIVE that a flow registered by `:rf.fx/reg-flow` has its initial output materialised, and every dependent recomputed, by the time the dispatching event settles. It is silent on the direct function, exactly as it was for clear-flow before rf2-g1zb.

FIRST STEP: reproduce. Seed app-db FIRST, then `reg-flow` a flow whose inputs are already present, then read app-db with no dispatch in between — the trap is that a probe which registers against an EMPTY db proves nothing, because there is no value to derive. Use the witness harness from `implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_direct_clear_settle_cljs_test.cljc`, which already carries the machinery: adjacency, a derive counter, a whole-stream :rf.event trace recorder with its own in-run positive control, and a drain-equivalence assertion. If the premise does not hold, that finding with its evidence is the deliverable.

IF IT REPRODUCES: the fix is likely one line reusing the seam PR #9204 added — `registry/set-settle-fn!` publishes an exact-owner settle installed by the facade, and `reg-flow` could call it under the same three fences clear-flow uses (inside the registration's exact-owner postcheck, out-of-drain only, inside the serialized region). Note the docs promise to reconcile: docs/core/flows.md currently states in prose that reg-flow's direct form does NOT make the matching promise about initial output and points readers at `:rf.fx/reg-flow`; docs/api/re-frame.flows.md documents the settle boundary on clear-flow only. Both would need updating alongside the spec subsection.

Consider also whether reg-flow's error surface changes: reg-flow already throws `:rf.error/flow-frame-not-live`, so a settling derive throw propagating to the direct caller is less of a departure there than it was for clear-flow.

title: surface-review(http): frame-scope managed request cancellation and supersession
description:
## Scope

Correct the frame isolation of implementation/http managed-request lifetime tracking: raw app-authored :request-id supersession, :rf.http/managed-abort, and actor-destroy cancellation. Keep the public :rf.http/managed args map and :rf.http/managed-abort effect shape unchanged.

## Correctness finding

The HTTP registry is process-global but both of its cancellation indexes use frame-local identifiers without the frame: in-flight is request-id -> handle and actor-in-flight is actor-id -> handles. managed-handler correctly captures the issuing frame, yet passes the raw request-id to next-issuance! and supersede!. managed-abort-handler receives frame-ctx but deliberately ignores it and aborts by the raw id. The actor-destroy hook likewise accepts only actor-id. Consequently two isolated frames running the same application code are not isolated at the managed-HTTP lifetime boundary.

A frame B request using the same ordinary stable id as frame A supersedes and suppresses A's live request. A manual abort dispatched in B can abort A even when B owns no request. Generated/fixed actor ids are also frame-local, so destroying an actor in one frame can walk the same actor-id slot containing another frame's handles. This is especially exposed by documented per-request SSR frames, Story/test variants, and side-by-side mounts: reusing code naturally reuses ids such as :articles/load.

## Steps to Reproduce

From implementation/http on current tip, the following read-only registry probe records a frame-A handle, then exercises the same production supersede selector a frame-B managed-handler calls:

  clojure -M -e "(require '[re-frame.http.registry :as r]) (r/clear-all-in-flight!) (let [seen (atom []) _ (r/record-in-flight! :shared nil {:frame :frame/a :abort-fn #(swap! seen conj [:frame/a %])})] (println (pr-str {:before (select-keys (r/lookup-in-flight :shared) [:frame]) :cross-frame-supersede-found? (boolean (r/supersede! :shared)) :aborts @seen :after (r/lookup-in-flight :shared)}))) (r/clear-all-in-flight!)"

Exit 0 output:

  {:before {:frame :frame/a}, :cross-frame-supersede-found? true, :aborts [[:frame/a :request-id-superseded]], :after nil}

A second probe invokes the real abort effect handler with frame B's context over frame A's registered handle:

  clojure -M -e "(require '[re-frame.http.registry :as r] '[re-frame.http.handlers :as h]) (r/clear-all-in-flight!) (let [seen (atom []) _ (r/record-in-flight! :shared nil {:frame :frame/a :abort-fn #(swap! seen conj [:frame/a %])})] (h/managed-abort-handler {:frame :frame/b :event [:cancel]} :shared) (println (pr-str {:caller-frame :frame/b :aborts @seen}))) (r/clear-all-in-flight!)"

Exit 0 output:

  {:caller-frame :frame/b, :aborts [[:frame/a :user]]}

This is not merely a test helper artifact. transport/run-attempt! publishes every live/backoff handle through registry/record-in-flight! using the raw normalized request-id; handlers/managed-handler calls supersede! with that same raw id before each fresh issuance.

## Source evidence

- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/handlers.cljc:207-220 and 253-267 capture :frame in the normalized context, proving frame identity is available.
- handlers.cljc:381-410 nevertheless calls next-issuance! and supersede! with request-id alone.
- handlers.cljc:413-428 names managed-abort-handler's first arg _frame-ctx and calls abort-in-flight! with request-id alone.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/registry.cljc:36-73 defines process-global atoms keyed only by request-id and actor-id.
- registry.cljc:87-179 clears, looks up, and aborts by unqualified request-id; 201-289 keys issuance and supersession the same way.
- registry.cljc:391-428 aborts actor work by actor-id alone, while the hook contract receives no frame.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc:1082 and 1701 are the live/backoff record-in-flight! sites; handles carry :frame, but the lookup key does not.
- spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:790 promises replies remain in their issuing frame; docs/core/frames.md:138-140 defines SSR and repeated mounts as isolated worlds. The lifetime side channel currently breaks that same isolation before reply routing.
- The repository already proved this class for higher-level consumers: commit 450cdd44a1 (rf2-sxyrzk) had resources/mutations synthesize [:rf.req frame-id work-id] because the process-global HTTP registry otherwise cross-cancelled identical frame-local work ids. That workaround does not protect direct :rf.http/managed users, whose ergonomic API accepts ordinary stable ids.

## Recommended bounded repair

Make the issuing frame part of HTTP's internal cancellation identity while preserving the caller's raw :request-id as the public correlation value echoed in replies and traces. Thread frame through request lookup/supersede/manual-abort/issuance and through actor-destroy cancellation (or use an equivalent compound internal key). A programmer should be able to write :request-id :articles/load once in reusable app code; the runtime, which already carries frame identity, should provide isolation automatically.

Keep the existing process-global atoms if compound keys are the smallest repair. Reuse the existing identity-conditional cleanup, retry handoff, finalisation CAS, and frame-destroy sweep. Update Spec 014 and internal comments that currently describe request-id keying as process-global to state the intended same-frame supersession law. Existing resource-generated qualified ids may remain if removing that redundant qualification would broaden the change; compatibility matters less than keeping this repair focused and mechanically safe.

## Posture rationale

This is a correctness and ergonomics repair, not extra machinery. Requiring every direct HTTP caller (and AI-generated app code) to remember to bake a frame id into an otherwise simple stable request id leaks a runtime implementation detail and makes reusable event code unsafe in the exact multi-frame/SSR modes the library advertises. Internal compound identity uses information already present and keeps the public API minimal. Do not add namespaces, registries, lease objects, user-facing tokens, or configuration switches.

## Non-goals

- No new public request-id type, frame argument, cancellation verb, failure kind, or compatibility alias.
- No transport, retry, decode, privacy, reply-envelope, or stale-trace redesign.
- No requirement to move process-global atoms into every frame; correct compound keying is sufficient.
- No attempt to make explicit cross-frame cancellation possible through this local effect. If such orchestration is ever needed, it deserves a separate explicit surface rather than accidental raw-id reach-through.
- No cleanup of the resources workaround unless required to keep its current behavior green.

## Related and duplicate search

Searched all-status beads with bd search/list across titles and descriptions for request-id, managed HTTP, in-flight registry, frame isolation, cross-frame, frame-qualify, frame-scope, supersede, and abort. No current or closed bead owns direct managed-HTTP cross-frame cancellation. The closest current HTTP issues are closed rf2-rsv2n (abort during body preparation), closed rf2-o9e15 (supersede-test flake), and closed rf2-lddbk (successful response metadata); all are distinct.

History search found commit 450cdd44a1 / historical rf2-sxyrzk, which fixed only resources and mutations by pre-qualifying their generated transport ids and explicitly documented the still-process-global HTTP registry. Commit d4f85afcac added frame-destroy aborts but its tests use distinct request ids per frame. The existing spec/conformance/fixtures/http-managed-frame-isolation.edn uses canned replies with no :request-id, so it never enters this registry. The full implementation/http JVM suite is green (506 tests, 3882 assertions, 0 failures/errors), confirming the current suite lacks this adversarial same-id/two-frame case rather than contradicting the reproduction.

## Uncertainties

The minimal internal signature migration needs care because resources calls the late-bound abort-by-id seam with its already-qualified token, and machines currently calls the actor-destroy hook with actor-id alone. The implementer should choose whether those internal hooks gain frame-id or accept a compound selector while leaving app-facing effects unchanged. CLJS is single-threaded but the same key collision exists; JVM/SSR additionally needs existing atomic/identity-conditional cleanup preserved under concurrent frames.
acceptance_criteria:
- A deterministic direct-managed-HTTP test creates two live frames, issues overlapping requests with the same raw :request-id in both, and proves both remain live; neither receives :request-id-superseded merely because the sibling frame reused the id.
- Reissuing that id inside frame A still supersedes exactly A's prior attempt, emits one stale-suppressed row with carried/current ids for A, and leaves frame B's handle and eventual reply untouched.
- Dispatching [:rf.http/managed-abort id] in frame A aborts only A's request; the identical id in frame B remains live and completes into B. The symmetric B case also passes.
- A cross-frame actor case uses the same generated or fixed actor-id in two frames; destroying A's actor aborts only A-owned HTTP and leaves B's actor request live. The actor-destroy hook carries enough frame identity to make this structural, not naming-convention-dependent.
- Frame destroy and epoch restore still abort every handle owned by the selected frame, including two sibling frames that reused a request id; retry-backoff handles remain continuously cancellable and clean only their own registry entry.
- App-visible replies/traces continue to echo the caller's original :request-id, not an internal compound key. Existing single-frame request-id, abort, supersede, retry-race, actor-destroy, and resource/mutation qualified-id tests remain green on JVM and CLJS.
- The two reproduction probes above no longer resolve or abort frame A from a frame-B selector through the supported production path; a negative control restoring raw global keying makes the new same-id/two-frame tests fail.
- Spec 014 and API/docs describe same-id supersession and managed-abort as frame-scoped, consistent with the isolated-world frame contract, without asking callers to manually qualify ids.
notes:
## Verdict (PR #9195)

PREMISE HOLDS, and was reproduced at tip before any edit. Spec 014 was SILENT
on cancellation scope — it said neither "frame-scoped" nor "process-global" —
so this settled the contract and implemented it (outcome 2 of the three the
dispatch named).

### Reproduced at tip (afe446ea71 / 835ea4804f), all four probes exit 0

- `supersede!` driven from frame B resolved and aborted frame A's handle:
  `{:cross-frame-supersede-found? true, :aborts [[:frame/a :request-id-superseded]], :after nil}`
- `managed-abort-handler` with frame B's ctx aborted frame A's handle:
  `{:caller-frame :frame/b, :aborts [[:frame/a :user]]}`
- `abort-on-actor-destroy :actor/x` aborted BOTH frames' handles.
- FOURTH finding the bead did not record: the issuance counter was shared too —
  frame B's FIRST issuance under a shared raw id read **2**, not 1, perturbing
  B's `:work/id` for a supersession that never happened to it.

### Contract settled against 014

Frame-scoping was chosen because process-global contradicts what 014 already
says: §Frame awareness promises multi-frame apps "work without extra
ceremony" (false unless every caller hand-qualifies ids); §Chain order and
frame scope already makes the sibling HTTP surface — the interceptor chain —
per-frame; §Sibling actors are not affected already asserts inter-actor
isolation. Spec 014 gains §Frame scope — a `:request-id` is frame-local, a
§Frame scope note under Abort on actor destroy, §Frame awareness extended from
reply routing to request lifetime, and the snapshot helpers' new arities.

### Fix

The issuing frame is now part of the INTERNAL key (`[frame-id id]`) for both
indexes and the issuance counters, derived from the `:frame` stamp the
transport already puts on every handle. Public `:rf.http/managed` args map and
`:rf.http/managed-abort` effect shape unchanged; the caller's raw
`:request-id` stays the correlation value echoed in replies and traces. No new
namespace, registry, lease object, user-facing token or config switch.

### Acceptance criteria

Met: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and the registry half of 4. Witness is
`implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_frame_scoped_cancellation_test.clj`
(9 deftests, deterministic — latched localhost `HttpServer`, no timing-
sensitive assertion). AC 7's negative control was run: restoring raw global
keying takes the suite to exit 1 / 21 failures / 3 errors with 7 of the 9 new
deftests red; reverted and verified by blob hash.

### Deliberately NOT done — see rf2-wjfm

AC 4's "the actor-destroy hook carries enough frame identity to make this
structural" needs the HOOK'S CALLERS to pass a frame, and both are outside the
dispatched fence: `machines/lifecycle_fx/finalize.cljc`
`abort-actor-in-flight-http!` (its caller in `destroy.cljc` has `frame-id`
bound one line above) and `core/frame.cljc` ~3983's machines-absent fallback.
The registry half IS done — the actor index is keyed `[frame-id actor-id]` and
`abort-on-actor-destroy` has a frame-bearing 2-arity — so the follow-up is one
line per call site. Its `[actor-id]` arity is retained as the documented
ANY-FRAME sweep so no flag day is needed. Filed rf2-wjfm (P2,
discovered-from rf2-o8ek) with both call sites named.

The resources any-frame seam (`:http/abort-in-flight!`) was left unchanged and
is correct as-is: its token is already frame-qualified
(`[:rf.req frame-id work-id]`, Spec 016), so at most one frame can match.

### Gates (captured exits, never read through a filter)

- `implementation/http` `clojure -M:test` BEFORE: exit 0, 506 tests / 3882 assertions
- same AFTER, on the final rebased base: exit 0, 515 tests / 3929 assertions
- `npm run test:cljs`: exit 0, 11,170 tests / 55,743 assertions
- `python -m mkdocs build --strict`: exit 0
- `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`: exit 0, and proven live — a planted broken
  anchor took it to exit 1 naming file, line and the planted anchor.

### Two test seeds needed a frame; neither was a production regression

Both production `record-in-flight!` sites stamp `:frame (:frame ctx)` from a
ctx whose value came through `require-frame-stamp!` (throws on nil), so a real
handle can never lack one. `flows_http_integration_test.clj`'s
`prime-in-flight!` and the `managed_http_counter` example's demo-only seed fx
both built handles by hand without it; the example already BOUND the carried
frame for its deferred dispatch and simply did not put it on the handle.
REOPENED by merged-PR audit of #9195 (2026-09-04). The compound registry keys correctly isolate the main managed-abort/supersede paths, but two cleanup paths still escape that scope:

1. `examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs` was changed to stamp `:frame` on its seeded handle, yet its `:abort-fn` still calls one-arg `(clear-in-flight! request-id)`. #9195 redefined that arity as an ANY-FRAME sweep. With the demo mounted in frames A and B under its stable `:http-counter/long` id, cancelling A invokes A's abort closure and deletes BOTH registry slots; B's fake long request becomes unregistered/unabortable and its UI can remain loading. A deterministic JVM registry probe using that exact closure shape produced `{:aborts [[:frame/a :user]], :a-live? false, :b-live? false}`. The new frame-lifecycle test explicitly notes that one-arg clear would take the sibling slot, but the changed example was not given the same handle-cell/identity-exact cleanup it models.

2. `clear-in-flight!`'s 2-arg nil-handle branch also delegates to the ANY-FRAME sweep. Both live-fetch host paths acknowledge a publication window between `record-in-flight!` and `reset! handle-holder`; on the JVM another thread can fire the just-published abort-fn there. A nil handle from frame A can therefore delete an already-live same-id frame-B slot. The comment that the window "precedes any successor" covers only same-frame succession, not a sibling frame that was already live.

Keep rf2-wjfm as the existing owner of the deliberately deferred actor-hook call sites. On this owner, make every cleanup path that possesses an issuing frame frame-exact, including the demo and nil/publication path, and add same-id/two-frame witnesses for both. Do not broaden the public effect API or remove the resource token's intentional any-frame seam.
REOPENED by merged-PR audit of #9202. The cross-frame cleanup paths are fixed, but the new frame-exact fallback does not close the publication race across the registry TWO indexes. record-in-flight! publishes the stamped handle to in-flight first (registry.cljc:142-143), then actor-in-flight in a separate swap! (144-146). A JVM abort between those swaps invokes the handle while its forward-reference cell is still nil; clear-in-flight-in-frame! removes the request slot and tries to remove the actor slot before that slot exists, then record-in-flight! resumes and publishes the already-aborted handle into actor-in-flight. Deterministic same-thread watch interleaving on current tip printed {:abort-fired? true, :request-slot nil, :actor-slot-count 1}. This is the exact publication window #9202 calls production-reachable from another JVM thread, for actor-originated requests carrying both ids. The result is a ghost actor handle, stale introspection and retained state until later actor/frame teardown. Preserve the frame-scoped and identity-conditional laws, but make publication plus cleanup coherent across both indexes (or make the stamped handle identity available to the abort closure before either publish). Add a controlled midpoint interleaving witness asserting both indexes are empty after the abort; the landed tests call cleanup only after record-in-flight! has finished and therefore cannot see this gap.

title: spec/006 §Cross-host: say that Hicasso's author-wins-a-collision guarantee is held at the canonical React slot, not at the key
description:
ONE SENTENCE, ONE SECTION. `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md` §Cross-host, in the paragraph beginning "**One clause is deliberately NOT taken: Hicasso emits no one-shot warning for a non-DOM root.**" — the clause that currently ends "...so fragments, `[:> …]` crossings, `defhost` islands and boundary heads are all skipped, and the author's own value wins a collision."

That sentence is TRUE as it stands (PR #9200 made it true again), so this is a sharpening and not a correction: it does not say WHERE the win is held, and the audit of PR #9191 showed that the difference is the whole of the contract. Replace the trailing clause "and the author's own value wins a collision." with:

  and the author's own value wins a collision — held at the CANONICAL REACT SLOT rather than at the key. Hicasso's codec accepts five spellings of one attribute (keyword, namespaced keyword, symbol, namespaced symbol and string) and folds every one onto a single React prop name, so a merge keyed by `=` would leave a body's `"data-rf-view"` beside the framework's `:data-rf-view` and let the attribute map's iteration order pick the emitted value — the guarantee failing nondeterministically rather than failing. The framework's entry is therefore dropped at any slot the author already claims, in any spelling, and the annotation a body did NOT write is still stamped beside the one it did (rf2-c5w1, audit of PR #9191).

WHY IT IS A SEPARATE BEAD. `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md` is a one-toucher hot-zone file and a peer worker (rf2-ss8x, the reagent-adapter teardown fix) held it during the wave PR #9200 landed in, having already committed to it on its branch. The mayor corrected the fence mid-task and asked for the prose rather than the edit. Sequence this after that peer's PR merges, and re-verify the quoted clause against the file at dispatch — the peer's change rewrites parts of 006 and the sentence may have moved.

GATES BY PATH. `spec/` is staged into the docs build by `mkdocs_hooks.py`'s `on_pre_build` on any invocation, so a bare `python -m mkdocs build --strict` covers it (`mkdocs` is not on PATH). `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` validates anchors and repo-relative targets; it exits 0 with an empty log on success, so prove it live with a plant before believing it. The edit adds no link and no heading, so neither gate inspects anything new — say so rather than citing a green that inspected nothing.
notes:
MAYOR SEQUENCING NOTE 2026-09-05. FENCED until reagent-a's PR for rf2-ss8x merges. spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md is a HOT-ZONE file and that live worker has already COMMITTED a change to it on its branch. A worker branching off main now would not carry that change and would silently revert it — the well-formed-revert failure that passes every check the tree has.

PROVENANCE, because it explains why this bead exists at all rather than being folded into rf2-c5w1's PR: I wrote rf2-c5w1's brief telling that worker it was "the sole occupant of spec/006 this wave". That was MY error — reagent-a had been dispatched onto the same hot-zone file first, which the project's own convention forbids. I caught it by reading both worktrees, confirmed rf2-c5w1's branch diff was still EMPTY while reagent-a had already committed a 006 change, and sent a fence correction telling the worker to hand the prose over rather than edit. It did exactly that, and this bead is the handover. Nothing was lost and nothing was reverted.

WHAT THIS IS NOT: not a defect on main. The worker was explicit that §Cross-host's existing sentence is TRUE as it stands — this is a sharpening that records WHERE the guarantee is held (at the canonical React slot, not at the key) and why a merge keyed by = would have failed nondeterministically. The code fix landed in PR #9200 without it.

ON DISPATCH: re-verify the target clause at tip before editing. reagent-a's PR rewrites parts of 006 and the paragraph may have moved. The edit adds no link and no heading, so NEITHER check_doc_slugs.py NOR mkdocs build --strict inspects anything new — say that plainly rather than citing either green as evidence, per the standing rule that a gate which inspected nothing you changed is not a gate for your change.

EVERY FACT THE NEW PROSE ASSERTS WAS CHECKED AT SOURCE, and all three hold at tip: (1) five spellings, closed set — codec/canonical-slot reads keyword/symbol keys through 'name' (namespace discarded) and takes a string verbatim via slot/prop-name, codec.cljs:192-196, and view_annotation_slot_cljs_test.cljs:48-57 pins that same five-element set; (2) they fold onto ONE React prop name — canonical-slot IS cached-prop-name (codec.cljs:202-208), and data-* is in dont-camel-case (slot.cljc:26-29) so data-rf-view passes through uncamelcased; (3) the framework's entry is dropped at any slot the author already claims, in any spelling — without-authored-slots (collector.cljs:907-929) compares canonical slots not keys, and annotate-root merges (without-authored-slots attrs maybe-attrs) under the author (collector.cljs:972). title: spec(004B): the ismap row is falsified against react-dom 19.2; record the boolean value disposition
description:
004B §Booleans and their neighbours names `ismap` in the boolean-attribute set explicitly — "the set is the react-dom/server 19.2.0 boolean-attribute list, probed row-by-row (S1b) — it includes `hidden`, `muted`, and `ismap` (React 19 dropped the camel `isMap` prop)". MEASURED AGAINST THE INSTALLED react-dom 19.2.0, THAT ROW IS FALSE. title: surface-review(ssr): hiccup emitter drops false ARIA and booleanish attrs, leaving SSR DOM semantics unlike React
description:
## Scope Correct the boolean-value classification used by the hiccup-to-HTML path in implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/html_helpers.cljc. This helper feeds both the public non-streaming re-frame.ssr/render-to-string path and the streaming hiccup walker. Keep the change at attribute serialization plus focused parity coverage. ## Correctness finding html-helpers/attr-string currently applies one rule to every attribute: true emits a bare name, while false and nil are omitted. HTML/React attributes do not share one boolean class. In particular, aria-* and data-* boolean values stringify, and booleanish attributes such as contentEditable, draggable, and spellCheck stringify both true and false. The current path therefore turns aria-expanded=true into a present attribute with the empty string, drops aria-expanded=false entirely, turns contentEditable=true into a bare attribute, and drops contentEditable=false. This is not a theoretical edge. Boolean ARIA state is ordinary SPA authoring, and contentEditable=false is the way a child opts out of an editable ancestor. Omitting that false marker changes the server DOM's semantics. Spec 011 also records that React attribute-only hydration mismatches are not guaranteed to be patched and do not reach onRecoverableError, so the wrong server attribute can survive hydration without the framework's mismatch signal. The separate structural-tree serializer already models the needed categories in implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/ui_tree.cljc. This is drift in the stock-Reagent-compatible hiccup emitter, not a missing design. ## Verified evidence Verified at source tip 52283022e9; the relevant html_helpers.cljc, ui_tree.cljc, and ssr_emit_test.clj blobs are byte-identical to origin/main at 82c112928c. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/html_helpers.cljc:563-626 — attr-string branches on the value alone. Lines 595-597 emit every true bare and omit every false/nil before considering the attribute name. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/emit.cljc:778-794 — the standard renderer sends DOM attrs through attr-string. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/streaming.cljc:391-404 — the streaming shell uses the same helper, so both hiccup SSR modes are affected. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr.cljc:48 and implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/emit.cljc:883-920 — this is the public render-to-string implementation installed into the headless/Reagent-compatible adapter path. - Focused JVM probe of the current emitter: aria-expanded true -> aria-expanded false -> contentEditable true ->
...

   unchanged, and the same deftest still pins it green. In Clojure `nil` is absence

   asserted the opposite of what the author wrote.
6. Two rules for one map shape would be the friction: `{:data-hidden false}` meaning
   omitted on <body> but `data-hidden="false"` on a <div>, with no cue at the call

WHAT LANDED. (1) The eight roster omissions the audit named, reconciled against the INSTALLED react-dom 19.2.0: presence gains disablePictureInPicture, disableRemotePlayback, scoped, seamless; the stringifying family gains autoReverse, externalResourcesRequired, focusable, preserveAlpha. (3) spec/011-SSR.md gains the structural lesson and both dispositions. 004B untouched.

WHY THE PROBE IS NOT CIRCULAR, since that is the thing a third carrier should check first. Both halves come from react-dom, not from us: candidate NAMES are the values of react-dom's own possibleStandardNames table (scraped from the dev build), and "is this a boolean attribute?" is React's own dev-build "Received `true` for a non-boolean attribute" warning. A candidate list taken from our roster would have reproduced the audit's blind spot verbatim. That warning is also what BOUNDS this to a roster correction rather than a react-dom clone: the numeric attributes (cols, rows, size, span, rowSpan, start) coerce a boolean into markup through arithmetic — `size={true}` really does render size="true" — but React warns on them, so React's own verdict excludes them and we do not model a fourth class.

THE TWO DISPOSITIONS, both DECIDED not deferred, and both PINNED so the premise changing is itself a failure. `value` stays :ordinary — react-dom stringifies a boolean `value` because `value` shares a serialiser branch with the booleanish names, not because it is one; that branch is the generic push-what-you-were-given path and a string or number `value` (the only kinds a form control carries) serialises identically under :ordinary, so the classification bites only for a boolean `value`, which on a form control is an author error rather than a state; and `value` is a 004B form-control special form whose meaning already varies per element, so reclassifying it from the shared SSR roster would have changed ui-tree's handling of that special form from outside 004B. `ismap` stays :presence on 004B's word, and that word is FALSIFIED against the installed React — react-dom 19.2 accepts no boolean ismap at all (warns, emits nothing), so it cannot appear in the evidence; ismap IS a real HTML boolean attribute so presence is HTML-correct, and what is unsettled is whether the grammar tracks HTML or react-dom where they part. title: surface-review(reagent-slim): the static-markup boolean roster has the same omissions rf2-r9kf fixed in SSR
description:
`implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/dom/server.cljs` carries its OWN boolean-attribute roster, independent of the SSR artefact's:

    (def ^:private boolean-attributes
      #{"allowfullscreen" "async" "autofocus" "autoplay" "checked"
        "controls" "default" "defer" "disabled" "formnovalidate" "hidden"
        "loop" "multiple" "muted" "novalidate" "open" "playsinline"
        "readonly" "required" "reversed" "selected" "itemscope"})

Measured against the installed react-dom 19.2.0 it is missing the presence names `inert`, `noModule`, `scoped`, `seamless`, `disablePictureInPicture` and `disableRemotePlayback`, and it models NO stringifying class at all — so `contentEditable`, `draggable`, `spellCheck`, `autoReverse`, `externalResourcesRequired`, `focusable` and `preserveAlpha` do not get `="true"` / `="false"` treatment, and `download` / `capture` have no overloaded-boolean arm. That is the SAME defect class rf2-r9kf fixed in `re-frame.ssr.html-helpers`: a false value that carries meaning is dropped, and the markup asserts the opposite of what the author wrote.

WHY IT WAS NOT CAUGHT. `reagent2.dom.parity-cljs-test` already renders both ways and compares byte-for-byte against `react-dom/server.renderToStaticMarkup`, which is the right shape of check — but it is CORPUS-DRIVEN, so it only catches what its corpus happens to contain. None of the eleven names above appears to be in it. That is the same blind spot in a different disguise from the one the rf2-r9kf audit found: there, a parity test between two consumers of a shared roster could not see the roster's omissions; here, a genuine external parity test cannot see what its corpus omits.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, IF THIS IS DISPATCHED. PR #9207 landed `implementation/ssr/test/react_dom_probe/boolean_attr_classes.cjs`, which derives its candidate names from react-dom's own `possibleStandardNames` table and its boolean-ness from react-dom's own dev-build warning — so the roster under test cannot bound the probe. reagent-slim's parity test runs under `:node-test` with live `react-dom/server` available, so it could enumerate the same React-derived name set directly at test time rather than through a committed fixture, which is strictly better than what SSR could do. That is the cheap version: drive the existing parity harness over a React-derived name list instead of a hand-written corpus.

SCOPE NOTE. Separate artefact, separate roster, separate emitter — nothing is shared with `re-frame.ssr`, and rf2-r9kf deliberately did not touch it. Whether reagent-slim should model the stringifying and overloaded classes at all is a real question rather than an obvious yes: it is a static-markup emitter for a Reagent-compatible surface, and its IMPL-SPEC §8.7 already allow-lists known divergences from React. Decide that before widening the roster.

value:
`bd show` RENDERS SEVERAL DISTINCT FIELDS AS ONE FLOW OF TEXT WITH NO BOUNDARY MARKER, so text belonging to `acceptance_criteria` reads as a continuation of `notes`. Measured 2026-09-05 on rf2-r9kf, where it put a false claim into a dispatch brief.

WHAT HAPPENED. rf2-r9kf was reopened by a post-merge audit. Reading `bd show`, I saw the reopen note run straight into "ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA 1. Add focused JVM tests …" and told the worker those numbered criteria were the audit's round-2 specification. THEY WERE NOT — they are the ROUND-1 acceptance criteria, already satisfied by the merged PR. The worker disproved it from the field-level history: `acceptance_criteria` is constant at 1204 bytes across ALL 118 snapshots, while at the reopen boundary only `notes` (4369 → 5521) and `status` (closed → open) moved. The round-2 specification was the two-paragraph reopen note alone.

WHY THE MISREADING IS EASY AND WILL RECUR. The rendered view is continuous prose. A field that was never touched by the reopen looks exactly like a field the reopen wrote, because nothing on screen says where one ends. It is the same class as `sed -n '/DESCRIPTION/,/^$/p'` collapsing at the first blank line, and as a path regex matching `spec/004-…` inside `tools/xray/spec/004-…`: THE RENDERING IS NOT THE STRUCTURE.

THE RULE: WHEN A BRIEF WILL ASSERT THAT SOME TEXT IS PART OF A PARTICULAR MUTATION, READ THE FIELDS SEPARATELY. `bd show --json` returns them keyed, and `bd history <id> --json` shows which ones actually changed and when — entries nest the item's fields under `.Issue`. Compare the field's LENGTH across the mutation boundary: unchanged length means that field was not part of that mutation, whatever the rendered order suggests.

AND ANCHOR THE COMPARISON TO THE BOUNDARY, not to the newest N snapshots. Walk newest-first to the first snapshot whose status differs, and compare that pair. On a bead that has settled since its reopen, the newest N read unchanged for BOTH a genuine audit and a bare status revert.

A GOOD OUTCOME ANYWAY: the worker answered the round-1 criteria by number regardless, confirmed all seven still hold, and reported the discrepancy rather than silently following my framing — which is the preamble clause working. But the brief should not have contained the claim.

RELATED: [[state-the-symptom-not-a-hypothesis-in-fix-briefs]], [[never-put-an-uncontrolled-extraction-in-a-brief]].

ADDING ANY NEW FILE TO A SURFACE THE ALIAS CAMPAIGN HAS BASELINED REDS THE RATCHET UNLESS ITS REQUIRES ARE CANONICAL — **FIVE occurrences in one session**, none by a worker doing anything wrong, and each cost a full fix-worker cycle.

WHAT HAPPENS. `scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py` holds each surface at a floor in `scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn`. A new file's `[re-frame.x.y :as y]` bare-leaf requires count as violations, so a branch that merely ADDS a test file pushes its surface above the floor and reds `Require-alias dialect ratchet` — plus `Lint required`, which is `lint.yml`'s `if: always()` aggregator carrying it. It is ONE defect, not two: the aggregator's only failing step is "Fail if any required lint job failed", it runs in ~5s, and one worker read its job log showing `needs results: success, success, success, skipped, success, failure`.

THE FIVE, all 2026-09-04/05:
  * PR #9191 — 8 new edges in a new hicasso test file: implementation/hicasso 1025 vs floor 1017.
  * PR #9200 — 2 new edges, same surface: 1019 vs 1017.
  * PR #9204 — 3 new edges in a new flows test file: implementation/flows 158 vs floor 155.
  * PR #9207 — 5 new edges in a new ssr test file: implementation/ssr 404 vs floor 399.
  * implementation/core's floor is ZERO, so a single bare-leaf alias anywhere under it reds immediately.

THE FIX IS ALWAYS TO CANONICALISE, NEVER TO RAISE THE FLOOR. `--write-baseline` is MONOTONIC — a floor may only FALL — so raising it is unavailable and would regress finished campaign work. Spell new aliases dotted (`:as rf.<leaf>`) per spec/Conventions.md §Require-alias dialect. THE RATCHET'S OWN OUTPUT NAMES THE WANTED SPELLING ON EACH LINE (`-> :as rf.hicasso.impl.codec`), so the repair is transcription, not judgement.

AND THE RATCHET IS TWO-SIDED, which is the part that bites the FIXER rather than the author: it exits 1 on a surface BELOW its floor as well as above. The log lists every pre-existing violation too — hundreds on an unmigrated surface — and canonicalising any of THOSE reddens it from the other direction. Land at EXACTLY the floor. That exit 0 is itself the two-sided proof that main sat on the floor and the branch added exactly N. Three fix workers hit this and all three correctly left neighbouring aliases alone.

PUT THE WARNING IN EVERY BRIEF THAT MIGHT ADD A FILE — WHICH IS MOST OF THEM. This is not a case-by-case judgement: three of the five briefs above were written BEFORE this memory existed and all three reded; the two written after it carried the warning and did not. One sentence in the original brief replaces a whole fix-worker cycle. Treat it as default boilerplate for any implementation dispatch, alongside the stance and the fence.

DIAGNOSING ONE: `gh api repos/<o>/<r>/actions/jobs/<job-id>/logs` with an EXACT job-name match (two jobs can share a substring). Grep the log for the surface's own new file to isolate the delta from the pre-existing listing, and control the grep against a file you know is in the log.
